Uganda is withdrawing from the Duke of Sussex’s Invictus Games, the country’s military chief said, out of respect for King Charles amid division over the “Harry-Meghan nonsense”.
Gen Muhoozi Kainerugaba, son of the Ugandan president, made the surprise announcement in a post on X on Wednesday.
Kainerugaba wrote: “In order not to be construed as being opposed to His Majesty King Charles III of the United Kingdom, whom we deeply revere, Uganda hereby withdraws from the Invictus Games. We shall not participate in anything that does not have His Majesty’s approval.”
The timing of the post suggests it may be in response to an official letter to UK senior government and military officials on behalf of Charles which reiterated the Duke and Duchess of Sussex were not working royals and would not use their HRH styles.
When asked by the Times about what had motivated the move, Kainerugaba is reported to have said: “I have factions in the Ministry of Defence that support that Harry-Meghan nonsense. I had to quash it straight away. I support the monarch. Period.”
The news, first reported by Uganda Pulse news website, will undoubtedly be a blow to Harry, who two months ago stood alongside Uganda’s defence minister, Kiryowa Kiwanuka, at an Invictus Games event in London to announce that the East African nation would be the 26th country to enter the multi-sport event for wounded service personnel.
At the time, Kiwanuka credited President Museveni for his “visionary leadership” and Kainerugaba, a Sandhurst graduate, for “championing our teams entry” adding their support “marks a new chapter for our service men and women.”
The decision to withdraw may be an unintended consequence of the official letter, issued on Monday by head of the royal household , the lord chamberlain, Richard Benyon, at Charles’s behest, and clarifying the position of the Sussexes after their return to the UK two weeks ago.
The letter directed that the couple were “no longer working members of the royal family”, that their charitable work “is a personal matter for them both and undertaken in their private capacity,” and “their position is akin to private citizens with commercial and charitable interests.”
Kainerugaba was appointed army chief in 2024, and is widely seen as his 81-year-old father’s successor to the presidency. He has made several provocative posts on X, including threats to invade neighbouring Kenya, demands that Jay-Z hand over his wife Beyoncé so he could marry her, and threats against Bobi Wine, Museveni’s principal political rival.
The Invictus Games and representatives for the Duke of Sussex have been approached for comment.

Flash floods at the Nepal-Tibet border have killed at least 543 people and more than 1,500 are missing. Hundreds were foreigners in the area to work, take guided treks or make pilgrimages.
Thousands have been rescued, with some of the injured taken to hospitals in Nepal’s capital, Kathmandu. The number of missing may vary because of progress in the ongoing rescue efforts and differences in how data has been collected and verified among agencies.
Here is how different countries have been affected.
Nepal
Nepal’s disaster management authority said on Friday the death toll in that country had risen to 538, with 977 people missing. The authority said 3,253 people had been rescued by helicopter, and more than 150 of the injured were taken to hospitals in Kathmandu and the districts of Rasuwa, Nuwakot and Dhading.
Local reports cited the National Emergency Operation Centre as saying on Thursday that the missing included 113 Nepali tourists, 85 personnel from the army and police, 161 residents from the Rasuwa district and one from the Nuwakot district.
China
State media reported on Friday that at least five people had died and 558 were missing in Gyirong County, Tibet. The state broadcaster CCTV reported that 260 of the 558 missing people were foreigners. In addition, nearly 100 Chinese citizens were missing on the Nepal side, China’s foreign ministry said.
India
India’s foreign ministry said 288 Indian nationals remained uncontactable, including 73 people who were working on a power project. Nepali officials said many Indian tourists were on pilgrimage to Mount Kailash in Tibet, a sacred site for Hindus.
US
The US state department said 90 of its citizens were unaccounted for in China and Nepal, but that it was not aware of any US deaths. Three Americans have been rescued.
Malaysia
Officials said 51 Malaysians were missing.
Ukraine
Ukraine’s foreign ministry said 55 Ukrainians were missing. The number includes two tourist groups, of 47 and seven people respectively, in addition to one Ukrainian woman travelling with a foreign tour group.
Australia
The Australian government said 39 Australians were missing.
Britain
Officials said 33 of the missing were from Britain.
Canada
The Nepal tourism board (NTB) said 25 of the missing were from Canada.
South Korea
South Korean government officials said nine citizens working on the construction of a hydropower plant in Nepal were missing.
Singapore
Eight Singaporeans were missing, according to the NTB.
Germany
The NTB said eight tourists from Germany were missing.
Russia
The Russian embassy in Nepal said eight of its citizens were missing.
South Africa
The NTB said six South Africans were missing.
Latvia
The NTB said six tourists from Latvia were missing.
Japan
Japanese media said five Japanese tourists were missing, made up of a couple and their children.
New Zealand
Five people from New Zealand were missing, the NTB said.
France
The NTB said four French citizens were missing.
Belgium
The NTB said three people from Belgium were missing.
Spain
The NTB said three visitors from Spain were missing.
Others
The NTB said two people each from Italy, Kazakhstan, Portugal, Ireland and the Netherlands were missing. It said 10 others – one each from Belarus, Finland, Hungary, Israel, Lithuania, the Philippines, Bulgaria, Switzerland, Serbia and Sweden – were also missing.

For some people, particularly youngsters, an AI chatbot is becoming the first place they turn to when they are distressed. It has its advantages: it is available at any hour, does not appear to judge them and can respond instantly. But when conversations involve thoughts of suicide, the limits of this interaction become consequential. Every conversation with an AI chatbot may not be harmful, but an apparently empathetic response could reinforce hopelessness, prolong rumination, or delay professional help in some people already at risk, say experts.
What the evidence shows
AI use for mental health support is now common. A U.S. survey of 1,009 people aged 12 to 21, published in JAMA Pediatrics found that 19.2% had used AI chatbots for mental health advice in 2025. Nearly 43% of these users did so at least monthly, while 5.8% used them daily or almost daily. Nearly two-thirds had not told anyone about this.
Another analysis of more than 620,000 publicly available ChatGPT conversations found that 4.9% could be classified broadly as involving mental health, although only 0.21% met a stricter definition involving an identifiable person explicitly seeking mental health help.
Studies have also found that chatbots are generally better at recognising very low- and very high-risk scenarios, but struggle to distinguish between intermediate levels of suicide risk. This is particularly concerning for psychiatrists, as suicidal distress is rarely expressed in a single, explicit statement and often emerges through a combination of subtle or changing cues.
When reassurance becomes a loop
“Suicidal distress is not always direct; people may hint, use humour or gradually disclose their thoughts,” said Mithun Prasad, consultant, psychiatry, SIMS Hospital, Chennai. Keyword recognition alone, he said, is therefore inadequate; the context and consistency of a conversation matter.
Sabaresh Pandiyan, consultant, psychiatry, Rela Hospital, Chennai, pointed to another issue: the ‘internal loop’, particularly among younger users, who may derive comfort from the empathetic part of an AI response, while ignoring advice to seek professional help. Repeated reassurance can also make suicidal thinking seem less urgent. “Talking about suicide or venting about suicide is not the problem, reinforcing hopelessness is,” he said.
Nithya M., consultant psychiatrist, Apollo Speciality Hospitals, Vanagaram, Chennai, emphasised that AI could amplify existing distress, prolong rumination or substitute validation for intervention.
In clinical practice, psychiatrists see patients use AI to discuss relationships, workplace problems and other personal concerns before speaking to family or friends. Dr. Pandiyan said around 60-70% of patients in his setting discuss such matters with AI first. For some, this may help them recognise a problem and seek care earlier. Others may spend months trying to manage difficulties themselves before consulting a professional.
Dr. Nithya said warning signs can include patients quoting AI responses verbatim, withdrawing from human confidants, resisting professional help or developing a rigid view of themselves or their relationships based on chatbot responses.
Not a substitute for care
There may be limited situations in which patients use AI alongside clinical care. Dr. Prasad said some patients use chatbots between appointments to record medication effects or organise their thoughts, and later bring a summary to their psychiatrist. This can provide the clinician with information about what happened between consultations.
But such use does not make AI a substitute for psychiatric assessment. A chatbot does not have access to a person’s psychiatric history, personality, psychological defences, adverse life experiences, protective factors or current mental state. It may validate an emotion without recognising when urgent assessment is needed. This is particularly concerning when a person has psychosis, mania or distorted beliefs.
Need for safety checks
Psychiatrists call for mandatory safety audits, independent clinical assessments and clearer liability frameworks. Companies should be required to investigate and report serious safety incidents. . Public education should also explain where AI is and is not appropriate.
Experts add that any response must also address the stigma that prevents people from seeking mental healthcare. Families and communities need to create safer spaces for people to talk about distress and seek help.
When a person is in a mental health crisis, experts said, the priority should remain timely human assessment and support. AI cannot take the place of that care.

The Bengaluru City Police have launched ‘Project Khushi’, a structured health and wellness programme aimed at supporting the long-term physical and mental well-being of police personnel, Home Minister Priyank Kharge said on Tuesday.
The programme will initially be implemented in the Electronics City police division, covering around 600 police personnel. Each batch will undergo a three-month programme comprising health check-ups, expert-led guidance sessions, and digital engagement activities.
The initiative will focus on preventive healthcare, nutrition, physical activity, quality sleep, and stress management, besides other lifestyle factors crucial for the long-term well-being of police personnel.
Pilot programme shows encouraging results
According to the Home Minister, an earlier pilot programme conducted as part of Project Khushi produced encouraging results. Around 61% of participants recorded a reduction in blood sugar levels, while 70% corrected Vitamin B12 deficiencies. In addition, 59% of participants reduced their body weight.
Mr. Kharge said that the results demonstrate that sustained and scientifically designed health interventions can have a positive impact on the well-being of police personnel.
Partnership with health and corporate organisations
“Our police personnel work every day in challenging and stressful conditions to ensure the safety of our communities. It is essential to pay continuous attention to their health. Healthy police personnel are the backbone of an effective and resilient policing system,” Mr Kharge said.
He added that equal importance must be given to mental well-being, a healthy lifestyle, and stress management, along with physical health.

iOS 27 adds a native Custom EQ for compatible AirPods with an H2 chip or later. Go to AirPods settings > Audio and Routing > Equalizer > Custom, then adjust lows, mids, and highs to tune bass, vocals, and treble to your taste.
Apple has officially started rolling out iOS 27 for eligible devices, and it brings a lot of useful additions. If you are using any Apple audio product, iOS 27 gets a new native custom equalizer to fine-tune the music from your AirPods and other Apple audio products (requires Apple’s H2 chip; you can see full compatibility here).
In this guide, you will learn how to use the new custom EQ for your AirPods and other Apple devices.
Table of Contents
How to Use the New AirPods Custom EQ in iOS 27
The new native equalizer is only available in the latest iOS 27. If your iPhone is eligible for the latest iOS 27, you can go to General > Software Update and update to the latest iOS 27.
Custom EQ Supported Device List:
Custom EQ for Apple iOS 27 is only available for audio devices with an H2 chip or later. Here is the official compatibility list.
- AirPods Pro 2
- AirPods Pro 3
- AirPods 4
- AirPods Max 2
Now, if your device supports it, follow the steps below.
First, Update Your iPhone to the Latest iOS 27
Step 1: Open Settings on your iPhone.
Step 2: Scroll down.
Step 3: Tap on General.
Step 4: Tap on Software Update.
Step 5: Tap on Update Now (if the update is available).
Please ensure that your iPhone is on the iOS 27 eligible device list.
Next, Update Your AirPods Firmware
Step 1: Connect your AirPods to your iPhone.
Step 2: Open Settings on your iPhone.
Step 3: Tap on your AirPods (you will see this option if your AirPods are connected to your device) and next go to Step 5.
Step 4: If you don’t see it, open Bluetooth.
Tap on the “i” icon next to your AirPods.
Step 5: Now, scroll down and tap on AirPods Beta Updates.
Step 6: Enable the option that says AirPods Beta Updates.
Ensure your iPhone is connected to the internet and your AirPods are connected to your iPhone. Your AirPods will automatically update to the latest software.
How to Use the Custom Equalizer on iOS 27
Step 1: Open Settings on your iPhone.
Step 2: Scroll down and tap on your AirPods.
Or else, you can go to Bluetooth and tap on the “i” icon next to your AirPods.
Step 3: Scroll down and tap on Audio and Routing.
Step 4: From here, scroll down and tap on Equalizer.
Step 5: Select the Custom option.
Step 6: Now you can adjust lows, mids, and highs based on your preference. You can move the slider to the top and bottom. The line above refers to high, and the line below refers to low.
1. Lows: Increase or decrease bass.
2. Mids: Meant for vocals, where you can increase or decrease the vocal presence, especially if the music has singer vocals.
3. Highs: Treble, which AirPods are mainly known for. You can adjust treble sound using high settings.
Step 7: If you want to reset, tap on the Reset option.
Step 8: If you don’t want custom controls, you can tap on “Recommended,” and it will use Apple’s default recommended sound signature.
Currently, the iOS 27 custom equalizer is very basic. Even though Apple has the best ecosystem, Apple only decided to give you basic controls to customize the sound output from your audio devices.
I know most people are fine with the default settings on the AirPods, but sometimes even I prefer more control over the music.
Adding custom equalizer settings natively on your iPhone eliminates the need to download third-party apps, which sometimes have compatibility issues. However, Apple’s basic equalizer still leaves room for third-party options. Apple also offers you the option to reset the changes you have made.
This is a good start. Hopefully, in iOS 28, Apple will bring more features to this custom equalizer to fine-tune the sound signature of the AirPods. Using EQ does bring a noticeable sound difference. If you don’t see this option or are facing any issues, you can comment below, and I am happy to help you.
FAQs about iOS 27 AirPods Custom EQ
1. Does AirPods Custom EQ Work on iPad and Mac?
Yes, AirPods Custom EQ is also available on iPadOS 27 and macOS 27
2. Can You Save Multiple Custom EQ Presets for AirPods?
As I said before, current EQ settings are basic. As of now, you can only have one custom EQ profile
3. Does Custom EQ Work With Spatial Audio and Adaptive Audio?
Yes, it works with spatial audio and adaptive audio, but those settings are different from custom EQ. Currently, custom EQ only allows you to adjust lows, highs, and mids.
4. Does Custom EQ Affect Calls and Videos or Only Music?
Yes, AirPods Custom EQ applies to all media playing on your iPhone, including videos, music, TV shows, and much more.
5. Why Is the Custom EQ Option Missing on Supported AirPods?
If you don’t see the custom EQ option on your iPhone, make sure that you update to iOS 27. Custom EQ options are available for AirPods that have an H2 processor. At the time of writing this article, current supported models include AirPods Pro 2, AirPods Pro 3, AirPods 4, and AirPods Max 2.

What Is the Good Life?
The philosophy professor Meghan Sullivan doesn’t just want to teach her students about virtue; she wants to make them better human beings.
Subscribe here: Apple Podcasts | Spotify | YouTube
David Brooks: Hi, I’m David Brooks. If you are listening to or watching this, you’ve stumbled across the first episode of a new podcast called The Permanent Questions.
The idea of the podcast is that there are a lot of shows about politics and business and health and tech, but there aren’t enough about the really big questions of life. How do you find your purpose? How do you confront death? How do you save a relationship that’s going through a rough patch? How do you build a just society?
Now, you may be asking yourself, “How the hell did a political pundit get into these deep waters?”
When I was 18, an incredibly lucky thing happened to me: The admissions officers at Columbia University, Wesleyan, and Brown decided I should go to the University of Chicago. I didn’t know anything about Chicago. I’d never visited. I never knew anybody who went there, but it was the only school I got into.
It turned out to be the perfect school for me. My favorite joke about Chicago: It’s a Baptist school where atheist professors teach Jewish students Saint Thomas Aquinas. And I fit right in.
There’s a saying, “If you catch fire with enthusiasm, people will come for miles to watch you burn.” My professors had caught fire with enthusiasm.
Those teachers were filled with a certain conviction. The conviction was, if you read important books, had important conversations, and addressed big questions, you would have the keys to the kingdom.
They gave us new things to love: new ideas, new heroes, new activities, new subjects. They tried to teach us how to see, not only to see with your preconceptions and the things you think you see, but to see with the clarity of a Tolstoy, the moral depth of George Eliot, the empathetic outrage of James Baldwin.
Mostly, they introduced us to the Great Conversation. The Great Conversation is a tradition of debate that goes back for thousands of years. It’s a collective attempt to find a workable balance between the inevitable tensions of life—the tension between autonomy and belonging, between freedom and order, between diversity and cohesion, safety and exploration, tenderness and strength, intellect and passion. The Great Conversation never ends, because there is no permanent solution to these tensions, just a temporary resting spot that works in this or that circumstance.
I never wanted to leave the Great Conversation, and I never have. I went off and became a journalist and a political pundit, and that was a worthwhile thing to do, and I still do it. A lot of the big questions in life are political questions. Who should lead us? What does a just society even look like? But none of my six books are about politics. They’re about the kind of questions my teachers asked me back in Chicago: How do you educate your emotions? How do you survive a setback?
As my career has gone on, I came to the conclusion that we as a society are over-politicized and under-moralized. That is to say, we pay attention to every little political scandal, but many people have been given no instruction on the basic questions of how to live, of how they should find their calling, what they should really want.
And over the last 15 years or so, this sensation has taken a deeper urgency. Like a lot of countries, America seems to be going through some sort of spiritual, relational, and social, and maybe moral crisis. You know all the stats: rising loneliness, rising despair, rising distrust, rising polarization.
We’re living through a period of great technological advance, but we’re losing our humanistic core. Because of technological improvements and social deterioration, our lives are objectively better, but subjectively worse. The elements of civilization that lift the spirit and nurture the affections are playing a smaller and smaller role in our national life. Religion, literature, art, theology, history, philosophy, friendship, even conversation.
In previous periods of technological advance, there was a humanistic counterreaction. Humanists said, “Okay, bring us your science. Bring us your machines. Bring us your efficiency. Bring us your technology. That’s fine. But don’t turn us into machines ourselves.” And the humanists made an aggressive counter-push to say, “We will preserve our humanistic core. We will preserve what is essentially human. ”
This podcast is an attempt to be a small part of that kind of humanistic reaction.
We asked Meghan Sullivan to be the first guest on the show because she’s the kind of great teacher I’m talking about. Meghan teaches one of the most beloved courses at Notre Dame University, which is called “God and the Good Life.” She’s won Notre Dame’s Joyce Award for Excellence in Teaching, and as you’ll see, she’s got a dynamic personality. She co-authored a book based on the course, called The Good Life Method: Reasoning Through the Big Questions of Happiness, Faith, and Meaning.
Meghan doesn’t just do education, providing students with facts they can regurgitate on a test. Meghan does formation. She helps students become better versions of themselves. And so it’s a great pleasure to welcome Meghan Sullivan to this table.
Brooks: Welcome, Meghan Sullivan. You are the first guest on The Permanent Questions. You are the founding figure of our podcast. So thank you for being here.
Meghan Sullivan: Heavy is the crown. This is a tremendous responsibility, David.
Brooks: I know. All future guests will be measured by your exemplary example.
Sullivan: Exactly. I’m hopefully gonna create a large ceiling for this podcast.
Brooks: So, you grew up in North Carolina, and I assume you had a moderately normal childhood. And then you became a philosopher. So how the hell did that happen?
Sullivan: I did not grow up in an academic family. My mom was a receptionist in a dental office, and my dad worked a bunch of different jobs, but for most of high school he worked at this company called Replacements. They basically replaced, like, broken plates. My dad was in the plate-replacement business. My mom was in the dental-billing business. So that was not particularly academic background, but very, very loving. And if you would’ve told me when I was a high-school student that I would end up a philosophy professor, I would have asked you to throw me off a bridge.
Most of my students have never met a professional philosopher before they take my class. But in high school, actually, one of my best friends, her dad was a philosophy professor at our local university, and we were very, very judgy, snotty teenage girls, and we devoted probably two years of high school to thinking, “We cannot understand this guy’s job.”
So in high school, I had a well-considered, extremely negative opinion of the profession of philosophy that was based on nothing but vibes about my friend’s dad’s books.
I got a scholarship and went to the University of Virginia, so this big public school where, as a freshman, you’re just sort of fed into the meat grinder. You just get whatever classes are left over after all of the big kids register for their classes. And my academic adviser was talking to me, and I was so stressed because I couldn’t get any of the pre-law classes that I desperately wanted, or econ classes. And he’s like, “I think that you would really love this ethics class called ‘Issues of Life and Death’ in the philosophy department. It’s really debate-y, and I just think given your background, you’re gonna have a blast in there. ”
So I was like, “Okay, fine. Philosophy. ” And I enrolled in that class, and I was hooked by the second week. The exact moment—I remember this really vividly—I was sitting in Alderman Library, in the library at UVA, and we’d just gotten our first assignment for all of our classes, our first writing assignment, and I was writing all these boring book reports for my other classes.
In “Issues of Life and Death,” the question we were assigned is: “Should you end your life?” And I remember talking to the TA being like, “Do you want me to write about what, you know, David Hume says about suicide?” And he’s like, “Absolutely not. I want the strongest possible argument about whether you should continue living.”
And I was like, “Are you allowed to ask me that? Like, is that allowed?” And he’s like, “Not only is it allowed, but there are better and worse answers, and if you don’t have a really tight, really well-argued position, you’re gonna get a bad grade in this class.” And I just remember sitting in the library, the kind of blinking cursor on Microsoft Word staring at me, thinking, Ah, we’re firing live ammunition here. Like, this is real. And that just totally got me hooked.
Brooks: Now, a lot of philosophers write abstruse academic articles with a lot of notations and numbers and diagrams. You actually teach this class, and you’ve written this book, on how to live. Why’d you become that kind of philosopher?
Sullivan: I had an epiphany my third year at Notre Dame. I was getting ready to go up for tenure, and I’d been teaching our big intro philosophy class. And when you go through the tenure process, at first, you’re only focused on keeping your job, and then you start to hit a point where you imagine a future where you’re just a professor and you’re not worried about getting fired all the time. And I was in that kind of mindset of thinking, What do I wanna do with the rest of my career after I hopefully survive this tenure vote?
And I felt very, very strongly that I wanted to focus the next chapter on my teaching. That’s what really I loved about my job. And I’d been teaching Aristotle. And we inflict Aristotle on every single freshman at the University of Notre Dame. And Aristotle has this line in the second chapter of his book about the good life that I’ve always loved, and I always assign students to write essays about.
He says, “We conduct this examination not so that we can know what virtue is, but so that we might be good.” We do all this not so we can know what dead people said about virtue and philosophy, but so that we can become happier people. Otherwise, there’s no benefit of it, he says. This whole enterprise is pointless if it doesn’t find some way to make us better.
Brooks: Now, you’re in the business of helping people become, as you said, happy and good. And this podcast is in the same business. I’m joining your team.
Sullivan: Yeah, all right.
Brooks: And so, as we enter this conversation, I thought I’d raise some objections to the life we have chosen.
Sullivan: Bring it. Objections are the love language of philosophy.
Brooks: So the first one is what’s—why is this necessary? I get up in the morning; I have my Frappuccino; I surf my media feed; I go to work, which is good, I like my work; I go home; I watch Netflix. Why should I read a bunch of complicated books and have hard conversations?
Sullivan: So one assumption I think we should challenge is that there are some people who do philosophy, a small number of people, like my friend’s dad, and then everybody else doesn’t do philosophy.
That’s like saying there are some people who exercise, and everybody else doesn’t exercise. I get why you’d make that assumption if you think that exercise or philosophy is this really, really narrow prescribed activity. But that’s just not true.

Go think about, instead, the ways that you can use your time to earn to give under this capitalist system.
And it’s a kind of radical idea, but also one that has a really logical deductive argument that gets you to that conclusion. Now it’s just taken as ethics in certain quarters, especially in the tech industry. Some of my colleagues in the econ department would say this just is ethics, doing a really rigorous cost-benefit analysis and opting for the option within your control that’s going to have the greatest possible impact.
I vehemently reject this worldview. And Aristotle and the philosophers from this virtue ethics tradition of the last 2,500 years that I deeply admire, they have considered this idea, and they have also vehemently rejected it. So you might ask: What’s wrong with trying to save people’s lives? What’s wrong with trying to use reason and skill to have the greatest impact in the world?
Well, one of the points that you made in your essay about this Princeton class that I thought was spot-on is: There is this foundational question about what a human being is. Is a human just a mechanism for redistribution in a society? So are you just an earner, somebody who receives money and then spits it out towards, hopefully, the best causes? Or do you have a rich inner life? Do you have a telos? Do you have a purpose that has to be cultivated and tended?
If you believe the latter, then you’re gonna have some serious questions about this effective-altruist strategy. One: What happens to you if you leave college and you go work in that high-frequency trading firm, and you’re around people that all day long only talk about making money? Like, what is that gonna do to the type of character you have, the type of person that you believe yourself to be? Maybe the first year you’re gonna be pretty tough. You’re gonna be living in your cheap apartment, you’re gonna be writing your checks to fighting malaria, and you’re gonna be able to tough it out.
But over time, you are gonna come to worship money. Because you’re gonna be thinking about it 24/7 all day at your job. And every minute that you’re not working, you’re gonna be thinking about what your money could be spent on curing out in the world. Money is going to be the sole focus of your life, and that is unethical. You have made yourself into something that’s less than what a human is called to be.
I think that’s gonna be one of the big tensions. Another big tension with effective altruism as a movement is, I think I would’ve been—I was more sympathetic with the movement maybe 10, 15 years ago, when the focus was on immediately relieving extreme suffering because of preventable diseases.
Like, they used to tell you, “Go earn a lot of money, and then use it to buy bed nets to stop kids from getting malaria tomorrow. ” So, all right, I can kinda feel the urgency of that. But this calculative system says you must devote your life to whatever is going to have the greatest possible causal impact. And one of the shifts that they’ve made in the last 10 years is realizing those kids with malaria, they’re a pretty good investment, but actually, right now, your dollars would be better spent building really well-aligned artificial intelligence that’s gonna help people 100 years from now in vastly greater numbers flourish much better than any human being could right now. Sullivan: Oh, it’s definitely part of Aristotle. Aristotle has four ways you could live your life when it comes to virtue. One is just pure vice. You know what the worst is, and you’re completely driven to go after it. And now we won’t name names, but I’m sure you could think of some celebrity exemplars where you think, there’s just no friction, they just know what the evil thing to do is, and they just, full speed ahead, go for it. Very few people are like that.
The other extreme is pure virtue. You know what the good is, and you just sort of effortlessly desire it and want it. And very few of us ever get even close to that category. Most of us fall somewhere in the middle, and the other two categories Aristotle has are “incontinence” and “continence.” So continence is, you know what the good is, you don’t always want it, but you realize that it’s out there, and you try to summon the will to go after it anyway, even though there’s some friction. And incontinence is the flip side of that equation, where you kind of have lost your grip on what the good is. You’re vaguely aware that you’re not happy with the direction that your life is going in, but you just don’t even have the will or knowledge to pull yourself out of it.
And most of us fall into some part of that spectrum of continence or incontinence. And your guy at the bar who’s very tempted by the beautiful woman but very aware of his wife, he’s probably about to fall into incontinence. He’s really on the precipice. And the problem is that if you don’t monitor which side of that line you’re on over the course of your life, you could get sucked into the pit.
Brooks: I think my views on character formation have shifted, actually. I wrote a book called The Road to Character, so I learned that writing a book on character doesn’t give you good character, and even reading a book on character doesn’t give you good character. But buying a book on character does, ’cause you get to—
Sullivan: Just, just owning the book and having it on your shelf. The more books you buy, actually, my publisher told me, the more character you acquire.
Brooks: Yeah, it’s absolutely true. So the theory of that book was self-confrontation. You say, What’s my key sin? And so one of the characters in that book is Dwight Eisenhower. And his key sin was anger. He had a temper problem.
Sullivan: I didn’t know that.
Brooks: He produced this persona of being this cheerful, country-club kinda guy, but that was manufactured. And so, in the middle of World War II, when he was general, he would take all the people he hated that day, and he would write their names on a piece of paper, and he’d shred it.
And that was his way of trying to purge his hatred for these people, these incompetents. And so that’s one form, and I still think that’s—it’s a useful exercise to say, What’s my key sin? And, What can I do about that?
Sullivan: What’s your key sin?
Brooks: I would say shallowness. I’m very prone to being shallow. And I’ve tried to spend my entire life being a little less shallow. So that’s definitely my key sin. I won’t ask you yours.
Sullivan: Actually, I would say pride, which actually in the Catholic world is a really, really bad one. You’re playing with nitroglycerin if you’ve got that in your life and you’re not really trying to address it. But,yeah, that’s a pretty bad one for me, with a little bit of anger.
Brooks: I’ll try not to cross you.
Sullivan: Exactly. I need to try the Eisenhower trick, though. Did it work? I wonder if it worked for him. If it gave him release.
Brooks: It doesn’t work. There’s been research. The idea of purging your anger, that doesn’t work, that doesn’t work.
Sullivan: You know, a really strongly worded email at 5 a.m. on a Saturday morning.
Brooks: That totally works.
Sullivan: That makes it worse.
Brooks: But now I think it’s loving the right things. I’m less impressed by willpower than I used to be. But if you can love the right things in the right way, in the right order, and mold your heart in that way, then—for example, giving up cigarettes and alcohol is really hard. But millions of women do it every year, because they get pregnant, and they love their kid more than they love cabernet.
Sullivan: It’s amazing.
Brooks: And so, but, how you mold your heart is a tricky thing, but being aware of, of loving things in the right order. I’m talking Augustine to a Catholic philosopher.
Sullivan: Exactly. The ordo amoris.
Brooks: The question is how you change somebody’s heart. Like how do you change their inner life? That seems really hard. I mean, let alone your—even changing your own is hard.
Sullivan: Yeah one of the biggest insights from social psychology and 2,500 years of philosophy is if you think that caring for your soul is a solo endeavor, like you write down your New Year’s resolutions and you commit yourself quietly in your own mind to following it, that’s a fool’s errand. No human changes their habits in that way. Change is inherently social and, you know, for a woman who becomes pregnant, the realization that I’m two people right now in this body, that’s a kind of social pressure. Not a bad social pressure, not like, your unborn child is not going to shame you about your decisions. But just this feeling of love creates a second self. It creates another self that’s permanently intertwined with your own, and that absolutely shapes your perspective about what your endeavor or journey is.
Brooks: The one I think that we don’t do enough of is basic skills, moral skills. Like, how do you sit with someone who’s depressed? How do you sit with someone who’s just lost a child? A lot of students, and a lot of people, nobody’s ever taught, and I would include myself in this. My friend suffered from severe depression, and I had no idea how to react, and I think I’m kinda literate. I don’t know. But I think we should do more basic skill building.
Sullivan: Oh, absolutely. We spend the first two weeks of the “God and the Good Life” course just on this question of how to ask questions at a dinner party. Most of my students don’t go to very many dinner parties, because they’re teenagers. They will later on in life, probably. But they think that all questions are created equal. And so they think you ask a question in class to just demonstrate how smart you are, if you talk at all.
Or to try to nail another student if you wanna have a moral debate. Like get them on record, like a prosecutor, of saying something that you’re then gonna attack. I think they must learn some of this in high school, too, but we spend the first two weeks just trying to deprogram them and help them realize you can ask a question of another person because you just wanna hear part of their story.
And the very best questions you might ask are ones where you genuinely have no clue what the person is gonna say next. And this is a revelation. We’ll have our students write down sample questions about whatever topic we’re doing in class. Should you be religious? How much money is enough to decide you would quit your job?
And they initially want to just lock into simple yes or no answers, and then start immediately offering their reasons. And we’re like, “Hold the phone. We don’t want your reasons yet. You’ve barely thought about this.” Instead, I want you to try to understand all of the other people that are in this conversation with you and where they might be coming from and what their possible reasons are.
Brooks: I find a lot of people don’t ask those questions. Well, either they’re not curious about people, or else they’re afraid they’re gonna invade someone’s privacy. And I would say, I’ve been a journalist since I was 22, and my job is asking people questions, often in difficult circumstances, and how often has anybody ever said to me, “That’s none of your damn business”? And the answer is zero. Zero. I’ve asked this of other journalists or people in the question-asking business. If you respectfully ask somebody to tell you the story of their life, no one has ever asked them, and they’re delighted to do this.
Sullivan: We started teaching this Good Life class 10 years ago, so it’s the 10-year anniversary. And one of the things we have all the students do is write this long confessional essay, basically, their confessions like Augustine, their apology like Socrates, where they share key moments from their life and then debate with themselves about what its significance is in light of the philosophy that we’ve been reading in class.
And this is 40 percent of their grade, this one big confessional essay. And I remember when we were unleashing the course, I got a lot of criticism from well-meaning but mistaken faculty who basically said, “You cannot ask a student to disclose aspects of their life like this. That’s professionally inappropriate. And you can’t grade them on it, you fool. This is not possible. ”
And we don’t grade them based on are they good people or not. We grade them based on their philosophical reasoning. But I have taught thousands of students in the last decade in this class. I have never once had a student complain about going through this exercise.
Sometimes they’ll complain about their final grade, but they never complain about the self-disclosure part. It’s the opposite. I get notes and emails from students, oftentimes from their parents, often like a year after they’ve taken the class, saying, “Hey, I just want you to realize that meant a tremendous amount to me at the time. Nobody had ever listened to me or paid that much attention to me in my life.”
Brooks: I’ve gotta ask, I was curious about this, about the apology. Like, they’re 18, 19, whatever. What do they say?
Sullivan: There are some common themes. They have to pick three of 10 possible topics.
Politics, money, work, moral responsibility, suffering, love, death, God, contemplation, et cetera. I think I got nine out of the 10. They tend to always pick three. They never pick politics. You’d be shocked to learn, they never think that political debate is a very important part of their lives, which is hilarious because we’re constantly pressured now as faculty to teach our students how to have political debates, this is all the rage right now, and I wanna tell them, none of my students actually care that much about this topic. Maybe they should, but they just don’t.
They usually choose work and love. My students are obsessed with work. That part of their essays tends to be very funny, because I will more often than not read these extremely sincere sections of their essays about their experiences with what Karl Marx calls alienation from your “species-being,” which is when you feel like the capitalist conditions you’re forced to operate under separate you from your deep sources of meaning and your essence. And they will say that their experience being the treasurer of the Ultimate Frisbee team has been a constant grind and has caused them to believe that they’re only valuable insofar as what they produce for the Frisbee club, and they’re experiencing burnout because of that.
But they do put a high value on work, and we let them. We indulge that. I give the students about four weeks on work and money in the class to just talk through all their questions, ’cause you can’t try to suppress it.
And then the second big theme is love. And one surprise, or I don’t know if this would be a surprise or not. You would think lovesick college students would write about romantic love and what it means to them. And we do a little bit of readings on that. They never write about romantic love.
The vast majority of my freshmen have actually never had a serious boyfriend or girlfriend by the time I get them. That’s still in the future for them. They write about their parents, and occasionally their siblings. And so I get to read a lot of really beautiful essays about their reflections on what these relationships have meant to them. I think a lot of them are experiencing some homesickness by the time I see them. But that’s very moving. And again, figures like Aristotle that we obsess about in the class, Aristotle gives a whole chapter over to parent-child relationships. These are extremely philosophically rich parts of our lives.
The most profound moment for this actually was in 2020. I was teaching my Good Life class, and I had two young women in the class. This was peak pandemic. Notre Dame went back in person in the fall, so we were all sitting there. We taught that class in the football stadium, and we were all wearing face masks in one of the sky boxes that the donors have in this massive room, and wearing face masks and struggling through the pandemic. And I had two young women in the class, and they’d just worked on the first draft of their apology essay, and they were crossing the street coming back from an event, and were hit by a drunk driver and killed.
And they were international students, and their family had to travel to the United States a few days later for the memorial masses for these two young women, and it was a huge ordeal. And Notre Dame, to their credit, put on this big in-person memorial service for these two women, even though it was really challenging.
And we got to give the parents the first drafts of these essays that these women had written, and they’d both chosen to write about love, unsurprisingly. When people are asked what really matters in their life, that’s one of the key sections. And one in particular had written about how much she loves her brother and what that feels like for her now that they’re separated.
And for us to be able to give—they’d never vocalized these things, or they had maybe in a quick text, like, “LOL, hugging face.” But it had never—their parents had never experienced five single-spaced pages of, “This is what love of you has meant in my life.” And to be able to take that artifact and give that to these grieving family members reminded me: This is the most important thing we could do.
I don’t care, you know, your “Compare and contrast Kant and Marx.” Yeah blah, blah, blah. That’s great. This is a little fragment of these women’s souls that we finally managed to wrap our hands around that we could give back to you when the rest of it is just grievously ripped from your hands.
Brooks: Wow. That’s an incredible story. Very moving.
So we’ve talked about love a lot in this conversation, and so my question to you is: Are you in the wrong business? I think of philosophy as about cognition. And so that would imply that being a good person is about having the right beliefs. You guys work on beliefs. But it doesn’t seem to me that being a good person is really mostly about beliefs. If it was, moral philosophers would be better than the rest of us. And sorry, you guys aren’t. I mean, you’re obviously better than the economists.
Sullivan: Yeah, for sure.
Brooks: But, but they’re not better than—
Sullivan: No, definitely not.
Brooks: But then when you think about, say, the church scandals. The guys who abused those children and then covered up for it, they had sat through a million sermons. They probably had the right beliefs. But we would say there was something poisoned in their soul that they are willing to damage another human being or cover up that damage.
So how do you think about the relationship between what I would call the desires and emotions, and reason? Are you too much in the reason business?
Sullivan: I think you could definitely accuse a lot of philosophers of that. My friend Eric Schwitzgebel did this really interesting study about, a social-psychology study, where he basically looked at whether your typical professional philosopher is more or less moral in everyday decision making than the kinda standard human. And you’ll be shocked, stunned to learn that your typical philosopher is a little bit less honest in ordinary situations, a little bit less moral than maybe their baseline American.
But this should not come as a surprise to those of us who study the tradition of philosophy. Aristotle, our guy, our main man again, addresses this in his second lecture in Book 2 of the Nicomachean Ethics. He says, Here’s the deal with philosophy and the good life. A lot of folks spend time collecting data, collecting beliefs, collecting ideas. But they don’t actually practice what these beliefs preach. They are like people who collect a lot of advice from physicians and then never follow it.
Your doctor says, “You need to get healthy. You need to stop eating so many fatty and sugary foods, and you need to exercise every day.” And I collect this, and I write about it on Twitter, but then I never actually do the thing, and then I’m shocked that I’m not healthy.
So many philosophers are like doctors who don’t exercise. They have studied the theory of the case pretty well, and it’s good that human beings have this kind of theoretical knowledge, but if you’re not willing to actually make this a way of life, you are not gonna receive the benefits of it.
And unfortunately, way too many professional philosophers and professional scholars generally are like the doctors who aren’t willing to give up the sugary treats. They just collect all the data, but they don’t actually make it any part of how they care for their souls. So that’s not surprising.
That’s not to say we don’t want the data, we don’t wanna think about the ideas. It’s just to say the ideas get you, like, 20 percent of the way there. The rest of the 80 percent is actually trying to have a way of life.
Brooks: I’ve really enjoyed our conversation, and I am so grateful and honored, and now proud, if I can say that—
Sullivan: Ooh, dangerous.
Brooks: —to have had Meghan Sullivan as our first guest on The Permanent Questions. Thanks so much for being here.
Sullivan: Oh, it’s great to be with you, and I’m so glad that this exists.

Bangladesh wants to ‘reset’ ties with India, calls Hasina-era relationship ‘uncomfortable’
Relations between India and Bangladesh came under strain over New Delhi's decision to provide refuge to ousted prime minister Sheikh Hasina.
Bangladesh wants to "reset" its ties with India and establish a new bilateral relationship centred on mutual interests, the country’s state minister for foreign affairs Humaiun Kobir said, adding that the relationship during the tenure of ousted prime minister Sheikh Hasina was "uncomfortable".
The remarks came days after Bangladesh said that Prime Minister Tarique Rahman would not attend the BRICS Summit in India as he was not “properly invited” to the event.
Notably, India had invited Rahman for a bilateral visit and also to attend the BRICS Summit as the chair of BIMSTEC. However, Dhaka reportedly did not formally accept either invitation, HT reported earlier.
Bangladesh says it wants to ‘reset’ ties with India
Relations between India and Bangladesh came under strain over New Delhi's decision to provide refuge to Hasina, who fled to India after being ousted from office amid a youth-led movement in August 2024.
Kobir told reporters in Dhaka on Sunday that Bangladesh wants to "reset" its bilateral relationship with India.
"We want to move towards a new relationship, which should be done through bilateral discussions, not through a multilateral forum," he said.
Kobir said Bangladesh should move away from what he called an "excessive preoccupation" with India and deal with New Delhi in a more balanced way. He said the focus should remain on shared interests and be viewed as part of its broader ties with other countries.
Replying to a question, the minister said, "Breakfast in India, lunch in India, dinner in India -- then when will you eat your own food?"
"We have to get out of the India fascination. India is just another country, and Bangladesh wants good bilateral relations with it," he said.
He clarified that his earlier comments were specifically about India and the need to rebuild ties through direct talks.
“What I said was mainly applicable to India. We want to build a good working bilateral relationship with India,” he said.
Bangladesh says reviewing 101 pacts signed with India
Nurul Islam Moni, the chief whip of the ruling Bangladesh Nationalist Party (BNP) in parliament, said on Friday that Dhaka was reviewing 101 agreements signed with India.
Asked whether agreements allowing ships from friendly countries to use the Chattogram and Mongla ports would be cancelled, Moni said, “We are reviewing the agreements, all 101 MoUs. You will get the outcome very soon, very soon.”
Kobir was asked about the review of the 101 MoUs. He told reporters that the agreements were being examined as part of the parliamentary process, Bangladesh's The Daily Star reported.

Frontline activists and leaders in the fight against female genital mutilation, which has affected more than 230 million women and girls worldwide, have welcomed an unprecedented $15.5m (£11.4m) fund aimed at creating “unstoppable momentum” to finally end the practice.
The launch of the fund comes as women’s rights are increasingly under attack and donor funding is in sharp decline, particularly for work led by FGM survivors in local communities. It is thought to be the largest single philanthropic contribution to ending the practice of FGM.
The United Nations has set a goal of elimination by by 2030, but progress is not on track as funding declines and legal protections are challenged.
Funding received by the largest initiative to end the practice – a joint programme operated in 18 countries by the UN’s sexual and reproductive health agency, UNFPA, and the UN humanitarian organisation for children, Unicef – fell by 45% last year, from $29.6m to $16.3m.
The Her Horizon Fund has been seeded with $14m from the Wallace Global Fund, plus an additional $1.5m contribution from an anonymous donor, making $15.5m in total.
The aim of Her Horizon Fund, set up by the US-based Wallace Global Fund, is to pool $100m from donors to reach a “tipping point” towards ending FGM within a generation.
Ifrah Ahmed, a Somali-Irish activist and survivor of FGM who set up the Ifrah Foundation to end practice in Somalia, where it is nearly universal, said: “By giving $14m, the global fund will ensure activists can continue their work in this area.”
UN funding worth $300,000 to her organisation was cut by UNFPA last year, but Ahmed managed to raise money from elsewhere. The Ifrah Foundation has helped push for anti-FGM legislation in Somalia, she said.
Three of Somalia’s seven federal member states have enacted anti-FGM laws, while in two other states bills banning the practice have been endorsed by cabinet and are awaiting parliamentary approval, albeit with opposition by religious leaders in some areas.
“If we don’t continue to raise money, the dream where this practice will end will have died for young girls,” she added.
Advocates warn that while international recognition of FGM as a human rights violation has grown, and countries such as Burkina Faso, the Gambia and Kenya have criminalised the practice, progress remains fragile.
In recent years, survivors and frontline groups have been trying to protect gains made over several decades.
The Gambia’s supreme court, for instance, is considering a constitutional challenge to the country’s 2015 ban on female genital mutilation and cutting. The case follows a 2024 parliamentary effort to repeal the ban, which lawmakers rejected after months of debate, amid strong resistance from women’s rights groups. In Sierra Leone, the new Child Rights Act does not prohibit FGM, despite sustained campaigning from rights groups.
Susan Gibbs, the Wallace Global Fund’s senior adviser on women’s rights and FGM, said: “Female genital mutilation is a global crisis, an extreme manifestation of gender-based violence and violence against children, and a public health emergency.
“There has been decades of progress, and UN data indicates declines in prevalence in a number of countries. But there have also been anti-rights pushback and political crises. Obviously, donor funding is in decline. So it’s a mixed picture.”
She added: “We’re at this critical inflection point. Most frontline organisations have been absolutely starved for resources, and so more direct funding would allow them to sustain and scale [up] their work.”
Gibbs, who attended a Justice for Girls global gathering in Kenya earlier this month, where the fund was officially launched, said the momentum at the meeting was “incredible”.
“Lasting change must be led by the frontline – it cannot be imposed from the outside. Frontline survivors, activists, they know their communities and they know what it will take. They must have the resources and power to lead.
“I’m convinced the impact [of the fund] will be catalytic,” she said. “There’s no doubt in my mind that with adequate funding, these frontline activists have what it takes to get this done.”
FGM is the partial or total removal of female genitalia for non-medical reasons. It has been endured by more than 144 million women and girls in Africa, 80 million in Asia and 6 million in the Middle East. The practice can cause immediate health complications such as severe pain, excessive bleeding and infection, as well as long-term consequences that include complications during childbirth, chronic pain and lasting psychological trauma.
A 2025 study estimated that FGM causes approximately 44,000 deaths each year in the 15 countries examined, making it one of the leading causes of death for women and girls in those countries.

Kosovo gets new government but political impasse persists
Kosovo lawmakers have voted in a new government led by Prime Minister Albin Kurti
PRISTINA, Kosovo -- PRISTINA, Kosovo (AP) — Kosovo lawmakers on Sunday voted into office a new government of Prime Minister Albin Kurti following an early election in June in the small Balkan nation that remains locked in a prolonged political crisis.
Kurti's government received support from a slim majority of 62 lawmakers in the 120-member assembly. Opposition lawmakers boycotted the session, accusing Kurti of violating postelection procedures.
Disagreements between key political players in Kosovo have led to an impasse over more than 18 months, which has not been resolved despite two early ballots.
Lawmakers failed to elect deputy speakers of the assembly. Opposition parties insisted on their election before the vote on the new government is held.
The crisis first started after an election in February 2025, when no party won enough votes to form a government. An early election in December 2025 ended with Kurti forming the government but parties could not agree on the president.
To choose a president, Kosovo’s 120-member assembly needs a quorum of at least 80 lawmakers, which Kurti did not have.
Kurti's ruling center-left Vetevendosje party again won most votes after the election in June, but less than the previous time as voter disappointment and frustration appeared to grow.
Opposition parties said they will take the alleged postelection procedural mistakes to the Constitutional Court. If the crisis drags on, it could push Kosovo into yet another early election.
Kosovo is among the youngest and poorest countries in Europe. The predominantly ethnic Albanian nation declared independence from Serbia in 2008 following a 1998-99 war that ended in a NATO bombing that forced Serbia to withdraw.
Kosovo has been recognized by the United States and most EU countries but not by Serbia and its allies Russia and China. Pristina and Belgrade have been told they must mend relations to move forward with their EU membership bids.

Beijing’s ‘trust issue’ with Hong Kong and what the city can promise in its 5-year plan
Hong Kong’s openness is both a strength and a weakness, so it must build robust security frameworks to reap rewards of national development, experts say
Now would be the time to focus entirely on economic growth and downplay national security, some experts have argued, warning the issue could deter potential investors.

Biscuitville may be far smaller than McDonald’s or Chick-fil-A, but when it comes to breakfast, the Southern chain continues to win over American diners. The family-owned restaurant has been named the nation’s best fast-food breakfast for the fourth consecutive year in the 2026 USA Today 10 Best Readers’ Choice Awards. It secured the top position ahead of much larger competitors, with McDonald’s ranking fourth and Chick-fil-A fifth. Burger King and Wendy’s followed in sixth and seventh place respectively. What makes the result particularly striking is Biscuitville’s relatively small footprint. The chain recently opened its 90th restaurant and operates only in North Carolina, South Carolina and Virginia. By comparison, the national brands it beat have locations across the United States and serve vastly larger customer bases. Biscuitville chief marketing officer Kristie Mitchell told Fox News Digital that the latest recognition was a reflection of the employees who prepare the food every morning, as well as the ingredients and cooking methods used by the company. The chain’s approach is deliberately different from the efficiency-driven model often associated with fast food. Its biscuits are made from scratch every 15 minutes using a three-ingredient family recipe that, according to Mitchell, was passed down from the founder’s grandmother. The restaurants also hand-crack eggs, while the company says food does not arrive partially cooked simply to be finished in the kitchen. That means more preparation and more labour behind the scenes, even though customers still expect their breakfast to arrive quickly, particularly when ordering through a drive-thru. For Mitchell, that extra effort is central to why customers keep returning. “We have no microwaves. There’s no instant anything in our kitchens,” she told Fox News Digital. Biscuitville’s menu extends beyond its signature biscuits. Customers can order bacon, egg and cheese biscuits, fried chicken biscuits, grits, hash browns and country gravy, along with pancakes and other breakfast options. The company also highlights locally sourced ingredients and partnerships with family-owned suppliers, including its eggs, chicken and bacon. Mitchell said the combination of those ingredients with scratch preparation helps distinguish the chain in an increasingly crowded breakfast market. But the appeal may not be entirely about what is on the plate. Southern breakfast has a strong association with comfort and family traditions, and that is something Biscuitville believes can connect with customers even if they did not grow up in the South. Mitchell said the company regularly receives feedback from customers comparing its biscuits with those made by their grandmothers. That sense of familiarity, she suggested, can make the meal feel like more than a quick stop for food. “I think it’s bigger than just the biscuit,” Mitchell said. “It’s all the things that go between that biscuit.” The idea appears to be resonating. USA Today’s 10Best contest saw Biscuitville chosen by readers after it was included among 20 nominees in the fast-food breakfast category. The public voting process ran for four weeks before the winners were announced on July 15. Biscuitville also placed third in the separate Best Regional Fast Food category. The company, which was founded in 1966, has said it eventually hopes to expand into states such as Tennessee and Georgia. For now, however, its focus remains on growing within its existing markets. That limited footprint has not stopped the chain from competing with America’s biggest fast-food names. If anything, its latest award suggests that a breakfast built around fresh preparation, familiar flavours and regional identity can still stand out in a market dominated by national chains. Saima Wazed, the World Health Organization’s (WHO) South-East Asia Region head and daughter of ousted Bangladeshi Prime Minister Sheikh Hasina, resigned on Wednesday (September 10, 2026) following fraud investigations by the U.N. agency and Bangladeshi authorities, according to sources.
The WHO placed Ms. Wazed, who took office in early 2024 for a five-year term, on unpaid administrative leave late last year. She was first sent on leave in July 2025, in a move that followed Bangladesh’s Anti-Corruption Commission filing cases for fraud, forgery, and misuse of power against.
The WHO accused Ms. Wazed of “committing financial fraud in relation to her travel to China” and of misrepresenting her academic credentials, according to a separate letter from her lawyers to the WHO on July 3, 2026. She has denied the allegations.
The WHO also alleged she had illegally acquired a plot of land in Bangladesh, according to her resignation letter to WHO Director-General Tedros Adhanom Ghebreyesus.
What Saima Wazed said in her reisgnation letter
Ms. Wazed said she acquired the land before she joined the WHO and was entitled to it under a Bangladeshi law that covered the families of the country’s independence leader, Sheikh Mujibur Rahman, osuted PM Hasina’s father. “I was elected to the position of Regional Director in order to serve the countries in my region, which I had sincerely done,” Ms. Wazed said in her resignation letter to Mr. Tedros sent late on Wednesday (September 10, 2026).
“Since you continue to prevent me from effectively carrying out my duties, I have lost all trust and confidence in your leadership of WHO,” she wrote. “Moreover, after nearly one year without any remuneration following your decision to place me on unpaid leave, my financial situation has become untenable. In these circumstances, I am choosing to step aside.” She declined to comment further.
Saima Wazed | Rise of the daughter
The role of WHO regional head
In the role of South-East Asia regional director, Ms. Wazed was mandated to direct international health work in 11 countries, an area with a population of over two billion people. She is a licensed school psychologist, nationally certified in the U.S.
Ms. Wazed’s appointment as Regional Director had also been under the scanner, with charges of having used her mother’s influence during the campaign, and of providing false information on her academic record during in her candidature for the post, allegedly violating Section 468 of the Bangladesh Penal Code (forgery for the purpose of cheating), and Section 471 (forging a document).
Regional directors are among the world’s most influential health policy officials, with their duties including responses to outbreaks and emergencies and adapting WHO policies to local conditions. They are elected every five years by member states, which include Bangladesh and India in the South-East Asia region.
Two sources told Reuters earlier that the U.N. agency was planning to formally remove Wazed. One of them said the WHO would announce nominations for the role on October 12, vet applications in December and hold elections on January 24. The sources declined to be named given the sensitivity of the matter.

Content warning: The following article has references to suicide. Please avoid reading if you feel distressed by the subject.
The semicolon, a punctuation mark often used while writing, signifies a pause -- one that is longer than a comma but shorter than a period. It signifies a break and not the end. And sometimes, such a pause might just be what a person needs -- to ensure that the end can stay away, if not forever, at least for the time being. This is what prompted Amy Bleuel to use the punctuation mark as the symbol for the movement that she founded to raise awareness on suicide prevention and mental health.
Today, the semicolon tattoo is one of the most recognised symbols of mental health awareness in the world. But how and when did it all begin?
Project Semicolon was founded in 2013 by Bleuel, a suicide prevention and mental health advocate, to honour her father, who died by suicide ten years ago. The intention was to create a space for people to talk about mental health openly and without any shame. According to the project’s website, the semicolon became a symbol for the movement as it “is used when an author could’ve ended a sentence but chose not to… the semicolon became a symbol for anyone who could’ve ended their own life but chose to keep going.” The movement caught the attention of people worldwide and so did the semicolon tattoo.
People began tattooing the semicolon on their bodies, either as a standalone or by adding it as an element within other hybrid tattoos. These tattoos were used by survivors to honour their personal mental health battles. People have also embraced the tattoo as tributes to their loved ones who had died by suicide, while others don their tattoos as an expression of solidarity to the movement and raise awareness about mental health and suicide prevention. “For many, it’s a daily reminder to keep fighting, to keep writing, to keep living,” reads a quote on their site.
The placement of the tattoo is a matter of choice and people sport them on various parts of their body including on visible locations such as the neck, wrists, etc., while others place it in more intimate areas. The tattoos are not just meant to express but also serve as a means of personal affirmation.
The project deals with spreading awareness not just on suicide prevention but also on various other aspects of mental health including depression, anxiety, post-traumatic stress disorder (PTSD), borderline personality disorder (BPD), and various other struggles. “What started as one woman’s act of hope has grown into a global movement — one inked semicolon at a time,” says the project’s website.
In 2017, Selena Gomez, Alisha Boe and Tommy Dorfman got the semicolon tattooed on their wrists to commemorate the premiere of their Netflix series 13 Reasons Why. The web series deals with themes of suicide and mental health and it was reported that the stars got the tattoo as a tribute to the show’s handling of the theme as well as the death of Bleuel, a victim of trauma, child abuse and rape.
Various regional organisations, projects, campaigns, etc., inspired by the semicolon project have come up in various parts of the world. India has also not shied away from embracing the movement. Semicolon (;) The Mental Health Awareness Project – India is one such initiative.
Founded by the Medical Students Association of India (MSAI) under the International Federation of Medical Students’ Associations (IFMSA), it was designed as a campaign model that could be leveraged by other local chapters. The project aims to create awareness regarding mental health and tackle the stigma associated with the same, among high school students from classes eighth to 10th.
If you are in distress, please reach out to national helpline 104 or any of these 24x7 helplines.

Telangana is exploring a proposal to make six months of robotic surgery training mandatory for postgraduate medical students, as the State looks to build a trained workforce to expand advanced robotic procedures across its government hospitals.
Health Minister C. Damodar Raja Narasimha said the government would approach the National Medical Commission (NMC) for permission to introduce the dedicated training period as part of the three-year postgraduate programme.
Speaking at the ‘State Level Multi-Specialty Robotic Surgery Workshop’ at the Marri Chenna Reddy Telangana Institute of Medical Sciences (MCR TIMS), Sanathnagar in Hyderabad, the Minister said training would be central to Telangana’s plans to expand robotic surgery, whether through a hub-and-spoke model or dedicated robotic surgery facilities at the district level.
The proposal comes as Telangana is already attempting to build a statewide pool of surgeons trained in robotic procedures.
MCR TIMS Director Dr A. Narendra Kumar said surgeons from 35 medical colleges and 47 hospitals, excluding speciality hospitals, are being trained in robotic surgery at two government institutions, Nizam’s Institute of Medical Sciences (NIMS) and MNJ Cancer Institute.

“The idea is to ensure that robotic surgery does not remain concentrated in a handful of premier institutions in Hyderabad,” he added.
Robotic surgery expert Dr. Sudhir Srivastava said such a model could allow specialist expertise to reach patients without requiring them to travel to major cities. He pointed to the financial and emotional burden faced by families from rural and smaller communities when they have to leave their homes to access specialised treatment.
Former NIMS Director Dr N. Bheerappa said NIMS had recently completed nearly 1,000 robotic surgeries and that the government was bearing the cost of such procedures for eligible patients through the Rajiv Aarogyasri health scheme.
Director of Medical Education (DME) Dr N. Vani said government medical colleges had a dual responsibility of providing patient care while training the next generation of doctors. Introducing young surgeons to newer technologies, she said, could have a multiplier effect across the government healthcare system.
She also stressed that young surgeons should not rely solely on the technology, but must combine it with clinical judgement, human touch and compassion.
Experts at the workshop also cautioned that expanding robotic surgery is about considerably more than installing machines. Government Medical College Nagpur Dean Dr. Raj Gajbhiye said robotic surgery was no longer merely a technology available at a few high-end private institutions.
For government hospitals, however, he said “the real objective should be equitable access to advanced surgical technology. “Success of robotics is not about purchasing a robot,” Dr. Gajbhiye said, pointing instead to the need for appropriate infrastructure, trained faculty, structured protocols, multidisciplinary teamwork and institutional support.
