Never use harsh cleaning products to clean your smartphone — do this instead
Put that bleach down.
Smartphones have become an essential part of daily life; for some people it's the last thing they touch before going to bed and the first thing they hold in the morning. How healthy that habit is is up for discussion, but what's definitely not up for discussion is how necessary it is to clean your smartphone. We use these devices everywhere from living rooms to conference rooms to parties and even the toilet in your friend's house. With that kind of usage, it's not hard to understand why the average smartphone is 10 times dirtier than a toilet seat. Thankfully, cleaning your phone is a pretty straightforward task.
Even though your smartphone is basically a glass sandwich, that doesn't mean you should use harsh products like Windex, compressed air, hydrogen peroxide or worse, bleach, to clean your phone. These products contain harsh chemicals that can permanently damage your phone's screen. To be more exact, they strip the oleophobic coating on your phone's display making it lose the fingerprint-resistant, oil-repelling properties that keep the screen smooth to the touch. To properly clean your phone, all you need is a lint-free microfiber cloth, a bit of soapy water or a dedicated 70 percent isopropyl alcohol solution (or wipe) — whichever is easier to keep on hand.
How to properly clean your smartphone
First things first, grab your cleaning materials, power off your phone, then remove the case if it has one. Now grab your microfiber cloth and gently dip it into your soapy water then squeeze out any excess water. If you're using 70 percent isopropyl alcohol, simply spray it on the cloth. The cloth should be damp, not wet.
Next, gently use the cloth to thoroughly wipe your phone. Make sure to get in between the camera lenses and side button, but take it slow around your phone's openings like the USB-C port to avoid moisture getting in. This method works for both your screen and back glass.
Circling back to phone cases. For most people their phone is almost always in its case, so it stands to reason that your case is probably as dirty as your phone if not more. How you clean your case depends on what it's made of; for silicone and plastic cases, use the same soapy water or alcohol wipe as you would for your phone. Leather is the exception, since alcohol dries it out and can cause cracking, so stick to a damp cloth with mild soap instead.
What not to do when cleaning your phone
Even with the right products, it's still possible to make a costly mistake when cleaning your smartphone. One of the most common ones is applying the cleaning liquid directly on the device. Any liquid that hits the phone directly can seep into the tiny openings around the screen, buttons or ports, leading to water damage even if the phone is waterproof.
Another thing to not do is clean your phone while it's plugged in. As you should know, combining any amount of moisture and electricity is just asking for trouble. Also, don't over-clean with alcohol wipes, as unnecessary repeated use even at the recommended 70 percent concentration gradually breaks down the oleophobic coating on the screen. Then lastly, avoid using rough fabric or paper towels to clean your device. Unlike microfiber cloths, which are soft and non-abrasive, these are abrasive at a microscopic level, so using rough fabric and paper towels to clean your phone will cause tiny scratches that get bigger and more noticeable the more you use those abrasive materials.

Barclays Bank is facing a formal complaint over its financial links to a coal-fired power station near the Sundarbans, the world’s largest mangrove forest and home to millions of people in Bangladesh and India.
Three complainants from the region have submitted a case to the UK government’s Office for Responsible Business Conduct, alleging that the British bank breached international guidelines by underwriting companies involved in the emission-heavy Maitree super thermal power project, also known as the Rampal power plant.
The coal-fired power station is situated near the Sundarbans, a Unesco world heritage site made up of more than 100 tiny islands across a river delta that supports hundreds of plant and animal species, including the Bengal tiger.
Sharif Jamil, an environmental campaigner based in the Bangladeshi capital, Dhaka, who is one of the complainants, said heavy-metal pollution from the plant and the industrial development surrounding it was entering the Sundarbans through its interconnected rivers and canals.
“The Rampal power plant is right on the bank of the Pasur River, which is the lifeline of the Sundarbans,” he said. “The health of the forest is in trouble.”
Last November, a study found elevated levels of mercury and arsenic in water samples taken from the Sundarbans, with the highest concentrations recorded in the Pasur River.
Researchers identified industrial discharge and port-related activities among the sources of heavy-metal contamination and said the Rampal power station posed “a significant environmental threat due to emissions from coal combustion and increased navigation traffic”.
Millions of people live in the Sundarbans, and many depend on the river and forests for food and other resources.
The claimants allege that Barclays failed to conduct sufficient due diligence on the environmental and human rights risks before providing financial services to organisations connected to the project.
Barclays underwrote debt of India’s state-owned NTPC Ltd (formerly the National Thermal Power Corporation), one of the joint-venture partners behind the plant, according to King’s Legal Clinic, which is assisting the complainants. It also says Barclays underwrote bond issues for the Export-Import Bank of India between 2016 and 2019, which provided a loan for the Rampal project.
The complainants argue that emissions from the plant will contribute to global heating, rising sea levels and extreme weather in a region already highly vulnerable to the climate crisis. Mangroves act as a natural barrier against cyclones and other extreme weather.
The power station faced sustained opposition during its planning and construction, including concerns raised by Unesco in a report in 2016, which concluded that “air and water pollution have a high likelihood to irreversibly damage the … World Heritage property”. Some financial institutions, including banks in France, refused to support the project because of its potential environmental and social effects, the complaint says.
Jamil said Barclays’ international standing obliged it to consider the consequences of financing. “The greater your reputation, the greater your responsibility to behave responsibly towards the planet and its people,” he said. “Barclays is a reputed global organisation, and that is why it also has a responsibility.
“Other banks and financial institutions were divesting from, or declining to finance, this project,” he added. “Barclays and other financial organisations should change their policies and examine how their operations can protect the planet from climate catastrophe.”
Jamil also called on banks to direct more funding towards renewable energy rather than imported fossil fuels. “Bangladesh has sunlight throughout the year,” he said. “Why should we expand fossil fuels when there is enormous potential to produce electricity from renewable energy?”
The other complainants include Animesh Mandal, a farmer and politician, and the Dakshinbanga Matsyajibi Forum, a trade union representing fish workers in West Bengal.
They are being assisted by students and lawyers at King’s Human Rights and Environment Clinic, part of King’s College London’s law school.
Sue Willman, a solicitor at the clinic, said: “Rural communities in the Sundarbans are on the frontline of the climate and nature crisis. We hope to persuade banks and financial institutions to think again before financing oil and coal developments that are contributing to that crisis.”
The Office for Responsible Business Conduct, part of the Department for Business and Trade, will assess whether to consider the complaint.
Barclays Bank and BIFPCL (Bangladesh India Friendship Power Company Ltd), the holding company for the Maitree super thermal power project, declined to comment.

Here's what you can use instead of a docking station
You might not need one at all.
If you're looking to get the most out of your laptop, chances are good that the baseline number of included ports isn't enough to get the job done. One of the easiest ways to remedy this is to get a docking station. However, many of the best docking stations can be prohibitively expensive, and they might not suit your specific setup needs.
Thankfully, docking stations aren't the only port solutions on the market anymore. There's now a new contender: USB-C hubs, which cover many of the same bases as a docking station. Either can be a good way to organize your desk setup, but docking stations and USB-C hubs do have some fundamental differences. Which piece of tech is right for you will depend on a variety of factors, particularly what you're plugging in and where.
What is a USB-C hub, and what makes it different from a docking station?
As colloquial terms, the definitions of "hub" and "dock" have become fairly blurred over the years, but when talking about USB-C hubs vs. docking stations, there remain a few key differences. One differentiator is size: Docking stations are generally bigger, often coming with a large number of ports, whereas a USB-C hub is smaller and lighter with fewer ports. The former is more centered around permanently transforming a desk setup, while the latter is designed for more on-the-go usage.
Power supply is the other big differentiation. Docking stations can plug directly into the wall, allowing the dock to provide power to external devices, while hubs tend to draw their power from the device they're plugged into. While externally powered hubs aren't unheard of, they aren't the norm either. Some USB-C hubs support power delivery passthrough, allowing them to charge accessories, but this can be quite slow unless you have a specialized hub.
What are common problems with a USB-C hub?
One of the most commonly encountered problems with USB-C hubs stems from the fact that many of them use power from your computer instead of utilizing a direct line to an outlet. Similarly, a USB-C hub is splitting its bandwidth from the laptop port it's plugged into, while a dock has its own dedicated bandwidth. These two limitations combined mean that not every piece of tech will run well on a USB-C hub. External hard drives, particularly SSDs, can struggle to get enough power and bandwidth to function properly, and the high-speed data needed for devices like HD webcams and external GPUs to function properly makes them a nonstarter with a hub. This is also why most USB-C hubs can only support one external monitor — there's simply not enough bandwidth for more.
Because they're designed to be more portable, USB-C hubs are also subject to the pitfalls of typical wear and tear. Compared to a stationary docking station, a hub is much more susceptible to things like debris buildup and internal damage from drops. Depending on how much you're traveling with it and how roughly it's treated, it might have a shorter lifespan than a dock. Despite their limitations, USB-C hubs can be a great option for users looking for more ports at their disposal, and their portability gives them a distinct edge over docking stations if you're not looking to plug in a huge amount of taxing peripherals.

US Open: Alexander Zverev sends out warning to Jannik Sinner and Carlos Alcaraz, claiming he is currently the best tennis player in the world
Alexander Zverev claims he is currently the best player in the world following his victory at the US Open over American hope Ben Shelton; you can also watch the Laver Cup at The O2 in London from 25-27 September live on Sky Sports
Monday 14 September 2026 04:09, UK
Alexander Zverev sent out firm warning to world No 1 Jannik Sinner and Carlos Alcaraz, claiming he is currently the best tennis player in the world following his US Open victory.
German Zverev beat Ben Shelton in the final on Sunday to the bitter disappointment of the home crowd in New York.
Zverev was playing in his sixth major final and Shelton his first, and it showed in a 6-3 7-6 (7-2) 5-7 6-2 victory extinguished America's hopes of a first male winner since Andy Roddick in 2003.

The 29-year-old has been the dominant player in Grand Slams in a season that has seen Alcaraz, who won this year's Australian Open, exit the US Open in a quarter-final defeat by Shelton after a long injury lay-off while Sinner pulled out injured before the tournament began after winning Wimbledon.
Zverev finally broke through to win his first major at the French Open, then reach the final at the All England Club, losing to Sinner.
He is 25-2 in Grand Slam matches in 2026 and Zverev believes he is currently the best in the world.
"You have to take everything into consideration," he said. "With Jannik Sinner being injured and Carlos Alcaraz coming back from injury after four months, right now, probably yes. Both of them healthy and both of them at the top of their game, maybe not.
"But if we say right, right now with Jannik being injured and Carlos coming back from injury, maybe. I mean, four, five months ago when both of them were healthy, I wasn't. I was losing to Jannik all the time. So if everyone is healthy, I think Jannik is still ahead. It's as simple as that."
Zverev: I forgot about the score and it helped me
Zverev was so focused on the job at hand, he did not even realise he had won the title when Shelton smacked a service return long.
As the umpire announced 'Game, set and match Zverev', the German headed back to the baseline, ready to receive Shelton's serve.
It took him a few seconds to register why the cheering fans were giving him a standing ovation - as he belatedly cracked a smile and ran to the net to embrace Shelton.
Speaking to Sky Sports Tennis, he said: "I thought the score was 5-1! I knew that I had broken him twice, but I thought he only held once.
"I was thinking: 'Okay, I'm going to have a relaxed service game here and then I'll get tight on the next one.' It was lucky for me!
"It's actually funny, teachers in tennis say play each point and forget about the score. Well I forgot about the score and it helped me!"
Shelton wants more of the same
Shelton said he was eager to get another taste of the spotlight on tennis' biggest stage.
"It's such a cool moment. Walking out on that court today, there's nothing like it. I've never felt anything like that before. Yeah, it's an addicting feeling being in positions like this," said the 23-year-old.
The USTA previously pointed to Taylor Fritz's 2024 campaign as a sign of progress, after announcing a massive overhaul to its player development programme in 2008.
The sport's national governing body has also moved to diversify its talent in a partnership announced last year with American Tennis Association, focusing on building Black representation in an overwhelmingly white sport.
Shelton made history just by stepping onto the court on Sunday as the first Black American man to play in the New York final in 54 years - since Arthur Ashe, the man for whom the tournament's showpiece court was named.
"I don't think I'm anywhere near the player that I want to be. I think I'm a great competitor. I think I compete really well out there on the court," said Shelton.
"I'm able it stay focused and stay there on the court for many, many hours. I think that's going to help me in the future moving forward."
Henman: Zverev has transformed from a player who was going backwards a year ago
"The perseverance and the way Zverev's game has improved over the last 12 months," said the 2004 US Open semi-finalist.
"I was looking back his Grand Slam results, and his game was going backwards.
"But he has transformed himself to be more aggressive, and when you reflect on this matchup, Zverev had beaten Shelton five times in a row.
"Shelton had to change the narrative, but Zverev looked so comfortable.
"Shelton did a great job getting that third set, but losing his serve first game of the fourth settled Zverev down and gave him more energy. He coasted to the line from there."

Police say it could take months to identify Philippine ferry fire victims
- Published
Philippine authorities said it could take weeks or months to identify victims of a ferry fire that killed 76 people last week.
"Most of them are already in a charred condition," Richard Allan Mangalip, a forensic specialist from the Philippine National Police, told reporters on Sunday. Family members have been asked to help identify victims with personal items or DNA samples.
The MV June Aster was heading from Manila to Coron in Palawan province, a popular holiday destination, when a fire started in its cargo hold and spread rapidly throughout the vessel.
Forty-three people survived the disaster, while 13 people remain unaccounted for, authorities said.
Mangalip said they were "trying [their] best to collect the possible identifying marks" from victims' remains.
But it was hard to give a clear timeline on how long the identification process would take because of the volume of specimens, he said, adding, "It could be weeks, or it could be months."
A coast guard official said on Saturday that the priority was identifying victims and determining the cause of the blaze.
The fire continued burning for more than a day, releasing heat and toxic fumes that impeded search and rescue operations. It took more than 40 hours before rescuers could board the ship in search of survivors.
The MV June Aster had set off last Tuesday from Manila to Coron, a popular destination among both local and foreign tourists, known for its beaches and WW2 shipwreck diving sites.
Besides tourists, there were also passengers on the ferry who had been travelling to Coron for work or to visit family.
Survivors recall hearing a loud explosion before seeing smoke and fire. When fire engulfed the ship, chaos erupted on board, they said.
One told the BBC that he had been trampled after falling on the floor. He jumped off the boat into the sea before being rescued hours later.
But many burned to death on the ship. Mangalip said at the press conference on Sunday that some victims' remains were found clustered together in parts of the vessel.
"Our thoughts are also with the survivors and families still waiting for news of their loved ones," the Philippine Coast Guard said in a statement on Sunday. "We recognise the pain and uncertainty they continue to endure as recovery and identification efforts remain underway."

Since the days immediately following the Sept. 11, 2001, attacks, U.S. President Donald Trump, a native of New York City, has made numerous claims about what he saw that day and his involvement in the recovery efforts.
One such claim Trump has repeatedly made is his assertion that he was at Ground Zero within days of 9/11 and that he sent workers to the recovery effort at the site of the World Trade Center.
In September 2026, multiple X users debated the veracity of the claim. For example, one user (archived) wrote, "There's no proof Trump sent a large group of construction workers to Ground Zero."
Other popular (archived) posts (archived) said there was no evidence Trump, himself, went to Ground Zero and helped with recovery efforts.
Another X post (archived) alternatively claimed, "President Trump is dropping VIDEO PROOF for every Fake News outlet lying to millions that he was nowhere near Ground Zero after 9/11."
(X)
Many Snopes readers searched the site to find out if Trump's claims were true.
A couple of days after the Sept. 11 attacks, Trump told multiple news media outlets that he sent at least 100 workers to Ground Zero to help pull people and bodies out of the rubble, with 125 to 150 more on the way. However, Snopes has never been able to identify any public evidence that crews he hired helped in the immediate recovery of the 9/11 attacks. Since we cannot independently confirm with certainty whether Trump had crews on site somewhere, we are leaving this claim unrated.
Footage of interviews Trump conducted in the immediate days after 9/11 placed him within blocks of Ground Zero. Trump said in those interviews that he visited Ground Zero to encourage the workers he said he brought to assist with clearing rubble at the site. It was not possible to find evidence showing Trump helped clear the pile of debris at Ground Zero, as some posts disputed.
In a phone call with a local news media station immediately after the planes crashed into the Twin Towers, Trump said he watched the towers fall from the window of one of his buildings.
Trump's September 2026 remarks
On Sept. 8, 2026, in a post on Truth Social (archived), Trump continued to maintain that he was at Ground Zero with construction workers after 9/11, clarifying that it was "obviously not on the same day as the collapse, but shortly thereafter":
The Failing New York Magazine wrote a story that I wasn't down at the World Trade Center after the Tragedy of September 11th, because nobody saw me there. Well, I don't think I would be the first thing on anyone's mind but, I was there, obviously not on the same day as the collapse, but shortly thereafter, with a large group of Construction Workers.
He then added he "was there as soon as the Law allowed."
The president was referencing a New York Magazine article disputing his comments about where he was on the day of, and the days following, the attacks.
Trump also made this claim (archived) in a Fox News interview two days prior, in which he added the additional context that he was constructing a new building in New York City. This is the reason, according to Trump at a 9/11 anniversary event on Sept. 8, why he had workers who he could bring to the rubble of the World Trade Center:
I was building a big building in New York and I took the whole crew down there right after this happened and they had no hesitation. Everybody went down with me. We went down as a big group of people. It wasn't too much we could do, I'll be honest.
What Trump told the media in 2001
Trump spoke to the media multiple times a few days after 9/11. On Sept. 13, he told a German news channel, that he had more than 100 men down at the site of the World Trade Center and more than 125 on their way. According to the German-speaking reporter, the interview was conducted a few blocks from Ground Zero.
That same day, NBC News interviewed Trump at what appeared to be the same location as his interview with the German news channel. Trump said he had "hundreds of men inside working right now" and was bringing down another 125.
PBS has a recording of another Trump interview from Sept. 13, in which Trump said he had 100 workers helping to dig people and bodies out of the rubble at the World Trade Center, with another 100 to 150 workers "coming." He told PBS that those workers were "digging out" at the site.
In another interview from that day, Trump told reporters his workers had been at Ground Zero "for about a day and a half." He said they were men from his company and that a couple had gotten hurt while working at the site. He also said he was just down at Ground Zero and was there to support them.
The evidence
When Snopes first researched this claim in 2018, we spoke to Richard Alles, a retired deputy chief with the New York City Fire Department, who later served as director of 9/11 community affairs for the law firm Barasch McGarry Salzman and Penson. Alles said that in all his time he spent at Ground Zero as a New York City Fire Department battalion chief, starting 20 minutes after the buildings collapsed, he never saw a large group of workers whom Trump had hired at the site assisting with search and rescue efforts. "This is the first I'm hearing of it," Alles said via phone call. "There would have been no need for that. Between police, fire and the construction crews, we had it all covered."
Alles added that the construction crews he saw at Ground Zero helping rescue workers were from the trade unions and were not hired by Trump.
John Feal, founder of the 9/11 first responder health advocacy nonprofit the FealGood Foundation, told Snopes at the time that he responded to Ground Zero on Sept. 12, 2001, as a construction demolitions expert and that he didn't see evidence of hundreds of workers hired by Trump at the site.
The Trump Organization was building in New York City in 2001, according to the Skyscraper Center database on skyscrapers. In fact, it finished a series of residential buildings in the city at Trump Place between 1998 and 2004. He was also building the Trump World Tower residential building near the United Nations Headquarters that year.
However, it was not possible to find verifiable information about how many people, either directly employed by Trump or contracted to work on one of the Trump Organization's projects, were working on these buildings and in New York City at the time.
A New York Times fact-check from July 2019 referenced Timothy O'Brien, the author of "TrumpNation: The Art of Being the Donald," who reportedly said the Trump Organization numbered "a little bit over a dozen people" at the time of the attacks, making it impossible to send as many workers to the relief effort as Trump claimed.
Neither the White House nor the Trump Organization responded to Snopes' requests for corroborating evidence in 2018. This lack of response is consistent with past attempts by Politifact, The Washington Post, The New York Times and Politifact again to reach out to the White House and/or the Trump Organization to corroborate evidence of Trump's claims.

In early September 2026, as Repulican U.S. Sen. Marsha Blackburn campaigned for governor of Tennessee, many people online claimed she announced a plan to bring segregation back to schools in the state if elected.
For example, a Facebook post stated:
BREAKING: Marsha Blackburn has announced that if she wins her bid for governor she will bring segregation back to Tennessee schools with the pilot program being in Chattanooga. "The supreme court will side with President Trump and I on this. The way we see it kids feel more comfortable with other kids that look like them."
(Facebook user, Chattanooga Enquirer)
Snopes readers emailed us to ask whether the claim was true.
The claim originated from an account that was satirical in nature. Blackburn did not say she would bring back school segregation in Tennessee. As such, this claim is labeled satire.
The post came from the Chattanooga Enquirer, a Facebook page that describes itself as a "Satire/Parody" media company. The introduction to the page states: "The one stop shop for Chattanooga's fake but maybe real news."
We searched for the purported quote featured in the post on Google, DuckDuckGo (archived), and Bing, and found no evidence of Blackburn ever making this announcement.
Blackburn has long been an opponent of diversity, equity and inclusion initiatives, and critical race theory in schools. On her Senate website, Blackburn calls CRT "a radical school of thought used by the political left to assign racial significance to objectively neutral concepts like history and mathematics." She adds, "This dangerous agenda insists that America is a racist country and teaches that all individuals are either oppressors or victims."
As Snopes previously reported, CRT looks to the law for answers as to why racial inequality persists even as American founding documents and aspirational ideals vaunt equality, and after the Civil Rights Movement brought about landmark legislation aimed at ending racism de jure.
According to data from the 2023-2024 school year collected by Stanford University, Tennessee is ranked sixth among the most racially segregated public schools in the country.
For further reading, Snopes previously reported on the false claim that Blackburn flashed a "white power gesture" during a Senate hearing.

'It's like a dog set loose on us' - fear over Kenya's crackdown on foreign traders
- Published
For Ndaikech Ali, who has been traversing the streets of the Kenyan capital eking out a living as a tuk-tuk driver for the past nine years, Nairobi's traffic - not xenophobia - has been his biggest concern.
During his time in the East African nation, the Burundian says he has always found Kenyans to be friendly and welcoming - that is until last week, when the president ordered a crackdown on foreigners working as traders or operating small-scale businesses.
"Now they have turned against us," he told the BBC at the Burundian embassy in Nairobi where many have been queuing this week for documents to allow them to travel back home.
"The threats are many… even from children," he said, adding: "It's a like a dog has been set loose upon us. We have been bitten."
President William Ruto made his remarks last week when addressing Kenyan traders gathered at state house - in reference to legislation before parliament that seeks to exclude foreign nationals from petty trade and to mandate the local sourcing of certain materials.
During his speech, he said that all foreign nationals operating small businesses had until 7 September to pack up shop, saying such low-level jobs should be reserved for Kenyans.
Ali, like others, panicked, saying it seemed the president's announcement had been interpreted by some Kenyans as a signal that foreign nationals were no longer welcome in the country.
"We face harassment and can't work," he says. "If our work is stopped, we lose the income that enables us to pay rent and buy food. When those jobs are taken away, the only option left is to return home."
Now he's gone, who will help me pay school fees"
Other Burundians and some other foreign nationals have rushed to border crossing points to leave the country, with reports suggesting that a number have ended up stranded there.
Some couples fear they will be forced to separate - and some families have already been divided.
"I have been here from 2019," said a Burundian man, who identified himself only as Prosper and who has a child with a Kenyan woman.
"When I heard the announcement, it was very painful because when I go, I'm forced to leave my family... and I love my family," he told the BBC.
In Nairobi's low-income neighbourhood of Majengo, Kenyan Grace Wamaitha said her Burundian husband had already gone - leaving the day after the president's 3 September directive.
She is distraught as she has been left trying to feed their five children - and has taken on extra work washing clothes.
"Now he's gone, who will help me pay school fees? I don't know what to do. Let them come back," she told the BBC.
In Nairobi and other major towns, migrants from the region can be found working in barber shops and salons, construction, operating motorbike taxis and street vending, as well as selling clothes, food and household goods.
Some have fled conflicts or economic hardship at home, while others have moved to Kenya in search of better opportunities. Within the East African Community (EAC), a regional bloc made up of eight countries, including Burundi and Kenya, the relative free movement of people is allowed - but employment and long-term residence do require permits.
Kenyan law also recognises the right of refugees to work and operate businesses, although they are also required to obtain the appropriate documentation.
Filmon Eyob, a co-ordinator within Nairobi's Eritrean community, agrees with concerns that the crackdown order will be used as pretext to harass foreigners.
He told the BBC that while many Kenyans had been supportive and welcoming, some Eritreans and Ethiopians had closed their businesses and stayed at home over the last week as a precaution.
The president's remarks also sparked a diplomatic row, with the Burundian foreign affairs minister warning that "hate speech against Burundi" could have repercussions for Kenyans abroad.
The authorities in Kenya have struggled to contain the fallout - and as the matter came to a head, Kenyan foreign affairs official Korir Sing'Oei visited and apologised to Burundians at the embassy this week, assuring them of protection from violence.
Critics argue that Ruto's remarks were a populist move that risked stoking xenophobia, although the government has denied this.
Since then, a series of official statements have sought to clarify the directive.
The government has now given a 90-day window for undocumented foreign nationals running small business to register and comply with local laws. During the process, those undergoing registration will be presumed to be living legally in Kenya.
Yet observers and those affected argue that it did not have to be this way.
Academic Hesbon Owilla told the BBC the president's comments were bound to be misinterpreted, especially by people who did not have the right documentation.
He says that while the proposed policy is good for Kenya and in line with global migration protocols, the communication about it ought to have been more diplomatic.
For those not in the audience, Owilla says people interpreted the president words as saying: "We are kicking these guys out."
The president did not stop at small-scale traders. A day later, he ordered India's Tata Chemicals to leave the country, saying the company had not provided sufficient benefits to the local Maasai community in Kajiado county.
Tata has been mining soda ash for years in Lake Magadi, a vast area often covered by a whitish salt crust. The lake's extreme briny environment sustains algae blooms that attract flamboyances of pink flamingos that thrive in the area.
Mining operations began at the lake in 1911 under a British colonial arrangement that is said to have remained largely intact, despite long-running land and resource disputes pitting the company and its predecessors against community and the government.
Economist Odhiambo Ramogi argues that the move to restrict foreign nationals from businesses is too broad - and could do with finessing.
He points out that Kenya hosts hundreds of thousands of refugees as well as other migrants, mostly from the EAC region, as well as other international investors.
Ramogi says that Ruto's intention seemed to go beyond "just protecting jobs for Kenyans".
The president's remarks have prompted a wave of support for foreign nationals, including by civil society groups and ordinary Kenyans who have criticised his approach.
In the wake of the criticism, Ruto, who is up for re-election next year, has sought to counter the backlash.
"Kenya will remain an open, secure and welcoming country, protecting opportunities for its citizens, safeguarding the rights of all persons lawfully within its borders," a statement by his spokesman said.
"Kenya's commitment to the East African Community of the African continent remains firm."
Ramogi says that in the end, it is Kenya that stands to lose when citizens of neighbouring countries are targeted.
He points out that Kenya earned $56m (£41m) in exports to Burundi last year, adding that the country would still benefit by allowing competition, as "locking out aliens simply means you don't want a competitive economy that gets to grow a lot faster".
"Now, if you got $56m out of a country, why are you worried about a hawker who's just trying to make, say, $200 in a month?
"It absolutely makes no sense what the president has done."
For Nairobi resident Lima Kabura, whose husband is Tanzanian, the president's remarks were just too hasty. She says he should have first established those who were in the country illegally.
"When they are forced out, I'm left with no work, no business and no husband," she said.
Additional reporting by Ahmed Bahajj

A Chinese rescue team has reached the all-but-obliterated Gyirong border crossing complex for the first time and found “nothing but ruins” as Nepal and China continue their arduous rescue operations in the flood-hit Himalayas.
Surveillance camera footage from the worst-hit Gyirong border crossing complex showed huge torrents of water and debris on Wednesday engulfing buildings and people trying to flee. Only on Friday were rescuers able to reach that area.
State media reported that the Chinese team of 21 rescuers and a search-and-rescue dog crossed mountains and valleys and used ropes to navigate forests and cliffs after roads to the complex, hemmed in by steep Himalayan slopes, were destroyed.
“There was no road … it was all virgin forest and sheer cliffs,” rescue worker Zou Mingqi said. At the complex, “as far as the eye could see, there was nothing but ruins.”
The glacier collapse which unleashed a deadly torrent through Himalayan mountain river systems has killed at least 579 people in Nepal and seven in China’s Tibet. The number of missing in Nepal has nearly doubled to 1,924, officials said on Friday. At least 558 were missing in Tibet’s Gyirong County, Chinese state media said. Among the missing are at least 540 foreigners, many of them Hindu pilgrims from India.
More than 90,000 people have been affected by the disaster, the Red Cross estimated.
Amid the deepening crisis, Nepal has now said it needs foreign help in specialised and technical areas in which it does not have expertise, but not in search and rescue.
Earlier on Friday, Nepal’s foreign ministry had said that Kathmandu could manage the rescue efforts on its own for now and declined foreign involvement.
The areas Nepal is seeking help include opening transport and communication services in places where bridges have been destroyed, identification of dead bodies, DNA testing and storing bodies for longer durations, foreign minister Shisir Khanal said late on Friday.
Asked about that stance of his government, Khanal said there was no need for assistance in general search and rescue which was being done by Nepali rescuers. “We think there is no need for repetition in this,” he said.
India and China, between whom Nepal is wedged, have been requested to supply bailey bridges to reopen transport and communication in an area where about two dozen bridges had been destroyed.
Nepal is continuing to monitor two barrier lakes upstream of the flood zone, with an official warning that flood risks will persist until both lakes fully drain.
Satellite imagery showed the second lake growing larger with no visible outlet, raising concerns that water pressure could still be building.
China’s state-run Xinhua news agency said that the first barrier lake was reducing in size, citing analysis by the water resources ministry. A Chinese government geo-hazards expert warned, however, that the lake may be unstable and that over 100 glacial lakes scattered throughout the area could pose a threat.
In Beijing, a politburo meeting chaired by President Xi Jinping called for stronger monitoring of glacier lakes and landslide risks, and for closer international disaster cooperation, Xinhua reported.
China’s Premier Li Qiang, the country’s No. 2 official, arrived in the area of Gyirong on Thursday afternoon, Xinhua said. The visit suggested Beijing was treating the disaster as a matter of the highest national priority.
In China, strict controls on the flow of information from one of its most sensitive regions are hampering the public’s understanding of events.
The BBC and NY Times have reported videos of the catastrophic floods, widely shared globally, have not appeared on Chinese social media sites.
Chinese state media has carried several broadcasts about the floods and dispatched their own journalists to the area, but reports have focused on the rescue efforts rather than the scale of the devastation. In one broadcast from a relief centre in Tibet, the journalist did not speak to any of the people sitting behind him.
Tibet, brought under Chinese control in the 1950s, is the most sensitive and tightly controlled region in the country.
The Gyirong border port plays a key role in China’s Belt and Road network linking the country to South Asia, with logistics zones and parking lots built there in the past decade.

Hyrox athlete sparks debate for continuing race after soiling herself
- Published
An athlete's Hyrox performance has sparked debate after completing a race in Beijing despite soiling herself midway through the event.
Footage of the woman competing in the indoor fitness competition despite her soiled legs has gone viral, with some people raising concerns around hygiene and others saluting her resolve to push through. Some also criticised race organisers for letting her to continue.
Hyrox said they launched a "major cleanup operation" after the event on Saturday, including by sanitising equipment and replacing sections of the carpet.
The German fitness company acknowledged the "legitimate concerns" but urged people not to direct their frustration at the athlete herself.
The company did not reveal the woman's identity, but it was revealed online and she subsequently received threats of violence.
"There is no place in our community for threats of violence or encouragement to harm an athlete," Hyrox said in a statement early on Monday.
"Any person identified as engaging in this behaviour – whether through comments, direct messages or social media – will be permanently banned from all Hyrox events," it said.
Some participants in the same event had demanded an apology and a refund, arguing that they were forced to come into contact with contaminated equipment, Chinese media reported.
In each Hyrox race, participants alternate between running a kilometre and doing fitness exercises, such as the sled push, burpee jumps, indoor rowing, and lunges while carrying a sandbag.
The competition has exploded in popularity since it was founded in 2017 in Hamburg, Germany, and is now held across the world. The sport debuted in mainland China in late 2024.
Some have questioned why those officiating the competition in Beijing last weekend did not intervene when the athlete soiled herself, given that Hyrox penalises acts including spitting and littering.
"From a basic health and sanitation standpoint, the athlete should have been stopped immediately, and any contaminated areas should have been closed off and properly cleaned before other athletes were allowed through," Erica Dodge, a US-based nurse, wrote in a comment on Instagram.
Joe Ho, who also took part in the Hyrox Beijing competition over the weekend, has criticised Hyrox's response to the issue and called on the organisation to "take responsibility when its own procedures fail".
"If the organisation accepts that something went wrong, why not offer affected participants refunds, credits, or some meaningful form of compensation?" he wrote.
Others in the fitness community have pointed out that this is not unheard of for endurance athletes.
One comment on Facebook, whose author noted that marathoners have similar experiences, while another wrote: "They've trained too long and too hard to give up just like that."
In 2005, British marathoner Paula Radcliffe famously stopped at the 22-mile mark during the London Marathon to relieve herself by the side of the road in full view of cameras and then went on to win the race.
Earlier this year, Chinese marathoner Li Meizhen made headlines after crossing the finish line at the Hengshui Lake Marathon with menstrual blood on her legs.
Hyrox has expanded rapidly across China, with gyms across the country cashing in on the craze. More than 500 affiliated gyms are offering Hyrox specific training, according to the state's Xinhua news agency.
The recent Beijing race faced such fierce demand that the organisers added an extra day, turning it into a four-day event to make space for even more competitors.
Additional reporting by Laura Bicker in Beijing.

It’s All Fun and Games Until You Give AI Your Credit Card
AI personal assistants are now acting on people’s behalf in the real world—and all sorts of strange things are going wrong.
In the race to develop intelligent machines, the leading AI companies have built bots that can whip up spreadsheets at a moment’s notice, write sophisticated code, and even solve long-standing math problems. But when it comes to the more mundane tasks of life—such as ordering groceries or booking flights—these tools sometimes still struggle. Now a new bot called Instinct is outperforming the AI giants.
Instinct lets people ask for help with all kinds of tasks by texting the bot directly through iMessage or WhatsApp. Lately, it has been all the rage in the tech world. Online, people are breathlessly sharing examples of what they’ve gotten the tool to do. One person reported that he has turned to Instinct to pay tolls, book a DMV appointment, and even negotiate prices with vendors in India while he sleeps. Another says he used Instinct to ship an Apple Pencil he had left behind at a hotel in Montreal back to him in Brooklyn. Noah Shinn, a 23-year-old Northeastern University dropout, launched the product to a small test group earlier this year, and his company is already worth billions of dollars. As of Thursday, the company is reportedly seeking $1 billion in new funds, which could make it worth the equivalent of Lufthansa or Pinterest.
Instinct isn’t the first AI personal assistant to draw attention this year. In the winter, the tech industry fawned over a similar tool called OpenClaw. But Instinct is comparatively much easier to use. Once you create an account, the bot can hook up to your credit cards and all kinds of digital services, including Slack, Google Workspace, and 1Password. Instead of finding a dinner recipe and opening up Instacart to manually add groceries, tell Instinct that you feel like making quiche Lorraine, and it can order groceries for you. But once AI tools start acting on people’s behalf in the real world, mistakes don’t just look like hallucinations. When AI agents have access to your email inbox and credit-card information, all sorts of strange things can go wrong.
I downloaded the tool this week to test it out for myself. Using the bot feels a lot like texting an actual person. It uses emojis such as 🫡 and 👀to react to requests as it receives them, and the infamous three dots appear when it’s writing a response. Sometimes, the bot even leaves you on read while it works. (Compare that with ChatGPT, which is always vomiting up walls of text and asking goading follow-up questions.) When I gave my agent a $25 budget and asked it to surprise my editor with a book, the bot read his previous writing (at my instruction), found a book he might enjoy—Material World by Ed Conway—and sent an email alerting him that it was ready for pick-up at his local Barnes & Noble. (Mercifully, Instinct didn’t hack his inbox to see whether he had previously ordered the book; these days, you never know.) The bot also helped me find an Airbnb for an upcoming vacation, track down new in-network primary-care providers, and reach out to cleaning companies to get quotes for a friend.
Other people are outsourcing even more tasks to Instinct. A colleague of mine who has also been testing out the bot used it to book tickets to a museum in Mexico City. The museum was sold out for the dates he wanted, but the bot dutifully monitored the portal for three days and eventually snagged tickets when spots freed up. After the bot paid for the tickets, it rearranged his itinerary—swapping around restaurant reservations—to account for the new schedule.
For the time being, Instinct is still available only to a private test group, and perhaps this is for the best. Although the bot is plenty powerful, it’s far from perfect. Online, the mishaps are starting to pile up. One user recently complained on X that Instinct lost him more than $200 after it prematurely cancelled his flight. He reported that the bot texted him the following: “Straight story: while pulling up the cancel terms, the cancellation actually went through before I could show you the cost first.” When a man in Los Angeles asked Instinct to scan for restaurant reservations for an upcoming trip, the bot apparently made a reservation without his approval at a place that charged a $200 cancellation fee. Another user temporarily lost access to his Resy account after trying to get a reservation at a hot West Village steak house—without his knowledge, the bot had been spamming the platform with requests. (Shinn, the Instinct founder, did not respond to a request for comment.)
Consider, too, the major risks that come with giving an AI agent broad access to your digital life. Ask the bot to respond to a scheduling text from a friend and it could accidentally leak private information: I can’t get lunch on Thursday morning because we have an appointment with our divorce lawyer. But how about dinner? Hackers could also trick the bot by telling it to ignore previous instructions and forward along any sensitive financial emails. “Despite our reasonable efforts to protect your information, no security measures are impenetrable, and we cannot guarantee ‘perfect security,’” reads Instinct’s privacy policy. While testing Instinct, I used a temporary phone number and did not connect the bot to my email or other important personal accounts; even the credit-card information I gave the bot was for a new, virtual credit-card that I disabled immediately after I was finished experimenting—at which point, I promptly deleted my account.
For all of its hazards, Instinct is a harbinger of where AI is headed. Earlier this week, Meta released its own personal-assistant product called Muse. In announcing Muse, Mark Zuckerberg emphasized the company’s security protections; how well those safeguards actually hold up remains to be seen. Google, OpenAI, and Anthropic may well follow suit by refining their own bots to have more Instinct-like capabilities. After all, the tech industry has long dreamed of a moment when a computer can serve as a genuinely competent personal assistant. Even if such bots aren’t quite ready for prime time, early adopters hint at how the technology might shape the world in the years to come. Contrary to the narrative of AI wiping out jobs, these new assistants could end up creating more work—in ways that are not always appealing. In one of the wildest Instinct examples that I encountered, Olivia Levine, an investor in New York, recounted using Instinct to track down footage of her and her boyfriend on the jumbotron at the US Open. As Levine tells it, the couple gave the bot a selfie and their seat numbers. The agent then put out a flurry of requests to the United States Tennis Association, the ticket office, the US Open’s production company, and an American Express media contact. By the following afternoon, a producer had emailed her the footage.
A world full of agents seems at once busier and lonelier. On Wednesday, Instinct added a new way for agents to coordinate between themselves. As Shinn explained on X, if you’re planning a weekend trip with friends or making plans with your spouse, you could just have your agents work together to figure out the logistics instead.
At least for now, the bots haven’t conquered everything. When I asked it for help finding a new desk chair, Instinct quickly tracked down a great option nearby on Craigslist and drafted a pick-up request to send to the lister. But when it came time to actually send the message, the bot was stymied by a CAPTCHA. I asked the agent to try harder, but it was stuck. “Nothing punctures the fantasy of autonomous intelligence like being defeated by nine blurry crosswalks,” the bot messaged me.

The interview Trump doesn’t want you to see
Why ABC won’t air an interview with a Democratic Senate candidate.
Welcome to The Logoff: President Donald Trump’s FCC wants to keep a Democratic Senate candidate off the air.
What’s happening? On Wednesday, late-night host Jimmy Kimmel announced that his upcoming interview with James Talarico, the Democratic nominee for Senate in Texas, would not air on TV. Instead, he said, “due to circumstances beyond our comprehension,” it would be posted only on YouTube.
According to Kimmel, Trump’s Federal Communications Commission “has threatened me, threatened our show, threatened our network, ABC, our affiliates, our local stations, based on simple, traditional editorial decisions — guest bookings it would seem they don’t like.”
Can Trump do that? It’s unclear — but he can at least make it painful enough for companies that they decide it’s not worth the headache. Kimmel said on Wednesday that his show’s decision was made “out of consideration for our local stations…who would have to deal with this nonsense” if they aired the interview.
Late-night shows like Kimmel’s Jimmy Kimmel Live! have long been considered exempt from something called the equal-time rule, which requires broadcasters to give equal air time for candidates contending for the same office.
In January, however, the Trump administration said that late-night shows needed to comply with the rule; the next month, CBS declined to air an interview with Talarico on its late-night show, The Late Show with Stephen Colbert. (That interview was also posted to YouTube, where it’s since garnered about 9.5 million views.)
What’s the context? This is not Kimmel’s first brush with Trump or the FCC. He was briefly suspended around this time last year after threats from Trump’s FCC chair, and Trump tried again to get him fired earlier this year, with less success.
Last month, ABC and its parent company, Disney, sued the FCC over its attempt to force a review of ABC’s broadcast licenses.
What’s the big picture? This kind of attack on the media is a familiar tactic from competitive authoritarian systems like Hungary, as my colleague Zack Beauchamp explained last year. Trump’s efforts to do the same in the US have often been clumsy or unsuccessful — but in this case, it seems to be working.
And with that, it’s time to log off…

More than 20 children killed in DR Congo school fire
- Published
At least 24 schoolchildren have died in a stampede as they tried to flee a fire that engulfed two schools in rebel-held Bukavu in the eastern Democratic Republic of Congo, officials there have said.
Adults are also reported to have died in the fire and there are fears that the death toll could rise further in the densely populated Kadutu commune.
Survivors have been taken to nearby hospitals, and footage of the scene shows children lying on hospital floors in pain.
Some 300 houses have also been destroyed in the fire, the cause of which is unknown.
Rebel‑appointed authorities released a provisional death toll of 24 on Thursday evening, confirming previous reports, but there are fears that more people may have died.
Pictures circulating on social media show young children lying motionless on the ground.
A witness quoted by Reuters news agency said the fire had been put out by afternoon but smoke was still rising from rubble and corrugated metal.
Bukavu, the capital of South Kivu province and one of DR Congo's most crowded hillside cities, was captured by M23 rebels in February last year.
Meanwhile the government in Kinshasa released a statement on X, without specifying numbers of casualties.
"The Ministry of National Education and New Citizenship expressed deep sorrow over the deadly fire," it said.
"With several lives lost and many injured, the toll remains provisional. The minister offered condolences, affirmed solidarity with families, and ordered assessments of affected schools to ensure learning continuity."
The tragedy follows a similar fire in Kinshasa last weekend, where residents died in a stampede at a wedding banquet hall.
In response, the government has ordered strict safety measures and deployed teams nationwide to enforce standards at public gathering places.

Experts say there is no universal clock time that works for everyone. What matters more is when dinner falls in relation to the body’s biological clock and bedtime. An earlier dinner may be beneficial, but there is no fixed 7 p.m. or 8 p.m. cut-off. The gap between dinner and sleep, the quality and composition of the meal, physical activity and individual health needs all play a role.
Insulin sensitivity and glucose tolerance generally decrease as the day progresses, so the body may not handle a heavy meal as well later in the day. However, dinner timing is only one part of the picture. The amount and quality of food, physical activity, sleep and health conditions such as diabetes and gastro-oesophageal reflux disease (GERD) also affect how the body responds to a meal.
The gap before sleep
“There is no evidence-based ideal dinner time,” said Aafrin Shabbir, medical director, senior consultant and diabetologist, Tambaram Medical Centre and CODE Clinic. The body’s metabolic efficiency is generally better during the daytime, she said, making a smaller and lighter dinner preferable.
She also cautioned against assuming that eating at 10 p.m. is unhealthy for everyone. Someone who sleeps at 1 a.m. has a different biological rhythm from someone who sleeps at 10 p.m. “One rule doesn’t fit all,” she said.
Saravana Bharathy S. P., internal medicine, Dr Mehta’s Hospitals, recommends leaving about two to three hours between dinner and bedtime. This is particularly relevant for people with reflux or digestive discomfort, as lying down soon after a meal can worsen symptoms.
Swathi Padmanaban, consultant, paediatric & adolescent endocrinologist and diabetologist, Rainbow Children’s Hospital, Chennai, said eating dinner earlier is generally better for metabolic health when practical. She advised against making dinner the largest meal of the day, particularly when it is eaten close to bedtime.
Meal timing is linked to the body’s circadian rhythm. The liver, pancreas and gastrointestinal tract have their own biological clocks that work with the brain’s central body clock. As the biological day progresses, insulin sensitivity and glucose tolerance tend to fall, meaning the same meal may cause a greater rise in blood glucose when eaten later.
Late eating
Studies have found that eating dinner at 10 p.m., compared with 6 p.m., led to higher overnight blood glucose and changes in fat metabolism, despite the meals having the same calories and nutrients.
“Late eating may have greater metabolic implications for people living with diabetes, prediabetes and obesity. A carbohydrate-rich meal late at night can cause a larger rise in blood glucose, particularly when physical activity is low,” Dr. Swathi said.
Late, heavy meals can also cause bloating, indigestion and acid reflux and may affect sleep. However, an occasional late dinner is unlikely to carry the same significance as a regular pattern of late-night eating.
Eating after a particular hour does not, by itself, cause obesity or heart disease. Overall calorie intake, food quality, physical activity, sedentary behaviour and sleep also play major roles. “People who regularly eat late may also snack more, sleep less or have irregular work schedules. This makes it difficult to separate the effect of dinner timing from other lifestyle factors,” Dr. Bharathy said.
Healthier dinner timing
For children and adolescents, the focus should be on regular meals, adequate nutrition, appropriate portions, physical activity and good sleep rather than restrictive eating windows.
If a late dinner is unavoidable, a moderate and balanced meal is preferable. Vegetables, protein and fibre can be included, while sugary drinks, sweets and fried or fatty foods should be limited. It is also better to avoid coming home extremely hungry and eating a large, carbohydrate-heavy meal just before bed. If possible, part of the meal can be eaten earlier and the later meal kept smaller. A short walk after dinner may also help with post-meal blood glucose control.
For people living with diabetes, meal timing should be planned around their medication, insulin requirements, blood glucose levels and HbA1c rather than a fixed cut-off.
The practical approach is to eat earlier when possible, leave about two to three hours between dinner and bedtime, keep late meals light and balanced, and maintain regular eating and sleep schedules.
