McInnes delivers togetherness & intensity in Old Firm gobsmacker
- Published
Fifty-five minutes into this Rangers romp at Ibrox, Martin O'Neill and Shaun Maloney stood beside each other in the Celtic technical area, chin-stroking, head-scratching, pointing, waving, drowning.
To them, in this moment, this Premier Sports Cup quarter-final must have felt like a surreal and nightmarish occasion - and it was only 1-0 at the time. Rangers had really only started to wreak their havoc.
Such was Rangers' dominance, their complete owning of their visitors in every conceivable category, the Celtic managerial brains trust seemed just as lost as every one of their players on the field.
Man for man, Rangers won every battle, not for 45 minutes but for the full ninety.
Simplicity of progression was surreal
No away fans, of course. Not that that had anything to do with it. Being locked out of Ibrox might have seemed like a curse to Celtic folk. In the end, it must have felt like the greatest blessing.
In his early months in the job, Derek McInnes has been looking for a marquee performance. Now he has it. He was looking for a formation that worked and personnel that were big enough and bold enough to execute it and he got that, too. This was 3-0 going on more. Plenty more.
The simplicity of their progression to the semi-final was a touch surreal. Neither of these were in particularly good form coming into this. They were both winning, yes, but they haven't been all that convincing.
This season, in their last eight domestic features combined - all won, in fairness - there was only a goal in it at the end in seven of them. Both sides had got themselves into a cycle of missed chances and, at times, uncomfortable days.
So the smart money was on a tight contest. Extra-time, maybe. Penalties? You wouldn't have ruled that out either. O'Neill is such a winning machine that many would have expected Celtic to find a way, somehow. So much for that.
Few Old Firm games surprise you anymore, but this one was a gobsmacker.
Rangers had all the intensity and all the togetherness. They had six players making their Old Firm debut from the start but if inexperience can be a challenge in this fixture then it was a challenge they met with gusto.
McInnes and his driven and vastly superior players neutralised Celtic, shut them down, rendered them impotent. Celtic captain Callum McGregor lords it over days like this, but the supreme central midfielder was Dan Neil, not just in his outstanding goals but in the control and the leadership he exerted.
With Nico Raskin beside him it was a no-contest in the middle of the pitch. James Penrice did a power of really good work in there, too.
Camilo Duran, playing wide again instead of through the middle, has been one of the players of the season so far, but he hardly existed, totally bossed by Olwethu Makhanya - calm in the maelstrom, classy in nearly everything he did.
Kasper Hogh needed a goal having scored in just one game in six - a hat-trick, albeit - but the record signing spent much of his day in Emmanuel Fernandez's pocket. He had no service and no sniff.
McInnes might have hit on something substantial
Where did this come from? Lord knows, but it makes life very interesting now, not just in the destination of the League Cup - Rangers will be massive favourites against Aberdeen in their semi-final - but in the race for the league title.
McInnes might have hit on something substantial. The big task, of course, is to repeat that energy, that belief, that ruthlessness.
You expected Celtic to stir and make a game of it, but they were never allowed to, in part because of their own awful shortcomings with the ball and in other part because Rangers didn't allow them to settle. They hunted them down, right from the opening minutes.
A mood, of sorts, was set as early as the fourth minute when Sam Johnstone, Celtic's jumpy new goalkeeper, passed a clearance straight to Kevin Kelsy, who slashed it wide.
Johnstone had been harried by Rangers' press, a big theme of the day. For Kelsy, it was a great chance to strike early, but if he failed then he made amends later on.
Kelsy is only in the door, but he looks to have personality and desire. He was playing with Ryan Naderi, an oft-criticised striker, a player you hear constantly is not Rangers class. Naderi was one of the totems of the day, a work rate that never stopped, a constant menace in hunting and gathering. Naderi might have changed a few Rangers minds on Sunday.
The opener was a microcosm; Naderi robbing Cameron Carter-Vickers, Kelsy then picking out Neil for a sumptuous finish. Rangers were physically and creatively on top, but there's always a feeling that one goal needed to become two to halt Celtic's assumed purple patch, a response that never came.
That was the bizarre thing. Total authority for an entire game is a rare enough thing in this contest. Usually there's a spell when the team that's ahead has to weather some kind of storm. Celtic couldn't throw a bucket of water in Rangers' direction not to mind a tempest. When McInnes' side made it two it was only what they deserved.
Penrice put in the cross, Naderi flicked it on and Kelsy banged in the volley. Neil's second and Rangers' third was a peach, a sign of confident uninhibited players enjoying themselves. The smallest of mercies for Celtic was that it stayed at three.
The second part of this drama comes on Sunday, a league game that could not have been better set up had Eddie Hearn been involved in the promotion. Rangers looking to lay down another marker going to Celtic's home, full of 60,000 folk baying for revenge. Given some of the vile songs that were directed at O'Neill at Ibrox then McInnes is in for some treatment. Sadly, he's heard it all over before, as has O'Neill.
McInnes was measured in the aftermath, more low-key than you might have expected and there was sense in that. This was one game and he knew it. They won nothing on the back of it and he knew that, too.
Apart from, that is, precious momentum and self-belief and the knowledge of what their standard can be when they get it right. And on Sunday, they got it spectacularly right.

On 26 August 2026, massive flash floods struck parts of Nepal and Tibet, causing widespread destruction (here, here, and here). In this context, a video is being shared on social media (here, here, and here) claiming it shows a mother and her daughter being swept away in the Nepal floods. Let’s verify the truth behind the video in this article.
Claim: The video shows a mother and her daughter being swept away in the 2026 Nepal floods.
Fact: The video does not show a mother and daughter being swept away in the 2026 Nepal floods. It shows two sisters being swept away by floodwaters in the Philippines in September 2025 before they were rescued by residents. Hence, the claim made in the post is Misleading.
A reverse image search of keyframes from the viral video led us to several media reports published in September 2025 (here, here, and here) featuring the same visuals. According to these reports, the incident occurred on 4 September 2025 in Barangay Balogo, Guihulngan City, Negros Oriental, Philippines, where two sisters were swept away by a strong current while returning home from school. They clung to tree roots and were later rescued by local residents.
To sum up, an old video of sisters trapped in a flash flood in the Philippines is shared as footage from the 2026 Nepal floods.

August was the planet’s hottest month ever recorded, capping a remarkably grim summer of heat records. With El Niño strengthening—and climate change continuing to heat things up—more records are likely in store well into next year.
Data from Copernicus, the European Union’s climate agency, shows that last month tied with July 2023 for Earth’s hottest month. (July is also usually the hottest month of the year.) This July also tied with July 2024 for the second-hottest July on record, while June 2026 was the second-hottest June ever recorded. The news comes on the heels of a separate announcement on Wednesday from the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration, which declared this was the hottest summer for the US, beating a previous record set during the Dust Bowl.
The sweltering summer is a grim sign of how burning fossil fuels is pushing temperatures up around the globe while unleashing more intense and longer heat waves.
“August 2026 was a remarkable month in the global climate record,” Samantha Burgess, the strategic lead for climate at the European Center for Medium-Range Weather Forecasts, said in a statement. “Combined with record global sea surface temperatures and the warmest summer on record for Western Europe, these observations show how climate change is driving extremes across both the atmosphere and the oceans. The impacts of these conditions are increasingly being felt by communities, economies, and ecosystems across the world.”
The global average temperature for August was 1.65 degrees Celsius (3 degrees Fahrenheit) above the preindustrial average, according to Copernicus. While it was hot globally this summer, the impacts played out with dangerous and sometimes deadly results locally.
Researchers estimate that as many as 35,000 people died during heat waves in Germany, France, and Spain this summer. Record-breaking fires also raged across parts of Europe, unleashing the first documented fire cloud in France and threatening a key NASA observatory in Spain. In North America, wildfires in Canada and northern parts of the US filled areas across the Northeast with smoke.
Climate change has boosted background temperatures, but the El Niño roiling the eastern Pacific Ocean has piled on more heat. El Niños usually coincide with a temporary uptick in global temperature from 0.1 to 0.2 degrees Celsius. This year’s El Niño is forecast to reach record strength and upend weather around the globe. But the full impact on the planet’s temperature won’t be felt until next year, meaning that next summer may be even hotter than the one we just lived through.
Climate scientists have warned that the world needs to prevent long-term average warming from breaching 1.5 degrees Celsius to avoid the worst impacts of climate change. While temperatures above the threshold for a single month don’t represent a permanent breach of this temperature, they’re a sign that the world is getting closer to this benchmark.
Earlier this month, the UN warned in a report that the world is likely to cross the 1.5 degrees Celsius threshold in a few years. To slow and eventually reverse the rise in global temperatures, the world needs to stop burning fossil fuels and lower carbon emissions.
“This summer’s scorching heat, raging wildfires, and deadly floods are a warning of what lies ahead,” UN Secretary-General Antőnio Guterres said in a statement. “We must make the overshoot above 1.5 degrees as small and short as possible. That demands an overshoot of ambition.”

More dropped points at Anfield - is it too early for Liverpool to worry?
- Published
Two Premier League matches at Anfield. Two draws.
For just the third time in 63 years, Liverpool have failed to win either of their opening home games of a league season - not exactly the flying start new boss Andoni Iraola would have been dreaming of.
After such an encouraging midweek performance against Atletico Madrid in the Champions League, full of urgency, Saturday's goalless draw against Fulham was a flat follow-up, especially with the Cottagers lacking in confidence and having conceded seven goals in their first three league games.
The Reds looked physically and mentally tired and, to put it bluntly, like an entirely different team to the one that won against a Diego Simeone side that made it to the Champions League semi-finals last season.
On the first real look at how Iraola's style will cope with two games a week, this was certainly not what the Liverpool head coach, nor the Anfield crowd, would have wanted to see.
Former boss Jurgen Klopp would often speak about recognising his team based on their identity and intensity rather than just their colours and judging by Iraola's words since he took over, the Spaniard wants the same too.
Iraola said: "What was lacking was quite clear, it is the first game we had problems to create chances and score goals and make the difference offensively, and that is the main reason we couldn't create chances."
His side are still unbeaten and it is hardly a crisis, but he will look at a return of six points from their first four Premier League games as disappointing, particularly by dropping four points at home to Nottingham Forest and Fulham, with another draw coming at Newcastle and their sole success at Ipswich.
Keeper Alisson told Sky Sports: "We are not happy at all with the draw. It is not something that should happen with Liverpool. To be unbeaten, but with three draws, is not something to celebrate too much with this shirt.
"If we want to do something special [this season] we have to cope with playing a game Wednesday, Saturday and then Tuesday.
"We need to have the right mental state and that was not the case from what we showed. Inside we have it, but we have to just put it out and put more energy on the pitch."
The £364m attacking trio of Alexander Isak, Bradley Barcola and Florian Wirtz started together for the first time in a league game and although Liverpool had decent chances, they created nowhere near enough.
Isak's 16 touches in 90 minutes was the second fewest for an outfield Reds player on record, having had the fewest (14) against Forest a fortnight ago.
German Wirtz looked a shadow of the player who was terrific in midweek against Atleti and while Barcola and Isak had a few encouraging moments, that is a partnership that will take time to develop.
"Bradley is one we are building up physically with games and the games will give him the condition we want," Iraola told Match of the Day.
"But it is not just Bradley, we lack the freshness. I only remember one clear chance [for Fulham] and we kept the structure but offensively we need to do much better."
'There is a lack of freshness - we cannot hide it'
Before the game against Atletico Madrid, Iraola was asked about how he sought to strike the right balance, with the intensity levels he craves and such a busy schedule.
His response was he didn't want his players to save energy because they had another game in three days.
"You play 55 minutes for me and you are dead and ask for a sub, then perfect," said Iraola. "We have a top-level 55 minutes and then a top-level 35 minutes."
By the hour mark against Fulham, all three of Iraola's changes to the starting line-up were replaced, with left-back Kostas Tsimikas taken off at half-time and Ryan Gravenberch and Victor Munoz replaced after 60 minutes.
Despite sending on Milos Kerkez, Cody Gakpo, Alexis Mac Allister, Rio Ngumoha and Jeremie Frimpong, Liverpool showed little improvement.
Iraola admitted: "The players were tired and there is a lack of freshness - we cannot hide it. This is the worst turnaround in terms of 60 or 70 hours [since the last game], but this is going to happen in the season and we have to adapt and it is these kind of games that you need to win sometimes with a set-play or a moment of brilliance."
It is still early, but already there is a realisation from Iraola and his players that when they have such short turnarounds between games, perhaps it is a case of adapting and finding ways to get a result.
With at least seven more Champions League games to follow and a Carabao Cup tie at home to Tottenham on Tuesday, Liverpool must adapt sooner rather than later as the fixture list cranks up if they are to show they can challenge for honours this season.

Six Nigerian nationals linked to an organized criminal network that allegedly swindled American women out of more than $6m through online romance scams were extradited to the United States on Friday.
South African police confirmed they were to be extradited earlier on Friday, while local news in Africa confirmed that the Directorate for Priority Crime Investigation, known as the Hawks, facilitated their handover to officials from the US Federal Bureau of Investigation and Secret Service at Cape Town international airport, in collaboration with Interpol South Africa.
The men, who were arrested in the South African city of Cape Town in 2021, face wire fraud and money laundering charges.
They are accused of belonging to a criminal network known as the Black Axe, which Interpol describes as being among criminal groups responsible for a significant share of the world’s cyber-enabled financial fraud, typically through romance, cryptocurrency and investment scams.
According to South African police, the men are alleged to have targeted more than 100 women in the US, defrauding them of more than $6m through online romance or love scams.
Among the alleged victims were pensioners and businesspeople who were reportedly targeted through sophisticated online relationships.
“Through the coordination of Interpol South Africa, the six will today be transported from a correctional facility in Cape Town to Cape Town international airport, where they will be handed over to officials from the FBI and the United States Secret Service, who arrived in South Africa this morning,” said police spokesperson Katlego Mogale.
A recent operation by Interpol targeting west African organized crime groups led to the arrest of 58 people and the identification of 263 suspects linked to various criminal networks involved in similar crimes, the multinational police body said last month.
The operation aimed to disrupt money laundering, identify high-value targets, seize assets, and support arrests and prosecution.
In South Africa, authorities raided seven locations in the city of Johannesburg linked to a syndicate that ran romance and investment scams targeting retirees in English-speaking countries.
In that operation in South Africa, police arrested 39 people, seized $2.67m and froze more than 250 bank accounts, Interpol said.

Seeking cash for AI, China’s Z.ai eyes new US$5b fundraising push after July share sale
The Chinese AI developer is courting more backers as it scales its models and infrastructure amid intensifying competition
Z.ai, the Chinese artificial intelligence model developer listed in Hong Kong, is seeking to raise about HK$15.7 billion (US$2 billion) through a placement of roughly 21.97 million new H shares at HK$714 apiece, according to a company filing on Sunday.
The company also announced a 20.14 billion yuan (US$3 billion) convertible-bond sale, according to its filing with the Hong Kong stock exchange.
The fundraising moves, which could help the company raise around US$5 billion, come as the company’s 60-day lock-up period following its July placement expires. The July placement raised HK$31.4 billion from the sale of 19.78 million shares at HK$1,588 each, shortly after a six-month lock-up on 25.68 million initial public offering shares held by cornerstone investors expired.
The company is also pursuing a listing on Shanghai’s Star Market. The firm has completed regulatory tutoring and secured shareholder approval for an offering targeting up to 15 billion yuan, though no application has been publicly accepted yet.
Z.ai’s repeated tapping of capital markets underscores the heavy costs of developing frontier AI models.

This as-told-to essay is based on a conversation with Braydon Barrett, 32, who moved to Asia with his family in 2024 but moved back to Utah eight months later. It's been edited for length and clarity.
Living abroad was never really on my radar until I got married.
My wife had always wanted to travel and live outside the US, and as I looked into it more, it started to feel like an experience we should try together.
We talked about it for years, but never followed through. Then, after our son was born in 2023, we felt it was the right time to finally give it a try. My wife is a stay-at-home mom, and since I run an online fitness coaching business, I could work remotely.
I spent a long time researching where we could go, and Thailand seemed the most feasible in terms of visa options.
We did a 10-day scouting trip to Thailand to figure out where we wanted to live, and to get a sense of what life there was actually like. In the end, we decided to settle in Pattaya, about a two-hour drive from Bangkok.
Back in Utah, we didn't own any property, so it was easy for us to move. We got rid of most of our belongings, kept some in a storage unit, and packed the rest into six suitcases.
On the day our son turned one in April 2024, we said our goodbyes and hopped on the plane.
Our plans unraveled at the airport
When we arrived in Thailand, I realized I'd made a major mistake with our visas. I had thought we would have 90 days in Thailand to sort out a longer-term option, but we only had 30 days.
We had planned to stay in Thailand indefinitely, so suddenly having to figure out where to go next was overwhelming.
We spent the next few weeks trying to see if we could make a longer-term visa situation work. When that wasn't possible, we decided to go to Malaysia, where we could stay for three months.
Near the end of our time in Malaysia, Thailand introduced the Destination Thailand Visa, a five-year visa for remote workers and digital nomads.
Applicants must be outside Thailand while awaiting approval, so when our time in Malaysia ran out, we moved on to Vietnam. From there, we applied for the Destination Thailand Visa.
My wife and I were approved almost immediately, but our son's application took longer. When our three-month stay in Vietnam came to an end, we had to leave.
On our way to the airport for our flight to Manila, Philippines, we finally received the notification that our son's visa had been approved. We had what we needed to return to Thailand.
When we arrived in Manila, it was late at night. Our son was upset and fussy, and we ran into an issue checking into our hotel because they couldn't find our reservation. Spending two hours trying to sort it out with security was the final straw.
By then, we'd had enough. We could have returned to Thailand, but I felt I couldn't do it anymore and needed a break.
Eight months after we left Utah, we came back home.
Visa issues weren't our only challenge
I thought it would be easier to manage my company from the other side of the world, but all of my clients and employees were based in the US.
Sometimes I was getting up at 3 a.m. to work, and other times I was taking calls at midnight.
When we came back to Utah, our families were happy to have us home. Coming back was bittersweet — I couldn't help feeling like I'd failed.
However, those eight months brought my wife and me so much closer together. We were in some stressful situations, but she remained calm and trusted me to take responsibility. It gave me a greater love and respect for her.
We still love Asia
Coming home didn't change how we felt about our time in Asia.
I loved the people, the culture, and the weather. America can feel high-stress and chaotic, but in Asia, people are more relaxed and courteous.
What stood out most was how people treated our son. Everyone was so kind and friendly to him.
Living abroad is a lot different from what social-media influencers make it out to be. There were a lot of great things about it, but people should not go in thinking the grass is greener on the other side.
Had we had everything figured out, we would still be in Thailand today. We genuinely loved it. It was my mistake that caused us to come home.
Even so, the possibility of our returning to Thailand remains. Our visas are valid for five years, and we would love to make it happen.

Are Apple's wired EarPods still worth buying?
Apple still sells its classic wired earbuds for a reason.
AirPods turn 10 this year, and they're everywhere now. They've also evolved over time; modern AirPods pack in noise cancellation, health sensors and even built-in live translation. If people ever had doubts about wireless earbuds, that's largely a concern of the past — though maybe not completely.
As it turns out, there's a niche group of people who still buy wired earbuds, like EarPods. Remember Apple's wired earbuds that used to come in the box with an iPhone? While using them now might seem like nothing more than nostalgia, there are a few reasons to prefer EarPods over AirPods.
What's different between AirPods and EarPods?
Comparing AirPods and EarPods isn't as simple as "wired versus wireless." AirPods are packed with modern features that make them go far beyond a simple pipe for transmitting audio. Take the AirPods Pro 3, for example, which can track your heart rate during a workout. There's also Spatial Audio and all the specs that make them sound great. In comparison, EarPods are just regular earbuds. They lack fancy gestures or voice commands.
Yet they can be better than AirPods in some ways. EarPods require zero maintenance. No battery means no charging, so they're ready whenever you are. Compare that to leaving your AirPods sitting off the charger for a few days and being greeted by a red battery icon. Having a cord also means zero pairing issues stemming from Bluetooth. There's no need to worry about re-pairing if you want to share your earbuds with a friend either.
The built-in EarPods microphone also delivers better voice quality. While Apple has done a good job of improving this aspect of AirPods, Bluetooth audio still doesn't sound as good as wired audio. They even come in three connection types: 3.5mm, Lightning and USB-C. That makes EarPods compatible with a wide range of gadgets, and they're cheap enough that you could buy separate pairs for different devices.
Due to the lack of a headphone jack on modern iPhones, though, using the Lightning or USB-C port for EarPods means you can't charge your phone while using your earbuds. If this poses a major issue for you, an adapter that splits the port into two is an easy fix, though it's not as convenient to carry around and have attached to your phone.
AirPods are better, but there's still room for EarPods
There's no denying that AirPods are better in many ways. Apple's wired earphones won't give you noise cancellation, which by itself is a compelling reason to choose AirPods. But sometimes you might prefer simplicity over high-end tech. Maybe you don't want to worry about recharging your earbuds, or perhaps yours always tend to die during an important meeting. Moments like this make it sensible to keep some wired earbuds around.
Then there's the price. The cheapest AirPods you can buy today cost $129, and they aren't even the best ones. For $19, EarPods are unbeatable. They aren't designed to be the best, but they cost a fraction of Apple's wireless earbuds. Maybe you'd rather spend $19 on EarPods than $69+ to replace your lost AirPod every six months. Or you can buy both and always have what the situation calls for.

Dominant Kerr wins $150K with GB's first Ultimate title
- Published
Josh Kerr ended a sensational season by being crowned Britain's first winner at the Ultimate Championship with a dominant 1500m victory - and earning $150,000 - as the inaugural edition of athletics' new global event concluded in Budapest.
Kerr smashed the 27-year mile world record at the London Diamond League and won Commonwealth Games gold in Glasgow this summer, after beginning an outstanding year by reclaiming the world indoor 3,000m title.
In the shape of his life, Kerr swept past American Yared Nuguse on the back straight in Hungary and would not be denied once he had made his move to the front, taking victory in three minutes 29.35 seconds.
"I am a major championship guy and I will always be that," Kerr, 28, told BBC Sport.
"From seven weeks ago in London, I went home, I chopped wood and carried water and I was ready to go again.
"Sometimes you have to come out of it to dig deeper inside and go further in life. Two weeks before [a race] I try to do something to get me out my routine and then I push myself for the last couple of weeks.
"I had a great build and, if I didn't finish with a win, then that was on me."
The 2023 world champion did not qualify by right for the Ultimate Championship, which is reserved for reigning global champions, Diamond League winners and others based on world ranking.
He was instead awarded an exceptional invitation by World Athletics, alongside rival Jakob Ingebrigtsen - although the pair's eagerly anticipated reunion did not transpire after the Norwegian withdrew following his 5,000m win on Friday.
Kerr was peerless as he seized the opportunity to put on one final show this season - and take his share of the biggest prize pot in the sport's history.
Over the past three nights, the world's top athletes competed for a new title and a total prize fund of $10m (£7.4m) at the innovative event, which World Athletics president Lord Coe hopes can play a key role in shaping the sport's future.
Kerr ignoring 'stick' in pursuit of major titles
Speaking after his victory, Kerr referenced the "stick" he receives for not competing as much as others.
But he is in no doubt that it is because of that approach that he is able to seize the career-defining moments when they arrive.
In response to criticism from Ingebrigtsen over his decision to skip the European Championships in Birmingham, Kerr said he "was not a robot" and would continue to approach each season by targeting only a few competitions to avoid injury and maintain consistent high levels of performance.
While the Ultimate Championship was not one of those dates at the beginning of the year, it was no surprise that World Athletics made sure he could be present - nor that Kerr took the sport's governing body up on the offer.
Kerr is, after all, blockbuster. He underlined his position as one of the sport's biggest draws when he boldly announced his record-breaking intentions months in advance before delivering his historic mile performance in front of 60,000 British fans in July.
There were also no mistakes in Scotland, despite the pressure which came with his role as headline act in front of an expectant home crowd.
It is just 12 months since Kerr's world title defence was ended by a calf tear in Tokyo.
But, having recovered to reach career-best fitness, the next three years now provide him with the opportunity to cement himself among the all-time greats.
With two World Championships - the second potentially in London - either side of the next Olympic Games, Kerr will continue to ignore the outside noise and follow his established winning formula.
"Obviously I get a lot of stick for not racing so much," Kerr said. "But it allows me to come here fresh and ready to go."
'Special' weekend for aspirational Hunt
Amy Hunt produced a season's best time in the women's 200m final to end her championship on a positive note following disappointment in the 100m.
The 24-year-old, winner of four European golds last month, said she did not feel she had done herself "proud" after placing eighth in the 100m final on Saturday.
But Hunt improved to fourth in the 200m, in a time of 22.10 seconds, as American Melissa Jefferson-Wooden became the third-fastest woman in history in completing her sprint double.
"Yesterday was bad but I came back today and used it as fuel and motivation," Hunt told BBC Sport.
"It was incredible to be part of an incredible race. This is what women in sport looks like; muscles, blood, sweat, tears.
"It has been really special to prove myself against the best in the world. It was the first time I have won a world semi-final. It is a massive confidence boost."
After running the joint-seventh fastest 100m by a woman in history just 24 hours earlier, world champion Jefferson-Wooden, 25, produced the fourth-fastest women's 200m time ever recorded with 21.47secs in the final event of the weekend.
"I did not see 21.47 coming tonight!" Jefferson-Wooden said. "I was thinking I could run this fast in maybe two years, but not tonight. I really have no words. This result is a good inspiration for the upcoming years."
Earlier, GB's mixed 4x400m relay quartet finished second to the USA following a superb anchor leg by Charlotte Henrich.

- Click on the UP NEET UG Counselling 2026 Round 2 registration link on the homepage.
- Enter the required registration details.
- Complete the counselling application form.
- Pay the applicable registration fee and security amount.
- Submit the application.
- Download the confirmation page.
- Take a printout of the confirmation page for future reference.
Candidates should ensure that their registration and security deposit are completed within the prescribed deadline.
UP NEET UG Round 2 Choice Filling
Candidates whose registration, security deposit and online document verification have been completed within the prescribed deadline will be eligible to participate in the choice-filling process.
During Round 2, candidates will see seats that remained vacant, were not reported against or were resigned from during Round 1 as “Clear-cut Vacancies.”
The choice-filling window will also include Seat Against Cancellation (SAC) options. These are treated as virtual vacancies. If a seat held by an already admitted candidate is upgraded, the vacated seat may subsequently be allotted to another candidate based on merit and choice preference.
There is no limit on the number of choices a candidate can fill. However, candidates have been advised to select only those colleges and seats where they are genuinely willing to take admission.
Candidates must also lock their choices after filling them. Failure to lock the choices will lead to exclusion from the seat allotment process.
Once choices are locked, they cannot be modified, and the DGME will not entertain requests for changes.
What happens if a candidate gets an upgraded seat?
If a candidate receives a different seat based on their preference for reallocation, their previously allotted seat will automatically become vacant and may be allotted to another candidate.
If there is no reallocation, the candidate will retain their existing seat.
Candidates seeking reallocation should therefore select choices other than the seat they have already secured. If the previously secured seat is allotted again, the candidate will have to report to the nodal centre and complete the admission process again, as applicable.
Round 2 Seat Allotment And Admission Rules
The UP NEET UG Round 2 seat allotment result will be declared on September 21, 2026. Candidates allotted seats can download their allotment letters and complete the admission process between September 22 and September 25.
Admission is mandatory for candidates allotted seats in Round 2.
If a candidate fails to take admission after being allotted a seat in the second round, the entire security deposit will be forfeited. Such candidates will be allowed to participate in the third round only after depositing the security amount again.
The same rule applies to a candidate who was admitted in Round 1 but fails to secure admission after reallocation in Round 2.
Where to report after Round 2 allotment?
The reporting procedure will depend on the type of institution allotted to the candidate.
Candidates allotted seats in government-sector medical or dental colleges, institutes or universities must report directly to the respective institution to complete admission.
Candidates allotted seats in private-sector medical or dental colleges must report to the designated nodal centre for completing the admission process.
Private-sector candidates are also required to deposit a CTS bank draft towards the government-prescribed tuition fee at the designated nodal centre. The draft must be drawn in favour of “Director General Medical Education & Training, U.P. (Payable at Lucknow)”.
Failure to deposit the prescribed fee through the required process will result in cancellation of the admission.
Medical Examination Mandatory
Candidates who are allotted seats must also undergo a medical examination conducted by the medical board constituted at the respective medical or dental college or designated nodal centre.
Candidates should therefore carry the required documents and follow the reporting instructions issued for their allotted institution.
Candidates are advised to rely on the official UP NEET counselling portal and DGME website for subsequent updates, revised schedules and admission instructions.

The American hopes of watching one of their own lift the US Open trophy in men’s singles for the first time since 2003 were dashed once again as Germany’s Alexander Zverev defeated Ben Shelton 6-3, 7-6(2), 5-7, 6-2 in three-and-a-half hours in Sunday’s final.
Six years ago, Zverev had squandered a two-sets-to-love lead in his maiden Major final against Dominic Thiem at Flushing Meadows.
When Shelton, who was playing in a Grand Slam final for the first time, broke Zverev’s serve in the 12th game to clinch the third set in front of home crowd at the Arthur Ashe Stadium, doubts could have crept in but the 29-year-old German stayed focused.
Zverev broke Shelton immediately in the opening game of the fourth set before securing an insurance break in the seventh. This time, there were no hiccups as the top-seeded German served successfully to clinch his maiden US Open title and overall, the second Major of his career. He also won this year’s French Open.
For USA, Andy Roddick’s 2003 triumph in New York still remains the last time an American man won a Grand Slam.

Five baby orangutans have been found in a forest in India, prompting authorities to investigate if they were trafficked into the country from south-east Asia.
The orangutans, native only to the islands of Borneo and Sumatra and known for their shaggy red fur, were found in Balasore district of Odisha state, thousands of kilometres away from their natural habitat.
Odisha’s environment minister, Ram Singh Khuntia, said wildlife investigators were trying to establish how the rare apes reached India.
“We suspect that an international racket might be involved in this,” Singh said.
International commercial trade in orangutans is prohibited under Cites – a global agreement governing trade in endangered wildlife.
The five babies were found by forest department officials who were patrolling in the Jaleswar range in Balasore district.
Officials believed the orangutans had been in the area for just a few days, and they have now been placed in quarantine at a zoological park in Odisha.
According to the World Wildlife Fund, about 104,000 orangutans remain in Borneo and Sumatra, down from more than 230,000 a century ago.
The Tapanuli orangutan (Pongo tapanuliensis), a third species, is classified as critically endangered, with fewer than 800 believed to survive in the wild.
In November, conservationists found the Tapanuli population had been reduced by 7% after severe flooding in Indonesia.
Between 33 and 54 Tapanuli orangutans were estimated to have been killed in widespread floods and landslides in North Sumatra province.
Previous research has suggested annual losses of 1% of the Tapanuli orangutan population would be sufficient to lead to eventual extinction.
The entire Tapanuli population dwells solely in the West Block of the Batang Toru, a forest threatened by mining, palm oil plantations and a large hydropower project.

The Supreme Court has put the Food Safety and Standards Authority of India’s (FSSAI) two-phase rollout of front-of-pack warning labels (FoPL) under the scanner, warning that the second phase could be “indefinitely postponed” in the absence of a clear timeline. The court also asked the Centre to consider introducing nutritional education in schools to help children understand food labels and make informed dietary choices.
Under the proposed rollout, warnings would initially apply to packaged foods high in two or more nutrients of concern — added fat, added sugar and salt — and would be extended in the second phase to products high in even one of them. The FSSAI had proposed the phased approach to give consumers time to adapt to the new labels and the food industry time to reformulate its products.
“Assessment of consumer acceptability or giving the industry adequate time for reformulation cannot be reason enough for this uncertainty in time. Therefore, a reasonable, scientifically justified and clearly defined timeline or transitionary period which divides the two-phases must be indicated, for the approach of the FSSAI to be a workable one,” a Bench comprising Justices J.B. Pardiwala and K. Vinod Chandran said in an order passed on Thursday (September 10, 2026) night.
It accordingly asked the FSSAI to consider an alternative model, under which products with the highest levels of nutrients of concern would be brought under the warning regime first, followed by those with progressively lower thresholds.
‘Nutritional literacy’ in schools
Acknowledging that children are particularly “vulnerable” to “impulse or uninformed dietary decision-making”, the Bench also asked the Union government to incorporate nutritional literacy into school curricula, including teaching children how to interpret nutritional information and front-of-pack labels.
The top court passed the directions while hearing a PIL filed by non-profit 3S and Our Health Society, represented by advocate Rajiv Shankar Dvivedi, seeking mandatory front-of-pack warnings on packaged foods high in sugar, salt and saturated fats.
‘Scientific basis’
The court also questioned why a warning should initially require a product to be high in at least two nutrients of concern when excess levels of even one could pose health risks. It noted the petitioners’ contention that the two-nutrient requirement lacked scientific basis and would leave many products outside the first phase.
The Bench also took note of concerns raised by stakeholders against placing ultra-processed foods on the same footing as minimally processed packaged foods, given the greater nutritional benefits of the latter. It accordingly asked the regulator to consider whether different thresholds could be formulated based on the degree of processing.
The FSSAI was further asked to clarify which “specified sweetened beverages” would be covered in the first phase and the thresholds that would apply to them.
‘Insufficient information’ on labels
The order also raised questions about the design of the proposed warning labels. The FSSAI has proposed a red hexagon carrying warnings such as “HIGH FAT”, “HIGH SUGAR” and “HIGH SALT”, but the court flagged that there was “insufficient information” on its size and placement.
It also pointed out that a “strictly word-based warning label” presupposes a certain level of comprehension and literacy among consumers, potentially limiting its accessibility across regions, languages and age groups.
“Ideally, an all-inclusive FoPL which effectively caters to the diverse population of this country should incorporate a combination of words along with pictorial representations of the individual nutrients-of-concern. This would ensure that the information provided in the FoPL is truly accessible”, the Bench said.
While acknowledging that the FSSAI had made “significant progress” in implementing its directions on warning labels, the Bench cautioned that reducing salt, sugar and fat in packaged foods could have the “unintended and unfortunate consequence” of prompting manufacturers to increase their use of artificial preservatives, emulsifiers and other additives to preserve taste, texture and shelf life.
It accordingly asked the regulator to “keep this danger in mind” while finalising the threshold limits and considering corresponding regulations governing the addition of such chemicals to packaged foods.
10 days time
The court directed the FSSAI to file an affidavit within 10 days setting out its responses and clarifications on the concerns raised and posted the matter for further hearing on September 28.
The order came a day after Additional Solicitor General Brijender Chahar, appearing for the Centre and the FSSAI, told the court that it was open to making warning labels mandatory for packaged foods high in even one nutrient of concern — sugar, salt or fat — marking a regulatory pivot from the earlier proposal to trigger warnings only when a product exceeded limits for two or more such nutrients.
Earlier, the top court had asked the regulator to take its directions “seriously”, stressing its concern over the impact of food safety standards on public health, particularly that of growing children. “We are concerned with the health of people, more particularly growing children. We have taken it up very seriously... We expect one and all to extend cooperation in a cause which is in national interest,” Justice Pardiwala had said.

The Midterm Conventions Will Continue Until Morale Improves
It isn’t over until the president’s tenor sings.
If only the GOP midterm convention succeeds in its aim of electing Donald Trump president, things will get a lot better in this country. Isn’t he already president? Hush! At the Unprecedented (But Very President-ed) Republican Midterm Convention, we reject such trivial objections! “I know many of you are still struggling thanks to Joe Biden and the Democrats,” said Richard Hudson, the National Republican Committee chair.
You have your orders: Imagine that Donald Trump is on the ballot, because if he were, the economy would get a lot better than it is under whoever is president right now—I have to assume Biden? But possibly, based on sheer volume of mentions, Abdul El-Sayed? Whoever it is, the guy is doing just terribly.
Donald Trump has fixed everything, but also, we need him to fix everything. He is the greatest president in our lifetime, if we can ever manage to elect him.
Also, everything is on the verge of being taken from us by Democrats. Sorry, not Democrats. Communists! “Communism is on the march, and it’s up to us to stop it in its tracks!” announced Donald Trump Jr. (whom the C-SPAN chyron demurely introduces as a 1789 Capital partner). Communists, he said, are “triggered at the sight of an American flag” and want to turn our cities into a “dystopian hellscape.”
“Democrats are advocates for evil,” warned the pastor introducing the second day of festivities.
Senator Ted Cruz denounced the “red-green alliance” of “Communists and Islamists”: “They hate Christians, they hate Jews, they hate capitalism, they hate the Constitution, and they hate America.” Things remained at this feverish pitch of Two Minutes’ Hate (sadly not limited to two minutes) for most of the convention. There were hearty scoops of anti-immigrant sentiment, Islamophobia (most speakers tackled El-Sayed’s name as though even attempting to pronounce it aloud was an unreasonable demand), and fearmongering about “TRANSGENDER FOR EVERYONE!” (as the president put it). It’s wonderful that things are going so well that we can take a step back and focus on what really matters: making this country a worse place for people to live in.
J. D. Vance stepped onstage on the second night and complained that “we were tired of being called racists for noticing that our country was becoming dirtier and poorer and less safe and less prosperous.” Can’t imagine why anyone would suggest that there were racist implications in a statement like that! He had some equally un-grotesque remarks to offer about James Talarico’s support for trans kids (“I never want to see that guy’s web-browser history”). Vance—more and more lifelike every day—got the warmest welcome he could possibly have wanted, often pausing his speech to bask in the applause, and even attempting to tell the women behind him that they looked good (“If you’re ever feeling down about our country,” he said, “just take a look at the beautiful ladies right behind me”) and to say that if they were having beverages, he wanted some too.
Some people even chanted “48!,” which left him starry-eyed. (“I got to say, it’s pretty cool to hear a crowd that’s this fired up chant your name.”) Said fired-up crowd was a sore subject that the president harped on in both of his speeches, urging people not to go to the bathroom lest someone snap a photo of their empty seat and draw incorrect conclusions.
After Vance’s speech, the night took an even more surreal turn. Trump returned to the stage and promised that he would not repeat the speech from the previous night. Then he began to repeat the speech from the previous night. As the desiccated corpse of the previous speech came shambling back to finish its unfinished business, I began to worry that we were all trapped in some kind of time loop. How to break it? Vote Trump? More tenor? Whatever beverage the beautiful women were having?
“It was bad, but now it’s good. And it’s going to soon be greater than ever before.” (This is what I, too, would say if I were trying to remember the general gist of the president’s Wednesday-night remarks but had no access to a teleprompter.) For a second night in a row, the president warned about the “mutilization” of children. He also repeated his promise of a $5,000 “let’s call it Trump dividend” for all Americans if they vote Republican majorities into both houses of Congress. (Is this legal?) This money would be for adults, Trump clarified: “We love our adults. It’s time we take care of our adults.” Yes! Those freeloading, nonvoting children have rested their tiny booties on our necks too long.
Then he forced everyone to listen to his “presidential tenor,” Chris Macchio, sing “Nessun dorma” as balloons fell. Also “All I Ask of You” from The Phantom of the Opera. No, I am not making this up. It’s 2026. No one makes anything up anymore, except the AI you are asking for urgent medical advice.
At one point during this ramble, after making everyone raise one hand and swear to bring their family to the polls (and cheat, if necessary), the president told everyone that if they did not vote, they would go to hell.
Sir, look around! We are already there.

తెలంగాణ బీజేపీ నేత, కేంద్ర హోం శాఖ సహాయ మంత్రి బండి సంజయ్ కుమార్ తన కుమార్తెను ఒక క్రైస్తవుడికి ఇచ్చి క్రిస్టియన్ పద్ధతిలో పెళ్లి చేశారంటూ కొన్ని పోస్టులు (ఇక్కడ, ఇక్కడ) సోషల్ మీడియాలో ప్రచారంలో ఉన్నాయి. ఇందులో ఎంత నిజముందో ఇప్పుడు చూద్దాం.
క్లెయిమ్: బీజేపీ నేత బండి సంజయ్ తన కుమార్తెను ఒక క్రైస్తవుడికి ఇచ్చి క్రిస్టియన్ పద్ధతిలో పెళ్లి చేశారు.
ఫాక్ట్: వైరల్ ఫోటోలో ఉన్నది బండి సంజయ్ సోదరుడి కుమార్తె సంజన. బండి సంజయ్కి ఇద్దరు కుమారులు మాత్రమే ఉన్నారు. ఆగస్టు 2026లో సంజనకు దొంతు రజనీక్రాంత్తో హిందూ సాంప్రదాయం ప్రకారం వివాహం జరిగింది. కావున, పోస్టులో చేయబడిన క్లెయిమ్ తప్పు.
ముందుగా బండి సంజయ్ కుటుంబ వివరాలను పరిశీలించగా, ఆయనకు ఇద్దరు కుమారులు మాత్రమే ఉన్నట్లు తేలింది. ఆయనకు కుమార్తె లేదు. 2024 లోక్ సభ ఎన్నికల అఫిడవిట్లో కూడా తనకు ఇద్దరు కుమారులు (సాయి భగీరథ్, సాయి సుముఖ్) ఉన్నట్టు ఉంది.
ఇక వైరల్ ఫోటోలో కనిపిస్తున్న యువతి, బండి సంజయ్ సోదరుడు బండి శ్రావణ్ కుమార్ కుమార్తె సంజన.
మీడియా కథనాల ప్రకారం (ఇక్కడ, ఇక్కడ & ఇక్కడ) , దొంతు హరిప్రసాద్, దొంతు రాణి దంపతుల కుమారుడైన దొంతు రజనీకాంత్తో(రజనీక్రాంత్) సంజన వివాహం ఆగస్టు 2026లో జరిగింది. వీరు క్రైస్తవులు అని ఎక్కడా పేర్కొనలేదు. పైగా, పెళ్లి, రిసెప్షన్కు సంబంధించిన వీడియోలను(ఇక్కడ, ఇక్కడ & ఇక్కడ) పరిశీలించగా, ఇవి హిందూ పద్ధతిలోనే జరిగినట్లు స్పష్టమవుతోంది.
చివరిగా, బండి సంజయ్ తన కుమార్తెకు క్రిస్టియన్ తో పెళ్లి చేశారంటూ జరుగుతున్న ప్రచారంలో ఎలాంటి వాస్తవం లేదు.

PM Modi checks on Xi Jinping mid speech at BRICS Summit, asks, ‘Is it okay?’
Chinese President Xi Jinping attended the BRICS Summit in Delhi. It was his first visit to India in seven years.
Prime Minister Narendra Modi briefly paused his BRICS Summit address on Day 1 to check on Chinese President Xi Jinping after appearing to notice that something was wrong. Click here for LIVE updates on Day 2 of the Summit
Modi, in the middle of his speech on Saturday, stopped and turned towards Xi, who was in India for the first time in seven years to attend the summit.
“Is it okay,” PM Modi asked the translator accompanying the Chinese president. He repeated the question moments later. It was not immediately clear what had caused Xi’s apparent discomfort.
Deep Dive
After a few seconds, Xi nodded in response, following which Modi resumed his address.
Modi-Xi bilateral meet
PM Modi and Xi Jinping held bilateral talks in New Delhi on September 12, on the sidelines of the BRICS Summit. The meeting lasted more than 50 minutes.
The talks focused on India-China relations, border peace, trade, market access and people-to-people exchanges. A key message from Modi was that peace and stability along the India-China border were essential for the broader relationship, HT earlier reported.

Modi spoke of the principles of “mutual respect, mutual sensitivity and mutual interest” while discussing bilateral ties. Both sides agreed that differences should not turn into disputes and reiterated the need to work towards a fair and mutually acceptable resolution of the boundary question.
Xi has described India and China as partners rather than rivals and called for a long-term approach to bilateral relations and cooperation.
Xi skips Modi-hosted gala dinner
Xi did not attend the gala dinner hosted by Modi for BRICS leaders on Saturday. The Chinese president was reported to have returned to his hotel to rest.

BRICS Summit 2026: Day 2
The second and final day of the BRICS Summit began at Bharat Mandapam in New Delhi. Modi received visiting leaders, who then posed for the customary family photo with PM Modi at the centre.
Opening the second day, Modi said India’s BRICS presidency focused on four pillars: resilience, innovation, cooperation and sustainability.
He said India had worked with other BRICS members to turn the grouping’s shared vision into practical, “win-win” cooperation.
Modi also warned that rising global tensions were increasingly affecting ordinary people. He cited pandemics, climate-related disasters and supply-chain disruptions, stressing that in an interconnected world, crises do not remain limited to one region.

BRICS to develop infectious disease early-warning system
Modi announced that BRICS countries had reached a consensus on a BRICS Integrated Early Warning System aimed at improving preparedness and response to infectious diseases.
He also said the grouping had formulated Early Warning Data Integration Guidelines for disaster management.
The initiatives are aimed at improving coordination and ensuring that member countries can respond more quickly to emerging risks.

You can read part one of the American Ground: Unbuilding the World Trade Center series here; part two here; and part three here.
American Ground was originally an Atlantic series, and an attempt to respond usefully to the terrorist attacks of September 11, 2001. As it became clear that the magazine was committed to a long and heavily charged project about the deconstruction of the World Trade Center ruins, I wanted to take some emotional distance from the tragedy, and to approach the narrative as if I were looking back on current events from several decades into the future. The result would be, I hoped, like a “history in the present tense.” It was a formulation that came often to mind as I proceeded.
My unwillingness to participate in the public displays of grief was partly just personal. But I also believed that the emotionalism surrounding the site, though at its origins genuine and necessary, had grown into something less healthy—an overindulgence, sustained by political forces and the media, that rather than serving as a catharsis only deepened the social anguish. And I thought that if American Ground was to have lasting value, readers should not be manipulated; they would bring their own feelings and thoughts to the text. My job was to observe for them, not as an “objective” journalist or an earnest encyclopedist, but more openly in the first person, as their agent on the ground. I spent six months immersed at the site, usually seven days a week, and another five months writing. I witnessed many sad moments, particularly when accompanying some of the families of the dead who came to contemplate their loss—but I did not write about that, because their grief was private, or should have been, and it was not my subject. My subject was construction, or more precisely deconstruction—the dismantling of the tangled steel and concrete, and all that this entailed. Now, nearly two years after the World Trade Center collapses, I still believe that the only way to communicate the essence of the cleanup, including the complexity of the emotions involved, was to maintain the narrative’s detachment. In American Ground the idea was to catch a glimpse of America itself, or of a certain slice of it at a certain time—unruly, unscripted, and in action. In the mix lay the bad as well as the good, but the book turned out to be hopeful—even celebratory—and all the more so because it wasn’t trying to be. Judging from the overwhelmingly positive response that followed publication, the narrative detachment did not diminish the book’s meaning to readers, or its emotional impact.
But the responses ran the other way, too. Some readers interpreted my refusal to embrace heroic imagery as disrespectful of the dead, or fundamentally biased against firefighters. They were also angry because the book mentioned looting at the site by firemen as well as by policemen and construction workers, and in particular described a confrontation that broke out when a crushed fire truck was discovered with new blue jeans inside. The street demonstrations in New York that followed the publication of American Ground were local, union-driven affairs, but when some of the press picked up on the story, American Ground became “controversial.”
In New York I was asked by reporters if I found the reaction surprising, and I answered no. I had seen and described these very same emotions in action on the pile, as the ruins were known. Moreover, the emotions were not unusual. Solidarity with a group, the possessive embrace of disaster, a sense of privilege, the searing or bittersweet sensation of sorrow—to various degrees most of us have known these feelings. I knew that the protesters had been through a tough and disorienting experience—the deaths of friends, co-workers, and in a few cases family, followed by the distorting glare of publicity and hype. Now time had moved on, but the feelings remained strong. I had written that the cool-blooded engineers had needed to learn a lesson—that the various emotions at the site had to be accommodated if the larger community was to function and the work was to proceed. America is a dynamic mess, not a dictatorship of rationalists. Now I was learning something, too, about writing nonfiction. “History in the present tense” can be so fresh that it’s alive—and still very raw. The book was becoming a small part of the story it told.
But the book was always just a partial history. Had a calm and open conversation been possible, I would readily have admitted that the account was biased in a particular way—in its emphasis on the deconstruction job. That is not to say that it was biased in favor of one group over another. When I first arrived at the site, I had warned Department of Design and Construction Commissioner Ken Holden and Mike Burton, the construction “czar,” that my presence represented a risk to them, because I would write about the project’s failure—if such it proved to be—as readily as I would write about the project’s success. Though I ended by admiring both men for their performance at the site, for many months this was not a sure thing, any more than success itself was guaranteed. Indeed, some of the principal construction men (and Burton in particular) were taken aback by the candor with which I described their motivations and work.
But for better or worse I certainly did pay more attention to the construction leaders than to anyone else. They were my subject, and this was no secret. From the very start I saw their role as interesting and forward-looking, in part because their challenges all lay ahead. That was the premise of my initial approach, and of the book that resulted, which, as the subtitle indicates, is about the “unbuilding” process. I wanted to tell the story fully, and this sometimes required me to grapple with implications and cross-connections, most significantly the extraction of the dead and the increasingly volatile social dynamics on the pile. But whenever possible I avoided straying into unrelated areas, of which there were many.
It has been suggested that I must have been glad to be the only writer with free access to the inner world of the Trade Center site, but the opposite is true. There was obviously more happening there than I alone could know or describe. More important, exclusivity is a cheap trick; transparency is good for everyone, and I would have preferred it. The presence of the daily press would have served the useful role not only of informing the public but also of clarifying the participants’ views of themselves. It is worth remembering that the Trade Center site was an intensely chaotic place. A huge number of worthy efforts were being pursued in all directions and almost spontaneously, in many cases with admirably little direction from above. For the first few weeks there must have been two dozen chiefs, each doing good work and believing to varying degrees that he or she was the one in charge. Certainly there was room for a variety of experiences and impressions. Volunteers working in the food lines would have had a very different view from that of the telephone-repair people, the National Guard, the police officers at the perimeter gates, or the sanitation crews working ferociously to clean up the surrounding neighborhoods. All of them would correctly have seen their roles as necessary for the functioning of the whole. But I was not writing about them.
I would hardly have mentioned the firemen either, had they not played such a pivotal role in the process of the unbuilding. Despite what the public believed, after the search for survivors ended, and the dust and smoke suppression was taken over by civilian water crews, the firemen’s role was not primarily physical. Beyond the increasingly careful raking of fine debris, and the immediate handling of human remains, which others could have done, the firemen’s position was largely symbolic. Their presence was crucial nonetheless, a forceful reminder of the human consequences of the attack, and of the importance of keeping people’s emotions in mind; it was also, as I have described, a source of friction and resentment on the pile, and ultimately a political challenge to the progress of the deconstruction. But in the climate of the times in New York, even short and neutral descriptions of any role or action that was not “heroic” constituted dangerous territory.
The demonstrators’ anger was real, and though it often seemed based on misunderstandings of the book, it also grew from a fundamentally different view of the Trade Center experience. This was to be expected, and there will surely be other, different versions, in print, of the story that I told. In the meantime, the demonstrating firefighters legitimately wanted to register their opinion that American Ground was wrong and unfair. I was doing my job, and they were doing theirs. They chanted and held up signs for the cameras, inflated a giant plastic rat (a well-worn union prop), and went home.
Heavily involved in these demonstrations was a group, small but vocal, that organized a campaign to have the book withdrawn and destroyed. Among others, its members included civilians who in the aftermath of the terrorist attacks had volunteered at the site, or in other ways had come into close contact with the firefighters, and had embraced their humanity and grief. They called themselves the WTC Living History Project, and announced their ambition to record and publish the oral history of this important event in the national experience. First, though, they fought against what they perceived as the injustice of American Ground. They organized e-mail campaigns against the book, disrupted public events, impugned my motivations, accused me of plagiarism, and pored over the text for factual errors. They found of course people from the site who were willing to dispute some of my observations and perspectives, and they called into question some of my information. They circulated to the press a long electronic document in itemized form, in which they attempted to lay out their case. Predictably, they had a more heroic “united we stand” view of the Trade Center site than did I. Again, all of this generated publicity, especially of the local television and tabloid kind.
It was reassuring to know that before publication, American Ground had been heavily vetted by The Atlantic’s rigorous fact-checking department. For five months, two veteran checkers had gone over the text full-time, verifying statements and descriptions, reading and rereading primary documents, and cross-checking details, often with multiple independent sources. Typically, with the campaign against American Ground under way, The Atlantic did not retreat into a hostile posture but called its readers’ attention to the Living History Project’s compendium (which was posted on the internet) and published angry and critical letters, along with some admiring ones. With an eye on the specific points raised in the various accusatory documents, it also undertook an extensive review of the earlier fact-checking.
I was very sure about the essence of what I had written. But despite the enormous effort that had gone into getting the details right, it was not unlikely that factual errors had slipped in. American Ground is a tight book, but a long and complicated piece of reporting. The publication of the paperback edition has offered the opportunity to make a few corrections. For example, the office into which Peter Rinaldi and Frank Lombardi escaped after the 1993 bombing was not associated with Brown & Root, as I had written, but rather with what was then the independent law firm of Brown & Wood. But the really striking result of the fact-checking review was that on item after item, the accusations proved to be incorrect.
As might be expected, there were gray areas. The emotional state of the American Airlines flight attendant Betty Ong was described one way in initial press accounts and another way in some later ones; tapes of Ong’s phone call have not been made public. In the paperback edition, I have omitted any reference to her emotional state. Often the discrepancies involved not just sources and perceptions, but time frames. I was accused, for example, of underestimating the size of the Fire Department. Well, the Fire Department when? We stuck with the obviously approximate number (14,000) that the department itself had given to us as the most relevant count for the period in question.
Time and again there were fundamental misunderstandings by the book’s critics, either of the site or of the text. In a passage about Mike Burton’s difficulty in ceding power as the work matured, I had written that “by the spring” the construction company Bovis had taken over day-to-day management of the job. The critics countered with a January 1 date, confusing the moment when Bovis became the sole “prime” contractor (initially a paperwork and billing rearrangement) with the much slower process of gaining significant operational control.
One of the peripheral points of contention by the Living History Project was that there had never been, as I had written, an attempt (presumably by workers with a cutting torch and heavy tools) to break into a huge Bank of Nova Scotia vault containing gold and silver, underground in the old H&M Railroad station at the site. I knew that the bank had denied an attempted theft at the time, even as the bullion was being urgently transferred to another location; police thought otherwise, and said so to the press. Now in the Living History Project document, a Port Authority police lieutenant was cited as saying that there had been no sign of an attempted break-in. Later, to the press, he wondered why no one had spoken to him. I was in the vault several times, and heard about a break-in attempt firsthand from the police and others standing guard there, some of them with shotguns. I was also told about it by an independent engineer who had a supervisory role in helping with the removal of the bullion, and by city and Port Authority officials who were directly involved. Contemporary newspaper reports in The New York Times and elsewhere refer to an attempted break-in. In the end there seemed to be no good reason to change the text.
As noted, these criticisms and more were posted by the Living History Project on the internet, and some were offered up at the public demonstrations and to the press. I responded repeatedly to the more important points, but tried to avoid sinking into the swamp of confused allegations and misinterpretations, many of them based on erroneous and perhaps naive assumptions. Some of American Ground’s critics seemed to be unacquainted with the concept of “spin,” or with the notion that people in nominal positions of authority might not know what was actually transpiring on the ground. In the free-for-all of the pile, the titular authorities often didn’t even know that they didn’t know. In such circumstances, there were frequent discrepancies between official reports and reality.
One genuine error that did emerge pertained to the early dispute between Port Authority police officers and firemen over whether to free a dead Port Authority policeman’s body by expeditiously amputating his leg. Though the book’s description supports the firemen’s view that amputation was the right thing to do, I wrote, “The police pointed out—correctly—that no dead fireman would have had his leg cut off.” Information received later suggested that there were cases I was unaware of in which firemen’s bodies had indeed been freed through amputation. As a result, in the paperback edition the sentence now reads, “The police maintained that no dead fireman …” The rest of the passage is unchanged, however. The Port Authority police officers were indeed angry because they believed that the firemen were interested only in searching for their own. The officers’ view was too crude to be fair, and I described it as such. But there is no doubt that for an astonishingly long time (months), the various categories of the dead were treated with different levels of ceremony and respect. The denial of this pattern was among the more audacious criticisms of American Ground. The differential treatment of the dead constituted one of the most glaring realities of the Trade Center site, and it exacerbated the tribal resentments that occasionally erupted into fights.
I wrote about looting at the site in a few passages. I was told about it first by policemen on the pile soon after I arrived. The looting started before the South Tower fell, as I wrote, “with the innocuous filching of cigarettes and soda pop,” and it rapidly spread and became more ambitious in the hours and weeks afterward. It involved firemen as well as other groups at the site. This was an open secret on the pile, well known to people there, as well as to more distant police and city officials, and to some reporters. After the campaign against American Ground began, a number of eyewitnesses came forward (including police officers, city officials, construction workers, and reporters) and privately offered me their moral support. A few went further and offered, if need be, though tentatively and with trepidation, to go public in the book’s defense with personal accounts of the acts that they had seen. I thanked them, but because I still hoped that the book would not become the carrying horse for this particular topic, I turned them down.
I included what little I wrote about looting because the looting was pervasive, and it affected working relations on the pile. To have glossed over it would have been dishonest, and would have required me to omit descriptions of some of the most significant social challenges that faced the project. It’s obvious that only a small number of people engaged in the looting. But their actions greatly exacerbated the frictions on the pile, and for that reason became a necessary part of the story. As for the specific misdeeds, I never felt they were pertinent to my subject. In the story of the deconstruction it was the tribal perceptions of the misdeeds that counted, whether right or wrong. But that point was lost in the din of controversy. In tabloid reduction, American Ground became simply “the book that accuses the firemen of looting.”
The most controversial passage turned out to be the description of an argument that broke out on the pile when jeans from a retail store were found in a fire truck that had been crushed and buried under the pile. One of the book’s critics, a professional writer independent of the Living History Project but with ties to firefighters, put considerable effort into reconstructing that fire truck’s final moments on September 11, to make the case that jeans from a retail store (apparently the brand was Structure, not Gap, as I had been told) had essentially become enmeshed with the truck as it was hammered down through shopping arcades rather than having been placed in the truck before it was buried. A reconstruction of the truck’s fate had no bearing, however, on the story I was telling in American Ground. That story was strictly related to the emotional and divisive social dynamics of a day in late fall, three months after the towers came down. It was not an account of whatever happened or did not happen on September 11, and it was certainly not intended as an exposé of the last moments of the fire truck’s crew. Nor was it the report of a rumor: Detailed descriptions of the argument, and the immediate context in which it took place, were provided to me shortly afterward by multiple independent eyewitnesses. These were people well known to me, who for months had proved to be reliable and steady sources, and who held important jobs on the pile. The reactions of the construction workers seemed to me to be unnecessarily provocative—as my description sought to make clear. But the argument over the jeans did not come out of nowhere. It occurred against the background of differential treatment of the dead, as well as of extensive looting in which firemen were known to have been involved. By placing the episode after these subjects had been explored, casting it in the past tense, and deliberately suppressing the identities of those involved, I tried to keep narrative attention focused on what mattered: a growing threat to the social order on the pile, which seemed to me to be a more important subject than looting, and certainly more pertinent to the unbuilding. I made that point explicitly a few sentences later: “The site would never stand united, as sloganeers said it should.”
That said, it is clear that the passage has been misinterpreted by some of the public, including people beyond the book’s critics, as an accusation. One reason is that in the course of the campaign against the book, pieces of the episode were frequently torn from context and acquired a life of their own as printed snippets and disembodied sound bites. But misinterpretation may also be due to my unintentionally ambiguous choice of wording. The construction “It was hard to avoid the conclusion that … while hundreds of doomed firemen had climbed through the wounded buildings, this particular crew had been engaged in something else entirely” can be read as my own assessment, rather than, as was intended, the explanation of an assessment by others who were preconditioned to construe it that way. Therefore in the paperback edition I have added at the start of the sentence the phrase “In their eyes” to clarify my meaning.
The World Trade Center site was an extremely complex place, loaded with emotion and political symbolism, full of action and confusion, with many interpretations possible. Having restricted my view to the engineering and deconstruction process, I wrote about it with complete candor, expressing my opinions openly, as I always do. I realized that the approach I took might offend a certain number of people who subscribed to different views—including the essentially two-dimensional one that has received so much publicity, and depicts the Trade Center project in maudlin and “heroic” terms. I do not perceive the project that way—and did not when I was there. More impressive, I felt, was another sort of American greatness that emerged at the site—a complex weave that included diverse acts and motivations, and also a culture of improvisational genius that seemed enormously encouraging about the future. There was no need to engage in propaganda. I wrote about the Trade Center with the assumption that candid descriptions would serve the subject best.
