In May, hundreds of malicious and spam packages were uploaded to RubyGems, causing a serious disruption for the host. Now independent researchers have said that a swarm of OpenAI agents were responsible for the attack. Not only that, but the AI tried to steal users’ API keys.
OpenAI’s rogue AI tried to hack another company in May
The previously undisclosed attack on Ruby Gems predates Hugging Face by more than a month.
At the time, RubyGems described it as a “major malicious attack” and shut down signups for four days as it tried to mitigate the damage and collect data. Researchers said that the contents of the packages that brought RubyGems to its knees were clearly authored by an LLM, and that the agents submitting those packages self-identified as being from OpenAI. They said the behavior observed very closely mirrored that of the swarm that began editing a German wiki, which OpenAI has confirmed its agents were responsible for.
The agents in this instance managed to bypass RubyGems’ email verification system to create a large number of accounts, then overwhelmed it with submissions. It then used the site’s automatic build system to remotely execute code and tried to exploit a vulnerability to steal user API keys. Though, it’s unclear if it ever succeeded.
OpenAI did not immediately reply to a request for comment.

The Birth of the New Legal Right
Forty-four years ago, a conservative legal convention offered disaffected students an identity—and hope.
America’s highest court didn’t take on a deeply partisan, conservative bent overnight. This transformation began decades ago, with a simple purpose: In the early 1980s, three law students were fed up with what they saw as a liberal monoculture at their elite universities. They wanted a place to freely debate conservative ideas and to refine their arguments. So the students—Lee Liberman, Steve Calabresi, and David McIntosh—decided to build one.
In late April 1982, their newly formed group, the Federalist Society, held its first conference, at Yale University. The formal title of the three-day affair was “A Symposium on Federalism: Legal and Political Ramifications,” but the snoozy name belied the energy of the weekend. Young Reaganites packed their sleeping bags and overnighted on the floors of fellow students they’d never met before. During smoke breaks, they chatted up Robert Bork, the famous Yale professor, and Antonin Scalia, then a lesser-known professor from the University of Chicago.
But if the attendees were idealistic about the Reagan era and the emergence of a harder-core strain of conservatism known as the New Right, they also understood that they were still a tiny minority in both the academic and legal worlds. Movements opposed to racism, sexism, and injustice remained the animating forces of campus life. Many students across the country were embracing Marxism and socialism. To make headway, young conservatives needed a voice—and a strategy.
To this end, Bork proved essential. He had recently been nominated by President Ronald Reagan to serve on the D.C. Circuit Court of Appeals and spoke with both knowledge and authority. Bork announced to his eager audience that media and academia had become left-wing machines. The Supreme Court was inventing new “rights” with no basis in the Constitution, he said, and the only path forward was to return to the words of the Founding Fathers.
Whether Bork truly believed in the conspiracies he outlined or whether he was merely exaggerating is unclear. But in his remarks at that first Federalist Society conference, Bork effectively mapped out what the right-wing legal movement would do over the course of the next four decades.
“We have a Court,” Bork declared in his speech, “which is creating individual rights which are not to be found in the Constitution by any standard method of interpretation.”
He went on to outline the formation of a nascent conservative approach called originalism. In the originalist view, constitutional rights existed only as the Founding Fathers imagined them, unless officially added via constitutional amendment. By embracing what Bork called a “strict” or “textualist” reading of the Constitution, conservatives could argue that recent social changes never specifically considered by the Founders were not constitutionally protected. The approach could return the country to its true, “conservative” values.
In championing this interpretation of the law, Bork proved to be ahead of his time. He saw benches and courtrooms as the final frontier in the right-wing culture war. Effete liberals either had persuaded judges to ignore the Constitution, he said, or had themselves colonized the bench. Bork railed against the media and academia as corrupting influences: “The institutions to which the court responds are the press and the law-school faculties. Those are the people they talk to; those are the people who are responsible for the reputations of individual judges.”
And those people were liberals. Bork cited a survey from the magazine Public Opinion, which concluded that the people who worked in American media were “heavily left liberal.”
More than 80 percent of the press, he continued, had voted for the Democratic candidate in every presidential election since 1968. The values of the press were “egalitarian and permissive.” And professors were no better: “They want sexual freedoms; they want freedom for abortions; they want the death penalty outlawed.”
Bork believed academic elites were bastardizing the First Amendment and the Fourteenth Amendment to suit their ends, creating “new constitutional values which are nothing more than the imposition of upper-middle-class values on society.” He blamed the “enormous industry in the law schools” and their faculty for these invented “rights.” If the professors had their way, he warned, they would indoctrinate a new class of law students that would promote liberal ideals on benches across the country. This all added up to, Bork stated with thinly veiled disgust, “the gentrification of the Constitution.”
Bork closed his remarks by outlining the constitutional means by which the New Right could overturn federal protection for abortion. Abortion and “acceptable sexual behavior” were matters for the states to decide—not constitutionally protected rights, as Roe v. Wade had recently found. Reproductive freedom, Bork advised, was “a classical case for local control. There is simply no national moral consensus about abortion, and there is not about to be.”
Soon, the Reagan administration would call upon the students that Bork had trained to carry out this strategy of curtailing rights, one case at a time. Four decades later, the Roberts Court would echo Bork’s language when it struck down Roe.
If the Federalist Society had begun as a campus alt-community, it quickly blossomed into something much more important. As Calabresi, one of its co-founders, later recalled, “Our conference was covered by the National Review and suddenly conservatives at fifteen other law schools began calling us and telling us they wanted to attend the conference and they wanted to form chapters, too. That was a process of almost spontaneous generation.” Less than a year after the 1982 Yale conference, 17 law schools across the country had a Federalist Society chapter.
Soon after its inception, the student group was on the White House’s radar. In attendance at that first conference were several members of the Reagan Justice Department, including the future acting solicitor general and the next assistant attorney general at the Office of Legal Counsel. By 1985, all three founding members of the Federalist Society—Liberman, Calabresi, and McIntosh—had positions at DOJ.
Half a century later, every sitting Supreme Court justice appointed by a Republican president is a member of the Federalist Society. During the first Trump presidency, 46 of his 54 nominees to the federal appeals courts were members. His White House counsel, two attorneys general, and deputy attorney general were all members as well.
From that very first conference, the Federalist Society awoke a power lying dormant among marginalized conservatives. It offered them an identity, a larger community, and hope—clarifying the battle at hand and, most essentially, suggesting that they might win it.
This article has been adapted from Alex Wagner’s new book, The Steal: Four Right-Wing Hard-Liners, One Republican Presidency, and the Raid on America's Courts.

If your laptop trackpad is popping out, stop using it immediately
A swollen battery can ruin your laptop and even cause a fire.
Trackpads on modern laptops are usually flat. But maybe you've noticed that yours has started to come loose, as if something were pushing it from the inside. It might even get to the point where the glass covering it cracks. If this happens to your laptop, you could have a serious trouble on your hands. The battery may be to blame, and you should stop using your laptop immediately. But don't throw your laptop away just yet — there are ways to fix it so you can use it safely again.
A loose trackpad could mean your battery is about to explode
To understand why, you should start by learning how batteries work. Pretty much every modern laptop has lithium-ion batteries inside. They're responsible for providing power when the laptop is unplugged. Overall, these batteries are quite safe if used properly. But they can put you at serious risk if you ignore certain safety precautions. A battery relies on many chemical reactions to work. And when it's overcharged or physically damaged, the internal chemical components can produce harmful gases.
The result is disastrous for your laptop. The battery starts to swell and pushes against all the components around it. And when it comes to laptops, the battery is usually located underneath the trackpad. Surface laptops and MacBooks are no exception. And you can imagine where that leads. A swollen battery pushes the trackpad out. A trackpad that pops out is usually a sign that your battery is nearing the end of its life. And that's not hypothetical — Apple already had to launch replacement programs for MacBooks with swollen batteries.
Your laptop stopping working wouldn't even be the worst-case scenario. A faulty battery can swell to the point where it explodes. The risk of it bursting into flames is very real. Sure, there are situations in which a trackpad might come loose due to other hardware malfunctions. Perhaps an internal screw has come loose, or your laptop has suffered an impact. But it's still worth taking every precaution to make sure it's not a battery issue.
Repairing and preventing accidents with swollen batteries
Have you noticed anything unusual with your laptop's trackpad? Is it popping up, or does the laptop case seem to be bulging? If the answer is yes, stop using your laptop immediately. Turn it off and unplug it. For most people, the best advice is to take your laptop to a repair shop. Dealing with swollen batteries can be very dangerous — one wrong move and it could catch fire. Having a professional take care of your laptop is probably the right choice here.
The good news is that laptops in this situation can be easily replaced in most cases. The trackpad snaps back into place once the new battery is installed. Prices for repairs like this can vary. Apple, for example, charges $149 to $249 to replace a MacBook battery — depending on which model you have. The price may be higher if the trackpad was damaged by the swollen battery. Most laptop makers will repair a bad battery for free if the device is still under warranty. It's worth checking to see if yours is still covered.
Also, some habits can help preserve your laptop's battery and keep it from overloading. Avoid leaving your laptop in extreme temperatures or in direct sunlight for long periods of time. Using original, certified chargers is also a good way to prevent accidents. And if you're going to store your laptop without using it for extended periods, keep it at about 50 percent charge. Try to turn it on and check it every three months to make sure everything is fine. Changing some settings on your laptop can also help reduce battery wear.

Emergency responders have rescued a Chinese man and a Nepali woman in two separate operations as authorities continued to search for thousands of people missing 10 days after massive floods hit Nepal.
The Nepali military said on Saturday a joint team comprising personnel from its army and South Korean disaster experts rescued the man from a 225-metre (740ft) tunnel in the Upper Trishuli-1 hydropower project, and that he was undergoing a health assessment. Pictures showed him being evacuated by helicopter after being carried out of the tunnel.
Rescue efforts have focused on a dozen hydropower projects across Nepal, where about 900 workers are missing, 500 of whom are thought to be trapped in huge tunnels. International rescue teams from India, China, South Korea and the US have been searching through debris and damaged structures at the projects to try to find survivors.
Two Nepali workers were rescued from another tunnel in a hydro-station on the Trishuli River on Friday.
Experts have said the possibility of finding missing people alive in the tunnels is diminishing.
The Nepali woman, 64, was rescued from a damaged house in the devastated town of Nuwakot. Photos published by the Nepali army showed rescuers discovering the woman submerged in mud before she was pulled to safety and airlifted to Kathmandu for treatment. 
 Members of Nepal’s police force cheered as she was pulled from the home, the lower half of which was buried in thick sludge.
Emergency responders have been working to find survivors from the devastating floods in Nepal, which were triggered by a glacial and rock collapse on 26 August. Their work has been complicated by the massive infrastructural damage caused by the floods, with more than 40 bridges having collapsed and rivers swelling unpredictably.
At least 1,375 people have been killed in the floods, with more than 5,000 missing, according to Nepal’s disaster management agency.

Marvel’s mishandling of its Blade reboot will likely go down as one of the studio’s biggest mistakes. There was a great actor in place to play the vampire hunter (Mahershala Ali), and a promising director set to take over the reins (Bassam Tariq). In retrospect, though, the disappointing demise of Blade might not be such a bad thing, because Tariq and Ali have collaborated on something much more interesting than a superhero reboot: the powerful hitman thriller Your Mother Your Mother Your Mother.
Your Mother Your Mother Your Mother will make you forget all about Marvel’s Blade disaster
Reviews from TIFF 2026: Your Mother Your Mother Your Mother, In Alaska, The Face of Horror, Babies, and Drifter.
That was one of five movies I was able to cram into a very hectic third day at the Toronto International Film Festival (you can see my previous reports here and here), and it was one of those days that drives home why events like TIFF can be so special. Each film I saw was drastically different from the last — there was everything from a drama about drifting cars to a throwback horror flick based on a famous Japanese ghost story — which was a great reminder that there are still plenty of new ideas left in the world of film.
So let’s get to it. Here are some rapid-fire reviews of everything I saw on day 3 at TIFF.
Your Mother Your Mother Your Mother
In theaters in October
Latif (Ali) lives a life of contradictions: he’s a devout Muslim and loyal father, but he also works as a hitman, albeit one who works under a specific moral code (only kill bad guys; never use a gun). But both his faith and his code are tested when his wife dies and he’s forced to become a single father to three kids, including a newborn baby. At the same time, his blood-soaked past comes back to haunt him, putting everyone at risk. We’re in a great moment for pure action flicks like Furious or the John Wick franchise, but Your Mother offers something very different. It’s a powerful character study, one where the action is comparatively fleeting, but all the more powerful and impactful because of it. It’s a film that always left me guessing just how Latif was going to get through this, and, despite being very serious and often solemn, the story also has plenty of laugh-out-loud moments. Ali is excellent as the morally questionable righteous killer, but I was also really impressed by John Cho as the villain, a charismatically unhinged leader of a right-wing church group.
In Alaska
No theatrical date yet
A slow-burning crime thriller, In Alaska, co-directed by Jaap van Heusden and Vinnie Karetak., follows a suicidal teen named Woody (Leo Matthew Temela) who, after a tragic mishap, finds himself wanted by the FBI for causing millions of dollars worth of damage to an oil pipeline. It’s a film of two sides: Woody’s desperate attempts at survival, and veteran agent Susan (Noomi Rapace), the only who realizes the damage wasn’t caused by eco-terrorists. In Alaska is a moodier take on the genre, and one that asks some difficult and important questions about both its leads, particularly Woody, who constantly grapples with whether he even wants to live at all. What starts out bleak ends on a much more hopeful note.
The Face of Horror
No theatrical date yet
Conceptually, Anna Biller’s The Face of Horror is a mishmash of styles and influences. It’s based on the influential Japanese ghost story Yotsuya Kaidan, but adapts the tale for 14th century England. It then renders the whole thing in the style of Technicolor horror classics. That curious combination works, though, as the film has a campy sense of theatricality to it, with over-the-top performances and classic-style special effects — including some truly memorable make-up work — that lend its grisly tale of murder and betrayal a distinct vibe. And it’s all held together by two strong lead performances: Eleanor (Kristine Froseth), the jilted wife-turned-nightmare of Edward (Jonah Hauer-King), a smarmy and morally-dubious knight who is the kind of asshole you can’t wait to see get what’s coming to him.
Babies
No theatrical date yet
A film that explores that nagging question many long-term couples are forced to answer repeatedly: when are you going to have a baby? Written and directed by Lauren Miller Rogen, Babies is centered on Annie (Anna Kendrick) and Aaron (Seth Rogen), the only childless couple in their social circle. But Annie can’t stop thinking about the question — there’s a lot of her internal monologue debating the pros and cons of having kids — and the couple are forced to really confront the idea when a close friend and her young daughter come to stay with them, providing a taste of parenthood. Babies works for two reasons. First, it’s hilarious: Kendrick and Rogen have a blast together, and the supporting cast includes the likes of Issa Rae, Zach Cherry, and Ed Helm. But it also feels grounded in a way that makes it very relatable, whether you have kids or not.
Drifter
No theatrical date yet
If Good Will Hunting and The Fast and the Furious were smushed together, you might get something like Drifter. The film is directed by longtime Fast star Sung Kang, who also plays the lead role of Tree, the janitor of a smalltown race track who moonlights as a driver for a drug kingpin. But all he really wants to do is drift, and events conspire to bring him to an event where he’ll go up against the best drifters in the world. The challenges are much more than just on the track, though; Tree has spent most of his life alone, so he’s forced to learn to open up to others, and he also has to contend with extracting himself from the world of crime. Unfortunately, Drifter leans too heavily on the established formula of underdog sports stories, which makes most of its beats feel predictable, with the exception of its completely improbable ending. Worse still is that, with the exception of Tree, none of the characters feel developed at all, and the crime thriller aspect doesn’t gel well with the feel-good story. At least there are some beautiful sequences that make drifting a car feel like an artform.

One blockbuster listing after another is keeping India’s startup IPO market buzzing. After Shiprocket’s strong debut last month, ESDS extended its post-listing rally for the sixth consecutive trading session on Friday, with the stock now up 306% from its IPO price of ₹429. Now, the spotlight is shifting to furniture rental startup RentoMojo. If its IPO subscription is anything to go by, investors are already lining up for the next big listing. The ₹1,256 Cr issue closed with a whopping 72.88X overall subscription, led by a strong QIB response, while retail investors subscribed 15.59X. The IPO, which opened on September 9 and closed on September 11, attracted bids for 158.7 Cr equity shares against 217.7 Cr shares on offer. The frenzy was not confined to the primary market either. In the grey market, Rentomojo shares were commanding a premium of around 37% on Friday, adding further fuel to the listing buzz. What makes RentoMojo’s subscription numbers striking is the crowded IPO calendar the issue had to contend with. The furniture rental company was competing for investor attention with five other mainboard IPOs that opened on September 9, with some issues attracting significantly more muted demand. If one is to look at the broader trend, a steady flow of money into mutual funds is keeping the sentiment around IPOs buoyant. At the same time, investors are increasingly shifting capital from the secondary market to the primary market, with even FPIs redirecting money towards new listings. "There is also a growing FOMO around companies that can show strong fundamentals. Recent listings such as ESDS Software, which has more than doubled from its IPO price in a week of trading, have given investors another reason to chase the primary market," an analyst said. While RentoMojo is not in the software game, it has the numbers to support some of this enthusiasm which may be trickling into consumer services. Its operating revenue rose 45.5% to ₹387 Cr in FY26, from ₹266 Cr in FY25, while profit after tax jumped nearly 142% to ₹104.3 Cr from ₹43.1 Cr. However, the latter was partly boosted by a ₹36.6 Cr tax credit. Beyond the numbers, is there a trigger behind investors flocking to back the IPO? RentoMojo’s Asset-To-Revenue Flywheel While RentoMojo is being seen as a consumer services business, its real moat lies in the physical infrastructure and the operations systems that power the furniture rentals and the subscription model. For the sake of simplicity, it can be viewed as an asset-utilisation business wrapped in a technology and subscription layer. In this case, RentoMojo buys the assets i.e. furniture and appliances and offers them through rentals to customers who pay a fee each month. When the tenure expires or the customer terminates the service, the company recovers the assets, refurbishes them and puts them back into circulation. By March 31, 2026, RentoMojo had 8.51 Lakh live items, with 83.34% of them being rented out. Management estimates that its furniture and appliances can remain useful for about 10 years. Some of its older assets are showing the benefit of that model. More than 56% of the assets added in 2017 and 60.92% of those added in 2018 were still generating revenue in FY26. Assets added in 2017 had already generated revenue equivalent to 5.12X their original cost. That is where the business can build a flywheel. The more often an asset is rented, refurbished and put back to work, the more revenue RentoMojo can extract from the original investment. The company describes this through three linked engines: ecommerce to acquire customers, subscriptions to generate recurring revenue and manage credit, and recommerce to recover and redeploy assets. RentoMojo says its supply chain infrastructure, operations systems and technology layer ties the three together. This includes tracking assets, forecasting demand and churn, optimising logistics and monitoring refurbishment. Redseer estimates India’s home furniture and appliance rental market grew from about ₹350 Cr in 2021 to ₹1,550 Cr in 2025, and could reach roughly ₹6,030 Cr by 2030. Rentomojo already had an estimated 42-47% share of the organised market in FY25. The Other Side Of The Model The same model that gives RentoMojo an easy route to operating leverage also increases complexities. The company has to not only spend money to acquire customers, but throughout the lifecycle of the customer and even after the customer has ended the relationship. The cost of collections, refurbishing and redeploying the asset has to be recovered through the rental fees and other costs paid by the customer during the lifetime of their relationship. Maximising this and recovering the cost faster will be the key challenge for RentoMojo. One way to do that will be to increase the cost of rentals, but this could adversely affect new customer acquisition. So the journey to maximising the profits will need the right spurs at different levels. In FY26, RentoMojo spent ₹28 Cr on logistics, ₹38 Cr on contractual manpower, ₹19 Cr on refurbishment and ₹21 Cr on performance marketing. These are recurring costs that can rise as the company adds subscribers and expands its asset base. As a listed company, these cost centres will become a key focus for investors examining the company’s trajectory. Depreciation is another important part of the equation. This rose 44% to ₹70 Cr in FY26 as the company invested more heavily in rental assets. At a certain point, assets will have to be written off and the model and category is such that procurement of new assets cannot halt. These are risks that investors have not yet had to consider because the company’s disclosures are only just beginning. The company needs to keep its assets productive for longer, control refurbishment costs and redeploy them quickly when customers return them. This makes the quality of RentoMojo’s profits an important metric to watch. RentoMojo has a growing market, a strong market position and the ability to generate revenue from the same asset multiple times. But investors will also want to see whether that growth can translate into sustainable profits. As of March 31, 2026, RentoMojo had 2.54 Lakh live subscribers across 29 cities and 8.51 Lakh live rental items, according to its RHP. Investors will be watching both numbers closely, particularly the company’s asset utilisation rate, as it expands. Competition adds another layer of potential risk for investors in the long run. Furlenco is said to be eyeing an IPO in the second half of 2027. The RentoMojo rival saw a 20X growth in profits in FY26, which has allowed it to start talking to investors to raise a pre-IPO round as well as a public listing in the next 12-14 months. RentoMojo’s First-Mover Premium RentoMojo is the first established player in its category to go public. This scarcity could work in the favour of the IPO investors and the listing could be at a high premium though nothing is certain. A similar pattern played out with Urban Company’s listing last year. Limited float and the scarcity value attached to a consumer tech IPO could result in high initial gains, but the real test anyway will be whether RentoMojo can sustain earnings after the listing. If the stock lists at a high valuation, the margin for error will be small. Investors are likely to watch the next three to four quarters to see whether profitability holds up as RentoMojo scales. The narrative is familiar in the startup ecosystem: companies can post strong IPO numbers, step up spending on new categories or markets after listing, and see profits come under pressure again. For RentoMojo, the primary objective will be to not be part of this narrative. Following the 25th-anniversary commemoration of the Sept. 11 attacks, news media outlets reported U.S. President Donald Trump planned to fly to Ireland for the weekend to take in the Irish Open at Trump International Golf Club in Doonbeg.
Snopes received a reader's email asking, "Is it true that in Ireland in flight path for Shannon airport is a F*** Trump message in someone's yard?" The reader attached an image of the alleged sign — apparently captured from a high-angle position, similar to that of a drone — showing a grassy field, with the "U" in the first word marked with an asterisk.
A reverse image search found users sharing the same image on Bluesky, Facebook, Threads and TikTok (archived), some also claiming the sign appeared along the flight path into Shannon Airport in County Clare.
(@electra75 via Threads)
Snopes could not independently verify the sign's authenticity as of this writing, but did note a report about the image from CorkBeo, a publication primarily covering matters involving Ireland's County Cork. We reached out to the White House to request comment about the subject matter and will update this article if we receive further information.
The CorkBeo article cited as its source a video that Irish personality Ray Foley posted on Sept. 9, interviewing a woman who said she asked her husband to help prepare the sign for Trump's trip.
Foley's post says the woman, not identified by name, sent a message and the image to him, saying she prepared a "warm welcome" on the flight path into Shannon Airport "for the guest this weekend" — referencing Trump. "We've already had a few black helicopter flybys," the message apparently read.
Speaking about her husband, whom she identified as Paul, the woman reportedly said the following:
I've been troubling him for a long time to do this because we knew he [Trump] was gonna be comin' and I just said, "Come on, come on, keep needlin', and keep putting the idea in his head," so, I think he just gave up and said, "Come on, we'll do it."
We contacted a Foley representative with Today FM's owner, Bauer Media Audio Ireland, to ask for contact information pertaining to the people who created the supposed sign and will add more details if we receive a response.
BBC reported Air Force One, with Trump onboard, would fly into Dublin Airport on Sept. 12, and into Shannon Airport later the same day. CorkBeo's article featured news of a second protest sign that appeared in Dublin, reading "No Kings," as well as mentioning Gaza, Iran and ICE. Reuters published a photo confirming the Dublin sign's authenticity.
For further reading, we previously investigated a rumor claiming an Irish priest said, "We pray for Donald Trump, the Lord will take him."

The construction of the approach road to the Pavangad–Puthiyappa railway overbridge (Pavangad ROB) is set to resume after the Roads and Bridges Development Corporation of Kerala (RBDCK) approved a revised design to overcome the hurdle posed by underground power cables.
The Kerala State Electricity Board (KSEB) had served a notice to the Public Works Department (PWD) directing it to stop piling work after 110-kV and 11-kV underground power cables were found passing through the site where the approach road was being constructed. The cables were detected during trial piling work.
KSEB had initially proposed shifting about 350 metres of the cables from the construction site to the service road. The relocation was estimated to cost around ₹5.5 crore, creating a substantial additional financial burden and making it difficult to complete the approach road using the funds already sanctioned.
RBDCK subsequently explored an alternative to avoid shifting the 110-kV cable. Under the revised design, the number of piles will be increased at locations where the high-voltage cable passes beneath the proposed approach road. At four locations, the number of piles will be increased from three to four, allowing construction to proceed without damaging the underground cable.
The revised design will also reduce the length of cable that needs to be shifted, thereby bringing down the additional cost. RBDCK has approved the structural modification, allowing the approach road to be constructed within the existing allocation.
The 11-kV cable, however, will have to be relocated. KSEB has submitted an estimate of ₹38 lakh to RBDCK for shifting the cable. The construction work is expected to begin after the PWD gives the required approval.
The Pavangad ROB was constructed 11 years ago at a cost of around ₹5.7 crore. However, it has remained unusable in the absence of an approach road. The State government sanctioned ₹12.82 crore for the construction of the approach road more than a year ago.

Sanika Chandrakant Mane’s early strike proved decisive as India qualified for the junior women's hockey World Cup by winning the AHF Junior Asia Cup title for the third time in a row after defeating China 1-0 in a closely fought summit clash, here Sunday.
Sanika struck in the 17th minute as the defending champions retained their continental crown.
The title clash began with nervous energy on both sides, with neither team able to establish control in the early exchanges. China enjoyed greater possession and looked to put India under pressure, but the defending champions remained composed, soaking up the pressure and working hard to negotiate the opening phase without conceding.
As the quarter wore on, India’s defensive structure grew stronger, ensuring the hosts were unable to create a clear-cut opening.
India, however, made their first real opening count. Two minutes into the second quarter, Sanika showed excellent awareness and intelligent off-the-ball movement to sneak in behind a Chinese defender and position herself just five metres from goal. She got her stick to a long slap-push into the Chinese circle and produced a deft deflection that beat goalkeeper Xu Mengjiao to put India ahead.
China came closest to restoring parity when they earned the only penalty corner of the match. However, their direct effort was ruled out after the ball entered the goal above the permitted height of the backboard, much to the relief of the Indian contingent and the disappointment of the home crowd.
India then came close to doubling their lead just two minutes before half-time when captain Khaidem Shileima Chanu found space for a shot on target, but the Chinese goalkeeper reacted sharply to palm the effort away.
India took their slender 1-0 advantage into the break, setting up a tense second half.
China resumed with renewed intent and came close to an equaliser seven minutes into the third quarter. A well-worked move saw a Chinese attacker overlap from the baseline before sending a dangerous cut-back into the area in front of goal, but India’s defence read the danger perfectly and intercepted the pass before it could reach its intended target.
The final quarter turned into a test of India’s defensive resolve. The defending champions stayed disciplined, compact and alert around their circle, closing down spaces and repeatedly frustrating the hosts’ attacking moves.
China pressed for the equaliser in the closing stages, but India held their shape and defended their slender advantage with composure to seal a memorable 1-0 victory and lift the trophy.
India finished the tournament unbeaten. After topping the Elite Pool with three wins and a draw, they thrashed South Korea 5-1 in the semi-finals before edging China 1-0 in the final to successfully defend their title and become three-time champions.
Hockey India announced a prize of Rs 3 lakh for each player and Rs 1.5 lakh for every member of the support staff.

In the days after the assassination of conservative activist and Turning Point cofounder Charlie Kirk, the online reaction was a mess. Graphic videos of the shooting were everywhere within minutes of his death, far-right figures called for violence and vengeance, and right-wing lawmakers and influencers called for the cancellation—and worse—of anyone celebrating. Then, the conspiracy theories began.
It’s been one year since Kirk’s death, and conspiracy theories about the shooting have persisted, supercharged by social media algorithms and right-wing influencers like Candace Owens, who has used her huge following to push baseless allegations about the incident.
Experts believe these conspiracy theories will continue for a long time to come. “There’s no reason to believe conspiracy theories about Kirk’s murder will lose steam anytime soon,” Jared Holt, senior researcher at Open Measures, tells WIRED. “If anything, I expect them to escalate further as the criminal trial against Tyler Robinson, the man accused of killing Kirk, plays out over the next year or so. The trial is bound to draw major media attention and offer conspiracy theorists a source of new material to work from.”
In the immediate aftermath of Kirk’s death, some conspiracy theorists claimed the assassination was a false flag operation designed to deflect attention away from President Donald Trump’s connections to Jeffrey Epstein. Others claimed the entire thing was staged. There was the AI-powered gun theory, the claim that the shooter was a Kirk supporter, and even claims that Kirk was still alive.
But ultimately, the baseless claim that persisted is that someone close to Kirk, or operating on behalf of Israel, was responsible for his death, that Robinson was simply a patsy and what really killed Kirk was an exploding microphone. This is the narrative that has been central to Owens’ months-long conspiracy theory campaign. Her Kirk content has racked up hundreds of millions of views.
Owens’ success is fueled in a large part by the way that social media platforms today encourage their users to post content. “X and YouTube are rife with speculation about Kirk’s death, where it is both still possible to recruit new audiences and monetize them,” Joan Donovan, assistant professor of journalism and emerging media studies at Boston University, tells WIRED.
The end result is that Kirk’s death has become yet another rabbit hole, or a way for viewers to distract themselves from reality. “Candace and other conspiratorial influencers make things seem much more mysterious and exciting,” Renée DiResta, an associate research professor at Georgetown University who tracks disinformation, tells WIRED. “For many, her explanations are preferable to the reality of an act of violence by a solo individual.”
There have already been real world repercussions: Researchers at the Network Contagion Research Institute recently found that “Candace Owens caused a measurable, statistically significant surge in death threats and calls for violence against [Charlie Kirk’s wife] Erika Kirk.” In May, a man was arrested for allegedly threatening to kill Erica Kirk ahead of her appearance at a Turning Point USA event in San Antonio, though the man has yet to be charged. Owens did not respond to a request for comment.
Erica Kirk and Turning Point have repeatedly called for Owens and others to stop spreading baseless rumours about the assassination. While those calls have not been heeded, Turning Point believes the impact the conspiracy theories are having is fading.
“The conspiracy theories have much less reach and potency now than they did six months ago, and I think I’ll say the same six months from now,” Andrew Kolvet, a Turning Point spokesperson, tells WIRED. “They won’t stop because many of these personalities were completely unknown and broke before Charlie was killed and this is their money maker, but their influence and credibility has collapsed and will continue to do so.”
But some experts disagree, arguing that conspiratorial thinking has been an aspect of American life for decades.
“Historically, this is quite normal,” Joseph Uscinski, professor of political science at the University of Miami and author of American Conspiracy Theories, tells WIRED. “Majorities of Americans have believed for decades that JFK was killed by a conspiracy rather than by a lone gunman. In fact almost 80 percent of Americans believed in the 1970s there was a conspiracy behind the assassination.”

Wisconsin congressman survives emergency plane landing, swims to safety
A Republican congressman from Wisconsin has described how he and a pilot had to swim to safety after the plane they were traveling in made an emergency landing in a lake.
Tom Tiffany said he was traveling aboard a small single-engine plane Saturday evening when the aircraft lost power as it approached Wausau Downtown Airport.
The Marathon County Sheriff's Office said in a statement the pilot Leonard Boltz made an emergency landing on Lake Wausau.
"As the plane began to submerge, we exited the aircraft and swam to a shallow area, where we waited until emergency responders reached us by boat," Tiffany wrote in a post on X.
Tiffany, Wisconsin's Republican gubernatorial nominee, said he was returning home from the La Crosse County Lincoln Day Dinner in Onalaska.
"The 911 call had come in from one of the occupants of the plane. They were able to exit the plane and made the call while they were basically standing on top of the plane," Marathon County Sheriff's Office Lt. Cory Gladden told Wisconsin Public Radio.
According to Gladden's timeline, Tiffany and Boltz were in the water for about 20 minutes before emergency responders located them. Gladden said initial information indicates the plane experienced mechanical failure.
Tiffany also shared online that he received stitches above his right eye and was released from the hospital. Boltz was also treated for minor injuries, according to the Marathon County Sheriff's Office.
The Federal Aviation Administration and the National Transportation Safety Board will investigate.
Wisconsin Public Radio's Hope Kirwan contributed to this report.

In 1920, Danish physiologist August Krogh was awarded the Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine “for his discovery of the capillary motor regulating mechanism.”
His work addressed a fundamental question: how does muscle receive enough oxygen when its demand rises sharply during exercise? Krogh showed how changes in the capillary circulation could help meet this increased demand by bringing blood closer to muscle fibres and increasing the surface available for oxygen exchange.
The work had important implications for medicine because understanding how oxygen reaches tissues is central to conditions in which blood supply is impaired, including cardiovascular disease, peripheral vascular disease, diabetes and wounds that fail to heal. The principles of microcirculation and tissue oxygenation that Krogh helped establish are now relevant to understanding tissue injury, wound healing, exercise physiology and the effects of impaired blood flow.
From zoology to physiology
Schack August Steenberg Krogh was born on November 15, 1874, in Grenaa, Denmark. He entered the University of Copenhagen in 1893, initially studying medicine before turning to zoology.
At the university, he joined the laboratory of physiologist Christian Bohr and became interested in respiration and the exchange of gases in living organisms. He obtained his zoology degree in 1899 and continued working in Bohr’s laboratory.
Krogh combined experimental biology with quantitative measurements and developed instruments for studying physiological processes. His research included respiration, gas exchange and water and electrolyte regulation.
In 1916, he became professor of zoophysiology at the University of Copenhagen.
The oxygen supply problem
Krogh focused on how oxygen moves from blood to tissue.
Muscles can increase their oxygen consumption considerably during exercise. Oxygen carried in the blood must diffuse from capillaries through surrounding tissue before reaching individual cells. The distance between a cell and a perfused capillary therefore affects oxygen delivery.
Krogh investigated capillary distribution in muscle and compared resting and active tissues. He observed that more capillaries appeared to contain blood when muscles were active.
In papers published in The Journal of Physiology in 1919, he combined these observations with mathematical calculations of oxygen diffusion. He proposed that bringing additional capillaries into functional use during activity would increase the available exchange surface and shorten the distance oxygen had to travel through tissue.
This work formed the basis of what became known as the Krogh cylinder model, a conceptual model describing oxygen diffusion from a capillary into the surrounding tissue.
The Nobel-winning discovery
Krogh went further than describing differences in capillary perfusion. He proposed a capillary motor regulating mechanism, through which capillary diameter and blood content could change according to the functional needs of tissue.
The Nobel Committee recognised this work in 1920.
In his Nobel lecture, Krogh described how the number of blood-filled capillaries varied with the activity of tissue. He argued that additional capillaries were brought into use during muscular activity, helping increase the area available for oxygen exchange.
The discovery shifted attention towards the microcirculation — the network of small vessels responsible for delivering oxygen and nutrients to tissues and carrying away metabolic products.
What modern physiology says
Some elements of Krogh’s original explanation have since been revised.
Modern studies do not support the simple idea that skeletal-muscle capillaries are routinely switched between completely closed and open states. Nor are capillaries considered the principal site of active blood-flow regulation.
Much of that regulation occurs upstream, particularly in arterioles. Modern microscopy has also shown that many muscle capillaries are already perfused at rest.
Capillary recruitment is therefore understood more precisely as changes in the pattern and extent of capillary perfusion rather than simply the opening of previously closed vessels.
Krogh’s central insight, however, remains important: the organisation of the capillary network and the distance oxygen must travel through tissue are crucial determinants of oxygen delivery.
From capillaries to insulin
Krogh’s career later intersected with another major medical development -- insulin.
In 1922, he and his wife, physician Marie Krogh, travelled to North America. Marie had diabetes and encouraged him to investigate the newly developed insulin treatment.
During the trip, Krogh visited Toronto, where Frederick Banting, Charles Best and their colleagues had developed methods for producing insulin. Krogh subsequently obtained permission to produce insulin using the Toronto method in Scandinavia.
Back in Denmark, he worked with physician Hans Christian Hagedorn and pharmacist August Kongsted. The first Danish patient was treated with insulin in March 1923, and Nordisk Insulinlaboratorium was established that year.
Scientific legacy
Krogh continued studying physiology after receiving the Nobel Prize. His work on respiration, gas exchange and the microcirculation demonstrated how physical principles and quantitative measurements could be used to understand biological processes.
The Krogh cylinder remains a useful conceptual model for studying oxygen diffusion, although modern research has refined the model using more detailed knowledge of blood flow, oxygen gradients and the three-dimensional structure of capillary networks.
Krogh retired from the University of Copenhagen in 1945 but continued his research. He died in Copenhagen on September 13, 1949, aged 74.
More than a century later, oxygen delivery to tissues is understood to involve cardiac output, blood flow, arteriolar regulation, capillary perfusion, blood oxygen content, diffusion and tissue metabolism.
Krogh’s original explanation has evolved, but his decision to study circulation at the microscopic level changed the understanding of how blood supplies individual tissues. His work established the capillary network and oxygen diffusion as central to the study of tissue oxygenation and microcirculation.

Mathematician and author Steven Strogatz starts to cry when he talks about the artificial-intelligence-driven breakthroughs in his field over the past week.
“The science is thrilling,” the Cornell University professor says, “but there's a lot of human unpleasantness going with it.”
On Tuesday, OpenAI said it had used tens of thousands of agents to solve a 90-year-old math problem, which had a $1 million prize attached. The solution—which still needs to be independently verified—builds on a strategy developed by Spanish mathematicians Diego Córdoba and Luis Martínez-Zoroa. The announcement was marred by claims from another mathematician, Tristan Buckmaster, who says that OpenAI rushed ahead to solve the problem after learning of his work alongside Anthropic researcher Levent Alpöge. Buckmaster claims OpenAI also tried to influence who got credit for the work.
The rupture is a symptom of the rapid changes taking place in the field due to AI advancements and what Strogatz—who cowrote Big Math, a book about how math is slipping away from human understanding that will be out in November—describes as corporate labs’ race to grab headlines ahead of blockbuster IPOs.
Last week, Anthropic said Claude had proved 29,500 small theorems while formalizing an existing proof of the infamous Fermat’s Last Theorem—a project other mathematicians had been working on for years. In August, OpenAI announced it had made advancements in 10 other long-standing mathematical problems. AI is making mathematical breakthroughs happen faster, Strogatz says, but what it means for the experts who have dedicated their lives to the field is decidedly less clear.
“I think the year 2026 is going to be remembered as either an annus mirabilis or annus horribilis for mathematics because so much has happened,” Strogatz tells WIRED, sitting in front of a wall covered in framed university honors. “You will not be able to compete without AI in the future if you want to do breakthrough math,” he adds.
His book collaborator, Alex Townsend has already been using the technology to accelerate their research. He recently used ChatGPT to help solve a decades-old numerical linear algebra problem. Toward the end of the interview, Townsend walks into Strogatz’s attic. Townsend and his coauthor said that without the technology, the volume of work required and cost-reward ratio would have been unfeasibly high. But while AI has helped his work, it’s also changing how Townsend views the field and his role in it.
"I actually feel kind of upset that I've dedicated 15 years of my life to research mathematics, and at a point in my career where I'm very productive and at my peak strength as a mathematician, that peak skill is no longer there. Something is able to surpass me,” he says. “Before, it was so exciting because you're world-class, doing great research, pushing back the frontier of knowledge, and now I don't feel like I'm the one at the frontier of knowledge. I'm the one with an AI agent, which feels very different actually. And I feel totally threatened by it."
For his part, Strogratz likens the current moment for math to a horror movie, as AI, driven by systems that are not well understood, creeps closer and closer. “But we're not at the end of the movie yet,” Strogratz says. “Instinctively, I'm really terrified.”
Here, he reflects on what the AI breakthroughs of 2026 mean for math, mathematicians, and humanity. His answers have been lightly edited for brevity.
On the significance of solving the Navier-Stokes existence and smoothness problem:
It's a very theoretical math problem of essentially no interest to a working engineer in civil engineering or aerodynamics. It’s a very, very arcane question.
This is a marketing device for them to prove how good their machines are. Nobody cares about the Navier-Stokes singularity problem; only a tiny subset of pure mathematicians care about that. It doesn't affect anybody except it's maybe worth a trillion dollars for OpenAI to show they're better than Anthropic.
On who deserves the credit for solving the problem, and the million-dollar prize:
I would love to see Córdoba and Martínez-Zoroa get the money, but let's be careful here because there's another pair of people who should be talked about, who are Tristan Buckmaster at New York University and a young mathematician named Levent Alpöge.
Arguably, you could say Buckmaster should get the money because Buckmaster posted a couple of days before OpenAI with Levent the solution to three very closely related problems to the Navier-Stokes. They're slightly easier cases, but they're very serious, important problems in their own right. They were on the trail, and I think they would've gotten there, but we don't know.
I don't know Buckmaster, but from what I can see, he is very scrupulous about giving credit. He's being a real gentleman about it. I have a lot of respect for how he's been handling it. I feel bad for him that he's not going to end up getting what he's devoted his career to.
On whether AI still needs human mathematicians:
We need proof digestion, which is explaining it in terms that human beings can understand and appreciate. Right now, the best digestion is still coming from human experts. Is that where we make our last stand? Are we going to be the great interpreters of the things that the machines do? I suspect that will be our role for a little while longer, that we will have that special skill of translating, though I do expect that will be surpassed by machines soon enough, too.
Applied math is messy because it deals with the real world. The messier the subject gets, the more resistant it will be to AI. So something like economics or international relations or sociology, these other disciplines, you would think will be relatively safe for a while.
You could do infinitely many things in math, but only some of them will be interesting to human beings. So who will be the arbiter of good mathematical taste? Will the machines have taste that will resonate with us? They've shown no sign of that yet. But I don't see why the machines couldn't train on aesthetic questions to become very good at that, too.
On what AI means for math:
Pure math is being devastated or revolutionized, depending on your point of view. A lot of the questions that we love are getting answered. A lot of us are not happy about it. We love those questions. We love the challenge of thinking about them. But if you only care about the answers and not the struggle, then you're happy.
But then let's take the other side of it: It's also very democratizing. Now everyone can participate in mathematics. That's a reasonable argument. I don't want to be in the ivory tower and say: ‘Oh no, it's gross. I'm 67. I put in a lifetime of training to be able to do this stuff. I don't want you guys getting in here without putting in the work.’
On what it means for human mathematicians:
There are people who were always thrilled being the first to climb the mountain. But what will be lost is that motivation. It won't be possible for us to even aspire to climb the highest mountains because the machines will always get there first. We'll lose every time. So if you were ever driven by that, that game is over.
Now you could say: ‘Why is that the only game in town?’ It's not. I don't play at Wimbledon, but I still play tennis. We're not as good as the best chess engines, but we still love chess. Is that the future of mathematics, that it's a beautiful game that we are second rate at, but we still enjoy it?
It could be, but that has a lot of implications. If that's all that math is, then why would anyone pay us to do it? When all that work is being done by AI, there's no need to put the money into human mathematicians doing that kind of work. And that seems like a very possible trajectory unless we stop it.
On what it means for humanity:
I feel like we're the first battleground here in math where we're on the brink of losing human understanding, and maybe fortunately the stakes are pretty low, but we're going to see what that feels like for humanity. Are we the canary in the coal mine for what's going to face humanity?

73 goals from dropping deep - we ask Kane to break down how he did it
- Published
As Harry Kane's career has progressed, the 33-year-old has taken an increasingly complete role, popping up to collect the ball as deep as his own box.
Many wonder why a talisman tasked with scoring doesn't spend more time closer to goal, but last season the England and Bayern Munich striker scored 73 goals - the highest tally of his career - while playing deeper than he ever has done.
When I mention this paradox, a grin spreads across his face.
"Until you really understand football and understand what we've been talking about, it's so easy to say 'stay high, you're going to score' but it doesn't work like that," Kane says.
I sat down to speak to Kane about the finer details of his game, shedding light on his unique role.
Watching Kane train, his professionalism is palpable. England's record goalscorer is one of the first out on the pitch. The younger players indulge in playful kick-ups as he watches, engaged in conversation with a member of staff.
From a distance, that makes it easy to confuse him with a coach but, given his role on the pitch, it is a fitting mistake.
Kane's style of play reflects who he is as a person, with those who know him saying he is well-rounded and humble on and off the pitch.
The season is in its infancy but Kane isn't basking in the success of the past 12 months. With only five days of pre-season training under his belt, the England captain completed 90 minutes of Bayern's 2-1 win over Borussia Dortmund to lift the German Super Cup.
As demanding as his roaming role is, he has taken the physical demands of it in his stride. Across the past six seasons, STATSports - a sports technology company Kane has invested in - found his distance covered, high-speed running and accelerations were up 8%, 22% and 42% respectively.
And given how the tactical landscape has changed over that time, it is particularly impressive Kane has been able to not only keep up, but stay ahead.
"Over the last five or six years, man-to-man pressure has become bigger," Kane says.
"European football is physical and top teams are trying to win the ball back high, trusting their defenders and midfielders to defend man for man to win their battles."
Given that change, the best teams have recruited physical athletes and brilliant dribblers who can beat their man when the game becomes a series of one-against-ones.
Kane, not known for his dribbling - and by his own admission "not the fastest", has thrived on his own terms.
Against Dortmund, there was a specific moment Kane dropped deep, looking to arrive in space unmarked. Recognising the danger, two players converged on the Englishman.
Kane's dribbling is cerebral. His speed of thought provides him solutions to problems others would attempt to solve with their feet alone.
After getting low and using his strength to shrug centre-back Waldemar Anton off him, Kane rose, slightly adjusting his body to the right. These micro-adjustments are a hallmark of his game and through them he is able to shift an entire team's momentum.
Fooled by this feint, Daniel Svensson and Jobe Bellingham found themselves wrong-footed as Kane snapped the ball back the other way, opening up the entire pitch from within Bayern's half.
1 of 4
Earlier this year, Bayern boss Vincent Kompany shed light on Kane's unique role, explaining it as being 50% coached and 50% Kane deciding what to do.
"I think it's partly instinct, using my football brain and getting the feeling on the pitch," says Kane. "If, for example, I want to drop and see if the centre-back really wants to commit, he might commit into midfield, but is he going to commit if I drop all the way to my box?
"After the first five or 10 minutes you really get an understanding of how the opposition are going to play, which dictates how I play."
There is a shared understanding at Bayern of an approach that allows team-mates to make sense of rotations that, to the naked eye, appear random.
Kane, who is given more freedom than most, is at the centre of it.
"I feel like my position now is as one of two 10s, and you work together," he says. "You can double up on one side to overload, which causes the opposition centre-backs a problem of who to mark.
"If they want to mark both, they've got to go man-to-man and then that leaves space for our wingers or full-backs to run into.
"It's posing all these questions to the opposition but, personally, I love having someone close to me who I can link with."
Kane built his reputation playing as a lone number nine, so it is interesting to hear him identify instead as a number 10 - in a front two.
"When you're the number nine on your own you can get marked by two centre-backs and you struggle to get touches on the ball," he says. "You're relying on everyone else to find you with the ball."
Showing Kane two clips from last season, I ask him to talk through what was going through his head.
"The thing with our formation is, as long as there's someone in each position, it doesn't really matter who it is. Lucho [Luis Diaz] in this clip is playing as one of those 10s.
"I've come off to try and create a bit of space and Lucho's gone through the centre."
Distracted by Kane's dropping-deep movement, one of the opposition midfielders is pulled towards him. This creates space, allowing Joshua Kimmich to punch the ball through to Diaz.
"I think it's Serge [Gnabry] making the run in behind which takes the defenders back, which allows me and Lucho that space in between. Lucho lays it off and whenever I'm in that position, around 20-25 yards out, I'm always looking if I can get my shot off."
It is one of many examples of Kane initially dropping deep before scoring.
"By playing deep when the play develops, I end up coming into a number 10 spot when everyone's dropped," he says. "I can get shots off from the edge of the box, which is a big strength of mine, or I'm running off the back of players where no-one's picking me up - because the midfielder finds it hard to [track]."
1 of 3
The second clip is from Bayern's Champions League tie against Club Brugge.
Usually Kane is marked by an opposition centre-back, but the Belgian club give that responsibility to their holding midfielder - something he recognises and exploits.
Lennart Karl scores without Kane touching the ball, but the striker's involvement is undeniable.
"These are the little runs, again, not everyone sees," Kane explains. "With Jamal Musiala and Lenny, they're so good at receiving the ball and dribbling so there'll be times where I will actually stay higher and let those guys get on the ball a bit deeper, and I'll try and make runs in behind.
"Without changing my game too much, I try and complement the players around me.
"I know Lenny is so good in those pockets and when he gets there, I'm more thinking of running in behind because, one, he can play me in and I can go through on goal, or two, he can dribble with the ball and do exactly what happened here.
"As soon as Lenny gets in that pocket I make the run and not always to get the ball, sometimes it is just to drag the defender away.
"Now he's one-against-one with a centre-back in the middle of the pitch and that's dangerous for any centre-back."
1 of 3
With the Ballon d'Or announcement on the horizon, Kane's name is in the conversation, primarily for the sheer volume of goals he has scored. What is easier to miss in that debate is the rest of his game.
Kane plays for the team in each phase of the game across the entirety of the pitch, while at the same time producing extraordinary individual numbers that match the likes of Cristiano Ronaldo, Lionel Messi and Erling Haaland.
He has described himself as playing in the role of a number 10, nine and six at times.
In a football world of specific and heavily drilled tactical roles, that is quite the achievement.

Scholar Rock on Friday received Food and Drug Administration approval for the first-ever therapy that targets the loss of muscle in spinal muscle atrophy, raising hopes that patients with the rare neurological disorder might have a better chance of moving and walking independently.
The FDA approved the drug, Isembyld, for use in adults and children 2 years and older who are currently receiving SMA therapies that target SMN2, a key gene for neurons that control movement. A late-stage clinical trial found that, when combined with an SMN2-targeting drug, Isembyld caused young patients’ motor skills to improve after a year, while those in a placebo group declined, a difference that was statistically significant.
“Today’s FDA approval of Isembyld marks a defining moment for the SMA community,” said David Hallal, CEO of Scholar Rock, in a press release. “After decades of failed industry-wide efforts to unlock the potential of myostatin inhibition, Scholar Rock has delivered a therapeutic breakthrough.”

The family of a British father who was found dead in the Caribbean in January is urging authorities in Grenada to work with UK police to uncover the truth about his death.
Andrew Frederick’s body was found in the property he was staying at in Grenada on 4 January. An autopsy, performed in the same week by a privately hired pathologist, concluded that the 47-year-old’s death was a homicide.
In June, Grenada’s director of public prosecution, Howard Pinnock, said at a press conference that Frederick’s and another pending case would be sent to the coroner to determine the cause of death “because there is no basis in terms of both investigations that any homicide has occurred”.
After a sustained campaign by the family, British authorities became involved and Frederick’s body was repatriated to the UK last month, where a second autopsy was carried out.
The UK coroner has noted that Frederick’s organs are missing and the death is currently “unascertained”.
At the start of an inquest at West London coroner’s court last week, senior coroner Lydia Brown said the Metropolitan police are now investigating Frederick’s death.
The family, who attended the court hearing by video link, said the coroner’s “decision to suspend Andrew’s inquest to allow the Metropolitan police to conduct a criminal investigation marks a significant turning point”.
In statement to the Guardian, they urged Grenada and the UK to work together to find out what happened to Frederick.
“We are encouraged and grateful that the Metropolitan police investigation is now under way. Justice for Andrew depends on everyone with the power to act, on both sides of the Atlantic, doing what is right,” the statement said.
It added: “Andrew was a deeply loved member of a close-knit family; a son, brother, father and grandson. He leaves behind his cherished daughter, who should be growing up with him beside her, not learning to live without him.
“Our family remain determined to uncover the truth about what happened to Andrew and to see justice follow. We hope this ruling is the step that finally enables a complete, properly coordinated investigation and that everyone who can assist will now do so.”
Earlier this year, the family had called for an urgent review of the policies governing UK assistance to the loved ones of Britons killed abroad, after they were forced to launch their own public appeals for information, and commission an independent forensic pathologist and a private investigation.
“Eight months have passed since Andrew was taken from us. In that time, we have learned what no family should ever have to learn, and fought battles no family should ever face alone,” their statement said.
It added: “We have relentlessly sought answers and support while carrying the weight of Andrew’s loss and the horror of what was done to him. We still do not have a complete account of what happened, and important questions remain unanswered.
“We hope the Grenadian authorities with knowledge of the case will now share that information and work collaboratively with the Metropolitan police, allowing the investigation to proceed without further delay. We are also seeking urgent answers as to why Andrew’s organs were absent when his body was returned to the UK for further examination.”
In Grenada, the Office of the Commissioner told the Guardian that “the matter will be progressing to the coroner’s court for the parish of Saint George”.
A Met spokesperson said: “The Met is investigating the death of 47-year-old Andrew Donald Frederick, who died in Grenada on 4 January.
“Mr Frederick’s family are being supported by specialist officers.
“No arrests have been made at this stage and inquiries are ongoing.”
Officers have contacted the Royal Grenada Police Force (RGPF) to offer assistance and discuss how the investigation can be progressed.
Inquest proceedings have been suspended pending the outcome of police investigations.

Himalayan ‘glacier bankruptcy’ threatens water security for 2 billion in Asia
Glacier mass loss is causing the region to approach ‘peak water’, the point when river flows stop rising and start declining
The Himalayas are approaching a tipping point as glaciers melt faster than a decade ago, threatening water security as the region approaches “peak water” by mid-century, according to a study released this month.
As glaciers retreat, they are leaving behind unstable glacial lakes held back by little more than loose rock and ice, above valleys where millions of people live, the study found.
The study was produced by Systemiq, a sustainability advisory firm, together with the Integrated Mountain Initiative, the International Centre for Integrated Mountain Development, and India’s G.B. Pant National Institute of Himalayan Environment.
Himalayan glacier mass loss has accelerated in recent decades, while only 21 glaciers were currently monitored on the ground out of an estimated 40,000 glaciers across the Hindu Kush-Himalaya region, the study found.

U.S. President Donald Trump on Sunday (September 13, 2026) called on Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy to halt strikes on Russian oil refineries and other infrastructure used to produce and distribute diesel, saying the attacks are causing a global shortage. He spoke after diesel prices in the U.S. hit a record on Friday (September 11, 2026), soaring past $6 a gallon on average.
Ukraine has for months been targeting Russia's oil and gas industry with long-range strikes, prompting fuel rationing across the country and causing Moscow to ban diesel exports in July, removing supplies from the already tight global market.
But the global crunch also came after the war on Iran curtailed oil shipments through the Strait of Hormuz.
Fuel prices are weighing on Americans as they prepare to vote in mid-term elections in November.
Mr. Trump was asked by a reporter if he had spoken with Mr. Zelenskyy following his recent conversation with Russia's Vladimir Putin. He responded by calling on Mr. Zelenskyy to halt strikes against Russia.
"Mr Zelenskyy has to do one thing. He has to stop knocking out diesel fuel in Russia," Mr. Trump told reporters on the sidelines of the Irish Open.
"We spoke to Mr Zelenskyy about it. There are plenty of other targets. Don't hit diesel fuel, because that's hurting, that's hurting the world," he said.
According to a report published by the International Energy Agency, net exports of diesel and gasoil from the Gulf countries in August stood at "just over a quarter" of what they were before the war on Iran began in February.
"Disruptions to Russia's refining system and a near-halt to product exports following intensified Ukrainian attacks have compounded these losses," the IEA wrote. It added that in February, combined next exports of diesel and gasoil from the Gulf and Russia "accounted for almost 45% of global seaborne trade."
Kyiv says Russia's oil industry both funds and directly fuels Moscow's more than four-year-old invasion of Ukraine.
Russia has ramped up its air campaign against Ukraine in recent weeks, using ballistic missiles and jet-powered drones to pierce Ukraine's defences. Moscow's attacks have targeted Ukraine's power grid ahead of winter in what officials say is meant to demoralise civilians.

“The Odyssey” continued its voyage at the summit of the South Korean box office during the weekend of Sept. 11–13.

Securing its sixth consecutive weekend victory, the blockbuster pushed its cumulative South Korean gross to $89.6 million from 10,782,715 total admissions since its Aug. 5 launch.
“Obsession” climbed to second place in its second weekend, pulling in $1.4 million from 176,479 admissions across 845 screens. The film accounted for 18.6% of the weekend market, lifting its cume to $3.7 million from 474,818 total viewers.

Last year, the District Child Welfare Committee in Chennai dealt with a case where a 15-year-old girl from Nepal had married a 28-year-old man working in Chennai, the two having met on Instagram. With the help of friends, they got married in Chennai.
A month into the marriage, the girl was traced after she made a call to her sister in Nepal. The girl’s family lodged a complaint with the police following which India Child Protection, a civil society organisation working in the area of child protection, intervened to rescue the girl.
Social media and online dating are increasingly exposing vulnerable girls to greater risk of child marriage.
“With advancement in digital communication, the modus operandi in child marriage is changing, making more children vulnerable,” says Bhuwan Ribhu, a child rights activist and founder of Just Rights for Children.
Bhuwan Ribhu says trafficking is a borderless crime, and it requires a borderless response. Online methods of enticement or grooming for marriage, sexual abuse and trafficking have become possible irrespective of distance and geography.
In a study taken by NGO Save the Children, they observed that girls in India faced greater online risk of child marriage and trafficking during the pandemic. The agency continues to work with children and teachers to raise awareness about staying safe online.
According to the National Family Health Survey (2019-21), the national average in India for child marriage is 23%. The prevalence rate in India for child marriage has fallen by 10 per cent. The Bal Vivah Mukt Bharat campaign launched by the Central Government in November 2024 promises to make India child marriage-free by 2030 and is seeing various state governments running different initiatives.
A dedicated CMPO needed
Natharsha Malim H, state coordinator - Tamil Nadu, India Child Protection, says while Tamil Nadu has been making steady progress in reporting and stopping child marriages, gaps continue to exist.
Tamil Nadu, he says, does not have Child Marriage Prohibition Officers (CMPOs) that are appointed to prevent marriages, gather evidence, raise awareness and report data. The District Social Welfare Officer (DSWO) is notified as the Child Marriage Prohibition Officer of the concerned district.
“This is an additional role that the DSWO takes up. We have been asking for a dedicated person to be appointed as many other states have done based on a Supreme Court recommendation,” says Malim.
For example, in Karnataka, the Department of Women and Child Welfare has included pre-university (PU) college principals as child marriage prohibition officers, whose responsibility is to prevent any girl child studying in their college from marrying before 18 years.
Dedicated officials tasked with curbing this practice is particularly required in places such as Salem, Dindigul, Namakal and Cuddalore which has reported maximum cases of child marriages, says Malim. Grama panchayats have to be empowered in these districts to curb child marriage
A rule book for intervention
Malim notes that State Governments have to draw up a Standard Operating Procedure (SOP) for elimination of child marriages.
“The Supreme Court came out with a landmark judgement on child marriages in October 2024, but Tamil Nadu is yet to come out with an SOP,” he says.
Panchayats that make an earnest effort to stop child marriage should be rewarded; and the bravery of young girls that resist coercion by family into child marriage should also be acknowledged.
Bhuwan Ribhu cites the example of a study done by India Child Protection in 2025, wherein cases in Assam dropped by 84 percent following a continuous crackdown by law-enforcement authorities.
How to report a child marriage
File a complaint with
* Child Marriage Prohibition Officer
* District Magistrate
* Nearest police station
* District Child Protection Unit
* ASHA Unit of District Legal Services Authority
* Bal Vivah Mukt Bharat portal https://stopchildmarriage.wcd.gov.in
Source: Ministry of Women and Child Development
Although Prohibition of Child Marriage Act, 2006 has been in existence for decades, enforcement leaves a lot to be desired.
“With amendments to the law and judgments by the Supreme Court, we have been able to see much impact on the ground, along with greater awareness,” says Ribhu, adding, “awareness needs to be supplemented with the enforcement of policies, accountability of institutions, and the use of technology for monitoring.”
Residents association in Chennai hails UN declaration
On September 4, 2026, when the United Nations General Assembly declared November 27 as the International Day for the Elimination of Child, Early and Forced Marriage, a residents group in Anna Nagar celebrated the announcement.
A small number of residents, close to 150, of Kambar Colony in Anna Nagar gathered at the park in the neighbourhood to watch the live proceedings of the United Nations General Assembly on the designation of November 27 as the International Day for the Elimination of Child, Early and Forced Marriage.
The programme was organised by the ICWO Tamil Nadu and Kambar Colony Welfare Association. The designation is a significant global commitment to strengthening awareness, prevention and action against child, early and forced marriage. This is a victory for children and civil society organisation that have been fighting to end child marriage.
Awareness banners and charts were displayed, and the gathering concluded with an oath-taking ceremony to strengthen the community’s commitment to end child marriage.
ICWO is a partner agency with Just Rights with Children in Chennai, working with educational institutions and communities on rights concerning children.
A.J. Hariharan, founder secretary, ICWO, says reporting is the key to preventing child marriage. He notes: “we work closely with schools and colleges to help eradicate child marriage. All what we ask them is report any cases of child marriage to the helpline number or a teacher.”
ChildLine Helpline 1098 can also be dialled to report a case.

In a boost for the pharmaceutical industry, a European Union Advocate General recommended annulling part of a directive that requires drug and cosmetics manufacturers to finance at least 80% of the costs of wastewater treatment.
The directive, which revised an earlier version and went into effect early last year, was designed to protect human health and the environment from harmful discharges of urban wastewater and ensure cleaner rivers, lakes, groundwater, and coasts across Europe. The effort was projected to save about $7.5 billion annually by 2040.
A key portion of the initiative is a “quaternary treatment stage” that involves removing micropollutants — which are mostly created by pharmaceuticals and cosmetics — from wastewater. Member states must ensure that companies contribute to programs to deal with the waste they generate by December 2028.
