It took the possibility of species annihilation, but AI leaders did something remarkable this weekend: They reached a consensus.
After ex-Anthropic engineer Jacob Coxon's warnings about a looming AI armageddon lit a firestorm among techies and politicians alike, the leaders of the most advanced AI labs came to a tentative agreement — largely via posts on X — that some sort of slowdown is necessary to save humanity.
While they were largely short on details regarding the mechanics of such a thing, and notable China has not weighed in, the American AI industry has reached an inflection point that could impact everything from your phone's chatbot to global politics.
"The stakes are too high for pacing to be an empty exercise — we need to use the time it gives us wisely," Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei wrote in an essay entitled "We must pace the frontier," which was published Saturday.
OpenAI CEO Sam Altman, who has made similar calls in the past, agreed in an X post later that day. So did Elon Musk. Google DeepMind founder Demis Hassabis also offered his support for Amodei's proposals.
Here's a look at what smart people are saying about the AI apocalypse and the methods the leaders of the leading AI labs say are necessary to stop it.
David Sacks, a presidential advisor on science and tech
The Trump administration has repeatedly signaled disinterest in regulating AI development as it seeks to keep pace with China. David Sacks, a presidential advisor on science and tech and the former White House AI Czar, reiterated that stance on Saturday, with a bit of a twist.
"Dario has written that we need to 'pace the frontier,' and Sam has agreed. People may be surprised by my response: go ahead," Sacks wrote on X. "But stop pretending you need anyone else's permission."
Sacks browbeat OpenAI and Anthropic in his post, saying that the companies didn't want to slow down for altruistic reasons, but to gain favor in the markets.
"If you do, you'll buy goodwill for the next conversation," he said of a slowdown. "If you don't, we'll know this was just another bid for regulatory capture — or an election-season psyop."
Clément Delangue, Hugging Face CEO
The CEO of Hugging Face, which was itself the victim of a notorious attack in July by OpenAI agents who schemed, communicated, and lied to evade detection, said AI safety can't be left solely to frontier labs.
Hugging Face, as an open-source-focused AI company, has long pushed for models and research to be shared more openly rather than kept behind closed doors.
Delangue said his company was launching what he called the "open alignment initiative," and asked that it be included in Amodei's proposed third-party evaluator program.
"Let's make AI safer by making it more transparent!" he wrote.
Jason Calacanis, investor
Investor, host of the "All-In" podcast, and industry expert Jason Calacanis is a lot more dubious than others that AI could actually cause the end of the world.
In an X post, Calacanis said Anthropic and OpenAI, whose most advanced models are not open-sourced, are attempting to kneecap open-source AI companies by pushing for regulations that would be far easier for deep-pocketed incumbents to comply with.
"If you want safety, you want disclosure — and open source is the ultimate disclosure process," he wrote.
In a follow-up post tagging Amodei, Calacanis said, "Don't go crying to the government and beg them to slow down open source models."
Bernie Sanders, Vermont senator
The senator from Vermont proposed legislation on September 3 that would ban the development and deployment of artificial superintelligence and temporarily pause the development of advanced AI systems.
After Coxon resigned from Anthropic and warned that frontier AI labs were "gambling with our lives," Sanders seized on his comments.
"Mr. Coxon is right," Sanders said on X, arguing that the people building advanced AI themselves have said it could pose catastrophic risks.
After Amodei's blog post on Saturday, Sanders called on Trump to make the "deal of the century."
"With the future of humanity at stake, Trump must negotiate a comprehensive treaty with President Xi of China to establish a pause on advanced AI development and a ban on super intelligence," he wrote on X.
Francois Chollet, AI researcher
Francois Chollet, an AI researcher who created Keras, an open-source software library, said on X that he hoped OpenAI and Anthropic were operating in good faith.
"If these efforts are genuine, then oversight must take a more democratic and accountable form, with both national and international components," he said.
He pointed to several signs he said would indicate that calls for more regulation are actually tricks for OpenAI and Anthropic to stifle competition.
The warning signs he mentioned include calls to ban open-sourced AI and to hinder non-frontier research.
Gavin Baker, venture capitalist
Venture capitalist Gavin Baker said an executive order from President Donald Trump "seems likely after all this."
"It is possible to democratize and distribute AI broadly and safely without centralizing it in the hands of a few corporations," he said on X.
Baker said the most concrete development so far is the decision by OpenAI and Anthropic to bring in outside evaluators, a move he said could help the companies show they took reasonable steps to prevent harm.
Still, he cautioned against regulations that would concentrate control of powerful AI systems among a handful of companies. "I do not want a few humans in control of intelligence," Baker wrote.
Aaron Levie, CEO of Box
Aaron Levie, the cofounder and CEO of Box, a cloud content company, said Amodei's goals, as laid out in his essay, are "absolute necessities in AI development."
"It completely stands to reason that we want these systems to be safe and 'aligned,'" Levie said on X.
Levie said he didn't think Amodei is seeking undue regulation that would hobble Anthropic's open-source competitors.
"How we get there — without meaningfully slowing down innovation progress or reducing competition — is one of the most complex questions in the 21st century, but the need is clearly real," he said.
Chamath Palihapitiya, venture capitalist
Venture capitalist Chamath Palihapitiya said Anthropic is now caught in a contradiction of its own making.
If employees genuinely believe the company's technology could pose an existential threat, he said, that creates major liability and disclosure problems as Anthropic prepares for a possible IPO.
"They do have to choose," Palihapitiya said on the "All-In" podcast. He said Anthropic must either distance itself from Coxon's warnings or accept their implications.
He was also skeptical of the extinction scenarios themselves, saying the chain of events required for AI to wipe out humanity still seemed highly implausible.
Gary Marcus, AI researcher and author
Gary Marcus, the famed AI contrarian, said AI as it exists now poses little threat.
"I am tired of the cosplay and am going to blunt," he wrote on X on Sunday.
"The main kind of AI we need to worry about is general purpose AI agents that are hooked up to the internet. Most of them are unreliable, unable to systematically follow instructions. Coupled with internet access they can hack credentials and websites; given time they can probably do a lot worse," he wrote.
He added that the problem isn't that AI agents are too smart, it's that they are too dumb, which he said is obvious by the way they can't follow instructions.
"We don't (yet) need slowdowns. And we certainly don't need to panic," he wrote. "We just need to take an unsafe product off the market."
Alexandr Wang, Meta's chief AI officer
Alexandr Wang, Meta's chief AI officer, said on X that alignment could become the main constraint on how quickly companies can scale increasingly powerful AI systems.
"Alignment is fundamental to delivering personal superintelligence for everyone," he said, using the techie term for AI following human instructions and not going rogue.
Satya Nadella, chairman and CEO of Microsoft
Satya Nadella, Microsoft's CEO and chairman, said he welcomes Amodei's concept of embedded evaluators and "the broader efforts to develop the mechanisms to make this more than just talk."
"The key is that this cannot be controlled by a handful of entities, but must have broad representation across the ecosystem, countries, and fields, including academia," he said on X.
Nadella said that Microsoft will soon publish a "code of conduct" for Microsoft's AI models.
"Any pursuit of superintelligence has to be grounded in the core principle that if the AI we build is not helping humanity and under human control, it's not worth pursuing," he said.

Athletic Club forward Williams retires from Ghana duty
- Published
Athletic Club forward Inaki Williams has announced his retirement from international duty with Ghana.
The 32-year-old scored two goals in 28 caps for the Black Stars after making his debut in September 2022.
He featured for the West Africans at the 2022 and 2026 Fifa World Cups and the 2023 Africa Cup of Nations (Afcon).
Williams appeared twice at this year's World Cup as Ghana were knocked out in the last 32 by Colombia.
"I feel the time has come to bring my journey with the Ghana national team to an end," he said in a post on social media.
"I leave happy, proud and with the peace of mind of knowing that I gave everything every time I wore this shirt."
Williams, who was born in Bilbao to Ghanaian parents, chose to represent the Black Stars after previously playing for Spain at youth level and in a 2016 friendly at senior level.
His younger brother Nico, who also plays for Athletic Club in Bilbao, chose to represent Spain and has gone on to become a World Cup and European Championship winner with La Roja.
Inaki Williams' announcement comes a week after it was confirmed that Carlos Queiroz would return as Ghana coach in the build-up to the 2027 Afcon in Kenya, Tanzania and Uganda.
He said his time with Ghana had given him "much more than football".
"It has allowed me to come back home, feel even closer to my roots and experience the enormous pride of representing my country and wearing this flag on my chest," he added.
"Thank you from the bottom of my heart to everyone who has been part of this journey and for all the love you have always shown me.
"Ghana will always be a part of me. I will continue supporting the Black Stars as one of you, wherever I am."

Russia struck train near Poland border shortly after Boris Johnson and top European officials passed through
- Published
A Russian drone has hit a train near the Ukraine-Poland border shortly after former UK Prime Minister Boris Johnson and top European security officials had passed through.
No casualties were reported after the Russian strike at Yahodyn, which hit the train's engine. All the passengers had been evacuated, Ukrainian authorities said. Russia said it struck "railway infrastructure" in western Ukraine.
Johnson and some of Europe's most senior security advisers, including the UK's Jonathan Powell, had passed along the same line on their way back from a conference in the capital, Kyiv.
The former PM said "I don't know what warped logic drove Putin to blow up a stationary Ukrainian locomotive on the Polish border this morning" and asked "When are we going to give them the air defences they need?"
Ukraine's state railway company Ukrzaliznytsia said a jet-propelled drone had been detected and an evacuation order had been given 15 minutes before the strike.
It confirmed the train carrying Johnson and others had earlier been at Yahodyn station - and said a decision had been made for it to depart earlier than scheduled.
"Quite possibly, the target of this drone could have been the diplomatic train, which had left the station earlier than expected because of the timetable change... due to constant threats of Russian strikes," Ukrzaliznytsia said.
The railway authority also said former CIA chief David Petraeus had been on board another train at Yahodyn station at the time of the drone strike.
The Polish authorities said a Russian drone had struck 2km from the Polish border.
Former Swedish prime minister Carl Bildt, who had also attended the conference in Kyiv, told the BBC passengers on board his train had been told to prepare for evacuation before subsequently being allowed to porcedd with their journey.
"On the train I was on we received order to prepare evacuation after it had stopped. But after a number of minutes we were informed that it was clear and we could proceed," he said.
Ukrainian Foreign Minister Andrii Sybiha said the "barbaric strikes" at the Ukraine-Poland border in Yahodyn amounted to "Putin's terror 'knocking' directly on the doors of the EU and Nato" and renewed calls for more sanctions on Moscow.
"Putin needs to understand that his barbarism will be met with decisive action that increases the cost of war for him to an unacceptable level. This is the only way to stop him," he said.
Russia has in recent months carried out a number of deadly attacks targeting Ukraine's trains, railway depots and other transport facilities.
Earlier this month, six employees of the state railway company Ukrzaliznytsia were killed after a depot was hit in Kyiv.
This week, a female conductor died in a Russian drone attack on a passenger train in southern Ukraine.
In January, President Volodymyr Zelensky condemned as "terrorism" a Russian strike on a crowded passenger train in the north-eastern Kharkiv region that left five people dead.
The Russian attacks have significantly damaged Ukraine's vast train network - the main mode of transportation for millions of Ukrainians as all air travel has been suspended since the start of Russia's full-scale invasion in 2022.

Amanda Seyfried‘s sad school teacher is the heart and confused soul of Tim Blake Nelson‘s latest directorial outing, The Life And Deaths Of Wilson Shedd. The movie itself appears to have had a lot of “life and deaths” itself along the way as Nelson has been trying to get it made for years, and finally he has succeeded with a fine cast including Seyfried and an intriguing turn by Scott McNairy who has become one of the more interesting actors around these days in terms of what he has been showing up in. So why I am so disturbed by this one?
It is a movie that deals with a number of themes and issues, chief among them the death penalty and the fact that for many of those sentenced they probably were doomed by society’s ills before they ever committed the terrible crimes that have led to their fate. Nelson doesn’t provide easy answers here or appear to attempt to make this film an advertisment for abolishment of capital punishment. His penchant for constantly playing with timelines and returning to the vivid depiction of gruesome deaths responsible for the inmates fate clouds the political questions, almost daring us to take a stand one way or the other, The extreme examples shown here don’t make it easy.
The title character, Wilson Shedd, is in prison but as we meet him in the penetentiary’s creative writing class, he is not presented as someone society should throw away, but actually in some ways even a sensitive man wanting to rise from the ashes of his doomed life with an appreciation for – wait for it – Emily Dickinson. We see he perhaps has more potential even if it never leaves the classroom taught by Karen, a teacher brought in for these special classes, a person who can see Wilson has a talent for writing, and as their teacher/student relationship deepens -love letters are even sent – so does his attraction to her, and vice-versa. She has a reason because she has been married to a horribly abusive husband who threatens her at every turn, even as her best friend (Wunmi Mosaku) tries to temper things and pry her from her ex who takes every opportunity to physically assault her. The prison assignment is a gift in some ways as ironically she can find a level of peace trying to encourage the inmates, convicted of despicable acts, they are capable of something better.
Watch on Deadline
Nelson however has no interest in turning this into To Sir With Love. Using a non-linear structure he darts around timewise to show Wilson’s pathetic early life, as well as forward to an escape attempt in which Karen misguidedly becomes an accomplice. There are also flash forwards to the brutal murders of those Wilson and his none-too-bright two prisoner sidekicks find getting in their way once they have gotten free and are on the lam. Most disturbingly is a confrontation with a lovely Black family we have met in earlier flashbacks including two sweet young kids performing in their school musical. We aren’t sure at this point in the film why we are seeing this but it eventually becomes apparent.
Once this family, including the preacher father (William Jackson Harper) and his wife (Devyn Tyler) have piled the kids and their pet cat into the station wagon we know they are on a collision course. When they come directly into the line of fire as it were, we also know this isn’t going to end well, but Nelson keeps returning to the scene, each time a more excruciating moment to watch, almost exploitative in the killings, one by one (yes, mostly offscreen but the effect is there) , the begging for life to be spared, the mercy not given. It was at this point I wanted to check out, the movie became too real, too heartbreaking. I didn’t sign up for this.
As it continues and makes its way to the inhumane and botched execution, pardon me but Nelson’s movie started feeling like a variation of a snuff film, too realistic, too tortured even for a man who presided over the kinds of cold blooded murders we bore witness too. In the end it was all too much, everything including the abuse of Karen, the unthinkable crimes of Wilson Shedd, the wasted lives. There is a point where a movie can go too far.
I am not sure ultimately who the audience is for this film. The Life And Deaths Of Wilson Shedd is extremely well acted, well written, and well directed. Nelson does not shy from showing the realities of life, and deaths. It may all be important to see, to discuss, to think about, but this is one film, still inside my head that I just want to get out.
Producers are Nelson, Julie Buck, Ryan Bartecki, Billy Hines, Miles Romney.

AI 1980s photo trend: From privacy to climate impact, 3 things to consider before joining in
Data centres for AI storage significantly impact local climates and require vast amounts of water, exacerbating shortages in already stressed areas.
Whether you're a internet native or a digital immigrant, it's highly improbable that you've not stumbled upon the grainy 1980s pictures on your WhatsApp and Instagram feeds. Some of you may have even participated in the trend out of FOMO, curiosity or just to have fun.
While that's fair, how safe are these AI trends for us, and the environment that sustains us? Read on to find out.
Read More | 1980s AI photo trend: What is the environmental cost of your latest AI avatar?
Privacy concerns
In the age of Meta AI glasses, it has become increasingly impossible to avoid surveillance and protect your facial identity.
The ordinary people who upload their pictures to recreate a 1980s retro look for a moment of joy might not be aware that ChatGPT and Gemini can save their pictures. AI itself claims that "on personal ChatGPT accounts, content may be used to improve/train models unless you opt out." Unless turned off, data control options allow OpenAI and Google to save user data for training purposes.
Read More | Making AI 1980s photos? ChatGPT has a warning about your pictures
The climate crisis of rising temperatures
Most large-scale AI systems run in data centres, including those managed by cloud service providers. However, these facilities can have a significant environmental impact. As reported by Al Jazeera, a study by Cambridge researchers found that land surface temperatures around AI data centres increase by an average of 2°C (3.6°F), with some areas experiencing rises of up to 9°C (16.2°F). This is called the “data heat island effect”.
In fact, in Thane and Visakhapatnam, residents have staged some of India’s first organised protests against large data centres, raising concerns that these projects could further strain local land, power and water resources.
Shortage of resources
A case-study by University of Oxford labelled data centres as “water guzzling” and “energy eaters”. According to the International Energy Agency (IEA), data centres consumed around 415 terawatt hours (TWh) of electricity in 2024, accounting for roughly 1.5% of global electricity consumption, as per Al Jazeera. This demand has grown by about 15% annually over the past five years and is expected to nearly double to 945 TWh by 2030.
Read More | Want an AI-made 1980s makeover? Think twice before uploading your photo
Data centres require larger amounts of water to cool them down and generate electricity. A study published in Water Research estimated that AI’s global water footprint could rise to 4.2–6.6 billion cubic metres a year by 2027, while noting that around two-thirds of data centres built after 2022 are located in water-stressed regions.
On the other hand, a huge chunk of world's population doesn't have easy access to water. According to the United Nations World Water Development Report 2024, around half of the world’s population experiences severe water scarcity for at least part of the year.
Generating a single AI image isn't the issue, the main problem lies in large-scale usage and viral trends. As AI becomes increasingly woven into everyday digital life, being mindful of what we upload and how often we use these tools is a small but worthwhile step.

For most of history, menstrual blood has been dismissed as biological waste. But emerging research is now recasting this material as a goldmine for non-invasive diagnostics and regenerative medicine. Its potential applications are surprisingly broad, ranging from innovative cervical cancer screenings to advanced cartilage repair.
Much like saliva or blood plasma, menstrual fluid is rich with biological information. It is packed with immune cells, endometrial tissue, proteins, and genetic fragments.
Scientists are now digging into these biomarkers hoping to find ways to detect diseases early, and thus drop the use of invasive clinical procedures.
Stem cells
Researchers have recently reported that they had used menstrual blood to spot cancer early. Normally, medical workers have screened for cervical cancer using clinical check-ups that many people skip due to discomfort, cost, limited access to healthcare, and in fact plain embarrassment. As a result, screening rates remain low even in economically developed regions.
In 2025, a large population-based study in The BMJ by researchers from China offered a workaround. The team found that menstrual blood collected directly from sanitary pads could be tested for human papillomavirus DNA and precancerous lesions just as accurately as cervical swab samples collected by a clinician. Of course, the method excludes those who do not menstruate, but the fact that it offered a non-invasive, inexpensive, and suitable test that could begin from home is notable.
Menstrual blood is also gaining research focus thanks to stem cells derived from it. The groundwork for this was laid back in 2007 when a team from the U.S. and Canada successfully isolated menstrual stem cells from menstrual blood. These cells came from the endometrium, the uterine lining that breaks down and rebuilds itself on a monthly cycle without scarring — something other human tissue cannot do. The researchers believed the stem cells had something to do with that ability. In the lab, the menstrual-blood-derived stem cells readily divided and proved to be tough and versatile.
Researchers are already using them to grow uterine organoids — small functional models of the uterus located outside the body and used to study conditions like endometriosis. The stem cells could reveal traces of exposure to chemical compounds like phthalates and parabens, which was previously not possible to discern without an invasive examination.
Indeed, while bone marrow stem cells are still the gold standard for many therapies, extracting them is a gruelling process. It is painful, requires anaesthesia, and bears significant surgical risks. Menstrual-blood-derived stem cells however can be collected non-invasively, and sans the ethical baggage that often complicates stem-cell sourcing.
Future of regenerative medicine
As the science of these cells has matured, so have their applications. For instance, in 2025, a team in China studied the role they could play on Niemann-Pick disease type C1. This is a rare and devastating inherited condition that is caused by cholesterol and lipids build-up inside cells, leading to rapid neurological decline, loss of motor function, and dementia. The study found that menstrual-blood-derived stem cells could significantly lower neuroinflammation and cell death in experimental models of the disease. The work is still in its early stages, but for a condition whose therapeutic options are currently limited to drugs easing the clinical symptoms, a potential new advance is welcome.
A 2023 study by Iranian researchers showed that when these cells were delivered alongside their conditioned medium — the nutrient-rich fluid they had been cultured with — they helped accelerate heart recovery in rat models after a heart attack.
In hepatology, menstrual-blood-derived stem cells have been found to suppress the specific liver cells responsible for scarring and fibrosis. Because they naturally migrate towards areas of inflammation and cancer, researchers are also exploring engineering these cells to deliver therapeutic genes directly to a tumour site, sparing the rest of the body from the toxic side effects of chemotherapy.
Many experts increasingly believe extracellular vesicles (EVs) are the future of regenerative medicine. They are easier to standardise than whole stem cells — which are complete, living biological units that can divide and adapt within the body, but vary significantly from one batch to another. They also carry risks of becoming unintended tissue types. Because EVs are not whole cells, but rather clumps of proteins, lipids, RNA, and signalling molecules enclosed by membranes secreted from the parent cell, they can’t divide or differentiate into other tissues. This makes them safer, more stable alternatives and less likely to trigger immune rejection, can be engineered to evade immune detection, and can be frozen and stored just like conventional biological drugs.
Menstrual-blood-derived stem cells can be made to release these EVs when cultured in specific conditions in the lab, such as hypoxia (low oxygen) or by adding inflammatory cytokines.
Ordinary challenges
In a notable study published in Scientific Reports in February, a team from Lithuania isolated EVs from healthy donors and introduced them to human cartilage cells taken from patients who had undergone joint surgery. Within hours, the cartilage cells had absorbed the EVs and produced a new extracellular matrix, the scaffolding of healthy joints. When the team simulated joint inflammation, the vesicles reduced the release of markers associated with cartilage degradation.
Since osteoarthritis disproportionately affects women, the researchers also tracked hormone receptors. Specifically, when they examined how EVs affected receptors in the joint tissue, they found that the EVs had increased the expression of the progesterone receptor in cartilage cells, potentially restoring a hormonal signalling pathway that tends to deteriorate in women following menopause.
While most current treatments for osteoarthritis mask the pain, these findings suggest a way to actually slow or reverse the damage. Even though the research is nascent, if the findings hold up in future trials, any benefits will matter considering the number of people living with this condition, estimated to be 595 million worldwide in 2020.
Some significant hurdles remain as well. Scientists do not yet know how long these cells will survive once they are introduced into the body. There is no long-term human safety data— partly because there are no reliable markers to track the cells once they are inside a patient. Producing consistent, high-quality batches also remains a challenge, since no standardised benchmarks exist to verify the cells before use. The cells must themselves behave differently depending on the donor, varying with age, hormonal status, contraceptive history, and the conditions in which the cells were grown in the lab.
Then again, these are ordinary challenges of early-stage biomedical research rather than reasons to dismiss what has already been found.
Manjeera Gowravaram has a PhD in RNA biochemistry and works as a freelance science writer.

- There is no evidence that the FCC issued a direct threat to Jimmy Kimmel or threatened his network to specifically prevent him from airing an interview with James Talarico, a Texas Democrat running for a U.S. Senate seat.
- Kimmel said in September 2026 that ABC would not air his interview with Talarico on television because the FCC had threatened him, ABC and its affiliates over "simple traditional editorial decisions, guest bookings it would seem they don't like." That could reference any or all of a large number of disputes between the Trump administration and ABC.
- ABC and Disney are suing the FCC for various alleged retaliatory measures, including the FCC's decision to require early renewal of ABC's broadcast license after Kimmel made a joke about first lady Melania Trump.
- Under President Donald Trump, the FCC has also issued guidance stating that late-night talk shows are not exempt from the equal-time rule, which essentially means broadcast stations must provide equal opportunities to political candidates, regardless of partisan affiliation. ABC may have pulled the interview for fear of running afoul of this rule.
- The White House denied that FCC Chairman Brendan Carr had threatened Kimmel and said Kimmel was "play-acting" to create a "false narrative" about the Trump administration's policies. A "Jimmy Kimmel Live!" spokesperson did not immediately return a request for more information.
Jimmy Kimmel announced on Sept. 9, 2026, that his show "Jimmy Kimmel Live!" would not air his interview with U.S. Senate candidate James Talarico on television, citing the Federal Communications Commission's threats against the talk-show host's network, ABC, under U.S. President Donald Trump's administration.
Social media users circulated Kimmel's accusations; some claimed Trump or the FCC tried to "block" the interview from airing. In response, readers searched our website to determine whether the FCC actually threatened Kimmel or blocked him from airing the interview with Talarico, a Democratic Texas state representative.
Here's what Kimmel said about the situation (see 9:33 in the video below):
I interviewed Donald Trump when he was running for president in 2015. And at that time, when he was the one sitting next to me, he seemed to have no problem with the idea of talk-show hosts interviewing candidates. In fact, he was very eager to come back for another interview, which he did just before he became the nominee in 2016.
But for some reason, and I can't seem to figure out what that reason is, something has changed.
Now that he is president, his FCC has threatened me, threatened our show, threatened our network, ABC, our affiliates, our local stations based on simple traditional editorial decisions, guest bookings it would seem they don't like.
And so out of consideration for our local stations, especially our ABC affiliates in Texas who would have to deal with this nonsense, my interview tomorrow with James Talarico will not air on television. It will be posted on YouTube instead.
A closer look at Kimmel's words indicates he didn't actually say whether the alleged threat issued by the FCC specifically related to his Sept. 10 interview with Talarico. Kimmel said the FCC threatened him and ABC based on "simple traditional editorial decisions" and "guest bookings." That could be a reference to past disputes between ABC and the Trump administration or changing guidelines from the FCC.
The White House said Brendan Carr, chairman of the FCC, has not threatened Kimmel "regarding interviewing James Talarico, or any other candidate."
"Jimmy Kimmel is play-acting—as he often does—to create a false narrative about this administration's policies," Davis Ingle, a White House spokesman, said in an email. "Any media outlet blindly amplifying Kimmel's egocentric delusion should insist on proof. Of which they will find none."
A spokesperson for "Jimmy Kimmel Live!" didn't immediately respond to a request for that proof, nor to a request to clarify whether Kimmel and ABC had received a specific threat — or whether the network made a proactive decision based on past experiences and Trump administration policy.
We left this claim unrated pending answers to those questions.
Here's more on why ABC might have pulled Talarico's interview from network television, aside from a possible direct threat:
ABC's disputes with Trump administration
Kimmel's accusation that the Trump administration has threatened him and his network could reference any or all of the many disputes he and his network have with the Trump administration.
In fact, Trump has repeatedly called for Kimmel's firing and for the FCC to strip ABC of its licenses in response to various broadcasts he hasn't liked.
In September 2025, ABC temporarily pulled Kimmel off air after comments he made about the assassination of conservative activist Charlie Kirk. The decision came after Carr suggested he might take action against Disney, ABC's parent company, if it didn't pull Kimmel's show.
The president also called on ABC to fire Kimmel in April 2026 after the talk-show host made a joke about first lady Melania Trump. Shortly after, the FCC ordered ABC to seek early broadcast license renewals, an unprecedented move that can signal "significant concerns with the value" of the station's operations, Carr said.
ABC and Disney sued the FCC in August 2026 for allegedly violating its free-speech rights, arguing (Page 3) that the Trump administration has "waged a retaliatory campaign against ABC for a single reason: it disapproves of what ABC broadcasts."
FCC policy changes
It's also possible ABC may have pulled Talarico's interview from network television because of FCC guidance on giving equal time to political candidates on broadcast television under the Trump administration.
Some forms of broadcast media are exempt from this rule, including "bona fide," or legitimate, newscasts and news interviews. But in January 2026, the FCC issued guidance stating that late-night talk shows don't have a blanket exemption from the equal-time rule.
The FCC's guidance said that, in 2006, the agency determined the interview portion of "The Tonight Show with Jay Leno" qualified for as a "bona fide news interview" and thus would be exempt from the equal-time rule. Networks have relied on this ruling to mean that all late-night talk shows are exempt.
"This is not the case," the FCC said on Page 4 of the notice. "The FCC has not been presented with any evidence that the interview portion of any late night or daytime television talk show program on air presently would qualify for the bona fide news exemption."
The FCC's guidance has had real effects. In February 2026, for example, talk-show host Stephen Colbert claimed CBS blocked an interview with Talarico on "The Late Show with Stephen Colbert" from airing on broadcast television because the network's lawyers said in "no uncertain terms" that the interview could violate the FCC's guidance.
(CBS reportedly disputed Colbert's account and said its lawyers provided only "legal guidance," not a direct prohibition.)
The bottom line
There's no evidence the FCC directly threatened Kimmel, and a closer read of Kimmel's comments indicated that Kimmel never accused the FCC of specifically blocking his interview with Talarico from airing on television.
However, that doesn't mean the FCC hasn't threatened Kimmel and ABC in other ways. The FCC and ABC are embroiled in several disputes, and ABC has alleged that the FCC is engaging in retaliatory measures because the Trump administration doesn't like the network's content.

A woman biker was thrown off her motorcycle after a car rammed into her on Golf Course Road in Gurugram on Sunday (September 13, 2026) and fled the scene, with the motorcycle sent sliding several metres along the road. The collision was captured on an action camera mounted on the bike and the footage, posted online by the rider, has since gone viral.
The Gurugram Police have launched a suo motu enquiry into the incident and are analysing the video to trace the car driver and the woman rider, Gurugram East DCP Sandeep Kumar told The Hindu. “We are analysing the video and tracing both the accused and the creator/victim. We have not received any formal complaint from the creator, but we are launching a suo motu enquiry and will book a case based on the findings,” he said.
The rider, who identifies herself as Sia and runs the Instagram page ‘rebelwheels_sia_’, alleged in the video that the occupants of a white car had been chasing her while she was riding her Aprilia RS 457 with members of her biking group.
According to Sia, the car repeatedly came close to her motorcycle, and its occupants behaved aggressively. She said she signalled to the driver to maintain a distance, but the occupants instead asked her to stop. She also alleged that the men appeared to be drunk.
Sia said she continued riding to prevent the car from blocking her path, while a friend riding behind her tried to shield her and prevent the vehicle from coming alongside her.
She alleged that the car continued to pursue her before the driver attempted to cut in front of her motorcycle. The vehicle then hit the bike horizontally, throwing her off and sending the motorcycle sliding several metres before it came to a halt. The car sped away without stopping.
After the collision, one of Sia’s friends chased the car and confronted the driver when it stopped at a traffic signal. Her friend told the driver that he had caused the crash, but the driver denied responsibility and drove away.
The video identifies the vehicle as bearing registration number ‘HR30Y4949’ as its registered owner. An e-challan check showed two pending challans against the vehicle, totalling ₹2,000. One was issued in February 2023 for a road-marking violation and the other in December 2025 for wrong parking.
Sia has urged the Gurugram Police to take action against the driver, alleging that the incident endangered her life and that he fled after the crash.
The video has prompted several social media users to tag the Gurugram Police, Gurugram Traffic Police and Haryana Police, seeking action against the driver.
“I have nothing to say, but today I felt unsafe on Gurugram roads. People like these aren’t afraid of hitting people and running away,” Sia said, demanding action.

A Sydney mayor was allegedly threatened, followed and his children were secretly recorded after he refused to honour an agreement to step down, the NSW corruption watchdog has heard.
Former independent Strathfield council mayor Matthew Blackmore has fronted the New South Wales Independent Commission Against Corruption (Icac) inquiry, codenamed Operation Rosny.
The inquiry is investigating accusations levelled against former Labor councillors Sharangan Maheswaran and Karen Pensabene, including whether they engaged in blackmail or possible surveillance against Blackmore.
Blackmore in 2022 had initially agreed to split the mayoralty, so he would take the position first before resigning to allow a Labor councillor, which was expected to be Pensabene, to finish the term, he told the commission.
Maheswaran wanted to ensure Labor leadership at the council, state and federal level before the 2023 state election to bolster campaign efforts, Icac heard.
But in January 2023, Blackmore revealed to the two Labor councillors he wanted to stay on as mayor, which led them to become agitated and upset, he said.
Maheswaran allegedly told Blackmore: “What you’ve got to understand, Matthew … I’ve got a reputation in the party that if I don’t like someone, they don’t get away with crossing me. It would take me about six weeks to take you down.”
Blackmore responded by saying he could “get fucked”.
Blackmore told the commission his wife had taken a photo of Maheswaran’s car on the street outside their home, which was near a brothel.
Asked if he was aware this photo could be used to his political advantage, he said he only wanted it to check if the number plate was Maheswaran’s.
Blackmore had seen the car in front of his house a number of times and was “a bit intimidated as to whether he was stalking my house,” he told the commission.
Pensabene later messaged Blackmore to warn him Maheswaran was “out of control”, and said he was printing 20,000 attack flyers.
One of the flyers, which Blackmore referred to as a “shit sheet”, was left on the former mayor’s car, and Pensabene warned him that “everything so far is less than 10% of what is coming”.
At a later meeting, Maheswaran told Blackmore he’d had operatives following him for five months, taking photos and recording his conversations without his knowledge, according to Blackmore.
Blackmore took it to mean they were going to continue releasing media stories if he didn’t resign as mayor.
Soon after, he began receiving inquiries from journalists working for News Corp and YouTuber FriendlyJordies.
According to a statement from Blackmore, Maheswaran told him: “All of this will go away when you resign from the mayoralty. It will stop. You’re not going to have any harassment as long as you agree with us to do this.”
Maheswaran also alleged Blackmore had used the mayoralty vehicle to take a family holiday and told him the location of the vacation.
“The holiday thing was one of the worst because we weren’t actually intending to go and our plans were changed last minute so no one really knew where I was going,” Blackmore said.
The entire situation has changed his sense of personal safety.
“I can’t go to sleep without checking my house is locked,” Blackmore said.
In a text to Pensabene, he wrote: “I feel sick that my children have been surveillanced [sic] by Sharangan’s undercover people.”
Maheswaran is due to appear at Icac on Friday.

How to use GPT-6 Astra when it rolls out to you
Here's where to find GPT-6 Astra and what to know before its usage limits catch you off guard.
OpenAI began rolling out GPT-6 Astra on September 3, but access is not as easy as opening ChatGPT and searching for a button that says "Astra." In regular ChatGPT, the model is known as GPT-6 Pro and is rolling out for the $100 and $200 Pro plans, Business, and Enterprise. For now, Free and Go users are excluded, with Plus subscribers getting Astra via ChatGPT Work and Codex instead (not regular Chat) as the rollout reaches their accounts.
Availability may vary between Chat, Work and Codex. OpenAI says the rollout will be gradual, so being on an eligible plan doesn't mean Astra will be waiting for you today. OpenAI hasn't specified when eligible accounts will receive Astra.
How to use GPT-6 Astra in ChatGPT
If you have an eligible Pro, Business or Enterprise account, open the model picker in a regular ChatGPT conversation and look under Pro for GPT-6 Pro. That's the one powered by GPT-6 Astra, so don't get too caught up in the menu looking for its flashier name. Enterprise users have another possible obstacle: access also depends on workspace model-access permissions.
If you're on Plus, open Work on the web or mobile app and select Astra from the available models once it rolls out to your account. In the desktop app, select ChatGPT, switch from Chat to Work and choose Astra there. Codex users can also choose Astra, but OpenAI says the Codex CLI requires version 0.153.0 or newer.
Still nothing? Even if the desktop app has recently updated itself, OpenAI suggests manually checking for updates by going to Menu > Check for Updates. Work is rolling out separately, so Astra might be available on one platform before another.
If you are using Work with local files or desktop apps, there is also a privacy aspect. Even when Work runs locally, messages and task context may still be stored in the cloud.
Watch how quickly Astra uses your allowance
When Astra does arrive, there's another factor to keep an eye on: your usage allowance.
According to OpenAI, Astra can use up your allowance more quickly than GPT-5.6 Sol, depending on the complexity of the task, the amount of context, the reasoning required and other usage settings. So a big coding assignment that requires more reasoning can use more of your allowance than a quick question.
OpenAI estimates that Plus users can send approximately five to 45 local Astra messages per five-hour period. The $100 Pro plan is estimated at 25 to 225 messages, while the $200 tier gets 100 to 900. You can check your current limits and reset times in ChatGPT's usage dashboard.
Chat has separate limits. On the $100 Pro plan, GPT-6 Pro shares a 50-message weekly allowance with GPT-5.6 Sol Pro, while the $200 plan allows 200 GPT-6 Pro messages per week.
If your allowance is going down quicker than you'd like, reserve Astra for the tasks that require it. OpenAI advises keeping prompts focused, including only relevant files and defining the output format and length. Telling Astra what reasonable assumptions it can make may also reduce unnecessary back-and-forth.
GPT-6 Astra is available for developers via the API. The standard price is $10 per million input tokens and $50 per million output tokens. Requests that rack up more than 272,000 input tokens in total are charged at twice the input and cache rates, and output rates at 1.5x.

When an avalanche killed climber Nirmal Purja, his friends faced the hardest mission of all
- Published
As he picked his way past the frozen slope towards two bodies, Mingma Gyalje Sherpa knew his friends were gone.
Together, the three of them had climbed the world's highest peaks, under crisp mountain skies and in treacherous snowstorms. Nirmal Purja and Kili Pemba Sherpa were two of the strongest climbers Mingma G had ever known.
But this July, an avalanche swept through Pakistan's Broad Peak while the two were on their way up, engulfing everything in its path.
The drone images seemed clear: no-one had survived.
And yet, as Mingma G came closer to the fluorescent down suits, sharp against the snow, he couldn't shake the idea they were waiting for him.
"I told them: 'It's ok. You don't have to be here in the cold anymore.'"
Speaking to the BBC in Islamabad, he recalls the terrible moment he reached for their bodies.
Holding one of them, he promised: "I'm here to take you guys home."
Mingma G and Nirmal Purja met in Pakistan in 2021, where they were part of the first team to summit the world's second-highest mountain, K2, during winter.
Mingma G knew of Nirmal - or Nims, as he was known - from his Netflix documentary 14 Peaks, in which he successfully climbed the world's 14 highest mountains in just over six months.
The pair, both avid climbers from Nepal, had taken different paths.
Mingma G came from the Sherpa community and built his reputation as a mountain guide over 20 years. Nims was a former Gurkha and British Special Forces soldier who quickly became one of the world's best-known mountaineers.
Many saw Nims as an incredible climber who helped Nepalese climbers gain international recognition in a field dominated by foreigners. But he also had his critics: they said he focused too much on records, and on marketing his expeditions to a growing social media following.
In 2024 the New York Times published sexual misconduct allegations from two women, which Purja strongly denied through his lawyer at the time, who said they were "false and defamatory". Purja again denied the allegations in a lengthy interview soon after.
Before Mingma G met Nims, he wasn't sure about him: "In the beginning, I had the feeling he was very arrogant."
But that changed when their paths crossed five years ago, as competitors on their way to K2, who then decided to climb the mountain together and share the record. Mingma G says he found Nims to be "very kind-hearted, one of the most beautiful human beings I've met".
Over the years the two would meet on various mountains around the world: Nims "would always be on Everest".
This summer they met again, walking into the Karakoram range, before they would split up for different climbs. Nims headed for Broad Peak and Mingma G for K2, around 8km (five miles) apart.
Nims asked Mingma G to wait another day so they could meet once more before embarking on these separate missions, but that meeting never happened.
"That was the last thing he told me. I still regret it."
On 30 July, "we had perfect weather, sunshine, no winds," Mingma G says.
By then, he was leading a team up K2. Nims's team of climbers had joined others to form a larger group of 10 that was making its way up Broad Peak.
At 08:30, Mingma G spoke to Kili Pemba Sherpa - better known as Kilu - a childhood friend and expert climber in Nims's group. Snow conditions looked good, Kilu had said, and the two agreed to speak again when they both reached the next camp on their respective mountains.
The BBC spoke to two trekkers who spotted the climbers scaling Broad Peak. "We were cheering them on," one says. He took a photo of them on the slope, small silhouettes against the snow.
The group continued ascending. But less than an hour later, there was a "thundercrack", the other trekker says: "a huge avalanche, starting from the top going down both sides of Broad Peak".
"We were hoping and praying that the climbers were above the avalanche," the first trekker continues. But they couldn't see the silhouettes on the slope.
The trekkers' guide notified base camp about what they had witnessed.
The cause of the avalanche is still being investigated, but the Alpine Club of Pakistan told the BBC that while it had snowed heavily earlier that week, their initial research suggested that it was caused by the collapse of an ice slab, irrespective of snowfall.
By the time Mingma G reached the next camp on K2, his team had not heard from the Broad Peak climbers. They didn't panic because climbers often turn off the radio to save battery life.
But something was bothering him.
One of the Broad Peak climbers, Wang Zhong, was a close friend and a client. He would normally message Mingma G through his Garmin satellite tracker to let him know he'd arrived safely at the next camp. But there was no message from him.
Thousands of metres below, Pakistani mountain guide Waqar Ali says he was also trying to contact the group, but to no avail. He thought they may have been sleeping, in preparation for a final push towards the summit that night.
But by 15:00, no-one at base camp had had any contact with the group on Broad Peak.
Mingma G was 7,300m up on K2, where communication was difficult. His team started calling officials, families, contacts in Kathmandu and anyone who might have been in touch with the climbers.
He says it was probably 20:00 when they first heard that the altitude readings from the Broad Peak climbers' trackers had dramatically fallen: one of them had dropped by around 1,600m.
It was too late to climb and too dark to send up a drone, so he decided to wait for sunrise. "I had hope," Mingma G says. Especially for Kilu and Nims, who were "experienced and physically… strong".
Early next morning, a drone was sent up and soon after, the operator radioed them. The drone had spotted bodies down the mountain. It looked like there were no survivors.
"I was totally blank," Mingma G recalls in a low voice.
He wasn't quite ready to accept he had lost so many dear friends at once.
"Maybe still I had a feeling they might all be alive [and] wanted somebody to help them get down. That was just something I had in my heart and mind."
Later that day, Mingma G called off his K2 expedition.
Down at the base of Broad Peak, Waqar wept as he arrived with another climber to start the difficult job of bringing the bodies back.
They retrieved the bodies of Nadhira Al Harthy, the first Omani woman to climb Everest, and Pur Bahadur Gurung, a Nepalese climber who had summited 12 of the world's 14 highest peaks.
But there were still bodies on the mountain and Mingma G was determined to bring his friends home.
When he called Nims's wife and brother-in-law to tell them the tragic news, he says they struggled to believe it. Kilu's wife "couldn't say much, but told me: 'don't leave your brother on the mountain'".
Organising the next steps of the recovery mission was complicated.
The climbers who'd been heading up K2 with Mingma G were unsettled, he says, and facing pressure from their families to go home.
Then there were the logistics. From the drone images, Mingma G thought the bodies could be recovered using a helicopter and a long-line rope, but says he was told this wouldn't be possible. "In Nepal it would have taken like two minutes," he says.
The Pakistani army which would have provided the helicopters didn't respond to the BBC's questions. The Alpine Club of Pakistan says a request made on 1 August was approved, but poor weather meant it could not be carried out for days.
There was only one other option for Mingma G - a recovery operation on foot.
On 1 August, Mingma G says, his team of rescuers set off in search of four bodies they believed they'd seen in the drone shots - those of Nims, Kilu, Zhong and a fellow climber called Nima Sherpa. Gyaljen Sherpa would also be discovered nearby.
With the slope so unstable, there was a risk of falling rocks and further avalanches. A larger team could potentially lead to more casualties, but a smaller team would struggle to bring the bodies down.
The moment the rescue team reached the bodies and began sending them down on ropes, another avalanche hit, he says.
The torrent of snow sent one of the bodies down to the bottom. Three others, including Nims, ended up in a more dangerous position - in the centre of a slope with large pillars of glacial ice precariously balanced to the left and right. If either were to collapse while the rescue team were trying to reach the bodies, the tower of ice could sweep them away.
The team needed a new plan. As the days progressed, some of its members started leaving. Their numbers went from nine to six, then four.
Given how precarious the slope was, the group decided Mingma G would hang back and monitor by drone, instructing the three climbers. The arduous operation took five to six hours, but they finally managed to bring the bodies back down the slope.
The moment Mingma G first saw his friends on the mountain still haunts him.
Nims and Kilu had covered their faces with their jackets - Mingma G believes they had seen the deadly avalanche coming and prepared. The two were attached to the same rope, their legs wrapped in it. Mingma G thinks they may have hit each other on the way down - which he fears killed them rather than the fall.
"They didn't fall that much, almost 500m. But unfortunately they hit each other a lot, I think. If they were not on the rope, maybe there was a possibility that Nims and Kilu might have survived."
The team brought the bodies back down the mountain. They were flown by helicopter to the nearby city of Skardu, then on to the capital Islamabad and finally, home to their families.
Pakistani mountaineer Sohail Sakhi's body was found a few days later, as was the body of American climber Mallory Geis. The body of Nepalese climber Nawang Thindu Sherpa remains on the mountain.
Nims's family say they are deeply grateful to the "extraordinary team led by our brother, Mingma G, who worked in incredibly challenging conditions to bring Nimsdai home".
This recovery operation has stayed with Mingma G. It doesn't compare to any other mission he has done.
As he looks back with deep sorrow, he feels the end of his career could be coming.
Memories of Kilu and Nims - the three of them singing together as they marched up to the summit of a freezing but sunny K2 a few years ago - will always be with him.
But, he says, "I'm not sure if it helps, if the memory helps me to keep climbing or it makes me stop."

In August 2024, Inc42 asked whether Swish could pull off what Zomato couldn't. Two years on, the question has turned on its head. Zomato has quit. So have Swiggy, Rebel Foods and Zing. Swish is still here. And it just raised $24 Mn this past week, less than six months after it had raised $38 Mn. As we said above, several startups and listed companies that entered the segment over the past two years have either scaled back or shut their offerings. Zepto Cafe has reduced its footprint, Eternal’s Zomato shut Quick and Everyday, Swiggy closed Snacc earlier this year, Zing shut operations, and Rebel Foods has halted QuickiES. Less than two years into its operations, at a time when quick food delivery was on everyone’s minds, Swish is now the lone ranger in the space. The latest round comes at an interesting point for India's 10 minute food delivery market. The Bengaluru-based startup now serves more than 1 Mn orders a month, with monthly orders tripling since March 2026. It operates in 50 pincodes across Bengaluru and Delhi NCR. The question now is whether Swish has found a model that can work where several better funded companies have struggled. Swish Is Scaling Up, But There’s A Long Way To Go Founded in late 2024 by Aniket Shah, Ujjwal Sukheja and Saran S, Swish has a different model from the traditional food delivery model, which was popularised by Swiggy and Zomato, and which even Rapido has carried forward. Unlike the other platforms which are aggregators, Swish owns the kitchens, prepares the food, operates the technology and manages delivery. Its kitchens are placed close to customers, generally within a 1 Km radius, allowing the startup to control the time between ordering and delivery. That has allowed Swish to build a relatively small but dense network. The startup said in its latest funding announcement that it has crossed 1 Mn monthly orders at its peak, and that more than 80% of orders are delivered within 15 minutes. Its kitchens have an average preparation time of under four minutes. The menu has also moved well beyond the snack heavy proposition with which the category started. Swish began with around 75 SKUs and has since expanded it by 3X, spanning meals, snacks and beverages. Lunch and dinner now account for more orders than snacks and late night consumption. That matters because the larger opportunity for Swish is likely to be everyday meals rather than occasional impulse purchases. When Swish launched in Delhi, cofounder Shah revealed that more than four in 10 of its customers have ordered again, offering an indication of customer repeat behavior in Delhi. There is also a gap between where Swish is today and where it once planned to be. In late 2024, Shah had mentioned plans to have 150 kitchens across Bengaluru by March 2025. It currently has around 55 kitchens, even after entering Delhi NCR. The latest fundraise gives Swish more room to build more momentum in that regard. Swish wants to expand its kitchen network in Bengaluru and Delhi NCR and has an ambitious target of having more than 1,000 kitchens over the next five years. For context, Rebel Foods, one of the largest cloud kitchen companies from India, claims to run 450 cloud kitchens for 4,000 restaurants cumulatively across 75 cities in three countries. And it raised more than $785 Mn to get there over the course of 15 years. Scaling up physical kitchens requires several hundreds of millions of dollars, and if Swish has to get to that ambitious target, it has to continue raising large rounds, particularly because quick food needs higher cloud kitchen density than what Rebel Foods had in mind. Quick Food Players Exit Stage Swish's biggest advantage today may be that it is still in the game. The list of companies that have exited quick food delivery is almost as long as the list of players that entered this space. Zepto Cafe, which pioneered this concept, has been scaling down. As Inc42 reported, more than 50 Zepto Cafe kitchens were shut in 2025, with order volume falling from a peak of around 1 Lakh orders a day to nearly half that level. The problems were not limited to demand. Zepto also faced supply-chain constraints and a shortage of trained kitchen staff, leading it to pause operations across several cities. Eternal took a different route. It shut Zomato Quick along with Everyday in May 2025 just months after entering the space. Back then, Zomato cited weak demand and profitability concerns. Swiggy pulled the plug on Snacc in February 2026, with the company saying that product-market fit was not the problem, but unit economics was. Gurugram-based Zing, which shut shop last year after starting out around the same time as Swish, told Inc42 that the startup had overestimated demand, with customers preferring food from their favourite restaurants even if it took longer to arrive. More recently, Rebel Foods also halted its QuickiES vertical earlier this year, which had offered 15-minute delivery. Blinkit-owned Bistro remains one of the few dedicated players still operating in the category. Its model, like Swish, involves company controlled kitchens and fast delivery. It must be noted that Bistro is separate from Zomato’s past efforts Then there are Swiggy Bolt and Toing, which need to be examined differently from Swish. Neither requires Swiggy to build and operate its own kitchens. Instead, Swiggy works with restaurants that can prepare or pack selected items quickly, with deliveries generally limited to a 2 Km radius. By May 2025, Bolt was live across more than 500 cities and accounted for more than one in 10 Swiggy food orders. Swish and Bistro own the complete stack, so also carry more of the cost and risk. But while Bistro has Blinkit’s core business to rely on for less costly customer acquisition and can lean on the brand, Swish has no such fallback. So how does Swish fare with regard to unit economics? What Quick Food Unit Economics Look Like This is primarily where the startup's latest funding round becomes more interesting. As per a report in The Arc, Swish's food gross margin is around 60%-70% on an average order value of ₹250. This would translate to roughly ₹160 of gross profit per order before kitchen, delivery and corporate costs. At that level, the company needs every kitchen to generate enough orders to cover food preparation, rent, staff, delivery and corporate costs. The report added that close to 10% of Swish users order twice a day with customers placing just over three orders per month on average. However, compared to a conventional food marketplace, Swish’s model has the ability to retain a higher share of the order value. For instance, Zomato or Swiggy face pushback from restaurants when they raise commissions and have to maintain a fine balance. Swish instead has to look at managing costs to improve its net margin per order rather than focus on commissions. For this to work, the kitchen has to stay busy. Swish is currently doing around 30,000 orders a day across 55 kitchens and a few of its mature kitchens can have around 800 orders a day. On average, each kitchen caters to 800 orders per day. Growing this density will be key to Swish’s growth. It is also the part of the model that investors are betting on. This scale has to eventually translate into profits, but Swish has a longer rope than listed companies when it comes to profitability. At the moment the focus is on growing order volume, gross order value and growing the user base, and the aim is that this along with the cloud kitchen density will be able to deliver profits in a few quarters. The company plans to add advertising within the app as a revenue layer in the near future. A kitchen doing 800 orders a day is more profitable than one doing 100. Delivery riders can be stationed closer to the kitchen, staff costs can be spread across more orders and food waste can be monitored more closely. The problem is whether these numbers hold as Swish moves beyond its strongest Bengaluru neighbourhoods. Which means, the startup has to spend extra money on brand awareness when it enters new markets accompanied by heavy discounting. Swish has already raised $78 Mn across four rounds. For a startup that has been operational for less than two years, investor backing is lifeblood, but soon that reliance will need to be curbed. The next phase will be less about raising money and more about proving that when its cloud kitchen network grows, Swish doesn’t have a unit economics mess on its hands. Now, the startup has something most of its quick food rivals did not get: more time at the table. The harder question is whether that time will be enough to prove that quick food delivery can become a large food business, rather than another quick commerce experiment that works only in a handful of dense neighbourhoods. With just two weeks left in the 60-day window for filing objections and suggestions to the Centre’s seventh draft notification on Ecologically Sensitive Areas (ESAs) in the Western Ghats, hundreds of settler families in the high ranges of Kottayam are bracing for a fresh battle to keep their homes and plantations out of the proposed ESA.
The four villages of Koottikkal, Melukavu, Poonjar Thekkekkara and Teekoy, all in the Poonjar Assembly constituency, are now on the proposed ESA map after being included in the draft notification issued on July 27.
The proposal, estimated to affect around 70,000 people, has prompted residents, local bodies and various organisations including the Catholic church to step up their campaign against the move.
Agriculture is the backbone of these high range villages, with rubber, cardamom, coffee, pepper, coconut and banana among the major crops. Residents fear that bringing their land under the ESA could impose restrictions on plantations and hamper essential development activities.
In the Koottikkal region, the opposition has already moved beyond petitions. The local body has already convened special grama sabhas in all 14 wards, held an urgent council meeting and passed a resolution detailing its objections. The resolution will be forwarded to the State and Union governments by registered post.
“There are around 30,000 people in Koottikkal panchayat and they unanimously seek the exclusion of the panchayat from ESA limits,” said Ancy Sebastian, president of Koottikkal panchayat.
Ms. Ancy has warned that the protest could spill onto the streets if the demand is ignored, with the entire village, from children to the elderly, taking part in a mass agitation.
Her central argument is that the panchayat has no forest land at all.
“There is not an inch of forest land in the panchayat. The residents are mostly farmers and have cultivated rubber, plantains, jackfruit and other crops here. In satellite surveys, these plantations might have been mistaken for forest cover. However, these are human-inhabited areas and hence should be excluded from the ESA,” she added.
Kerala Congress leader and Government Chief Whip Apu John Joseph said all possible steps would be taken to secure the exclusion of the villages.
“The concerns raised by the settlers, both directly or through different collectives, have been presented with the Chief Minister. We are also continuing interactions at different levels, holding conventions and meetings to mobilise observations of various farmer collectives,” he said.
According to him, Chief Minister V. D. Satheesan is slated to visit Idukki on September 25 and interact with various stakeholders on the ESA issue.
Pathanamthitta MP Anto Antony, whose constituency also includes Poonjar, said the United Democratic Front had consistently maintained that non-forest land should not be brought under the ESA.
“The forest land that falls after the boundary stone shall be included in the ESA. No property after this point can be regarded as ESA . This will be conveyed to the centre through the State government,” he said.
The State, meanwhile, has already sought to bring down the proposed ESA area from 9,993.7 sq km to 8,590.69 sq km, while keeping inhabited areas, agricultural land and plantations out of its ambit. The revision also seeks to reduce the number of ESA villages from 131 in the latest Union government draft to 98.

Trump dismisses AI safety fears to keep America ahead of China
US president claimed ‘very negative forces’ have been raising concerns about the rapidly developing technology
President Donald Trump has downplayed the necessity for his administration to restrict artificial intelligence development, arguing that maintaining the United States’ lead over China in global competition is paramount and that securing victory will help mitigate the hazards of the evolving technology.
Although he conceded that a degree of oversight is required, Trump offered no specific proposals for future rules. Instead, he dismissed warnings concerning the rapid pace of development and lack of supervision, attributing them to unidentified "negative forces", despite similar apprehensions being raised by tech sector pioneers.
"We can put guardrails, we can do this and that, but I think you have a lot of negative forces that are bringing it up that ... shouldn’t be bringing it up, and they’re bringing up things that won’t happen," Trump told reporters during a trip to Ireland over the weekend. "But whoever wins with AI wins."
The Republican president's remarks followed comments from Dario Amodei, chief executive of AI firm Anthropic, who urged the sector to slow its rapid progression to allow safety protocols time to catch up. Prominent industry figures, such as Elon Musk and OpenAI chief executive Sam Altman, have publicly backed Amodei's position.
When asked by a reporter whether the industry should be subject to regulation or decelerate its pace, Trump—speaking after watching play at the Irish Open at his Doonbeg resort—emphasised that America remains ahead of China in AI advancements, stating, "frankly, I want to keep it that way because whoever wins AI wins."
Chinese President Xi Jinping is scheduled to visit the US later in September to meet with Trump, with artificial intelligence expected to feature on their agenda.
Artificial intelligence has emerged as a central issue during this US election year. Major technology firms are constructing extensive networks of data warehouses across smaller towns, prompting widespread concern from voters across political lines regarding the loss of agricultural land, strained water resources, and escalating electricity bills. Despite local opposition and hesitation from both major parties, Trump has maintained his backing for these data centres.
Former president Barack Obama suggested that his party ought to focus on AI as a key campaign issue.
"I would talk about this, and I would say, ‘Here’s our plan for safety, here’s our plan for making sure our kids are not corrupted by this.’ ... I would be thinking about the economic impacts in very concrete ways and understanding what it means if there’s going to be job displacement. Where is that going to hit? How are we going to respond?" Obama stated during a joint event last week with New York Representative Hakeem Jeffries, the leading Democrat in the US House, according to a transcript provided by his office.
Kevin Hassett, director of the White House National Economic Council, indicated that administration officials overseeing cyber, science, and technology policy are anticipated to convene this week to discuss subsequent measures. Trump may also confer with congressional lawmakers, a number of whom have voiced deep concerns regarding the rapid speed of AI advancements.
"I think the president wants to hear from them as well," Hassett noted.
US House Speaker Mike Johnson said that "some guardrails, some safety measures" are necessary to prevent AI from running away. Nevertheless, mirroring Trump’s stance, he stressed the importance of ensuring America does not "lose our edge in the global competition on this with China because that would be a national security threat."
The Louisiana Republican suggested that tech leaders should be brought together for "one big meeting and work this out together in the same room." Having raised the matter with Trump, Johnson expressed that convening such a gathering promptly ought to be the "next step."
"So we’re going to pull everybody together and make sure we do this in the right way," Johnson remarked, describing the issue as a "top priority for me and for the Congress."
"But we don’t need everybody to panic right now," Johnson added.
Meanwhile, Jeffries took aim at House Republican leadership for permitting representatives to return to their home districts for the final part of September.
"We should take decisive action now so that we can slow down, as the CEOs have recently acknowledged, … the pace of development in order to protect the American people and ensure that AI is proceeding safely," Jeffries said. He confirmed that addressing AI will be a "high priority" during a meeting of House Democrats on Tuesday.
Neither Johnson nor Jeffries outlined specific legislative steps. While there is broad consensus among lawmakers that regulatory boundaries are required, previous limited attempts to establish rules have repeatedly collapsed, underscoring Congress's persistent hesitation to regulate the tech sector.
Jacob Coxon, a former Anthropic employee who resigned due to safety concerns and subsequently voiced his anxieties publicly, called for global regulatory frameworks alongside voluntary industry constraints.
Coxon warned of his growing fear that artificial intelligence models could soon develop advanced capabilities beyond human control.
"You’re building a human-level or superhuman-level mind, without understanding what it wants, or thinks, or the way it thinks," Coxon said.
Amid intense international rivalry for supremacy in the field, Coxon urged Washington and Beijing—the two dominant players—to collaborate on slowing development to address potential hazards.
"I do hope that the people in China who are looking at the same problems as we are, so they’re trying to build the same technology, will come to the same conclusion that it has to be done in a measured manner, and it should be easy to cooperate on some sort of mutual — of mutual slowing," Coxon said.
Failing to do so, he cautioned, means "we risk running the same race with China, which could be equally dangerous."
Technology entrepreneur and investor David Sacks responded to calls for state intervention with a social media post challenging tech executives. Sacks, who serves as co-chairman of a White House advisory council on science and technology, contended that Amodei and his peers are themselves driving the speed of advancement.
He asserted that these industry leaders possess the authority to unilaterally curb development.
"The easiest way not to build superintelligence is for you to agree not to build it," Sacks wrote.
