As a rock star, Chrissie Hynde has always been a bit of a paradox — gnarly but cerebral, ferocious yet guarded. And “Pretenders,” Joss Crowley’s sensational and revealing music documentary, shows you that there was a paradox — a glorious one — built into her band.
Formed in London in 1978, the Pretenders emerged from the moment when “punk” had morphed into “new wave.” But there were still musicians around who could claim to be both, and Hynde was one of them. When you listen to “Precious,” which is totally a punk song (it has the potent high-speed sizzle of something by the Ramones), the ice-cold defiance and gutter snarl of Hynde’s singing (“Made me wanna…”), the song’s total fuck-it-all vibe, are undiminished by time. Hynde, with her shag haircut and androgynous toothy scowl, had emerged from the original punk scene (she’d moved to London in her early 20s and even tried to join the Slits), and it left its mark on her. She was a blistering rocker who was going to be no one’s doll.
And yet…as fierce and defining as a song like “Precious” was, it doesn’t represent what I ultimately cherish about the Pretenders. To say what that is, I have to use a word that risks sounding innocuous: They were tuneful. They came out of the world of rage and nihilism and buzzcuts and heroin, but there was an incandescence to the songs Hynde wrote, and to how the band sounded. For years, rock critics of the post-new wave era struggled to come up with different words to communicate the concept of “jangly guitar.” But it was James Honeyman-Scott, the lead guitarist of the Pretenders, who owned jangly guitar, and in some ways invented it. He had a sound that rang. And Hynde, though she had the feeling of punk in her bones, was the most romantic songwriter of that scene. I don’t mean romantic as in “love songs,” but as in conjuring the majestic romanticism of life. Just listen to “Kid,” a song so happy and sad at the same time that it’s worthy of the Beatles.
Popular on Variety
“Pretenders,” which is built around astonishing archival footage as well as a lengthy interview with Hynde (Crowley also talks to many fascinating people in her orbit), is a movie that understands that side of the Pretenders — that they were making music so shimmering in its timelessness that it transcended the new-wave aesthetic and a lot of other things. How Chrissie Hynde wound up being that kind of songwriter is anyone’s guess. Songwriting is one of the true mysteries: a gift that drops into certain people from the heavens. But Hynde’s vocal expression was just as magical. She sounded like she was singing directly to you, and she had that unique slow vibrato, which could suffuse a single note with heartbreak.
Born in 1951 and raised in Akron, Ohio, she grew up in what’s described in the film as a “cookie-cutter postwar family.” She loved her parents but experienced their ’50s squareness as if they were aliens. At Kent State University, she was close to one of the four students killed there by the National Guard on May 4, 1970, and by the time she moved to London in the early ’70s, she was ready for anything. Which is what she got.
She was majorly into drugs. She became a pop-music critic for New Musical Express, mostly writing scathing put-downs. But she couldn’t find a band that would have her! She met Mick Jones and attempted to work with him, but he went off and formed the Clash. She tried to join the Damned, but they weren’t biting. (She finally joined a band called the Moors Murders, who were so disreputable that they all performed in masks.) Yet she was writing songs, and her gift was pure; we hear her singing a demo of “Precious” from 1976, and the Hynde mystique is there, fully loaded.
The only solution was to form her own band, which she did, joining forces with a bass player, Pete Farndon (they were in a relationship together), then inviting in James Honeyman-Scott, who turned out to be a karmic addition. Hynde just thought she needed a guitarist, but Honeyman-Scott, who was only 22, was as visionary a guitar player as The Edge. The ferocious drummer Martin Chambers, with his knifey sideburns, completed the quartet.
So here was Hynde, an American girl with a smoldering stare, and her three British male back-up musicians. That sounds like a novelty, but Hynde ruled the stage with such verve, and such effortless punk-ruffian moves, that when you looked at her, you didn’t think that this was pretty much the first time in history that a woman with a guitar slung around her neck had led a rock ‘n’ roll band. She made it look like something that had always been.
The first song their producer, Nick Lowe, wanted to put out as a single was “Stop Your Sobbing,” Hynde’s cover of a 1964 track by the Kinks. If you listen to the original, it’s got a C&W-meets-British-Invasion stodginess that makes it sound like one of those slightly boring covers that filled out the Beatles’ first few albums. But Hynde makes the song as accusatory, and grandly symphonic, as a great Phil Spector track. In her hands, it’s a brand new song, one that squares with the vantage that would define the Pretenders — a grounded yearning for love, in its very imperfection, to become a higher love. As the single was getting ready to be pressed, the band still didn’t have a name, so Hynde, inspired by the Platters song “The Great Pretender,” came up with it at the last moment.
Here’s another side of the Chrissie Hynde paradox. At 17, she became a vegetarian, and still is, mostly driven by the animal-rights aspect of it all. But as she discusses in the documentary, she also had a thing for bikers — and I don’t just mean that she liked the sexiness of riding on the back of a chopper (though she did). She was hanging out with biker-gang members who were, by her own description, homicidal, and that was part of the excitement. So when it came to her belief in punk danger, this animal-rights vegetarian wasn’t playing.
That spirit was the yin to her melodic yang. She wrote “Brass in Pocket,” a masterpiece of jangle, and didn’t even want to put it out as a single, though it went to number one and became defining. What lyrics! The song is so resonant that it’s like a movie, and it’s also one of the most romantic songs I’ve ever heard. It could be the anthem of a teenage girl (“‘Cause I’m…gonna make you see,/There’s nobody else here, no one like me”). It could be the anthem of anyone who’s looking for someone to fall for them.
The Pretenders, for a while, had a satisfying life on the road. Hynde was a disciplined performer, and the guys enjoyed the perks of rock celebrity. But they indulged too much. Watching “Pretenders,” we wait for the dark side, and when it arrives it’s simple and devastating. Pete Farndon became a heroin addict, and spiraled down to the point that they had to kick him out of the band. Okay, that happened; it’s part of the rock ‘n’ roll story. He was fired from the Pretenders on June 14, 1982. Exactly two days later, James Honeyman-Scott, who was not a junkie (he was just a rock star who liked to party too much), died in his sleep of a heart attack. He was 25 years old and had been up for four nights straight, doing cocaine. This was a genuinely shocking rock death. Just like that, the band…was no longer a band.
As “Pretenders” captures vividly in the conversation it features with Chrissie Hynde, she’s a straight-shooter who can be extremely prickly and defensive. She was, and still is (at 75, looking great in a black-leather jacket), a strutting rock star who hates to see herself on camera. She smashed through the rock ‘n’ roll glass ceiling before it was even named, yet she doesn’t like the label of feminist or groundbreaker or anything else of that ilk, because she doesn’t want to be stuck in the role-model box. She had a fierce bravado on stage, yet claims that she took no pride in her performances; she just thought she was getting away with something. Maybe that’s why she called herself a Pretender? In “Pretenders,” she’s as real as it gets.

World's tallest totem pole comes down in Alert Bay, B.C., after more than 50 years
Emotional day as the tallest totem pole in the world, representing unity between tribes, comes down
The world’s tallest totem pole was brought down this week in Alert Bay, B.C., a community off the coast of northeast Vancouver Island.
For two 'Na̱mǥis chiefs, the pole — recognized in the Guinness Book of World Records — represented much more than its height.
"This pole was so much more," said Ho’miskanis Don Svanvik, hereditary chief and elected chief councillor of the 'Na̱mǥis First Nation.
"It was a beacon for our people coming out of a pretty dark time in history," he said, referencing the potlatch ban — the federal law that outlawed potlatching on the coast for more than 60 years.
Svanvik said his great-grandparents were jailed in the 1920s for taking part in potlatch.
"The pole, in some ways, represents people being who they always have been and continue to be," he said.
- Mi'kmaw mask carver wins Canadian Crafts Federation award
- Members of Okanagan Indian Band mourn loss of forests and irreplaceable artifacts in wildfire
"This is who we are. This is how we govern ourselves. This is how we celebrate and acknowledge things, through our ceremonies … this was a time when that was all coming back, coming into the forefront of things."
Crews began dismantling the 173-foot pole on Wednesday in a carefully staged, multi-hour process, after the 'Na̱mǥis First Nation confirmed the structure had become too unstable and hazardous to remain standing.
The nearby Gukwdzi (Big House) and its surrounding parking area were closed the evening before to establish a safety perimeter, and community members gathered nearby to witness.
Nothing lasts forever
The original pole was raised in 1973. It was one tree spliced into two connected sections, according to 'Na̱mǥis Hereditary Chief William Wasden Jr.
He said the pole was designed to carry the crests of 22 Kwakwa̱ka̱ʼwakw tribes — a deliberate statement of unity.
Tribes have amalgamated since then, Wasden said, but it was a powerful symbol of solidarity, an essential theme of the times.
"Our Big House was finished around then too … it was the same theme … somewhere for everybody to come and utilize," Wasden Jr. said.
"Alert Bay was like Grand Central Station, it was almost like the center of Kwakwa̱ka̱ʼwakw territories physically, but people were amalgamating there and so it almost became Kwakwa̱ka̱ʼwakw central."
When the pole came down, Wasden said he felt proud.
"Nothing lasts forever, especially the cedar tree," he said, sharing a story of an ancestor who recognized in ancient times that neither a cedar tree nor a mountain would always stand.
For Wasden, the pole’s takedown is part of a much older pattern, one where each generation is left to answer for itself.
"It’s our ancestors challenging us now," he said. "Are you gonna ride on our coattails, or will you be as great as we were, by doing the things you need to do to uplift your people?"
The pole was carved by a number of carvers at the time, overseen by Jimmy Dick.
Wasden named Jimmy Dick’s son "Blackie," Ben Dick Senior, as the main carver. He named other carvers like Adam Dick, Andy "Beanie" Beans, Gus Matilpi and Dick Dawson.
Svanvik named Henry Hunt and Henry Speck, along with others who may have dropped in at the time.
Both acknowledged Dora Cook who learned to carve alongside the men, one of very few women to do so at the time.
"She was ahead of her time," said Wasden.
Both Wasden and Svanvik remember the pole being carved when they were kids.
Svanvik jokingly said he played a small role when he was called over by the carvers to "squirt oil on the saw" they were using. Wasden carries a photo of himself and his friends sitting on the pole before it was raised.
Both said they look forward to what’s next.
"This is not the end of anything," Svanvik said.

EXCLUSIVE: Industry vet Ziad Kebbi is taking charge at MForMedia with a remit to take the Dubai-based production biz in a new direction built on the ownership of IP. “The best stories from this region have not been told yet,” the exec said as he stepped into his new role.
Kebbi becomes Managing Director at MForMedia, which Khalil Homeissy and Ralph Matar launched a decade ago. The founding duo will stay and oversee group strategy.
The company has a track record of producing big international formats regionally. Its credits include the local version of Carpool Karaoke, The X Factor and Takeshi’s Castle.
With Kebbi as MD, the plan is to re-engineer MForMedia into a studio built on creating and owning IP across scripted and unscripted. The other pillars of the new-look biz will be digital content and AI production.
Watch on Deadline
Kebbi is a seasoned player. The Lebanese-born exec’s previous roles include stints as Managing Director of Endemol Middle East, President of Sony Pictures Television Arabia, and CEO of Talpa Middle East. His credits include nine seasons of the huge regional hit The Voice Arabia.
“What drew me to MForMedia is what Khalil and Ralph have built: a real production company, with real delivery muscle and relationships earned over a decade,” Kebbi said. “The region is living its most exciting chapter, and the next great wave of Arabic content will belong to those who can move across genres and platforms without compromising on craft.”
He added: “My focus is exactly that: building on this foundation to create, source and produce content across non-scripted, scripted, and digital, shaped by the tools and thinking of what is coming, not what has been.”
Matar said: “Khalil and I have built this company on a simple promise: deliver, every time, at the highest standard. You protect what you have built by preparing it for what comes next, and there is no one better prepared for what comes next than Ziad.”
Homeissy added: “This industry is moving faster than it ever has, and the companies that will lead it are the ones that combine deep production craft with real creative networks across the region and beyond. Ziad brings both.”

Welcome to Edition 9.10 of the Rocket Report! This week we’re celebrating a historic moment in Europe when a German rocket company successfully put its launch vehicle into orbit. Isar Aerospace became the first purely commercial European company to reach orbit, and impressively it did so on just its second launch attempt. How quickly can they scale up operations? How quickly will the second European launch firm reach this goal? Big questions, which for now we don’t have answers to.
As always, we welcome reader submissions, and if you don’t want to miss an issue, please subscribe using the box below (the form will not appear on AMP-enabled versions of the site). Each report will include information on small-, medium-, and heavy-lift rockets as well as a quick look ahead at the next three launches on the calendar.
Isar Aerospace takes a huge step forward. Isar Aerospace, founded in 2018 by three students at a German university, successfully launched a privately developed rocket into low-Earth orbit on Saturday from a Norwegian spaceport inside the Arctic Circle. The two-stage rocket, Spectrum, became the first fully commercial launch vehicle in Europe to reach orbit, Ars reports. With Saturday’s success, Isar becomes the clear leader among a pack of several European launch startups vying to inject some competition into Europe’s stagnant launch market.
Private capital emerges … It took eight years for Isar to get to orbit, a timetable similar to other successful commercial rocket startups in the West. In that time, the company raised roughly $1 billion through several private financing rounds and now has a workforce of nearly 500 employees. European space officials hope a jolt of competition will light a fire under the continent’s rocket industry. European governments are accustomed to footing the bill and having a say in where rockets are built, a procurement model known as geographical return, or geo-return. The paradigm is different with companies like Isar, which established themselves on a privately funded basis, with ambitions to eventually attract commercial and government business.
Long-forgotten space plane is back? Ars Technica has written precisely one article about Ravn X, an autonomous aircraft and launch vehicle under development by Aevum. This was back in December 2020. We haven’t covered it since, I think it’s safe to say, there is a fair amount of skepticism about whether the project to build the space plane was all that realistic. And time has largely proved us right. The company’s initial target of an orbital mission in 2021 came and went. We largely forgot about the vehicle. Then something mysterious showed up at Long Beach Airport.
Don’t get too excited … TWZ reports that a handful of aviation photographers got a surprise eyeful of a very sleek and large aircraft silhouette last week at the airport and later learned that it was likely a mockup of Ravn X. Later on, in posts on X, Aevum founder Jay Skylus said the company “conducted Test 2 of Ravn X SN0 early this morning. Ravn X completed its first fully autonomous taxi. ~37 minutes of autonomy. We’re reviewing the telemetry and test data now and will share more as soon as I can.” We are not expecting any flights imminently. (submitted by Onychomys)
The Ars Technica Rocket Report
The easiest way to keep up with Eric Berger’s and Stephen Clark’s reporting on all things space is to sign up for our newsletter. We’ll collect their stories and deliver them straight to your inbox.
UK invests big time in northern spaceport. This week, the United Kingdom unveiled a new national space strategy that seeks to “drive growth, strengthen security and back everyday technologies.” As part of efforts to reindustrialize the country, the government is investing 7.8 billion pounds ($10.5 billion) through 2030. About 40 percent of the funding will go toward strengthening connectivity, including the Connectivity in Low Earth Orbit and SKYNET defense communications programs, which “play a pivotal role in keeping our Armed Forces connected wherever they are in the world.”
German rockets to launch from there … The UK government also wants to help push forward a spaceport under development in Shetland, an archipelago north of the Scottish mainland. The government will provide 30 million pounds ($40.5 million) for the SaxaVord Spaceport in Shetland, with the aim of “helping Britain and our partners to launch satellites without relying on countries further afield while creating new jobs.” No orbital rocket has ever successfully launched from the United Kingdom. The main tenant of SaxaVord is German launch company Rocket Factory Augsburg. (submitted by iCowboy)
Firefly to launch from Sweden. Firefly Aerospace announced on Wednesday a multi-launch agreement with SSC Space for two Alpha rocket launches from Sweden’s Esrange Space Center. Targeted to launch no earlier than 2028, the missions will serve Sweden’s national security customers as well as additional commercial rideshare customers.
More to come … Jason Kim, CEO of Firefly Aerospace, said more Alpha launches will follow. “These first two missions are just the start of a long-term, multi-launch partnership with SSC Space that will provide assured access to space for years to come,” he said. SSC Space secured the full payload capacity and can allocate payload space to its government and commercial customers, providing flexible accommodations and launch opportunities for the European satellite market.
Avio seeks higher flight rate. Avio is looking to boost the pace of Vega-C rocket flights to six missions per year, roughly double the current level, and potentially go another 50 percent higher, Aviation Week reports. “We are working to increase, as a first step, the cadence of Vega to six per year, and potentially a second step to nine per year,” Giulio Ranzo said Wednesday during the International Space Summit in Paris.
Solid production is not so solid … The Vega-C rocket is used heavily by institutions for launch in Europe, where demand is rising. “We will follow what they need, what they ask us, and we will try to adapt to continue providing the service,” Ranzo said. One of the challenges in ramping up is that the Vega-C used the same solid rocket motors employed on Ariane 6, which is also looking to boost output. The combination is creating supply-chain bottlenecks that industry and government are trying to address.
Stoke Space eyes larger rocket. Stoke Space announced Tuesday that it has raised another significant round of funding, $1 billion, as it makes a final push toward its debut launch next year. The Washington-based launch company also revealed plans for a larger medium-lift vehicle, Ars reports. The quantity of new funding will enable the company to accelerate work on a larger “Block 2” version of the Nova rocket, capable of lifting 15 metric tons to low-Earth orbit in a fully reusable configuration.
Block 2 will rock you … “We have already started development on a larger vehicle, and we felt like now is the time to pour gas on that fire and really start full-force development of the larger vehicle, and so that’s the reason for the timing,” Stoke co-founder and Chief Executive Andy Lapsa said. The Nova Pathfinder vehicle has a diameter of about 12.5 feet, slightly larger than SpaceX’s Falcon 9 vehicle, although it is considerably shorter. The Block 2 version of Nova is intended to have a 15-foot diameter, Lapsa said. Stoke is targeting 2029 for the debut launch of Block 2.
Ariane 64 gets with Amazon for some more. Arianespace and Amazon Leo announced Wednesday an agreement at the International Space Summit in Paris for six additional Ariane 64 launches to continue deploying the Amazon Leo constellation into low-Earth orbit. The new order brings the total number of Amazon Leo launches with Arianespace to 24, up from 18, with missions scheduled through 2031 from Europe’s Spaceport in French Guiana.
Arianespace, the on-time provider? … To the surprise of some observers, including your humble correspondent, Arianespace has proven to be a more reliable launch partner to Amazon than the other two providers who inked deals with Amazon in 2022, United Launch Alliance and Blue Origin. But Ariane 6 has gotten through its teething pains without major issues, unlike Vulcan and New Glenn. “We committed early because we believed in what Arianespace was building, and they’ve executed mission after mission,” said Chris Weber, vice president of Amazon Leo business and product. “Expanding from 18 to 24 launches reflects our confidence in Ariane 6 and our continued investment in European launch capability.”
Nyx will fly on Ariane 6. Arianespace and The Exploration Company announced this week that Nyx, the reusable space capsule developed by The Exploration Company, will launch into orbit on an Ariane 6 rocket from French Guiana. The Exploration Company chief executive, Hélène Huby, has said she is targeting late 2028 for the launch of this spacecraft, which is due to fly a cargo mission to the International Space Station.
Commercial cargo redux … The launch deal follows the award of a service contract to The Exploration Company by the European Space Agency worth 760 million euros ($880 million) to support the development of Nyx, a demonstration mission, and two operational cargo missions. “We started the development of Nyx with private funding only, and we are now at a technical maturity level where ESA and Member States’ public funding can support us massively, as anchor clients, to help us finalize the vehicle,” Huby said.
Does Europe need a massive rocket? Speaking of Huby and The Exploration Company, the company also announced a $450 million Series C funding round this week, Ars reports. As part of this, the company will continue development of the Storm rocket engine, which is projected to have a thrust of about 400,000 pound-feet. This would be used to power a reusable rocket intended to launch 40 metric tons in reusable mode and 60 tons in expendable mode.
How to stay relevant … The expendable Ariane 6 rocket, by contrast, has a maximum lift capacity of about 20 tons. “If Europe wants to stay relevant—we will not be relevant without a massive rocket at a massive cadence,” Huby said during a teleconference with reporters on Tuesday. “And to do that we need a massive engine, and right now this is something we just do not have in Europe.” An aggressive timeline for the rocket’s development, she said, is 2033.
Terran R gets on-ramped by NASA. NASA said this week it has awarded a “Launch Services II” contract to Relativity Space that allows for on-ramping the Terran R rocket into the agency’s launch services program. Accordingly, the Terran R launch service will be available to NASA for future missions, including science, research, and human spaceflight.
Don’t expect Terran R to win awards right away … NASA still wants to see a new rocket like Terran R, which has yet to make its debut, demonstrate success in flight. Trump downplays AI risks after dire expert warnings and calls to slow development down
- Published
US President Donald Trump has downplayed risks posed by artificial intelligence following days of dire warnings by experts.
"You have a lot of very negative forces that are bringing it up that shouldn't be bringing it up and they're bringing up things that won't happen," Trump said during a visit to Ireland.
One of the warnings came from a former Anthropic researcher who said "there is a strong chance that we could all die in the immediate future" if the current pace of development continued.
On Saturday, top industry bosses agreed and called for a slow-down. Trump did not directly address the idea, but said: "We're leading China on AI... and, frankly, I want to keep it that way because whoever wins AI, wins."
Trump spoke on the same day AI researcher Jacob Coxon - who quit Anthropic a few days ago - told the BBC staff who were developing the systems were "genuinely frightened" for the future of humanity.
Coxon – who has also worked at OpenAI – welcomed the idea of a slowdown but said it would need to be co-ordinated with China.
On Saturday, Elon Musk, owner of xAI, and Sam Altman of OpenAI, backed a warning from the head of Anthropic Dario Amodei that the pace of development should be slowed "to reduce the risk that something goes seriously wrong".
The Anthropic CEO said any slowdown would have to be limited to avoid allowing China to pull ahead.
The issues surrounding AI have prompted fierce debate - and present a dilemma for many world leaders.
On one hand, the sector is seen as huge opportunity to boost economic growth and a way to improve outdated digital systems and ways of working.
But there have also been a number of incidents where AI appears to have gone seriously wrong.
In August OpenAI said it had slowed down training some of its most advanced AI models to improve security.
The ChatGPT-maker said it was adding new measures after its AI agents bypassed safeguards and hacked the tech start-up Hugging Face.
And the same month it was disclosed two of the world's most powerful AI tools created fake human profiles to try and trick people in attempted cyber-attacks.
The UK's AI Security Institute (AISI) said in the most serious case, Anthropic's Mythos AI tried to gain access to a service by sending private messages, having set up fake accounts mimicking real people - then hid the evidence.

What to know as a Philippine region with a history of conflict holds its first parliamentary polls
Voters in an autonomous southern Philippine region will cast their ballots Monday in the region's first parliamentary elections
MANILA, Philippines -- Voters in an autonomous southern Philippine region will cast their ballots Monday in the region's first parliamentary elections, seen as a crucial step in the quest for self-determination and lasting peace after decades of insurgency and violence.
The Bangsamoro Autonomous Region in Muslim Mindanao, or BARMM, covers five provinces, three cities and 63 villages across eight special geographic area clusters. It has nearly 2.4 million voters, with election officials aiming for an 80% turnout after polling was postponed for several years.
Here’s what to know about the Sept. 14 vote.
There are 80 seats at stake in the elections that will determine members of parliament, the region’s legislative body. These include 40 political party representatives, 32 district representatives and eight sectoral representatives.
Unlike the direct voting under the presidential system of the national government, the region’s chief minister, who heads the executive branch, is not elected by voters. Members of parliament will choose the chief minister from among themselves by a majority vote during their first parliamentary session.
Voters will choose one regional party, one district representative and six sectoral representatives. The 40 regional party-representative seats will be distributed to nominees based on a party’s vote share.
Centuries of colonialism by Spain, the U.S. and Filipino Christian settlers turned Muslims into a minority group in resource-rich Mindanao, the southern third of the Philippine archipelago from which the BARMM was carved out. The region has seen decades of intermittent but bloody conflicts over land, resources and political power.
Since the 1970s, about 150,000 combatants and civilians have died in the southern Philippines, while development was stunted in the country’s poorest region. Western and Asian governments feared the tenacious insurgencies could help foster Islamic extremism in Southeast Asia.
The presence of private armies and long-running clan wars has added to the violent mix.
Under a 2014 peace deal brokered by Malaysia, the largest Muslim rebel group — the Moro Islamic Liberation Front — gave up its goal of a separate Muslim state in the south of the largely Catholic country in exchange for broader autonomy. The group’s 40,000 fighters would be “demobilized” and given livelihoods and other help to bring them back to normal life.
The Bangsamoro region was established under the peace deal to replace a poverty-wracked five-province autonomous region with a larger, better-funded and more powerful area, which has been governed by former guerrilla leaders under a transition period that ends with the first regular elections on Sept. 14.
The Moro Islamic Liberation Front last year suspended the disarming of its remaining 14,000 fighters after claiming that the government has not fully complied with socio-economic commitments it made under the 2014 peace deal. Then-presidential assistant David Diciano, who had been helping oversee the transformation of the Bangsamoro region, said in a statement at the time that the Muslim rebel front’s central committee had decided “to postpone the decommissioning of 14,000 of its combatants and 2,450 of their weapons.”
The Institute for Autonomy and Governance, a nonprofit policy and research center based in the region, has noted that the incomplete decommissioning of the Moro Islamic Liberation Front’s combatants as well as the organization’s split into two rival political parties vying in the elections pose a potential danger of violence that may affect voters’ confidence to go out and vote.
More than 20,000 military and police personnel are being deployed to secure the elections, officials said.
“We have just one goal: for them to be able to vote. All our preparations and efforts would be in vain if our fellow citizens couldn’t vote,” Commission on Elections Chairman Erwin Garcia said.
Michael Henry Yusingco, a senior research fellow of the Ateneo Policy Center, in an article published by the online portal Access Bangsamoro, said: “Without a party ethos that is rooted in collective responsibility, mutual respect, and orientation toward the common good, parliaments risk devolving into arenas of personal rivalries, factional disputes, or transactional politics."
He said it is the right time for regional parties to show they can embody such party ethos to sustain parliamentary democracy.
“Clearly, the BARMM’s history of clan politics, electoral violence, and patronage-based loyalties presents formidable challenges.”

Although the photograph recirculated in 2026, it dates back to at least December 2018.
"In 1973 Japan planted trees in concentric circles as part of an experiment in forestry spacing. This is what they look like today from above," one Reddit post (archived) captioned the photograph.
(Reddit u/Impressive_East_)
That image and other photographs showing the same formations have circulated online for years, appearing on platforms such as Instagram, 9GAG, Facebook, Pinterest and X.
In short, the photograph was real, and the claim about the forest was also accurate. It showed two experimental plots of Japanese cedar near Nichinan, a city in Miyazaki Prefecture on the island of Kyushu. According to the Miyazaki Southern Forest Management Office, the experiment was established in fiscal year 1973 to study how different planting densities affected tree growth and wood quality. As such, we have rated this claim as true.
The photograph circulating in 2026 was not new — we traced it to at least December 2018.
The same forest has attracted attention before. We previously investigated similar photographs of the experimental plots in September 2024. One of the images circulating at the time was also available in The Associated Press' image archive.
Origin of the photograph
The photograph first gained attention when Japanese news outlet Sankei News published it in a story about the forest.
(www.sankei.com)
The outlet credited the image to Miyazaki Southern Forest Management Office, a regional office of Japan's Forestry Agency. Its caption (translated from Japanese via Google Translate) read, "A circular pattern visible in the mountains of Nichinan City, Miyazaki Prefecture."
The image later appeared in numerous social media posts and articles.
What the photograph shows
The photographs circulating online show Japanese cedar trees arranged in two groups of concentric circles in a national forest near Nichinan, in Miyazaki Prefecture. An AP caption describing the forest said the trees in the outer ring were approximately 20 meters (66 feet) tall, about 5 meters (16 feet) taller than those near the center.
The circular forest was also discoverable on Google Maps and Google Earth, as the Miyazaki Southern Forest Management Office gave its location as 31°43'50.0"N, 131°23'05.0"E.
According to the office, the experiment was linked to changes in the local timber industry. Obi cedar was planted sparsely in the area for shipbuilding timber, but demand later shifted toward wood for general construction.
Researchers created the experiment to study how different planting densities affected tree growth and wood quality. It was established in fiscal 1973, with the cedar seedlings planted in March 1974. The trees were arranged in concentric circles at different distances from one another, creating planting densities of about 377 to 10,027 trees per hectare. Seen from above, this produced the circular pattern that earned the site the nickname "mystery circles."
Later surveys showed that planting density affected the trees' size and growth. A 2011 study concluded that around 2,000 to 2,800 trees per hectare was suitable for lower-cost forestry. The experiment's final report, completed in fiscal year 2023, concluded that planting densities of 1,500 trees per hectare or fewer could be effective in terms of financial returns and afforestation costs.
For further reading, in January 2015 we investigated whether a law in Japan makes it illegal for citizens to be fat.

Intensifying vaccination of dogs and ensuring that people bitten by dogs receive timely and complete rabies post-exposure prophylaxis (PEP) could save far more lives in Keralam than routine pre-exposure prophylaxis (PrEP) vaccination of children, according to a new modelling study on the cost-effectiveness of rabies interventions.
What the study found
The study, published in The Lancet Regional Health – Southeast Asia, estimates that routine childhood PrEP—vaccinating children against rabies before any animal exposure — would prevent only about 10 additional deaths over 10 years, while adding an estimated $10.5 million to $36.5 million to healthcare costs.
In contrast, comprehensive vaccination of dogs, combined with improved post-bite treatment and efforts to close gaps in PEP, could reduce rabies deaths by 83% compared to the current strategy, the study says. Scaling up vaccination of both owned and free-roaming dogs to 70% coverage could potentially bring human rabies deaths down to zero in Keralam within three years, according to the model.
The research was led by the University of Glasgow in collaboration with researchers from the Directorate of Medical Education, Kerala University of Health Sciences, the School of Public Health, the Directorates of Health and Animal Husbandry in Keralam, and the London School of Economics and Political Science.
Rabies in Keralam
Rabies prevention is already one of Keralam’s most intensive public health interventions, with more than 9,00,000 people receiving free treatment every year following animal bites. The State also has a PEP completion rate of over 90%. Yet human rabies deaths continue to occur, with 33 deaths reported in 2025, including among children.
The findings add a new dimension to the ongoing debate over whether Keralam should introduce routine PrEP for children as a rabies prevention strategy. Paediatricians and several public health experts have advocated childhood PrEP because children are particularly vulnerable to severe bites, including injuries to the face and hands, which could become fatal, despite post-exposure treatment.
The study does not rule out PrEP. Instead, it argues that PrEP may be more appropriate for specific high-risk populations who face difficulties in reaching healthcare facilities quickly after exposure, including some geographically dispersed tribal communities.
It argues that given Keralam’s relatively strong access to PEP, universal childhood PrEP may produce relatively little additional mortality reduction for the huge resources required, whereas improved dog vaccination and better wound management and timely PEP may produce greater population-level gains.
Cost effectiveness
“The study is a comparison of the cost effectiveness of PrEP against other interventions as a population-level strategy to reduce rabies. It points out that, as a public health strategy, investing in dog vaccination is more cost effective because it stops virus transmission in the community, and takes us closer to rabies elimination,” said Zinia T. Nujum of the School of Public Health, KUHS, who led the research in Kerala.
According to Martha Luka, researcher at the University of Glasgow’s School of Biodiversity, One Health & Veterinary Medicine and lead author, PrEP for children is unlikely to be the best use of public health resources in Keralam, where access to post-bite vaccination and completion of the regimen are already high.
Canines are the reservoir of the rabies virus and accounts for 70% of the rabies cases. Vaccinating the dog population interrupts transmission before people are exposed, whereas PrEP mainly protects vaccinated individuals while the wider risk remains.
The researchers modelled 12 different combinations of dog vaccination, post-bite treatment and PrEP over a 10-year period from 2026-2035. The study’s sensitivity analysis underlines the importance of improving access to PEP. Raising the proportion of bite victims who seek medical care from 70% to 95% could prevent more than 1,100 additional deaths—over 20 times the mortality reduction achievable even with maximum PrEP coverage in the model.
Vaccination of domestic dogs
The researchers also found that increasing vaccination coverage among domestic dogs alone could produce substantial health gains. “About 70-80% of dog-bite cases in the State are due to domestic dogs. Mandatory licensing and vaccination of domestic dogs, can help improve coverage. We could focus on completing domestic dog vaccination and then move on to vaccinating strays,” said Dr. Nujum.
However, she pointed out that the population of free-roaming dogs in Keralam could be at least five times the official estimate, highlighting the need for better data to plan vaccination programmes. The researchers argue that the State’s priority should therefore be a sustained One Health-based dog vaccination programme targeting at least 70% coverage, involving local bodies, Animal Husbandry and Health departments, veterinary teams, NGOs and communities.

The forum, marking the 10th anniversary of the King Salman Humanitarian Aid and Relief Centre (KSRelief), witnessed key agreements and pledges aimed at addressing ongoing humanitarian challenges in the Middle East and beyond.

September is typically the time when television gets serious again. The summer’s biggest TV shows have aired their finales, the fall schedule is kicking into high gear, and streamers are rolling out everything from high-concept sci-fi to prestige dramas. There’s plenty of familiar IP in the mix, but also some genuinely original shows worth putting on your “to watch” list.
While plenty of outlets will tell you what everyone is watching (see: Reacher), that’s not our goal. As always, the TV shows we’re watching this month reflect the kinds of stories WIRED covers every day—shows that explore technology, science, politics, culture, and the sometimes unsettling ways they intersect.
From returning favorites to ambitious new series—and at least one show that might rekindle your love of traditional anime—these are the TV shows we think you should make time to stream this month.
The Paper
What happens when a newspaper attempts to not just survive, but thrive, in a world where digital media has become the norm? The Paper, a spinoff of The Office from Greg Daniels and Michael Koman, follows the staff of a struggling Midwestern paper as they attempt to revive it.
Ultimately, its idealistic new editor-in-chief Ned Sampson (Star Wars and Harry Potter alum Domhnall Gleeson) and his hungry young reporter Mare Pritti (Chelsea Frei) end up grappling with what journalism looks like in the digital age. Season 2, which arrived on September 9, finds their Toledo Truth Teller newly revitalized and searching for its next big scoop, making the show a surprisingly sharp comedy about the future of journalism—and who gets to shape it.
Lego Star Wars: The Mandalorian
Though this summer’s The Mandalorian and Grogu (which is streaming on Disney+ now) seriously underperformed at the box office, Lucasfilm is partnering with Lego to take another stab at the fan-favorite Star Wars series—which might be exactly what the franchise needs right now. Lucasfilm and Lego are going back to the beginning, reimagining all three seasons of the Pedro Pascal-starring live-action series as a 49-minute animated comedy.
For anyone who somehow managed to miss Mando and Grogu until now, the story follows Din Djarin (Pascal in the live-action series, Gavin Hammon in this iteration), a bounty hunter known as the Mandalorian, who takes a job transporting a mysterious Force-sensitive child. That child, of course, is Grogu, aka Baby Yoda. What starts as a simple assignment turns into a galaxy-spanning adventure as the pair become unlikely partners. Consider this version an entertaining way to play catch-up.
South Park
It’s hard to remember a time when the world didn’t have South Park. For nearly 30 years, audiences have watched as four potty-mouthed fourth-graders—Stan, Kyle, Cartman, and Kenny—navigate life in the bizarre mountain town of South Park, Colorado, in this very much adults-only animated comedy. Along the way, they’ve encountered alien life forms, celebrities, and Elon Musk (yes, the real one). They’ve also watched Kenny die on at least 100 occasions.
Last year, the seemingly never-ending comedy reinvented itself as a particularly pointed political satire by taking aim at figures including JD Vance, Pete Hegseth, Kristi Noem, Donald Trump, and Donald Trump’s manhood. The White House, unsurprisingly, had thoughts. And so did the Emmys; the show just took home the 2026 award for Outstanding Animated Program. Clearly, creators Trey Parker and Matt Stone have no plans to take their foot off the gas; they just announced they’re taking a page out of Trump’s renaming book and rechristening the show South America for its 29th season, which premieres on September 16.
Slow Horses
What if television’s best spy show was also one of its funniest? If John le Carré and (the original) The Office had a baby, it would look and sound a lot like Slow Horses, which returns for a sixth season on September 16.
Based on Mick Herron’s Slough House book series, the series follows a dysfunctional team of MI5 misfits who are banished to the infamous Slough House unit, where they work under the notorious Jackson Lamb (Gary Oldman), a foul-mouthed, flatulent, chain-smoking wreck of a man who also happens to be the most brilliant operative in the room. It’s a prestige spy thriller that doesn’t take itself too seriously, bouncing effortlessly between shoot-outs and the kind of droll office banter you’d expect from the best workplace comedies. In a career full of memorable performances, and an Oscar to show for it, Slow Horses just might be the role Oldman is best remembered for. It’s also the project that has made Jack Lowden oddsmakers’ top pick for the next James Bond.
City of Blood
In City of Blood, an eight-episode miniseries from Germany, climate change has turned Berlin into a sweltering city teetering on the edge of collapse—and vampires are ready to take advantage of the chaos. While the privileged few live beneath a climate-controlled dome, the rest of the city’s denizens are left to battle the heat, crime, and corruption that have become part of everyday life. But when estranged sisters Bea (Lea Drinda) and Phoebe (Soma Pysall) reunite, they uncover a nefarious political plot and learn that, thanks to that aforementioned undead population, blood has become the city’s most coveted commodity. It’s a perfectly strange mix of climate dystopia, family drama, and vampire thriller. And it arrives on September 16.
MobLand
Season 2 of MobLand is almost here—whether Tom Hardy likes it or not. (Despite all the recent headlines surrounding the Oscar winner’s behind-the-scenes drama, he has already signed on for Season 3.) The highly underrated, or perhaps just underseen, crime drama returns with the Harrigan family’s criminal empire under threat from rival forces, forcing their street-smart fixer Harry Da Souza (yep, Hardy) to navigate increasingly bloody internal tensions.
As Harry works to keep the fractured family from tearing itself apart, he’s aided by his trusty sidekick Zosia (Jasmine Jobson), a tech specialist who brings a distinctly 21st-century skill set to their old-school criminal enterprise headed up by Conrad (Pierce Brosnan) and Maeve Harrington (Helen Mirren). Meanwhile, rival forces close in, loyalties shift, and violence spreads through every corner of the family’s world. Expect more bloodshed, shifting allegiances, poor decisions, and one of television’s most kickass theme songs (Fontaines D.C.’s “Starburster”) when Season 2 premieres on September 18.
Outlander: Blood of My Blood
Before there was Jamie and Claire, there were their parents. Like its predecessor, this Outlander prequel follows two separate timelines as it details the courtship of Jamie Fraser’s parents, Brian Fraser (Jamie Roy) and Ellen MacKenzie (Harriet Slater), in 18th-century Scotland, alongside the story of Claire Beauchamp’s parents, Henry Beauchamp (Jeremy Irvine) and Julia Moriston (Hermione Corfield), in World War I-era England. Their two love stories unfold across different time periods, weaving together romance, family drama, and the time-traveling forces that kept Outlander fans enthralled for eight seasons. The series’ second season arrives on September 18.
American Horror Story
Season 13 of Ryan Murphy and Brad Falchuk’s horror anthology is shaping up to be what has at various points called an Avengers-esque “endgame-level event” of “greatest hits.” While the details, as always, have been kept rather quiet, what we do know is that the new season of American Horror Story will pull bits and pieces from each season of the series, with a heavy emphasis on its witchcraft-laden “Coven” and “Apocalypse” storylines.
We also know it is reassembling an all-star cast of past stars, some of whom will play double—or even triple—character duty. Among them: Murphy mainstays Sarah Paulson, Evan Peters, Jessica Lange, Kathy Bates, Emma Roberts, Billie Lourd, and Angela Bassett. The new season arrives on September 26, which gives you plenty of time to brush up on your AHS lore.
Neon Genesis Evangelion
Before Netflix gave it a new English dub—and, depending on who you ask, stirred up a lot of feelings—there was the original Japanese-language version of Neon Genesis Evangelion. The landmark anime, released in 1995, follows a group of teenagers recruited to pilot giant biomechanical weapons called Evangelions, or Evas, as they defend a post-apocalyptic Tokyo (now known as Tokyo-3) from mysterious creatures, aka Angels. But what starts as a fairly straightforward battle-for-humanity story soon becomes something far stranger, delving into trauma, loneliness, identity, and human connection.
The Criterion Channel is bringing all 26 episodes of the classic (pre-Netflix) English dub to streaming for the first time, alongside the original Japanese-language version for all you purists. It’s a fitting return for one of anime’s most boundary-pushing series.

Trump Will Never Mail the $5,000 Checks
Deconstructing a policy proposal that makes no sense on any level
Donald Trump’s new promise to give a $5,000 check to every adult American citizen if Republicans win the midterm elections may be an effort to answer a variant of an age-old riddle: Can Trump devise a policy so ill-conceived that even Trump’s intelligence is insulted?
Candidates often make inducements part of their campaign pitch. One obvious peculiarity of this plan is that Trump’s party already controls both chambers of Congress. Why, then, should the bonus checks be contingent on voters giving Republicans another two-year majority?
Trump has told reporters that he could distribute the loot without congressional approval. This is untrue. (It’s a facially unconstitutional infringement of Congress’s spending authority.) If it were true, however, it would make his decision to hinge the checks on the election’s outcome even more mysterious. If the choice were his alone, the outcome would seem totally irrelevant.
Under certain economic circumstances, distributing checks to everybody can make sense. In a deeply depressed economy, in which consumer spending is too low to maintain high employment levels, juicing it with a cash infusion can help keep it alive.
However, current circumstances are quite different. Unemployment is low and growth is healthy. The problem is that inflation is running well above target levels. Injecting roughly $1.2 trillion (the one-year cost of the checks) into the economy would likely make inflation worse—more cash would be chasing the same number of goods and services, driving up their price. This, in turn, would probably force the Federal Reserve to raise interest rates to tamp down inflation, which would throw recovery into jeopardy.
J. D. Vance has suggested that the checks could be paid for with tariff revenue. In theory, that would offset the inflationary effect of the new spending. But the tariffs are already in place, meaning that he’s citing a current revenue source to fund a new cost—at a moment when revenue is nowhere near sufficient: The U.S. government is running a deficit of nearly $1.8 trillion.
Trump, for his part, explained to reporters that he intends the checks not as an economic policy but as a treat: “I’m doing it as a reward for people having to put up for five years and four years of a horrible situation caused by Biden … It’s almost a reward for the people having to put up with Biden’s policy.”
When Trump ran in 2024 against Joe Biden’s policies, the “reward” was supposed to be having Trump and his policies in place. Now he seems to be suggesting that Trump’s incredible economy is not enough. This explanation is also impossible to square with his claim that the bonus would be contingent on Republicans winning the midterms. Why do Americans deserve a retroactive bonus for living in Biden’s America only if Republicans win the midterm elections? By Trump’s logic, if we were forced to endure two years of Democrats sharing power, that would make us more, not less, deserving of compensation.
The pretense that these checks have any economic logic has proved too great to bear for at least some Republicans. Senator Ted Cruz of Texas and Florida Governor Ron DeSantis dissented mildly, causing Trump’s advisers to heap them with ridicule. “Ron and Ted—the co-captains of your old high school Math-Lete Team—will nerd out on this while jockeying for 11th place in ’28,” a senior adviser to the White House told Politico Playbook.
In a normal administration, These guys understand high-school-level math is a credential, albeit a minimal one, to opine on economic policy. Only in the Trump era can it be presented as a disqualification.
The actual defense of the policy, obviously, is that it’s never going to happen. Last February, Elon Musk floated a DOGE dividend (which never arrived, in part because DOGE never produced meaningful savings). That year, Trump repeatedly promised tariff-rebate checks, which also never happened.
The Fox News host Laura Ingraham asked Trump why he doesn’t simply send the checks out now. He replied, “Because the Democrats can’t do it. Because for them, it’s negative growth. With us, it’s so positive.” What does this answer mean? Does it mean anything at all? Does Trump even believe it has any meaning, other than constituting a string of sentence fragments conveying the general sentiment Democrats bad; me good?
The actual divide within the party pits the Republicans who think that their voters are dumb enough to fall yet again for Trump’s free-money promise against those who suspect that the ruse has worn thin. Trump has spent his career betting against the intelligence of the American voter. The $5,000-check promise may be the moment he finally underestimated his audience.

The dream box-office run of a rom-com and the enthusiastic audience response to two new releases have instilled hopes among the exhibtors in Malayalam film industry to end the September quarter on a positive note.
Filmmaker A. D. Girish’s Bethlehem Kudumba Unit, featuring Nivin Pauly and Mamitha Baiju in lead roles, has crossed the 300-crore mark in worldwide collections as of Sunday (September 13, 2026), according to the estimates by the Film Exhibitors’ United Organisation of Kerala (FEUOK).
“It has surpassed the record set by director Dominic Arun’s Lokah Chapter 1: Chandra that had collected over 300 crores worldwide,” said Suresh Shenoy, member of the executive committee of FEUOK.
“Bethlehem Kudumba Unit, which was released on August 21, 2026, has earned a Kerala gross collection of about 150 crore, along with an overseas and rest of India total turnover of around 120 crore and 30 crore, respectively, as of Sunday (September 13, 2026). The repeat audience for the movie has shot up its performance at the box-office,” he said.
Exhibitors said that the enthusiastic response to the movies Pradhama Drishtya Kuttakkar and Aasha released on September 11 along with the extended run of Bethlehem Kudumba Unit have eased the situation in September after the much-expected movie I’m Game featuring Dulquer Salmaan in lead role did not rise up to the expectations.
P.V. Basheer Ahamed, president of the Kerala Film Exhibitors’ Association, pointed out that the footfalls for both movies have gone up after the first day of its release. “These movies are receiving a positive response in view of its strong content. It has been proved again that an interesting script will always bring the audiences into the cinemas,” he said.
Directed by Shahad, ‘Pradhama Drishtya Kuttakkar’ has Parvathy Thiruvothu, Vijayaraghavan, Mathew Thomas, Unnimaya Prasad, and Sidharth Bharathan in lead roles. The cast of ‘Aasha’ directed by Safar Sanal includes Urvashi, Joju George, and Aishwarya Lekshmi.

The rock guitarist whose killing shocked India's north-east
- Published
When Chongtham Vikram Singh finally came home to India's north-eastern state of Manipur, his old friend Dhiren Sadokpam went to the airport to receive him.
It was not the homecoming he had imagined. Vikram arrived in the cargo hold, inside a steel container.
Three days earlier, the 54-year-old musician had been beaten to death outside his home in south-east Delhi.
"Nobody seemed to have the strength to speak," Sadokpam told the BBC. "What could be said?"
Vikram had spent much of his life travelling with his guitars, carrying his music from small stages in Manipur's capital, Imphal, to jazz clubs, classrooms and concert halls in Delhi.
According to police and his family, he had gone downstairs late on Sunday night after a group of men were shouting and drinking outside his apartment building. When he objected to the disturbance, the men allegedly attacked him.
His wife, Joshna Chongtham, said Vikram returned upstairs but was pursued and assaulted outside the family's apartment.
Hours later, after complaining of breathlessness, he was taken to hospital by his 20-year-old son. He died there early in the morning.
Seven men and a juvenile have been arrested in connection with his killing. Police say they are investigating the circumstances of the attack.
The death has prompted an outpouring of grief and anger, and renewed concerns about the discrimination faced by people from India's north-east in Delhi, where members of the community have for years reported racial abuse, harassment and violence.
Police say they have so far found no evidence of a racial motive. But north-eastern groups have held protests and demanded an impartial investigation.
The case has also drawn attention to Vikram himself - a familiar figure in Manipur's music scene who, over four decades of playing and teaching, gathered around him a large circle of students, friends and admirers.
At a press conference two days after his death, his wife Joshna said: "We are not seeking revenge. We are seeking justice. He had a name, a family and a life that mattered."
For most of his 54 years, that life had revolved around music.
Vikram grew up around it. His mother, Chongtham Kamala, was a celebrated singer who lent her voice to Matamgi Manipur, the first feature film made in the Manipuri language.
As a boy, he accompanied her to All India Radio for recordings. Before long, he had auditioned there himself and become a child artist, playing the accordion.
There is an old black-and-white photograph of Vikram from those years. He is kneeling stiffly in front of a microphone with an accordion balanced across his lap. Beside him, another boy sits behind a pair of drums. Both wear the grave expressions of children who have been told that a photograph is being taken.
The boy with the accordion would soon discover guitars - first Hawaiian and Spanish, then electric - and, somewhere along the way, acquire thick black glasses and a splendid moustache.
By the mid-1980s, Imphal had become an unlikely outpost of rock music. The sound travelled there largely on cassette tapes, bringing with it the hard rock and heavy metal being played thousands of miles away.
Young men formed bands and crowded into local halls, working with whatever they could find - modest sound systems, locally made amplifiers, guitars turned up as loud as they would go. They listened, copied, experimented.
Vikram was studying at Don Bosco School then and still playing accordion and Hawaiian guitar. Years later, he remembered how he and his friends would ask the priests for permission to leave school to watch a local band perform.
"Those were sweet and innocent days that actually inspired me to go for rock," he recalled in a 2014 interview, external.
Soon, watching was no longer enough. Vikram took up the electric guitar and began playing in bands himself - first Ultra Vires, then Phoenix and Eastern Dark - becoming part of the generation that was giving Imphal's new rock scene a sound of its own.
It was around this time, in 1987, that Dhiren Sadokpam first met him.
They were setting off from Imphal to study in Shillong, and Sadokpam remembers them waiting at a temporary interstate bus terminal with backpacks, steel luggage boxes and bedding for the long journey.
Vikram was boyish and energetic, he recalls, but mostly kept to himself.
"He would spend long hours in his room, mastering each and every composition that came his way," Sadokpam said.
With each band, Vikram's playing evolved. Ultra Vires became a place to experiment. Phoenix, which would become one of the defining bands of Manipur's early rock scene, brought greater precision and a devoted following that endured long after its heyday.
By the time he joined Eastern Dark, Sadokpam remembers the quiet young man disappearing into the instrument, making its six strings "cry and sing".
In the early 1990s, he spent two years in Calcutta (now Kolkata), where he encountered musicians at the Calcutta School of Music, a century-old institution with a strong tradition of Western classical music, and was drawn more deeply into jazz and classical music. His own playing began to range across styles, from rock and blues to jazz and fusion.
By the 2000s, Vikram had moved to Delhi, where he built a life around performing and teaching music.
In 2010, he reconnected with an old musician friend and formed Fubar Ghetto. The band played jazz, blues, rock and fusion, with improvisation at the centre of it. Their first performance was a charity concert near the Yamuna river.
From there, they worked their way through Delhi's live-music circuit: universities, clubs and cultural festivals, the National School of Drama and, on one occasion, the Czech Embassy.
Vikram never became a major star. Instead, he built the quieter reputation of a working musician - among the people he played with, the students he taught and the musicians he helped along the way.
Since his killing, many of those people have remembered the man who was gentle, generous and largely uninterested in recognition.
Former student guitarist Sachidananda Angom remembered him as "always kind, helpful" and someone who "could really light up a room".
Mame Khan, the Rajasthani folk singer with whom Vikram performed for several years, told The Indian Express, external that Vikram was "a really kind and lovely person" who never picked arguments with anyone.
Sadokpam is careful not to make more of their friendship than it was.
They had met as young men in 1987, lost touch for two decades and found each other again in middle age. In between, Sadokpam followed Vikram's musical life from a distance, as a fan and a friend.
They last met in Delhi in 2019, when Vikram invited him home for dinner.
"Vikram picked up his guitar and played and spoke excitedly about his students," he recalled.
When it was time to leave, Vikram asked him to come again soon. Sadokpam said he promised he would.
"I never made it back."

How did the first Ultimate Championship go?
- Published
As poster boy Armand Duplantis performed the Ultimate Championship's official song and fireworks lit up the sky above the newly crowned winners, athletics had taken its first strides in a new direction.
Across three fast-paced evenings the inaugural event played out in Budapest, where a record $10m (£7.4m) prize pot was distributed among the sport's biggest stars.
It looked different. It felt different. And, after three successive sell-out crowds and positive feedback from the athletes, it appears it is here to stay.
"It's a good first step towards changing track and field for the better," said Usain Bolt, event ambassador and the greatest sprinter in history.
"The athletes are loving it. It's a different energy, a different vibe."
World Athletics and its president, Lord Coe, worked for three years to tackle the absence of a season-ending pinnacle event.
Rather than keeping to an established formula, the Ultimate Championship was a bold, innovative undertaking - and it is hoped it can exist as a testing ground to help shape the sport's future.
"We walked out, we came through the little starlights and we all looked at each other and said, 'this is unbelievable'," Britain's four-time global relay medallist Imani-Lara Lansiquot told BBC Sport.
"It's so rare that things really live up to the expectation, the hype. I'm so, so glad, having been in this sport for many years now, to actually see us be put on a platform and celebrated in this way."
Athletics has long grappled with the issue of maintaining the interest and excitement which it generates at the Olympics throughout the rest of those four-year cycles.
The structure of the season has not always been clear for occasional viewers, while showdowns between the world's top athletes can be inconsistent. From a storytelling perspective, that is far from ideal.
They are all issues World Athletics has sought to begin addressing with the biennial Ultimate Championship, while also compensating the athletes with record prize money.
The premise is accessible: condensed, fast-paced sessions, with the best competing against the best for a global title and significant prize money.
A striking new appearance and several innovative features ensured the Ultimate Championship provided a notably different feel to that of the sport's established global championships.
An infield painted black sought to focus attention on the illuminated live events, while the horizontal jumps were decided in a bright pink sandpit.
A new trophy waited for the winners on a plinth, with their crowning moment marked by sparklers and celebratory music.
New features for TV audiences attempted to enhance the viewer experience, with athlete headshots, win probabilities and projected finishing positions flashing up on screen.
They did so with varying success.
Norway's Jakob Ingebrigtsen was unimpressed by his predicted finishing position of 12th before winning the 5,000m title, while Britain's 1500m champion Josh Kerr was expected to finish last - a result of both athletes racing lightly over recent seasons.
There was a notable athlete-centric feel to the event beyond the increased financial rewards.
The world's top athletes arrived on the eve of the championship for a red carpet event featuring photoshoots.
Athlete videos were played inside the stadium before events and winners held centre-court style interviews before being escorted to a champions' enclosure, where they joined Bolt and master of ceremonies Noah Lyles.
On the videos, Britain's Georgia Hunter Bell said: "I do like the fact that it builds personality and character for, hopefully, people to connect with the athletes. That storytelling is something that's really interesting.
"If you think of superstars like Carlos Alcaraz, Serena Williams or Tadej Pogacar, obviously they're great athletes, but it's their personality coming through that makes it fun."
BBC commentator and former 1500m world champion Steve Cram said: "The key is the exposure of it. It's good for the sport. It's really good for the profile of the athletes."
But the championship did not avoid criticism - the biggest its exclusion of certain events.
World Athletics took the decision to include events based on viewer behaviour, including pulse rate and sweat response.
That meant that distance track events, including the 3,000m steeplechase and 10,000m, were omitted, while only selected field events were included. Shot-putters and discus throwers were excluded entirely.
The event format was also altered. Round progression in several field events meant increased jeopardy, with the competition whittled down to the top four athletes by the fourth and final round.
British long jumper Jazmin Sawyers told BBC Sport: "Some field events didn't get any attention because they're not here. The championship is worse off for not having them.
"It looks amazing in stadium and broadcast. It's dynamic. It's exciting. There's a place for it alongside regular championships.
"I don't think I would like to see it replace regular championships, but I like the idea that this is something that exists alone."
On the long jump competition format, she added: "I would love to see all eight [athletes] get all four jumps. It makes it more interesting.
"I was able to come from fourth to second. What if the person who was eighth could go from eighth to first? That's more exciting."
On the matter of the excluded events, Coe said the disciplines held at the Ultimate Championship were "not in tablets of stone".
Looking ahead to the next edition in 2028, the Ultimate Championship will be positioned at the end of a season which is headlined by an Olympics.
It remains to be seen how it will fit alongside the Diamond League - the sport's season-long series - in the schedule of the athletes.
Former Olympic heptathlon champion Denise Lewis told BBC Sport: "People have wanted to see something that looked different and felt like a different product. World Athletics has delivered.
"I don't think we know what it will do to the global calendar of athletics.
"The overall picture and the landscape isn't clear. There is place for this, but I do think it is unclear what yet."
Coe accepted before the weekend that there would be "no guarantee we're going get everything right" and said a "slightly different format" might be considered in future.
But, regardless, the competition was a statement of intent as the sport seeks to engage with new, bigger audiences while ensuring its star names are rewarded with prize money closer aligned to that of other sports.
Speaking after become Britain's first Ultimate champion in the 1500m, Josh Kerr said: "I welcome anything that can push this sport on to make it more entertaining for people to watch and athletes to go out and compete.
"There is one last thing that we can do to get it right and that is to let athletes wear their own brands versus their country.
"I love my country and competing for them, but we don't make money from that. We don't have the pay cheques other sports do just yet.
"My $30,000 pay cheque just came through from winning the World Indoors, so $150,000 is a huge jump and I'm massively appreciative."

Swedish left-wing bloc edges ahead in knife-edge election results
Final results are not expected before Wednesday, when local election boards count postal votes that arrived too late for polling day, along with ballots cast from abroad
Sweden's centre-left opposition has edged ahead of the ruling right-wing government in a knife-edge general election, with days of uncertainty expected before a final result is confirmed.
The left-leaning bloc, led by Social Democrats leader Magdalena Andersson, was projected to win 176 seats in the 349-seat Riksdag, based on votes counted from 6,195 of Sweden's 6,312 electoral districts, the country's election authority said.
The right-wing governing bloc of prime minister Ulf Kristersson trailed with 173 seats, separated by roughly 20,000 votes, with around 94 per cent of the vote counted on Monday morning.
Exit polls from public broadcaster SVT had initially shown the left-wing parties ahead by several percentage points, prompting jubilation at the Social Democrats' election night gathering in Stockholm, though the mood shifted to quiet waiting as the closer preliminary results came in.
Sweden elects its parliament through a proportional representation system, with parties needing at least 4 per cent of the vote to win seats. More than 8 million of the country's roughly 10.6 million people were eligible to vote.
The country's political landscape is split between two four-party blocs, on the left and the right, meaning the outcome hinges less on any single party's result and more on which side can assemble a majority.
Final results are not expected before Wednesday, when local election boards count postal votes that arrived too late for polling day, along with ballots cast from abroad.
Speaking early on Monday, Mr Kristersson said the outcome remained genuinely uncertain, though he pointed to what he described as a broader ideological majority in parliament.
"There is a very clear non-socialist majority, or non-left leaning economic majority in the Swedish parliament," he said.
"When we have the final result it's a good idea to look at possible combinations. I will actually take note of that and at least figure out whether there are any possibilities."
No major media outlet had called the result. Ms Andersson urged her own supporters to wait for the final count.
"We must wait for the final election result," she said. "Right now we are leading, but we have to wait for the final result."
Mr Kristersson has governed Sweden since 2022 at the head of a three-party centre-right coalition, relying on outside support from the Sweden Democrats, a party with far-right roots that has moved toward the political mainstream, to secure a parliamentary majority.
The Sweden Democrats had been promised cabinet posts this time had the governing coalition been returned to office. In a break from a longstanding taboo, Mr Kristersson pledged before the vote to bring the party directly into government as he seeks to build a majority right-wing coalition. Since taking office, his government has abolished permanent residency for refugees, tightened welfare rules and stepped up expulsions of people without the right to remain in the country.
Ms Andersson, who served as prime minister from 2021 until losing power at the last election, would need to secure a coalition agreement with other parties to return to office, and her own bloc faces internal tensions of its own, with disagreements over migration policy, a proposed tax on billionaires and the construction of new nuclear reactors. Her Left Party and Centre Party partners, in particular, differ sharply on economic policy, which could complicate efforts to pass a budget even if her bloc secures a majority.

An Indian-origin individual has been declared a fugitive in the U.S. after allegedly defrauding the Medicare healthcare scheme of $93 million by submitting false claims for genetic tests.
The Department of Health and Human Services said Khadeer Khan Mohammed purportedly submitted, or directed others to submit, claims for laboratory genetic testing ineligible for reimbursement.
Over the course of the conspiracy, Mohammed used American Premier to submit approximately $93 million in alleged fraudulent Medicare claims, resulting in payments of at least $65 million, the Office of the Inspector General, Department of Health and Human Services said.
In 10 days in 2023 alone, Medicare paid approximately $13 million in suspected fraudulent claims.
According to the Department of Health, Mohammed is believed to be in Hyderabad, India.
It said from about August 2023 to October 2024, in the Northern District of Texas and elsewhere, Mohammed allegedly used physicians' personal identifying information without their knowledge or consent to submit claims for genetic tests for beneficiaries with whom the physicians had no treatment relationship.
"These tests were not ordered by the physicians and were not used in the care of the beneficiaries," the Department of Health said.

Supreme Court to offer Hindi summaries, audio-video bulletins
The initiative, announced on Hindi Diwas, is aimed at making the Supreme Court’s important decisions and their implications more accessible to ordinary citizens and litigants
The Supreme Court on Monday announced a new Hindi public information service under which simple Hindi summaries of selected important judgments and orders will be made available along with daily 15-30 minute audio and video bulletins explaining key rulings.
The initiative, announced on Hindi Diwas, is aimed at making the Supreme Court’s important decisions and their implications more accessible to ordinary citizens and litigants, particularly those who may find lengthy legal documents difficult to read or understand.
A press statement said that the Hindi service would be launched shortly after the necessary arrangements are put in place. Each summary will also carry a link to the corresponding official judgment or order, allowing users to access the original court document.

The audio and video bulletins are intended to provide a more accessible means of understanding important rulings, their impact and the course of action that may follow from them. The Supreme Court said the initiative would also benefit persons with disabilities.
The service will initially be available in Hindi, with the court planning to extend it in phases to other Indian languages. The move is intended to make concise information about important Supreme Court decisions available to citizens across linguistic regions in languages familiar to them.
The statement added that the initiative was also intended to link the recognition and respect for Indian languages with judicial public information and further the broader objective of making access to justice more accessible.

Spanish racers Fernando Alonso and Carlos Sainz had a home race to forget at the Spanish Grand Prix at the new ‘Madring’ circuit.
The two collided on track while fighting for position and it led to an angry rant on the radio from the two-time World Champion.
“He squeezed me into the wall,” Alonso said. “[At] the start, he crashed into two people; now he squeezed me into the wall on breaking.”
The Williams driver received a five-second time penalty for the incident and was eventually forced to retire from the race with an issue. Alonso finished 17th carrying damage from the clash and continued his angry response to the incident after the race.
“At 340 kph, I’d rather no one squeeze me against the wall. I’d rather be alive at the end of the race,” Alonso said.
I didn’t touch anyone, I was a centimeter from the wall and someone came and sent me into the wall at 340 kph,” he added.
Sainz, however, defended his action that preceded contact between the two cars and said Alonso forced the stewards to punish him with his explosive radio messages.
“There isn’t much to say. It’s the nature of the corner when you turn,” Sainz said. “The nature of that corner is always going to cause these kinds of incidents, because there’s only room for one car.”
