Russian drone hits train near Ukraine-Poland border soon after dignitaries passed through
KYIV, Ukraine — A Russian drone struck a train near the Ukraine- Poland border on Sunday shortly after senior visiting officials — including the former prime ministers of the U.K. and Sweden -- passed through, Ukraine's state rail operator said.
According to Ukrzaliznytsia, a diplomatic train carrying Boris Johnson, Carl Bildt and security advisers from several European Union states had purposely left the station at Yahodyn ahead of schedule. The visitors were on their way back from a security conference in Kyiv.
"It is highly probable that the Russian drone 's intended target was in fact the diplomatic train, which had departed the station earlier than scheduled," the company said in a Telegram post.
Bildt, the former Swedish PM, shared a video on X of the attack at Yahodyn station, near the Yahodyn-Dorohusk border crossing with Poland.
"This wasn't our train, but the one just minutes after us by the Polish border crossing," Bildt said. "It was evacuated as the Russian drone approached and no one was hurt. Very good safety system. Our train just had an evacuation warning."
Bildt, Johnson and fellow passengers had been in Kyiv for the Yalta European Strategy conference, which is an annual gathering of leaders and experts across politics, business, security and media.
Another train, with former CIA Director David Petraeus on board, was still at Yahodyn station when the drone struck, according to Ukrzaliznytsia.
There were no immediate reports of casualties on any of the trains.
Ukrzaliznytsia said it "constantly adjusts train schedules" to guard against strikes.
"I don't know what warped logic drove Putin to blow up a stationary Ukrainian locomotive on the Polish border this morning," Johnson wrote in a post on X.
"What we can say for sure is that this is the kind of random and senseless attack Ukrainians are enduring every day — even on civilian railways," he added.
Earlier on Sunday, a Russian drone hit a truck less than a mile from Polish territory, according to border guards, forcing the temporary closure of the Yahodyn-Dorohusk crossing.

The song carries a devotional appeal as it praises the glory of Lord Ram. The music of Rahman adds a serene feeling with Shreya’s vocals reverberating stillness. The music video of the song features visuals from the film with Ranbir Kapoor as Ram and Sai Pallavi as Sita exhibiting their charm.
Speaking about the song, Rahman said in a statement, “At the heart of ‘Jai Jai Ram’ is the simple and powerful repetition of Shri Ram’s name. Musically, the intention was to preserve the purity and intimacy of a prayer while allowing the composition to grow into a cinematic song. Arijit Singh and Shreya Ghoshal bring their own distinct emotional expression to Dr. Kumar Vishwas’s words, while always remaining true to the devotion at the centre of the song.”
Kumar Vishwas added, “While writing the song, my endeavour was not to describe Shri Ram, because his meaning cannot be contained in words, but to express the relationship every devotee shares with him: as our guide, our strength and our refuge. The language has been kept simple and direct because true devotion needs no ornamentation.”
Ramayana also stars Yash as Ravana, Sunny Deol as Hanuman and Ravie Dubey as Lakshman. The adapted screenplay is written by Sridhar Raghavan and Nitesh Tiwari with dialogues by Shreyas Jain and Nitesh Tiwari and the film is shot by Pankaj Kumar and Mahesh Limaye. It is among the most expensive Indian films ever made with the budget reportedly crossing Rs 4,000 crore.
Ramayana is produced by Namit Malhotra’s Prime Focus Studios along with DNEG and Yash’s Monster Mind Creations. The first part in the series will be released in theatres on Diwali 2026 followed by the second part in 2027.

Albertans to vote on opting out of federal programs — while keeping cash
It’s 1 of 4 constitutional questions on October ballot, but ‘yes’ vote alone can’t change this
When referendum day arrives in Alberta on Oct. 19, the focus won’t just be on separation and immigration.
Albertans will also be presented with four constitutional questions that range from abolishing the Senate to whether Alberta should appoint the judges who sit on the province’s higher courts.
Third on the list will be a question tied to federal programs like pharmacare. The federal government provides funding to provinces for these programs, sometimes with conditions attached.
The Alberta government wants that to change.
As part of the referendum, voters will be asked if they support a government push to try to amend the Constitution.
The stated goal? To allow provinces to opt out of federal programs “that intrude on provincial jurisdiction such as health care, education and social services” without losing any associated federal funding for use in social programs.
“What Alberta is gunning for here is an attempt to limit what we call the constitutional spending power,” said Geoffrey Sigalet, director of the UBC Research Group for Constitutional Law.
Power of the purse
By constitutional spending power, Sigalet is referring to Ottawa’s ability to transfer money to provinces and attach conditions to it.
Today, provinces can decline federal funding if they don’t agree with the conditions attached.
But if agreements between provinces and the federal government aren’t reached, that can also mean leaving money on the table, which can be politically unpopular.
“Different constitutional scholars take different perspectives on this,” Sigalet said.
“Some will be more in favour of centralizing this kind of thing. … My own sense is that Alberta has a point here.”
In Sigalet’s view, setting conditions on federal funding sent to other levels of government can look a lot like policymaking in another's jurisdiction.
He noted that some scholars have argued that the spending power is unconstitutional, and others have said it could be open to future litigation.
David Schneiderman, a law professor at the University of Toronto, argued the federal government only oversteps, constitutionally speaking, when it “imposes" programs.
“When it attaches conditions to spending in an area of provincial jurisdiction, a province can simply refuse to accept federal money,” Schneiderman wrote in an email.
“Note that there has not been any serious constitutional challenge to the exercise of the modern federal spending power. Provinces prefer to accept the money — and then erode conditions, as in the case of healthcare.”
This isn’t the first time the federal government’s spending power has been debated.
Not a new debate
The Meech Lake Accord in the 1980s was a failed attempt to amend the Canadian Constitution. One of the proposed amendments was allowing provinces to opt out with "reasonable compensation" of national shared-cost federal programs — with a notable condition.
“Under the language of Meech Lake, it was still a little limiting,” Sigalet said.
Under Meech, provinces could opt out if they established a program compatible with national objectives.
Alberta’s referendum doesn’t mention such a condition. Voters will simply be asked whether they endorse Alberta pursuing a constitutional change.
That change, as the province sees it, would allow provinces to opt out of federal programs “without a province losing any of the associated federal funding for use in its social programs.”
But as for then setting up a comparable program?
“We won’t make assumptions about the outcome or what decisions should follow until Albertans have had their say,” wrote Kyle Warner, a spokesperson for the province, in an email.
Schneiderman sees an issue.
“Alberta could negotiate with the feds. It is hard to see any federal government agreeing to something short of the Meech formulation,” he said.
Much like the other constitutional questions on the ballot this October, a “yes” vote doesn’t mean immediate change.
Developing an opt-out rule, in whatever form it might take, would require the support of Parliament, as well as at least seven provinces representing at least half of Canada’s population.
Impact on federal programs
All of this might sound familiar to Albertans.
For instance, take Alberta Premier Danielle Smith’s statement in 2024 that the province would pull out of the Canadian Dental Care Plan by 2026.
There are, of course, less than four months to go in the calendar year, and Alberta has yet to exit that plan. A spokesperson for the provincial government said officials continue to work with Ottawa to ensure the province “receives its fair share” of federal funding to further expand its coverage.
- Why Alberta's government wants out of the federal dental care plan — and who it could impact
- Alberta wants to opt out of national pharmacare program
Fiona Clement, director of the Centre for Health Policy at the University of Calgary's Cumming School of Medicine, said that in her view, the federal government is in charge of a funding method, not a way to deliver the program.
“I would hope if we were standing something up in Alberta on its own, we would also be attracted to concepts like universality and comprehensiveness,” Clement said.
“On a general stand, I think many of the things that are done by the federal government, you are stronger together … there’s a lot of these processes that make a lot of sense to do at the national, federal level.”
The debate around how this money is spent has been going on for decades.
On Oct. 19, Albertans will have the opportunity to weigh in on whether they feel the current arrangement is working, or whether they think Alberta should fight to try to take control of those dollars — no strings attached.

There are many, many strange things about the stew of conspiracy theories that fall under the umbrella of “9/11 Truth”—the false, often antisemitic worldview purporting that the US government had inside knowledge of or even actively participated in the September 11 attacks. But perhaps the strangest is that the seed of these theories was planted three months before the attacks themselves.
It was June 28, 2001, when Milton William “Bill” Cooper took to the air on his national radio show after watching a news report on CNN. “Supposedly, a CNN reporter found Osama bin Laden, took a television camera crew with him, went into Osama bin Laden's hideout, interviewed him and his top leadership, his top lieutenants and colonels and generals in their hideout,” Cooper told his listeners. “He came out and told everybody, ‘Within three weeks, Osama bin Laden is going to attack the United States and Israel.’”
Cooper had part of the story right—a reporter had indeed just reached the inner sanctum of al Qaeda in the mountains near Kandahar, Afghanistan, but he was actually a correspondent for a Middle Eastern broadcaster. And that reporter, the MBC correspondent Baker Atyani, had actually interviewed al Qaeda’s military chief, Mohammed Atif, not bin Laden. “In the coming weeks, there will be a big surprise; we are going to hit American and Israeli installations,” Atif told Atyani. “The coffin business will increase in the United States.” According to Atyani, bin Laden—who was present for the interview—smiled and nodded.
To Cooper, speaking on the radio that day, the interview represented either a major embarrassment for the US government, which had been hunting bin Laden for years, or it was evidence that the government was lying about the threat from bin Laden.
“Now, don’t you think that’s kind of strange, folks?” Cooper said. “The largest intelligence apparatus in the world, with the biggest budget in the history of the world, has been looking for Osama bin Laden for years and years and years and can't find him. The FBI, also under the leadership of Louis Freeh, has been looking for Osama bin Laden for years and years and years and years and years and many years and can’t find him. Some doofus jerk-off reporter with a camera crew waltzes right into his hideout and interviews him?”
“Now that tells us two things: Either everyone in the intelligence community and all of the intelligence agencies of the United States government are blithering idiots and incompetent fools, including the entire apparatus of the FBI and all of their personnel—or they're lying to us. They're not looking for him at all.”
Cooper went on to say that “the CIA created Osama bin Laden” and that “they're now using him to help bring about world government by making him the big boogeyman because they can't use [Iraqi dictator] Saddam Hussein anymore.”
Cooper argued that the whole threat from bin Laden was a farce—what would now be called a “false flag” operation. “If you believe it, you are one of the stupidest jerks that ever lived on the face of this earth, and whatever’s going to happen they’re going to blame on Osama bin Laden.”
About 10 weeks later, Cooper’s comment would come to be seen as a prophecy.
The events and aftermath of 9/11 altered almost every aspect of American society: from the ever-present security theater of daily life—the 3.4-ounce liquid bottles at airports, the defensive bollards that now dominate so many urban landscapes—to the expansion of the surveillance state, to 20 years of war in Afghanistan, to the backdrop of fear and anxiety that permeates the culture. Few, though, rightly recognize one of the most important and pernicious impacts of 9/11: how it changed our society’s very understanding and relationship to facts and truth.
It’s a story that not many people fully understand, one with roots in the UFO conspiracies of the 1980s and with tentacles that stretch to the National Mall on January 6, 2021—and one that helps in particular to explain the transformation of Alex Jones from a fringe Austin, Texas, talk show host to one of the most important (and disruptive) political forces of the 21st century. This transformation began in the first minutes after the September 11 attacks.
Cooper first came to prominence in the 1980s, among the first of a group who would come to be known as “UFO whistleblowers,” former military or intelligence veterans who purported to have insider knowledge about the government’s cover-up of alien civilizations, captured spacecraft, and recovered alien life-forms. It was the first golden age of modern conspiracism, as trust in government cratered following Vietnam, Watergate, and the revelations of dark assassination plots by the Pike and Church committees; books about cover-ups and urban legends like the Bermuda Triangle and the “Philadelphia Experiment” became bestsellers.
Cooper claimed to have been a naval intelligence officer in the 1970s and said that, as part of his work with a high-ranking admiral, he’d been able to covertly paw through the contents of the admiral’s cabinet of classified material. As Colin Dickey wrote in a review of a Cooper biography, the cabinet became “a repository of secrets known only to Cooper, whose contents seemed to change and evolve over the years, fitting whatever need Cooper’s current conspiracies had.” In early iterations, Cooper hinted it contained the truth about the JFK assassination and the government’s contact with aliens.
In the 1990s, amid the rise of far-right talk shows like that of Rush Limbaugh, Cooper became a national radio figure as well; his shortwave The Hour of the Time focused on a witches’ brew of sinister government conspiracies, alternate histories, warnings about the New World Order and secret societies, and a healthy dose of general-purpose skepticism; Cooper often exhorted his audience, “Wake up, sheeple!” (Much of his conspiracism contained thinly and not-so-thinly veiled antisemitism.)
For a brief period, Cooper was one of the nation’s most famous “UFO-ologists,” but few believed him—he feuded frequently with others in the field. He eventually laid out a grand conspiracy account in his 1991 memoir/fever-dream of a book, Behold a Pale Horse.
Behold a Pale Horse is a wacky piece of writing—there’s almost no other word for it. At one point it quotes the entire text of the Protocols of the Elders of Zion, a fabricated antisemitic screed from the early 1900s that alleged a secret Jewish plot to overthrow Christianity. Cooper’s work was basically QAnon three decades early, outlining a vast global conspiracy, decades-long and all-encompassing, to steal America and our freedoms from real Americans, all to serve some global super elite. The book became an underground bestseller—it still is today—and took off particularly within the militia movement.
This newfound fame coincided with the start of his talk radio career on WWCR, World Wide Christian Radio, in January 1993. With a 100,000-watt signal, he could reach huge swaths of the country from his home in Arizona. And over time, Cooper developed two important—and later infamous—superfans. One was a young Gulf War veteran named Timothy McVeigh, who in the early spring of 1995 journeyed with a companion—their exact identity is disputed—to Arizona to try to talk to Cooper at his home. “The last thing he said before they left in their green Mercury Marquis station wagon with a puke-yellow interior was, ‘Watch Oklahoma City,’” Cooper would later recount. Soon after their meeting, McVeigh attacked the Alfred P. Murrah Federal Building, killing 168 people and injuring nearly 700.
Then there was Alex Jones, a local public-access talk show host in Austin, Texas, who first came onto the national radar for his fundraising work to rebuild the church at the Branch Davidian compound in Waco, Texas. The site had burned down in 1993 at the end of a 51-day siege by the US government, as federal agents tried to arrest the leader of the Branch Davidian cult, David Koresh. In the end, agents in armored vehicles tried to fill the compound with tear gas; the buildings caught fire—it was never clear how the fires started—and most of the Davidians who remained in the compound died in the blaze. There were 75 fatalities, including about two dozen children. The Waco siege was a key flashpoint for the far right in the 1990s.
Jones saw inspiration in Cooper’s model, and Cooper became something of a mentor to the budding radio host, calling in for an interview on Jones’ early shows. Jones’ show on KJFK-FM lasted until 1999—he was even voted “Best of Austin” radio host by a local newspaper, which called him “either Austin’s great exposer of truth or a black helicopter conspiracy nut, depending on your worldview.” But his conspiracism made getting sponsors difficult, and KJFK fired him in December 1999. Jones quickly latched on to a new venture on the expanding internet: Infowars.com.
On September 11, 2001, Cooper was outraged by the attacks and warned of what would come next. “Folks, I can assure you that 72 hours from now, we will be at war. We will be bombing two or maybe three countries … Because that’s how it works. When governments are attacked, they lash out. Thousands of people who had nothing whatsoever to do with what is happening at the World Trade Center and the Pentagon are going to die,” Cooper said. “Nothing will be the same after today.”
Broadcasting that day on Infowars and about 100 syndicated stations, Jones did one better: “I went on the air and said, ‘Those were controlled demolitions,’” he later told Rolling Stone.
In the weeks ahead, Cooper and Jones diverged politically. Cooper had come to see Jones as a copycat, a fearmonger, and a liar. (On September 26, 2001, Cooper’s show was titled simply “Alex Jones—Liar.”)
Amid the aftermath of the September 11 attacks, Jones dove deeper into budding 9/11 conspiracies, and Cooper—who had stopped paying taxes, was drinking heavily, and was engaged in sometimes violent disputes with his neighbors—began prophesying his own death. In November 2001, law enforcement arrived at his Arizona compound to arrest him on an outstanding warrant on suspicion of aggravated assault; Cooper opened fire, shooting one deputy in the head, and was killed in the returning police gunfire.
The field was clear for the rise of Alex Jones.
In the years that followed, Alex Jones became a key force in the spread of 9/11 conspiracies. The movement, which came to be known as “9/11 Truth,” encompassed a host of different theories: that United Airlines Flight 93 had been downed by US fighters; that the Pentagon had been struck by a missile, not a plane; that the World Trade Centers had been brought down by space weapons.
By even the first years after 9/11, the ideas had become so widespread that the government’s 9/11 Commission took pains to document in careful factual detail the impossibility of some of the conspiracies, hoping to avoid the ambiguities that dogged the Warren Commission’s report into the JFK assassination. Popular Mechanics devoted a special issue—later turned into a book, with a foreword by Senator John McCain—to debunking the most popular ones.
But the conspiracies took root in the early internet of the 2000s: Arguably the first viral online documentary, known as Loose Change, took the conspiracies to the broader public, becoming one of the most-watched videos on Google Video and the early era of YouTube. (Jones would even get an “executive producer” credit on one version of the film.) The DVD box promised, “What you will see inside will prove without a shadow of a doubt that everything you know about 9/11 is a complete fabrication.”
The reality is that the film offered no conclusive evidence of government involvement or conspiracy, but would be familiar format-wise to anyone online today in its “We’re-just-asking-questions” tone, cherry-picking quotes and evidence out of context to broadly hand-wave at surely sinister machinations behind the scenes.
9/11 conspiracism found a home politically on both the right, with Jones and his acolytes, and the left in the 2000s, as Democrats protested the documentable lies and mistruths that helped lead the nation into war with Iraq. Documentarian Michael Moore released a blockbuster movie in 2004, Fahrenheit 9/11, a polemic that tied George W. Bush’s administration, Saudi Arabia, and Iraq together in a sinister warmongering and corporate profiteering conspiracy; it became one of the highest-grossing documentaries of all time and won the prestigious Palme d’Or at Cannes.
According to a May 2006 Zogby poll, some 42 percent of Americans believed that the US government and the 9/11 Commission “concealed or refused to investigate critical evidence that contradicts their official explanation of the September 11 attacks” and that “there has been a cover-up.”
I’ve spent much of the past decade writing about 9/11 and have spoken at hundreds of public events; rarely do I make it through an event without an audience question that’s at least conspiracy-adjacent.
Jones, in particular, found conspiracism wildly profitable. As Nicole Hemmer, a Vanderbilt professor who studies the far right, told me, “Because he was a critic of the war in Iraq, he becomes seen by many people outside of the Alex Jones universe as somebody who bridges the left-right divide. Even though he is a far-right figure, he can feast off this credibility that he has as being somebody who is above politics—and that really helps elevate him into, increasingly, a household name.”
Jones became nationally infamous for arguing that later tragedies, like the elementary school shooting at Sandy Hook, were also false-flag operations. In the first Trump term, amid the Covid-19 pandemic, Jones became a fierce voice against government lockdowns, and as the aftermath of the fall 2020 election unfolded, he and his “InfoWars Battle Tank”—an armored truck worth some $300,000—became a ubiquitous presence at Stop the Steal rallies leading up to the protests at the Capitol on January 6. Throughout Donald Trump’s rise and first term, conspiracies loomed large. Trump himself first came to political prominence amid the birtherism movement, and his supporters embraced Pizzagate and the broader QAnon conspiracy.
In recent years, Jones, of course, has suffered a remarkable comedown; his vicious lies finally caught up with him in lawsuits from the families of the victims of the Sandy Hook shooting, and after a lengthy court battle, his InfoWars.com domain has been acquired by The Onion.
But if Jones has lost his most recent battles, it’s hard not to see that his conspiracism has won the broader war. Today, as the nation marks the 25th anniversary of the 9/11 attacks, it’s notable that the anti-government conspiracists have effectively taken over the US government itself—from Health and Human Services secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr.’s Covid and vaccine denialism to President Donald Trump’s own fetid swamp of a social media feed. In news that would make Bill Cooper particularly proud, Trump has even promised to release the government’s files on the truth about UFOs. For the most part, though, we’re still waiting.

Benjamin Netanyahu's rule is at a crossroads. Former war cabinet member Gadi Eisenkot could unseat him
Benjamin Netanyahu is facing the battle of his political life, with the man he once tapped to be the nation's defence chief firming as the favourite to topple him as prime minister when Israelis head to the polls on October 27.
The election could be one of the most consequential in Israel's almost eight-decade history, following years of wars on multiple fronts and intense social upheaval which has threatened to tear at the fabric of the country and put immense pressure on its international standing.
But any shift in government is unlikely to prompt a major change in key policies on the war in Gaza or the occupied West Bank.
If current polling is to be believed, the right-wing coalition led by Mr Netanyahu and his Likud party will be challenged by an opposition bloc, led by former IDF lieutenant-general Gadi Eisenkot and his newly established Yashar party.
The name of the political movement translates from Hebrew as "straight" or "honest", reflecting what its leader has argued is a need to be up-front with the electorate after four years of alleged obstruction and deceit from the incumbent.
"You have to understand that Eisenkot is everything that Netanyahu is not," Gideon Rahat, professor of political science at Jerusalem's Hebrew University, told the ABC.
"Eisenkot has lost his son and nephew in the [Gaza] war, one of the Netanyahu kids at least spent most of the war in Miami.
"Netanyahu is a player, he knows how to talk very good English — Eisenkot, his English is not so good, he's quite, I would say, a popular person … a regular person."
That sentiment was shared by one of Mr Eisenkot's candidates, former senior finance ministry bureaucrat Shaul Meridor.
"When he says things, he means them — and he's a mensch," Mr Meridor quipped.
"With a lot of interactions we had, I saw a man that really got into the things, to the essence of them, and tried to solve them."
'A religious Sparta'?
Mr Netanyahu has only held on to power during this term due to a complicated coalition agreement, involving at least five different parties.
His government has been described as the most right-wing in Israel's history, particularly given the influence of ultra nationalist parties led by controversial ministers Bezalel Smotrich and Itamar Ben-Gvir — two men subject to international sanctions, including from Australia, for their policies and rhetoric against Palestinians.
For months, the polling data from multiple Israeli media outlets has suggested surging support for Mr Eisenkot.
The most recent gauge of public sentiment from Israeli television network Channel 13 showed his Yashar party could become the largest in the Knesset, securing 22 out of 120 seats, narrowly edging out Likud on 21.
It suggested Mr Eisenkot could secure 53 seats if he were to band together with other leading opposition parties, while Mr Netanyahu's current coalition would also secure 53 seats.
Neither man would have enough seats to control an outright majority, leaving them to either govern in minority or court parties led by Palestinian citizens of Israel, for support.
Other polls from outlets such as Channel 14 — often described as the most conservative broadcaster in Israel and a mouthpiece for the government — put the prime minister and Likud in a much more comfortable position — securing a majority alongside the parties in the current right-wing coalition government.
"Every election is significant, but I believe that these elections are really significant for many people," Professor Rahat told 7.30.
"These are elections that will show, will indicate where Israel goes — to become an extreme right, religious Sparta, like Netanyahu mentioned, or a liberal democracy among liberal democracies in the world," he said.
What Netanyahu's government 'forgot'
Yashar is banking on simmering anger directed at Mr Netanyahu and his coalition to secure votes from the centre of the Israeli political spectrum.
At a small community rally in a comfortable suburb of Motza Illit, on the outskirts of Jerusalem, Mr Meridor asked those gathered what they feared most.
Israel is often ranked as one of the most expensive places to live among OECD countries, so cost-of-living was mentioned, but issues such as civil war, conflicts and international isolation were also shouted out from the crowd.
"I think in the last few years, we see our leadership as a leadership that does not talk to the world,"
"Other than the Trump administration, which is very important, we have a lot of other friends in the world — whether it's in the United States and all around in Europe, Australia, New Zealand — and I think we need leaders to start talking back.
"Yes, there is a lot of things that we might not agree on, but we have to talk to our friends, and I think that's something that this government really forgot."
Mr Meridor says that Mr Netanyahu is no longer in touch with modern Israel.
"Bibi is the prime minister in Israel; he was elected," he said.
"But I think in many ways, the majority of Israelis do not feel that he shares their values.
"What you'll find in Gadi Eisenkot, I think myself and others that we are running with, is a different Israel."
Top general to political opponent
The prime minister and his challenger have a history that stretches back a decade.
In 2015, Mr Netanyahu appointed Mr Eisenkot to the top job of IDF Chief of the General Staff.
After almost 40 years in the military, Mr Eisenkot served his full four-year term before retiring.
In 2022, he entered the Knesset and was appointed as a member of Mr Netanyahu's emergency cabinet, following Hamas' deadly attacks on Israel and the outbreak of the Gaza war.
By mid-2023, he quit the war cabinet, accusing Mr Netanyahu of making decisions to prolong the war, influenced by increasingly loud right-wing voices in his governing coalition, at the expense of Israelis still being held captive by Hamas.
This dispute has formed the basis for political attacks on Mr Eisenkot, with Mr Netanyahu and his Likud party accusing him of wanting to capitulate to the terror organisation which killed 1,200 people and took 251 hostages on October 7, 2023.
That messaging has expanded to Hezbollah in Lebanon and the Iranian regime, with Mr Eisenkot accused by his political opponents of wanting to surrender to Israel's arch enemies.
Mr Eisenkot quit the Knesset in July last year, and announced the creation of his own party in September of that same year.
While Yashar is promising to be more open with the international community, the status quo could largely prevail in regard to some of the issues which spark the most global condemnation and criticism of Israel.
Mr Eisenkot is flagging greater engagement with mediators but is shying away from any suggestions of major change in the approach towards the Gaza Strip.
"I'm not sure you'll see a big change in the aspect of security, in that we will not withdraw from Gaza until Hamas is really demilitarised," Mr Meridor said.
Mr Eisenkot has insisted there will be no Palestinian state under his prime ministership.
The former general is also the author of the so-called "Dahiyeh doctrine".
The policy was developed while he was in charge of the IDF's northern command, and advocated for disproportionate force and widespread destruction of civilian infrastructure, in a bid to pressure enemies like Hezbollah to surrender.
"I know for Western ears, what you guys want to hear is, 'We can live side-by-side with these terrorist organisations,''' Mr Meridor said.
"Our answer is no, with a capital N, and the Dahiyeh doctrine, I think, was a very essential thing.
"We don't want to hurt civilians in any way, but if Dahiyeh is the headquarters of Hezbollah, it will be hit if we need to, because that's the way they work."
October 7 inquiry?
Central to Mr Eisenkot's pitch to voters are two issues that have torn Israeli politics apart over the past four years.
The headline pitch is the establishment of a fully independent commission of inquiry into the failures that led to Hamas's October 7 attacks.
Mr Netanyahu has resisted calls for such a probe, suggesting it would be a political witch hunt against him and his right-wing government.
The former general also insists that the country's ultra-Orthodox Jewish community should have to serve in the military, with a few small carve-outs.
In 2024, a Supreme Court ruled that the sweeping exemptions for the Haredi, as they are known in Israel, were unlawful. Previously, they had been able to avoid conscription if they were studying at Yeshivas, or Jewish religious schools.
It is an issue the conservative elements of the Netanyahu Government have insisted needed to be restored, and has prompted massive protests across Israel in recent months.

Thank you for joining us for our continuing coverage of the aftermath of Wednesday’s catastrophic flash floods in the Himalayan mountains near the Nepal-Tibet border.
Poor weather has hampered aerial rescue operations in Nepal as the search for thousands of people missing enters its fourth day.
Nepal’s finance minister says his country will need up to $5bn to rebuild after the floods, believed to have been caused by a melting glacier high up in the mountains that set off a deadly cascade of water into the valleys below.
Finance minister Swarnim Wagle told Reuters today those figures are “just an estimate” and that “loss and damage is being assessed”.
Here’s a summary of what we know so far:
Nearly 3,000 people are missing. Nepal’s disaster agency on Saturday said 2,426 people were missing on its side of the border, while China’s Xinhua news agency reports the total number of missing in Tibet is now 554.
The death toll in Nepal has now risen to 626, while China’s Xinhua news agency earlier today reported seven people confirmed dead in Tibet.
More than 3,700 people have been rescued in Nepal so far but at least 93,000 people are estimated to have been affected by the disaster, according to the Red Cross.
At least 777 foreigners are missing, with Nepal’s disaster agency on Friday reporting 517 foreigners unaccounted for – which could include tourists and foreign workers – and Chinese officials putting the number of foreigners missing at 260.
India said it is increasing surveillance of glaciers and glacial lakes in its Himalayan regions bordering Nepal and China.
The deadly floods on the Nepal-Tibet border were believed to have been triggered by a glacial collapse that was detected as a magnitude 5.2 seismic event by geologists. You can read this explainer to find out more about how a collapsing glacier can generate a powerful flood, and whether the climate crisis is contributing to the risk.
Madan Kaushik, state disaster management minister in India’s Himalayan state of Uttarakhand, said: “Since we share a border with Nepal, as a neighbour, and also have a similar geographic situation … we have asked our department to monitor all the glaciers and known glacial lakes in the region.”
Uttarakhand is one of the most ecologically sensitive regions of India, with 1,266 glacial lakes. As glaciers melt, water can accumulate in lakes held back by natural barriers. If those barriers fail, vast volumes of water can be released suddenly, triggering devastating floods.
“We have asked our teams to be vigilant and monitor if a similar situation is emerging anywhere in the state,” Kaushik told AFP.
‘The flood took everything I have’: survivors grieve for relatives and homes swept away in Nepal
The Guardian’s south Asia correspondent Hannah Ellis-Petersen and journalist Gaurav Pokharel report from the Nepalese town of Bidur, where rescue efforts are being coordinated. They spoke to survivors mourning loved ones and confronting the loss of their homes and livelihoods after devastating floods swept through their communities.
Among those caught in the floods was Sangke Dolma Tamang, who described the moment she watched her husband being swept away and returned to find her home and village destroyed:
Sangke Dolma Tamang, 61, had been cheerily cooking snacks in her village of Mailung in the Rasuwa district when the floods came without warning. The whole family ran uphill for safety, but as she grabbed for her husband, he slipped from her grip and was washed into the dark, fast-moving waters.
“Others tried to pull him to safety, but the flood swept him away,” she said, tears rolling down her weathered cheeks. There was, she said, nothing left of her village now. She had spent a night sheltering on higher ground, until an army helicopter arrived and brought to her safety at the barracks. Her son too was missing since the disaster, and she waited anxiously for any news.
“Now I have nothing left to live for,” said Tamang. “The whole house is gone. We couldn’t salvage anything.”
Nepal’s government has appealed for financial help as it faces the daunting task of recovering from the devastating flash floods and braces for the possibility of more flooding.
Entire communities have been swept away, leaving families homeless or sheltering in temporary facilities.
“Multiple bridges have been washed away and major roads disrupted, leaving some of the worst-affected communities extremely difficult to reach,” the Red Cross says.
At least 18 schools have been destroyed and another 20 damaged, leaving about 10,000 school-age children affected, according to the UN Children’s Fund.
The disaster comes just ahead of the anniversary of last year’s 8-9 September mass anti-corruption protests that toppled the government.
Nepal is now led by prime minister Balendra Shah, a 36-year-old rapper turned politician widely known as “Balen”. The former Kathmandu mayor swept March elections on a wave of euphoria calling for political change.
The risk of a lake formed after the glacier collapse bursting near the China-Nepal border where the devastating flood occurred earlier this week has decreased, Chinese authorities said today, as its size appears to have shrunk.
Satellite images from Thursday this morning suggest water in the lake – straddling the China-Nepal border at the confluence of two rivers – has been slowly flowing through, decreasing the reservoir gradually, state broadcaster CCTV reported, citing the water resources ministry.
The ministry said satellite imagery of the surface area of the lake at Purepu Tsangpo river showed it was 99,000 sq metres in size this morning – around the size of 14 football fields combined – having shrunk by 21,000 sq metres compared with images from Thursday.
Experts and authorities have warned of the extremely high risk of secondary disasters in the valley, especially from the lake that was formed by glacier debris, potentially endangering rescue operations downstream.
State-owned engineering and rescue enterprise China Anneng, which has been monitoring the lake since Thursday, dispatched a 15-member team on Friday with reconnaissance drones, portable satellite stations and mobile surveillance cameras to gather more data about the lake.
An overflow from the lake on Friday temporarily halted rescue work before further assessment deemed the risks manageable.

Worldwide, traditional medicine is used by billions of people for their health and well-being. At a signing ceremony in Geneva, the Government of India committed US$ 85 million over 10 years, 2022–2032, to support the programming of the WHO Global Traditional Medicine Centre. India’s 10-year financial contribution will support a cross-sectoral program of work to strengthen the evidence base for traditional medicine by providing data and evidence on traditional medicine policies, practice, products, and public use.
The WHO-India donor agreement is part of a US$ 250 million investment from India in support of the establishment of the WHO Global Centre of Traditional Medicine in 2022, which includes financial support for the workplan of the Centre, interim premises and a new building. This support will scale up WHO’s capacities on traditional medicine across technical divisions and regions in the spirit of global collaboration and solidarity. Part of this substantial contribution from the Government of India will also be included in WHO’s Investment Round to resource WHO’s core work during 2025–2028.
Photo: WHO/Lindsay Mackenzie
“India’s commitment and leadership in expanding the evidence-based contribution of traditional medicine to the health and well-being of all people and the planet, comes at an opportune moment,” said Dr Bruce Aylward, Assistant Director-General of the Universal Health Coverage and Life Course division of WHO. “Traditional medicine, supported within national health systems, can allow us to reach those most often left behind. Integration of traditional practice and knowledge is critical to achieving health for all.”
“The signing of this donor agreement is a major milestone towards achieving the shared vision of Honourable Prime Minister of India Shri Narendra Modi and WHO Director-General Tedros for the development of the WHO Global Traditional Medicine Centre at Jamnagar in India,” said Vice Minister Vaidya Rajesh Kotecha, Secretary of the Ministry of Ayush, Government of India.
“India remains committed to supporting WHO in its work to strengthen traditional medicine systems globally for achieving universal health coverage and serving the entire humanity, especially through this Global Centre in Jamnagar, which would help focus these efforts to benefit all Member States,” said Ambassador Arindam Bagchi, Permanent Representative of India to the UN and other International Organizations in Geneva.
The WHO Global Traditional Medicine Centre is is a knowledge hub focusing on five inter-connected areas of work: research and evidence; primary health care and universal health coverage; Indigenous Knowledges and biodiversity; digital health applications; and the biennial WHO Global Traditional Medicine Summit and collaborations. The Centre is led by Dr Shyama Kuruvilla, Director a.i.
The first WHO traditional medicine global summit was held in August 2023 in Gujarat, resulting in the a multistakeholder action agenda, the Gujarat Declaration. The next WHO Global Summit is planned for November 2025, following up on the anticipated launch of the 2025–2034 Global Strategy for Traditional Medicine at the 78th World Health Assembly in May 2025.
India’s support for traditional medicine has been expressed through a variety of long-standing partnerships with WHO. In 2023, India signed a five-year agreement to support the technical work of WHO’s Traditional, Complementary and Integrative Medicine (TCI) unit. The unit is supporting the development of the Member State-requested new WHO traditional medicine global strategy (2025 - 2034), and publishes key benchmark documents, standardized terminologies, and other evidence-informed technical products to support the safe and effective integration of traditional medicine in national health systems.  
The Centre and TCI collaborate closely with teams across WHO to advance WHO’s multisectoral agenda on traditional medicine, including through regular meetings of the WHO Technical Expert Network, coordinated by the WHO Global Traditional Medicine Centre and TCI, to promote a One WHO approach on traditional medicine across headquarters, regional and country office.

One Nation’s latest immigration policy would “smash the Australian economy” and force hospitals and aged care facilities to close, Labor has warned, while the university sector has urged against a “race to the bottom” on cutting overseas arrivals.
One Nation said on Monday it would cut the number of temporary migrants in Australia by more than 750,000 over three years, targeting international students and family members of skilled migrants.
The One Nation leader, Pauline Hanson, claimed the new policy would “reset” Australia’s immigration system and help ease pressure on housing and public services.
Temporary visa numbers would be returned to 2017 levels, under what Hanson says would represent a net-negative arrivals rate for the first three years. That would mean the net overseas migration (Nom) total would be 130,000 under the One Nation plan.
The home affairs minister, Tony Burke, said a halt on immigration “would smash the Australian economy” and warned regional communities would be the first to suffer.
“Hospitals and aged care facilities would be forced to close,” he said.
“There’d be a chronic shortage of backpackers to work in hospitality and tourism, or to help farmers pick their crops.
“The construction sector would grind to a halt. Regional universities would have to radically shrink or go broke.”
Burke said Hanson should be honest and upfront with Australians about the effect of the new policy.
Luke Sheehy, the chief executive of peak body Universities Australia, said the plan would do lasting damage. He said One Nation was joining Labor and the Coalition in a “race to the bottom” with plans to dramatically cut student visas.
“You can’t take skills, jobs and billions of dollars of economic activity out of the country and pretend there will be no consequences,” he said.
“International education is one of Australia’s biggest exports. It supports jobs across the economy, helps build the skilled workforce we desperately need and strengthens our relationships around the world.
“It also helps keep our universities going.”
Immigration debate
Hanson’s announcement comes as Labor and the Coalition consider new cuts to overseas arrivals, in an increasingly charged contest before the next federal election. Hanson will hope her plan plays well in the lead-up to the Victorian state election, due in November.
“I know Australians are doing it tough,” Hanson said. “Families are competing with hundreds of people for rental accommodation. Patients are stuck in ambulances because there are not enough hospital beds. Young Australians are being locked out of home ownership while wages and infrastructure fail to keep up.”
The target is to reduce student visa numbers, including visas for accompanying family members, to 350,000 over three years. According to education department data, about 680,000 international students studied in Australia between January to May this year.
A single student graduate program visa will be created, with numbers capped at 20,000 new visas per year. One Nation’s target is to reduce graduate visa numbers from 270,000 to 40,000.
The policy could also drive division within One Nation, with the lower house MP David Farley previously expressing concern that big cuts to immigration could deny his electorate of Farrer the workers needed to care for elderly people and work on farms.
Hanson said One Nation would give “illegal migrants” three months to leave, with those who departed voluntarily allowed to apply for visas in the future.
“Those who remain unlawfully after this period will be subject to immigration enforcement and a lifetime ban from re-entering Australia,” she said.
The Pacific labour mobility scheme for agriculture would remain in place under One Nation’s plan but temporary skilled migrants would lose the ability to apply for visas for family members.
“We will take back control of who comes here and how many we accept, train more Australians, restore living standards and put the safety and security of Australians first.”
The prime minister, Anthony Albanese, and the opposition leader, Angus Taylor, have held talks on Labor’s delayed migration package. It is expected to further drive down net overseas migration.
But Labor has struggled to finalise the plan and delayed its announcement by more than a month.
Australian businesses ‘at risk’
One Nation’s policy was widely criticised by business groups.
Business Council of Australia boss, Bran Black, warned One Nation that migrants were needed for growth in the economy.
“The starting point for any conversation with respect to migration cannot simply have the objective of cutting numbers, it has to be: how do we go about delivering the growth that ultimately locks in and secures our way of life?” he said.
Australian Chamber of Commerce and Industry chief executive, Andrew McKellar, said the business community would not support damaging cuts.
“Many Australian businesses would be put at risk by major cuts to the migration program. Pubs, cafes, hotels and accommodation providers desperately need chefs.
“Aged care homes and hospitals are short of staff already. Farmers and resources sector businesses continue to face persistent workforce shortages. Housing projects are being held up, while others remain unviable because of lack of workforce and skills shortages.”
National Farmers’ Federation boss, Hamish McIntyre, warned food prices could rise due to worker shortages.
“One in seven employees on our farms across regional Australia now are working holidaymakers or backpackers,” he told Channel Nine.
“We need these people now.
“It’ll prohibit us from planting some of these crops. We rely on these people. We won’t be able to take the risks to spend all the money, we spend up front obviously to produce these crops, so we’re not going to take a risk if we can’t harvest them.”
Taylor dismissed the policy as “absolute nonsense”.
“I’m interested to know the details of One Nation’s plan. I don’t know what their non-numbers were. A few days ago, their immigration numbers were 130,000. Now it’s something different. Well, what is it, each year over the next three or four years?
“What are those numbers? They’re not in their releases. They need to explain it.”

At BRICS, India's Modi warns geopolitical tensions and supply chain shocks threaten global stability
Indian Prime Minister Narendra Modi has warned that rising geopolitical tensions, supply chain disruptions and climate crises are affecting people worldwide
NEW DELHI -- Indian Prime Minister Narendra Modi on Sunday warned that rising geopolitical tensions, supply chain disruptions and climate crises are increasingly affecting people worldwide and called for strengthened cooperation and support across the Global South.
Addressing the BRICS summit of leading developing nations on its second day in New Delhi, Modi also warned that the “weaponization of technology and critical minerals” could hinder global development and shared prosperity.
Founded in 2006 by Brazil, Russia, India and China, BRICS has expanded to 11 members representing about half the world’s population and a significant share of global economic output. It has sought greater representation for developing countries in global institutions and promoted alternatives to Western-dominated financial systems.
“The number of conflicts and tensions in the world is continuously increasing, and this is having an increasingly negative and far-reaching impact on the lives of ordinary people,” Modi said, alongside bloc leaders, including Chinese President Xi Jinping, Russian President Vladimir Putin and Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian.
“Pandemics, climate disasters and supply-chain disruptions have shown that in today’s interconnected world, no crisis remains confined to a single region,” Modi said, while announcing that the bloc agreed to establish an integrated early warning system for infectious diseases, aimed at boosting preparedness and response to future outbreaks.
In his closing remarks at the summit, Modi urged the bloc nations to convert the summit’s agreements into tangible and time-bound action and move them from “files to real-life impact.”
The discussions over the past two days, he said, reinforced the belief that “BRICS is not merely a group of countries, but an ecosystem of solutions.” He wished China success as it takes over the BRICS chair for the next term.
The group in a joint declaration Saturday had expressed concern over escalating tensions in the Middle East and Sudan, and called for disputes to be resolved through dialogue and diplomacy.
The bloc reiterated support for a multipolar world order and reforms to the United Nations, including its Security Council, as well as global financial institutions such as the World Bank and the International Monetary Fund.
The leaders opposed unilateral sanctions and coercive economic measures and criticized sanctions not authorized by the U.N. They also criticized rising tariffs and nontariff barriers, saying they undermine global trade and supply chains.
The bloc backed greater use of local currencies in trade and stronger cross-border payment systems, while calling for cooperation on food security, energy, digital infrastructure, artificial intelligence and climate action.
The declaration was a significant breakthrough, as forging consensus among Iran, Saudi Arabia and the United Arab Emirates — which hold competing positions on key regional and geopolitical issues — posed a complex diplomatic challenge amid ongoing conflicts and heightened tensions.

More than 30 missing from ferry that sank in Vanuatu
A search in waters off the Pacific Island nation of Vanuatu is continuing for more than 30 people who officials said were missing after a passenger ferry sank
WELLINGTON, New Zealand -- A search in waters off the Pacific Island nation of Vanuatu continued Monday for more than 30 people who officials said were missing after a passenger ferry sank.
The ferry MV Matui was traveling between the islands of Ambae and Santo with 47 people on board when it sank Friday, local news outlets reported. Searchers in boats pulled 15 survivors from the water over the weekend, a statement Sunday from the prime minister’s office said.
One body was also recovered, according to the statement, while more than 30 people were still missing. The search would now focus on a coastline where currents might have carried survivors, rather than on open waters.
“This loss appears to be the result of strong winds and marine warnings not being heeded, and possibly of negligence including overloading of the vessel,” the statement said. The country’s meteorological service issued a marine warning for strong winds and high seas on the day the ferry sailed.
Vanuatu is an archipelago of 83 islands in the South Pacific Ocean, located about 1750 km (1090 miles) east of northern Australia.

Huntington’s disease (HD) is an inherited neurological disorder in which nerve cells in parts of the brain gradually break down and die. While there is currently no cure, doctors can treat some of its symptoms and researchers are investigating therapies aimed at slowing or preventing the underlying disease process. Here’s all you need to know about it.
What is Huntington’s disease?
Huntington’s disease is caused by a change in the HTT gene, which carries instructions for producing the huntingtin protein. The abnormal gene contains excessive repetitions of a three-base DNA sequence called CAG (Cytosine, Adenine, and Guanine).
According to information from the National Institutes of Health (NIH), most people have fewer than 27 CAG repeats and are not at risk of developing HD. Those with 27 to 35 repeats are unlikely to develop the disease but may be able to pass an expanded repeat to their children. People with 36 or more repeats may have the disease-causing expansion.
The abnormal huntingtin protein can become malformed and damage brain cells. The basal ganglia, a group of brain structures involved in coordinating movement, and the cortex, which plays a role in thought, perception and memory, are among the areas most affected, according to the NIH’s National Human Genome Research Institute.
HD is an autosomal dominant disorder. This means that a person needs only one copy of the altered gene to develop the disease. Each child of a parent who carries the HD gene has a 50% chance of inheriting it. If a child does not inherit the altered gene, they will not develop HD or pass the gene on to their children.
What are the symptoms?
The symptoms of Huntington’s disease vary from person to person and generally become more severe as the disease progresses. They broadly involve movement, thinking and behaviour or mood.
According to the NIH, one of the most recognisable movement symptoms is chorea — uncontrollable, dance-like movements that can affect the fingers, feet, face or torso. These movements may become worse when a person is nervous or distracted.
Early symptoms can include mild clumsiness, problems with balance or movement, difficulty walking, stiffness or rigid muscles, involuntary shaking or tremors, and dystonia, in which muscles tighten involuntarily and the body can become fixed in unusual positions. Unusual eye movements may also occur early in the disease.
As the condition progresses, people may develop problems with speech, swallowing and eating. Difficulty eating and swallowing can lead to weight loss, choking and lung infections. Other physical symptoms include fatigue, low energy, sleep problems and, in some cases, seizures.
HD also affects cognitive abilities. People may have difficulty concentrating, making decisions, solving problems, judging situations, organising or prioritising tasks, learning or remembering new information, or putting their thoughts into words. These problems can progressively interfere with work, driving and the ability to care for oneself.
Behaviour and mood can change as well. Symptoms may include irritability, mood swings, depression, anger, loss of interest and withdrawal from friends and family. Severe depression, suicidal thoughts and psychosis can occur.
How is it diagnosed?
Doctors diagnose HD by considering a person’s symptoms, family history and neurological examination, supported by laboratory and genetic tests and, where appropriate, brain imaging.
A neurologist may assess reflexes, balance, movement, muscle strength, walking, hearing, thinking, memory and mood. Other specialists, including mental health professionals, genetic counsellors and speech-language therapists, may also be involved in diagnosis and care.
The most accurate way to confirm HD is a genetic test. A blood sample is used to analyse DNA and determine the number of CAG repeats in the HTT gene. The attached NIH material notes that people with 36 or more repeats have the disease-causing expansion, while those with fewer than 26 repeats do not have the condition.
MRI and CT scans can show structural changes in the brain as HD progresses, including shrinkage in affected regions. However, such changes can occur in other conditions and scans can be normal in people with early HD. So, conventional brain imaging is not a replacement for genetic testing to confirm the disease.
Latest research says that a new type of MRI technique could eventually allow researchers to see more than just the shrinkage of the brain and get an indirect picture of the cellular damage caused by HD.
According to The Conversation, researchers used soma and neurite density imaging (Sandi), a diffusion MRI technique, to assess cellular changes in the brains of 56 people with HD and 57 healthy volunteers.
In the basal ganglia of those with HD, the scans showed lower apparent cell-body density, larger cell bodies and more space between cells — changes resembling those seen in postmortem brain tissue.
The measurements were also linked to disease severity and motor performance, and in some striatal regions helped explain up to 63% of observed brain shrinkage. Researchers say Sandi could eventually help track disease progression and assess whether treatments are protecting brain cells, but larger, longer-term studies are needed before it can be used clinically.
What are the treatment options?
According to the U.S. National Institute of Neurological Disorders and Stroke, there is currently no treatment that can stop or reverse HD. Treatment focuses on managing symptoms and improving quality of life.
For chorea, medicines including tetrabenazine, deutetrabenazine and valbenazine can be used to affect the brain signals involved in controlling movement.
Antipsychotic medicines, including risperidone and olanzapine, may help reduce chorea as well as psychiatric symptoms such as severe irritability, unusual thoughts or hallucinations. However, some antipsychotic medicines can worsen movement-related symptoms, so doctors need to monitor patients and adjust treatment where necessary.
Medicines can also be used to treat depression and anxiety. Treatments may have side effects such as tiredness, sleepiness, difficulty concentrating, restlessness or increased activity. Beyond managing symptoms, research is increasingly focused on finding ways to alter the underlying disease.

Ex-Tehelka editor Tarun Tejpal surrenders before Goa court after 2013 sexual assault conviction
In August, the top court called in Tejpal to surrender before the court after he was convicted in a 2013 rape and sexual assault case.
Tarun Tejpal, former editor-in-chief of Tehelka magazine, surrendered before the Mapusa Court in Goa on Monday. As per reports, this comes after the Supreme Court of India called on the journalist to surrender before his appeal against the conviction is taken up.
In August, the top court called in Tejpal to surrender before the court after he was convicted in a 2013 rape and sexual assault case.
Appearing for Tejpal, senior advocate Kapil Sibal, argued for the surrender exemption, saying that the incident was of 2013 and the journalist had earlier spent around six months in jail in the case.
"He (Tejpal) has throughout been on bail since then. The high court has directed him to surrender within four weeks. This court may fix the main appeal for hearing on August 31," he told the court.
Rejecting his plea for exemption, the Supreme Court directed Tejpal to submit his surrender certificate and stated that his appeal will be heard only once he does so.
"In case the surrender certificate is filed on or before September 21, 2026, the registry shall list the criminal appeal for hearing on September 22, 2026 before the regular court," the court said.
On August 6, the Goa bench of the Bombay high court convicted Tejpal of rape and sexual assault. He was sentenced to 10 years in prison.
The case pertains to allegations made by a female journalist who accused Tejpal of sexually assaulting her inside a hotel elevator on November 7 and 8, 2013.
Following the conviction, Tejpal told reporters that he will file an appeal to challenge the conviction and his surrender.
