For over a month and a half, residents of Chitpur Jyotinagar Colony in Cossipore, North Kolkata, have been without regular water supply after five public taps serving the colony ran dry following pipeline work in the area. Home to around 5,000 people, the 200-metre-long stretch is largely inhabited by people belonging to the Muslim community, and from lower-income backgrounds.
Residents, whose daily lives and livelihoods have been disrupted, alleged that water supply has been deliberately cut off by the state’s Bharatiya Janata Party (BJP) government to target them on the basis of their identities and force them out of the slum.
It is worth noting days after the election results were declared, local BJP MLA Ritesh Tiwari had pledged not to do anything for Muslims in his constituency. “Today, in front of Baba Bholenath, I swear, I will not do one job for them (Muslims) in the next five years. Will not issue any certificate for them. I am saying this live. I do not care about what anyone else says or thinks,” he had said.
Residents of Jyotinagar this colony, around 95% of them Muslims, depend on informal jobs for their sustenance. While women manage household chores in the morning before working at nearby factories in the afternoon, where they clean glass bottles and break glass panels into shards, most men work as daily wage labourers, masons, drivers, rickshaw pullers, or at factories.
How Did Water Supply Stop?
Alt News visited the water-deprived area, located a few meters from the over 200-years-old Cossipore Gun and Shell factory. The colony has five taps, which used to supply water from 5 am to 11 pm daily. Since July 29, after water supply was cut off, all five taps have been dry, locals said.
Locals said that water supply was perfectly normal and no complaints from the neighbourhood was made to the local civic body or any authorities, and yet, pipeline work was carried out in the area by the Kolkata Municipal Corporation (KMC) from July 26-28.
“Pipeline work was happening, they had dug two pits, one at the beginning of the slum and another at the end, marking the slum. On July 28, the water supply stopped around 11 pm. The next morning, we were waiting for the water supply to return. It has not been restored since,” said a resident, Mohinudeen Sheikh.
Sheikh, along with other residents, alleged that the pipelines were shut during the night while the roads were being repaired. “They used the cover of midnight to close the pipelines and mend the streets. We had no water from the early morning onwards,” he claimed.
‘They Also Took Away Electricity’
Residents said the water crisis was accompanied by a disruption in electricity supply as well. “They took away both water and electricity,” one youth said.
“They thought we were drawing electricity illegally from the main line, so they stopped the supply,” said a resident, Pinki Bibi. “All our houses have separate electricity connections and we receive separate bills. Then how can they say we are drawing electricity illegally?”
Residents claimed that electricity was restored after more than a week, following an incident during the Kanwar Yatra when poor visibility allegedly led some Kanwariyas to fall into the pothole-ridden lane. Alamgir Biswas, secretary of the Jyotinagar Colony, said that the supply was restored 10-15 days after the Basti Unnayan Samiti protested against the disruption.
Locals alleged that Calcutta Electric Supply Corporation (CESC) said the main-road connection had been shut to verify whether allegations of illegal electricity tapping were true. However, electricity supply remained available in the lanes branching off the main road. After seven days, CESC was able to verify that no illegal tapping was taking place and restored the connection, they added.
‘They are Trying to Evict Us’
Residents alleged that the disruption of these essential services was a part of a concerted attempt to evict the slum dwellers. Alamgir alleged: “The plan was to cut off the basic needs of water and electricity so that we leave the area. In this area, there is absolute communal harmony. Hindus and Muslims live harmoniously together. However, this government is trying to create a rift between us.”
Morjina Begum, who works at the glass factory, also alleged, “They are trying to evict us from this colony and therefore employing these tricks of cutting off the water supply. We are not new to this place. I was born here. My grandfather had settled here years ago,” while asserting, “We are not going to leave this place so easily. We will fight.”
Begum said residents had also approached the local councillor, Suman Singh, but has received no meaningful assistance as of yet. Alt News tried to speak to Singh, but he did not answer our calls till press time.
Saraswati Biswas, a 60-year-old Hindu resident, alleged that Tiwari, the newly elected MLA, had referred to the residents as “Bangladeshis and encroachers”. “He is calling us Bangladeshis and encroachers. How am I a Bangladeshi? My forefathers used to live here. I have proper documents proving that I am an Indian. I voted this year,” she said.
Legal Entanglement With Kolkata Port
While investigating the possible reason behind the elongated water supply disruption, Alt News found an intricate legal entanglement between the residents of the colony and the authorities of the Kolkata port.
As per legal records, the entire colony is built on a parcel of land measuring approximately 3478 square metres officially belonging to the Syama Prasad Mookerjee Port, Kolkata. On February 23, the estate officer of the port issued an eviction order for the colony.
Alt News accessed the order, and found that it was issued based on the Public Premises (Eviction of Unauthorised Occupants) Act, 1971. The notice terms the residents of Jyotinagar Colony as ‘unauthorised occupants and/or trespasser to the port property’. The estate officer ordered the residents to vacate the land within 15 days of date of publication of this notice. Before the eviction order was passed, a hearing took place, wherein, port authorities submitted that ‘there is potential threat to communal unrest’ due to the existence of the colony.
According to legal documents accessed by Alt News, the residents of the colony came to know about the existence of this eviction order on June 9. The residents alleged that after the change of government in West Bengal, local BJP supporters started to campaign for the demolition of the slum. The locals claimed that they began deeming the colony as “a den of illegal Bangladeshi infiltrators”.
In order to seek legal protection from the eviction drive, residents appealed before the chief judge of the city civil court, Calcutta, however, on August 18, the court declined to grant any immunity from eviction to them.
The Port authorities in their submission before the city civil court had mentioned that ‘unlawful activities’ were ongoing in the colony. They described the premises as congested and unsafe for human habitation, citing the presence of inflammable materials and several uninsulated electrical wires that could potentially cause a fire. They also lodged two police complaints at the North Port police station on September 9, 2020 and July 25, 2022.
On August 19, the residents appeared before the Calcutta high court, seeking protection from eviction. The court granted an interim stay order on the eviction process till September 18. In the meantime, the water and electricity disruptions happened, which residents believe was done to purposely disrupt their lives to expedite the eviction.
Nine residents of the colony: Alamgir Biswas, Pinki Bibi, Mafajel Gazi, Sk Mainuddin, Rahima Bibi, Saraswati Biswas, Anita Prasad, Lima Bibi and Bonani Bibi appeared as petitioners before the high court. In their appeal, the residents had informed the HC that although the proceedings recorded before the estate officer of Kolkata Port mentioned two persons: Hafizul and Tarcina Bibi as respondents from the colony, the order does not record that any notice for eviction, under section 4 of the Public Premises (Eviction of Unauthorised Occupants) Act, 1971, was issued publicly.
It was also submitted before the HC that the order issued by the Kolkata Port does not record that the petitioners were called upon to show cause against the proposed eviction, were afforded an opportunity to produce evidence or were given an opportunity of personal hearing.
According to Section 4 of the Public Premises (Eviction of Unauthorised Occupants) Act, 1971, all concerned persons, that is all persons who are in occupation of the public premises, have to be given the opportunity to show cause why they wouldn’t be evicted.
Section 4(3) of the Act clearly mentions: The estate officer shall cause the notice to be served by having it affixed on the outer door or some other conspicuous part of the public premises, and in such other manner as may be prescribed, whereupon the notice shall be deemed to have been duly given to all persons concerned. However, the order issued by the estate officer makes no mention of any such notice being issued or served. This issue was also raised in the petition before the high court.
A team of lawyers including Bikash Ranjan Bhattacharya, Samim Ahammed, Md Nasirul Hoque and Ivi Banerjee represented the residents legally. Speaking to Alt News, Ahammed said, “The Port authorities are claiming that the land in question is their property. But in reality, it is public property. Therefore, a government body like the Syama Prasad Mookerjee Port, Kolkata, must ensure the fundamental rights of the public, in this case, their right to shelter.”
The State has the power to regulate and make sure people follow the law and cannot occupy public property illegally. They are exercising this power through the Public Premises (Eviction of Unauthorised Occupants) Act, 1971. But while doing this, the State cannot treat people unfairly or take away someone’s home and leave them without shelter. Having a place to live and being able to live with dignity are part of a person’s inalienable rights protected by the Constitution, he explained.
Simultaneously with the HC appeal, another appeal was submitted by the residents before the chief judge of the city civil court seeking the restoration of water connection. This prayer, however, is still pending.
According to the port authorities, the total damage incurred due to the existence of the colony, starting from 1990, has reached approximately over Rs 61 crore. As per the legal records, the estimated monthly damage amount is calculated to be more than Rs 19 lakh rupees, and the port is losing more than Rs 2 crore annually in terms of revenue due to the colony.
Questions Of ‘Communal Targeting’
The geographical location of the water disruption has become a point of contention for residents, who have alleged that this is a form of communal targeting.
When one walks along Khagendra Chatterjee Lane towards the Ganges, with the Gun and Shell Factory on the right, the road turns left towards the river after two temples, and becomes Chitpur Strand Road. The Cossipore Jetty is on the right, followed by Jyotinagar Colony.
Residents showed Alt News the two points where pipeline work had been carried out. They said the entire stretch between the two points had remained without water. They also alleged that the points where the road was dug up correspond to the boundaries of Jyotinagar Colony, which has a predominantly Muslim population. According to the residents, taps immediately before and after this stretch, located in predominantly Hindu residential areas, continue to receive water.
Alt News checked the taps inside the colony and found them dry. Taps located immediately before and after the stretch where the pipeline work had been carried out, however, had water supply. We found that the tap directly opposite a temple, just before the first point where the road had allegedly been dug up, had water supply. The tap at the other end, near the second point where digging had taken place, also had water. In between, however, an approximately 150-metre stretch, had no water supply.
‘A Basic Need’
For residents, the suspension of water has led to tremendous daily struggle. “Water is a basic need. There are so many people in our colony, and there is no water. People have to stand in queues to fetch water from the taps that are present in the nearby areas. Though people are sharing their taps, they prioritise their own needs. This affects our work,” a resident said.
A woman in her mid-twenties, while cleaning utensils, showed buckets filled with water fetched from the river. “Look at the condition of the water we are using to clean. It is so muddy and filthy. At this point, all we can hope is we don’t fall ill,” she said.
The monsoon season has made it more difficult. “The water level is very high in Ganga now, so it becomes dangerous to bathe in the river or fetch water. The river water is muddy and unfit for consumption. But we are left with no option,” an elderly woman said. “We are scared that our children will develop skin infections. There are already a few cases,” said a woman in her thirties, while standing in queue to bathe her children.
Residents have to walk some distance from their colony to a functioning tap to fill water, which they then transport back on vans.
Locals Allege Administrative Apathy
Alamgir elaborated that after water and electricity supply was cut off on July 29, the following day, locals reached the corporation office and complained. “They took my number and told us that they would look into the matter. But nothing happened. On the following day, we submitted a written complaint at the main corporation office in Hatibagan. They also told us they would try to look into it. However, as everyone can see, nothing has changed as of yet,” he said.
Several residents had approached the local police station, the councillor, and MLA Tiwari, seeking their intervention, but no official visited the colony to inspect the reality so far, they lamented. Residents also said that when a group of women approached Tiwari, he dismissed them stating he was not responsible for the disruption of water supply and refused to restore it.
Further, Pinki Bibi alleged that Tiwari had used communal slurs and threatened the locals with eviction. “While talking to the people, he threatened them, ‘If I want, I could demolish the mosque that was built in the colony. And evict the entire colony with it,’” she said.
Morjina Begum told Alt News that residents believe they are being purposely treated this way because of their Muslim identities. Asked why they felt this was the case, she referred to speeches by chief minister Suvendu Adhikari and the local MLA following their election victories, in which they said they would not work for Muslims because Muslims had not voted for them. “Where are we supposed to go? There are so many of us?” she asked.
Also Read: I swear I won’t do anything for Muslims, says Bengal BJP MLA Ritesh Tiwari
Burdened by the uncertainties of their future in the colony, an elderly woman in her 70s, sitting on the threshold of her house, said, “I pray that in my next life I am not born as a Muslim in this country.”
On September 9, Minakshi Mukherjee, CPI(M)’s central committee member, visited the locality along with other workers and leaders, and expressed her solidarity with the residents and protested against the eviction drive. At the initiative of the party, a water tanker visits the colony every two to three days to provide residents with an alternative source of water.
MLA Ritesh Tiwari Responds
When Alt News asked Tiwari about the predicament of people in his constituency, he distanced himself from the issue, saying, “The plot belongs to the Port. The people have a feud with the Port. The Port had ordered them to vacate. Later, the high court ordered them to refrain from taking temporary coercive action. The water supply is provided by the KMC. So, what role do I play here? What can I say here? The matter is sub judice, and it is better for political leaders to refrain from making any comments.”
When asked whether he could stand by the people of his constituency and help restore their water supply, he said, “This is not my job…they [residents] have sought the assistance of established political leaders… so they should keep faith in the people they have called. Should they lose that faith so quickly?”
Upon being further prodded on why he was not helping people in his own constituency, the MLA replied (in Bengali), “Why don’t you do my part of the job!” (“Amar bhaag er kaaj ta apni kore deben”)

With an eye on expanding its financial services offerings, Amazon Pay is now reportedly doubling down on insurance in India. Speaking with Reuters, Amazon Pay India CEO Vikas Bansal said that the company is expanding its insurance offerings to include travel insurance and other products. As per Bansal, the expansion plans are reportedly part of Amazon Pay’s strategy to evolve from a mere payments processor to a broader financial service platform comprising credit, insurance and savings and investment products. “Obviously travel...there could be others in the future as well," Bansal reportedly added when asked if the company plans to launch other insurance products in the future. This comes barely a day after Amazon Pay partnered with HDFC ERGO to foray into the health insurance space. “Health is our next frontier,” Bansal reportedly said, adding that health insurance is an important area for expansion as a relatively small proportion of Indians have personal health insurance. It is pertinent to note that Amazon first entered the insurance distribution business in 2020, when it partnered with ACKO General Insurance to offer car and two-wheeler insurance. The ecommerce giant’s fintech arm operates as a registered corporate agent, allowing it to distribute insurance products from licenced insurers. Since then, Amazon Pay has onboarded HDFC ERGO and ICICI Lombard to offer vehicle insurance. Amazon's insurance push is part of a broader effort to build out its financial services stack in India. As of now, the fintech platform allows users to transfer money, pay bills, buy insurance, travel tickets, invest in mutual funds and purchase digital gold. But it is diversifying. Earlier this year, Amazon Pay partnered with multiple non-banking financial companies (NBFCs) and small finance banks to roll out pan-India fixed deposit (FD) service. At the recently concluded Global Fintech Fest 2026, Amazon Pay also partnered with Kotak Mahindra Bank to launch a co-branded credit card for small businesses registered on Amazon Business, the company’s dedicated B2B marketplace. On the financial front, Amazon Pay India reported an operating revenue of ₹2,097 Cr in FY25, down 8.3% from ₹2,287 Cr in the year-ago fiscal. Meanwhile, net losses declined a mere 5% to ₹866 Cr from ₹911 Cr in FY24.

The two Left parties — Communist Party of India (CPI) and Communist Party of India (Marxist) (CPI(M)) — have decided to contest the ensuing byelections to the Dharapuram and Madurantakam Assembly constituencies without aligning with any other formations. CPI will contest the Dharapuram seat, while the CPI(M) will contest Madurantakam, said CPI State secretary M. Veerapandian on Sunday (September 13, 2026).
With the Left parties’ decision to contest as a separate front, the upcoming bypolls have become a five-cornered contest. The alliances led by the TVK, the DMK and the AIADMK have already announced their candidates while Seeman-led Naam Tamilar Katchi (NTK) is to face the byelections alone.
Speaking to reporters at Balan Illam, the CPI State headquarters in Chennai, Mr. Veerapandian said the candidates of the Left front would be announced on September 15. “In the prevailing political situation in Tamil Nadu, the CPI had already decided not to be part of any alliance. At the executive committee meeting held on Saturday and Sunday, there was also a strong view that the same stand should continue,” he said.
“Respecting the verdict given by the people, the Left parties extended outside support to the TVK to form the government, to avoid Governor’s rule and, indirectly, the BJP’s rule. We are neither a part of the Cabinet nor a part of the alliance,” he said.
According to him, the upcoming bypolls in the Madurantakam and Dharapuram constituencies are not normal byelections, but what he termed as byelections imposed on people.
“It has been decided that the Left parties will face this election from the position we have already taken, that is, the position of not being part of any alliance. The CPI will contest in Dharapuram and the CPI (M) will contest in Madurantakam. We appeal to various democratic forces to extend their support to the Left parties,” he said.
“We believe that students and youngsters are intellectually strong, aware of what is happening around the world and politically conscious. We believe that the Left will have a place among them,” he added.
‘Outside support will continue’
CPI(M) State secretary P. Shanmugam said that though the two Left parties had decided to contest alone in the upcoming bypolls, the CPI(M) would continue to extend outside support to the TVK-led government.
Speaking to journalists after the State executive committee meeting of the CPI(M) that was held in Tiruchi to discuss in detail the stand to be taken for the forthcoming bypolls. Mr. Shanmugam said the Left parties had already decided that they would function independently.
The forthcoming bypolls were neither a general election nor intended for a regime change. Hence, it was decided that the CPI(M) and the CPI would contest in one Assembly seat each, he said.
Asked whether the CPI(M)’s decision to contest would indirectly provide strength to the DMK, Mr. Shanmugam categorically reiterated that his party’s outside support to the ruling TVK-led government would continue.
The political stand taken by the CPI(M) for the bypolls would not endanger the present government. It would be wrong to say that the CPI(M) had taken the stand to support the DMK, he said, adding that his party would field its candidate against the three fronts.
‘Wrong decision’
The candidates selected by the TVK to contest in the two Assembly constituencies had won as AIADMK candidates in the 2026 Assembly election. Within days of their victory, the two MLAs resigned from the AIADMK and joined the TVK. However, they could not cite any fair reason for this move. The CPI(M) had made it clear then that it was a wrong decision, as it went against the people’s sentiments, Mr. Shanmugam said.
Asked whether the support to the TVK government on the one hand and contesting alone in the byelections on the other would confuse the people, he said the Left parties would clarify their political stand during the course of the campaign for the byelections.
The byelections to Madurantakam and Dharapuram are scheduled to be held on October 6.

The Himalayas are melting faster - and India's economy is 'at risk'
- Published
The Himalayas are approaching a dangerous threshold as glaciers melt faster, glacial lakes grow more unstable and the mountains face a widening gap in monitoring, according to new research.
The findings come in the aftermath of devastating floods in Nepal and Tibet, which killed more than 1,300 people and caused widespread destruction, highlighting the growing risks from a rapidly changing Himalayan environment.
Himalayan glaciers are now losing mass 65% faster than they were a decade ago, the report by global consultancy Systemiq, produced with the Integrated Mountain Initiative and with technical contributions from the International Centre for Integrated Mountain Development (ICIMOD) and GB Pant National Institute of Himalayan Environment, says.
Yet only about 21 of the estimated 40,000 glaciers across the Himalaya-Karakoram region are being monitored in detail and on a sustained basis, according to the report.
That monitoring gap matters because the physical landscape is changing rapidly.
As glaciers retreat, they can leave behind expanding lakes held back by unstable deposits of rock and ice. At the same time, warming is destabilising permafrost - permanently frozen ground that can thaw as temperatures rise - and high mountain slopes, increasing the possibility of cascading hazards, the report says.
India already has evidence of the scale of the risk.
Some 18% of Indian land is Himalayan, yet the region accounts for about 35% of disasters, according to the report.
The government told parliament in July that 56 glacial lakes had been classified as "very high risk", external following a 2025 scientific assessment of 189 high-risk lakes in the Indian Himalayan region. The Central Water Commission is monitoring 2,485 glacial lakes larger than 10 hectares across India's Himalayan river basins, the government said.
The Himalayas have already seen devastating examples of what can happen when glacial lakes burst their natural dams.
In 2023, a glacial lake outburst flood in Sikkim killed at least 70 people and caused widespread damage to roads, bridges and hydropower projects. In 2021, a similar disaster in Uttarakhand killed more than 200 people after a massive flood swept through the Rishiganga and Dhauliganga valleys.
But the danger is not confined to spectacular floods.
The Himalayas are a vast natural water system feeding rivers that sustain hundreds of millions of people across South Asia. ICIMOD says "peak water", external is expected around mid-century in most Hindu Kush Himalayan river basins - the point at which glacier runoff reaches its maximum before declining as glaciers lose mass.
The new research puts an unusually large economic number on that dependency.
It estimates that Himalayan water underpins roughly 20% of India's GDP, sustaining wheat, rice, tea, hydropower and pilgrimage economies. Yet the mountain states capture only about 5% of that value, it says.
"The Himalayas are the Third Pole," said economist Lord Nicholas Stern, chair of the Grantham Research Institute on Climate Change and the Environment at the London School of Economics. "Unlike the Arctic or Antarctic, this pole has hundreds of millions of people living beneath it."
"This is national and international infrastructure," he said, warning that the ecological system underpinning it is "approaching a tipping point".
Not all the forces driving glacier loss are beyond the region's control.
The Systemiq research estimates that roughly a third of Himalayan glacier melt is driven by black carbon, much of it originating from brick kilns in the plains. Soot deposited on snow and ice absorbs more sunlight and accelerates melting.
Unlike global greenhouse-gas emissions, black-carbon pollution is a lever that India and its neighbours can act on directly, the report argues.
"The Himalayas are approaching a tipping point, with millions of lives and livelihoods hanging in the balance," said Arushi Chopra, Systemiq's senior director and lead author. "Glaciers are melting faster than they were a decade ago."
The report proposes 10 priority transitions, ranging from reducing black-carbon emissions and expanding glacier monitoring to improving disaster early-warning systems and changing the way tourism is developed in the mountains.
One priority is to strengthen disaster preparedness, with governments agreeing in advance what action to take when hazards emerge - from evacuation to protecting vulnerable infrastructure.
Another is to rethink tourism. The Indian Himalayan region receives roughly 400 million tourist visits a year, according to the report, and researchers argue that the objective should shift from maximising visitor numbers towards generating value that is retained and reinvested locally.
Pema Gyamtsho, director general of ICIMOD, said the risks were becoming increasingly complex.
"Glaciers are retreating, permafrost and high-mountain slopes are becoming increasingly unstable, and communities and infrastructure downstream face growing risks from complex and cascading hazards," he said.
And those risks do not stop at the borders drawn across the Himalayas. Such hazards, Gyamtsho said, "do not respect national borders, and no single country can address them alone".
That makes cross-border monitoring, shared risk information and early-warning systems, and joint investment in resilience increasingly urgent - not just to save lives, but to protect the livelihoods and economies of hundreds of millions of people who depend on the mountains.

The Joy of Being Asked to Help
Deciding to go it alone can end up depriving loved ones.
This is an edition of The Wonder Reader, a newsletter in which our editors recommend a set of stories to spark your curiosity and fill you with delight. Sign up here to get it every Saturday morning.
Learning how to drive is a rare instance in a teenager’s life, Liz Krieger argues in a recent article: “This wobbly uncertainty, this return to a kind of innocence, is the rarest condition in a 16-year-old, and it lasts about as long as a learner’s permit does.” The best part of teaching her daughter how to drive, Krieger writes, is being allowed to help.
Even once we move beyond the fierce teenage desire for independence, asking for assistance can feel awkward and vulnerable—espsecially in America’s culture of individualism, Julie Beck noted last year. But deciding to go it alone ends up depriving loved ones of the joy of participating. “Pushing through discomfort to accept the help that was offered” in planning her wedding, Julie wrote, made it “feel less like a product we had purchased and more like something special that we had created with our friends, family, and neighbors.” Today’s newsletter explores what asking for help does for the people helping.

An interesting shift happens when a kid is learning to drive, and you’re both inside a box with your fear, moving 40 miles an hour.

Police say Assam man accused of beheading wife died after jumping off vehicle
Goswami’s family refused to accept his body, claiming this was not an accidental death but a so-called “encounter” killing
A 30-year-old Guwahati man arrested for beheading his wife and storing her severed head in a refrigerator died after allegedly attacking the Assam Police personnel accompanying him from a hospital following medical examinations, jumping off a moving vehicle, and falling into a gorge, an officer said on Monday.
Anjad Brahma, the officer-in-charge of the Hatigaon Police Station where Ramanuj Goswami was being taken, said that the incident happened in the early hours of Monday and the body has been sent for postmortem.
A second officer said Goswami suddenly attacked the police team escorting him back to the police station. “He jumped from the vehicle and fell into a gorge near the Narakashur Pahar area.” He added that Goswami was rescued with injuries and was taken to hospital, where the doctors declared him dead.
Records showed Goswami was brought to the hospital at 2:41am and declared dead on arrival. Doctors said he had severe head injuries. His seven-day police remand was to end on Monday, and the police were to produce him before the court.
Goswami’s family refused to accept the body, claiming this was not an accidental death but a so-called “encounter” killing. It said they were preparing for post-death rituals of Goswami’s wife, Riya Talukdar, but cancelled them after the report of Goswami’s death. The family said these rituals according to Hindu customs cannot be continued after his death.
Goswami allegedly beheaded Talukdar, 25, on September 3 at a Guwahati flat for allegedly cheating on him. Neighbours reported a foul odour, leading police to recover the severed head and fingers inside a black polythene bag in the refrigerator.
Goswami, who had fled, surrendered on September 6 and was sent into seven-day police remand. He said he had no regret for killing his wife when he was taken to the crime scene on September 8. “No regret, no apology. I killed her with a sharp weapon, and I will kill her sugar daddy if I ever come out of jail.”
Police said they recovered a blood-stained machete, the suspected weapon used in the murder. Goswami told police he was intoxicated when he killed his wife, and empty alcohol bottles were recovered from the apartment.
Talukdar family said that Goswami had a history of drug addiction, concealed medical issues, and a prior arrest for financial fraud in 2019.
Goswami’s death in custody is the latest in a series of such deaths in the state. A death in police custody is treated as a custodial death regardless of the cause, whether it is an escape attempt or of natural causes, warranting a magisterial inquiry.
In 2025, the Supreme Court directed the Assam Human Rights Commission (AHRC) to investigate a series of alleged extrajudicial killings in the northeastern state, saying the use of excessive or illegal force cannot be justified. It overturned a January 2022 AHRC decision to close a case on the alleged extrajudicial killings, citing a pending plea on the issue in the Gauhati high court.
The Supreme Court directed the commission to reconsider the matter and conduct the probe, including allegations of injuries from illegal police action, popularly known as encounters. It asked the AHRC to approach the matter with sensitivity and the Assam government to cooperate fully and remove any institutional barriers.
Lawyer Arif Jwadder moved the Supreme Court over the alleged extrajudicial killings after the high court rejected his plea seeking action. His plea alleged 171 fake “encounters” between May 2021, when the Bharatiya Janata Party (BJP) returned to power for a second time, and August 2022.
In January 2023, the high court said people were killed and injured in police action, but the state government had registered first information reports to probe them. Jwadder’s petition said 54 people were killed and 140 injured in police action.

This as-told-to essay is based on a conversation with Laura Lee Ehrlich, 54, who lives on Long Island. Ehrlich has cared for five older loved ones over the last two decades and gave up her job to be a more present caregiver. It's come at a cost to her savings and emotional well-being. This interview has been edited for length and clarity.
I'm the youngest of five siblings. My mom held numerous jobs when we were little, and my dad worked in the city. When he worked strange hours, my older brother was the man of the house.
My mom, who worked for a surgeon, got me a job with his practice, where I worked for 17 years. My sister and I worked for my family's medical billing business. I also did insurance verification, and I'm currently in nursing school.
I wish I had listened to my mom to pursue this when I was 18.
I've been my family's caregiver
For the last two decades, I've been on and off working because of my family's illnesses. I was the one who wouldn't work anymore and stay home to take care of my father.
In 2002, my son was an infant when my dad was rushed to the hospital. We had a cardiologist come see him, and he pulled strings to get my father into a Manhattan hospital. He wound up having open-heart surgery after doctors discovered he had a widowmaker heart attack.
Doctors told us he had six months to a year at the most, but he wound up sticking around for six more years. His body took a toll little by little, and he started having mini strokes. He was basically homebound, and my mom would stay home with him. If she weren't there, I would be. I lived with them at that point. He would fall constantly, and we would have to rush to him frequently over a period of two months before he died in 2008.
My husband died in July that same year. It was completely unexpected. The hospital considered his mom and dad as the next of kin, and they kept him alive for four days while checking his organs for donation. It was too much for me.
Shortly after that, my father-in-law was diagnosed with prostate cancer. I took him to the hospital for radiation therapy and handled some of his errands, as he only had his sister in the US, who lived in Florida.
When my father-in-law became sick again in 2021, we got him into a nursing home because he couldn't care for himself anymore. I've dealt with all the red tape for him, and I became his power of attorney.
I was able to get Family and Medical Leave Act money, and when that ran out, I went back to work. I couldn't handle it anymore because of how many calls the nursing home gave me. I had some money saved up and had a 401(k) I wound up using.
I used up my retirement money
Then, my aunt was diagnosed with pancreatic cancer, and I became her full-time caregiver at that point. I took her to her chemo appointments, and I would stay with her for four to six hours after each treatment to make sure that she wasn't getting sick. Being out of a job wasn't so bad, and they would give me some money for my caregiving.
After she completed her chemo, she fell and needed back surgery to fuse two of her vertebrae. I became her caregiver again, and I would do her wound care. She recovered quite a bit, and we decided that she would do OK with just a cane. For a few years afterward, I wasn't a full-time caregiver, and I moved to Tennessee with my kids for a year.
My sister arranged a trip for my mom to go to Georgia to see her niece and nephew. She broke her pelvis while there, as well as her thigh bone, a few bones, and her wrist. After three days of arguing about what to do, we got her into a rehab facility. Her mind was slipping quite a bit. My siblings and I made sure my mom had everything she needed. After trying out aides who were not helpful, my sisters and I moved in with my mom on a rotating schedule, 24/7.
She didn't know where she was or who the people were. This probably lasted for a year and a half. At the start of the pandemic, she broke her femur, and she was only in the hospital. We got a hoist lift, but she really degraded quite a bit. She died in 2021.
My aunt offered for my kids and me to live here permanently, but it became obvious very quickly that she was developing Alzheimer's disease. I would have to babysit her all day to make sure she wasn't getting scammed or doing anything wrong. I had to take over control of her medication. I hired an aide to take her out during the day to give me a break, and that went on for a year and a half. Then, we took the car away from her.
One day at the mall, she fell and broke her femur. She went to rehab, and I got her placed at an assisted living, which I haven't been thrilled about. She's been there for about a year. There hasn't been much for me to do in her case, and I know I should be more active, but I can't handle it.
I became her trustee, and I get a living stipend that I draw on, which is enough to get by. I don't have to pay for her house.
I'm caring for my mother-in-law, who is 85, and is not requiring any medical care except for driving her to all of her doctors. I've taken over her bills and mail because she can't see very well. I'm there to clean the house and fix anything. I'm probably with her for four hours, three times a week. I'd suspect caregiving costs are between $1,000 and $2,000 monthly.
I'm waiting for my life to start
I'm taking it one day at a time. I don't have any plans for my life except taking care of my mother-in-law. When she's no longer here, that's when my life will start. I'm hoping to complete nursing school and find a good job somewhere, ideally traveling to people's homes to care for their physical needs. This way, I'll have something to support myself.
I still haven't dealt with the loss of my parents, my husband, or my father-in-law. It's just been putting up a wall and going on to the next person who needs help. It's very taxing and emotionally draining. You do what you have to do to get through the day and go on to the next one. I have a new granddaughter, who has been the light of my life.
I tell people that when you're 18, buy long-term care insurance. By the time you need it, you won't be able to afford it. I'm 54 and can't pay $800 a month. I'm better off being a Medicaid recipient so I don't have to worry about nursing homes. It's important to stay close to your family because you're going to need them. It goes a long way for mental health.

There is something wrong with the tractor. The water-in-fuel sensor, a small device embedded in the John Deere machine that monitors the integrity of its diesel engine, is disconnected. And I’ve got to fix it.
I’m not a mechanic or a farmer. I’m poking at a laptop at John Deere’s corporate office in Santa Clara, California. There’s a cable connecting the computer to a 5130ML tractor sitting on the grass nearby. A bright red notification sits on the screen, telling me something is wrong. I type in a question and the software pulls up instructions and a few images from the user manual that matches the serial number of the machine.
I wander over to the tractor and find the parts modeled on the screen. I spot the sensor, with two very obvious dangling wires that need to be connected together. I press them together, hear a little click, then step away and look back at the screen. The notification has cleared. Everything seems to be fine. In just a couple minutes, all by myself, I’ve fixed the water-in-fuel sensor. This fix was an easy one. It’s a WiF, really.
The John Deere employees surrounding me offer their congratulations. They’ve all been very patient with me, someone who has written several articles for WIRED about their company’s seemingly steadfast reluctance to let anyone but its official technicians repair its products.
In the group is Jahmy Hindman, senior vice president and chief technology officer of John Deere, who has flown in from Illinois. Hindman has worked for the company for 30 years. In that time, John Deere has thrived in an era of technological advancement. He’s here now to show off the company’s self-repair software Operations Center Pro Service, a system that pairs with nearly every electronic-enabled machine John Deere has made.
“It is owner-friendly,” Hindman says. “I think that’s always been our intent.”
Lots of farmers would beg to differ.
Oh, Deere
John Deere is the largest agricultural machine manufacturer in the US. In the past couple decades, machines of this ilk have become far more technologically advanced, loaded up with controllers, radios, and sensors. Many newer machines are equipped with 4G wireless connections that enable the collection of precise location data and other metrics. Some tractors can even run without a human operator at all, guided by built-in software systems to run autonomously on predetermined paths.
Over the last decade, John Deere has become a big target of the ever-growing right-to-repair movement. The company’s high-tech software systems also come equipped with digital locks, which require official, dealer-sanctioned approval to access. If you want to fiddle with a part, or replace it with an aftermarket alternative, those software restrictions can block those attempts.
That frustration has manifested in multiple lawsuits and even federal action. In April, the company agreed to pay out a $99 million settlement to its equipment owners to pay back burdensome repair costs. In July, the company settled a separate lawsuit brought by the US Federal Trade Commission that would require the company to make its products more repairable. John Deere did not admit wrongdoing in either case. Repair advocates say the two measures have been insufficient, both in financial terms and as requirements that will actually change Deere’s behavior. (Both settlements are not yet final until a judge issues a final ruling.)
Pro tip
John Deere disagrees, of course, citing its recent efforts to make the case that its self-repair program works just fine.
The company introduced its Pro Service in 2025. Prices start at an annual cost of $195 per individual machine. For bigger operations or independent repair shops, the price to access every machine in John Deere’s fleet starts at $4,995 a year. That access for agricultural and turf services costs $5,995 per year.
Pro Service lets owners connect Deere’s software to their equipment via Wi-Fi or cable. Based on the serial number of the machine, the software can be used to find information from manuals and John Deere’s broader data services to diagnose any maintenance the machine needs. John Deere also recently introduced an AI chatbot called JD to its Operations Center self-repair software tool, but I did not have a chance to use that version during my visit. The AI features are meant to make it easier to find information about the components in any given machine.
“As the tractor products grow in size, they also grow in number of controllers that are necessary in order to make it all work,” Hindman says, noting that in some cases tractors can have upward of 50 controllers. “So it can be super complex.”
Theoretically, Pro Service is the ultimate platform to find any equipment information and diagnose any problem. If something goes wrong, the software will guide you through a fix. Some features in Pro Service can be downloaded and used offline in case a connection isn’t working when something needs fixing. You can customize the layout to your liking and keep track of the full history of the software updates on each machine. If you need a new part, the software will helpfully serve you a link to the product in John Deere’s shop. It feels as smooth as scrolling through an Amazon page.
Kelli Sullivan, a group product manager of marketing automation and governance at John Deere, is the person leading the demo. She says owners are in full control of their data and can choose whether to share it with John Deere or an independent repair shop, or keep it private.
Data as a service
The thing John Deere does seem to struggle with is enticing people to use its Pro Service, or even making its customers aware of it. (That’s the reason I’m here at this demo.) A year on, John Deere says its service has about a thousand daily users—a relatively small number, given that there are somewhere around 1.8 million farms in the US.
“We’re just trying to get the word out,” Sullivan says. “We have a suite of tools that are already available in our customers’ hands that allow them to do those things.”
Jared Wilson is a farmer in Missouri who uses Deere machines to care for his 3,000 acres of corn and soybean crops. He is also a named plaintiff in the $99 million lawsuit against John Deere who has called that payout ruling “fundamentally flawed.” When I describe my demo experience to Wilson, he laughs, saying the service works best on particularly simple repairs.
“If you have multiple failures, you have to figure out where to start,” Wilson says. “If you have three different or four different diagnostic codes, where do you start in the tree to figure out what’s wrong?”
Wilson does not use Pro Service. He doesn’t know anyone who does, saying the farmers he knows tend to use cracked versions of the software they find on gray markets instead of giving their money to John Deere. Even with Pro Service, he says, farmers don’t always trust that John Deere will give farmers the tools they really need to fix their stuff.
“It’s taken a class action lawsuit and FTC action to get them to come this far,” Wilson says. “If you believe what they’re saying now—that this is actually it and we’re getting everything we’ve asked for—then I’ve got some oceanfront property in Arizona to sell you.”
One of Wilson’s biggest concerns with using a service like Pro Service, he says, is that it’s almost impossible to compare the dealership version of the software with the customer version of the software for parity. (Hindman says the versions of the software are all the same.)
Part of the problem are PIPs, or product improvement plans, which is a term John Deere uses to identify potential or existing problems in its machines. John Deere can issue a PIP, which then goes out to let people who own a particular piece of equipment know there’s an issue with the machine. But those missives only go out after the system has gathered the information that an improvement might be needed in the first place.
If a user faces a novel problem with how a machine works, it would still take time for that issue to get back to John Deere, which would verify it, then issue a PIP in Pro Service. In the meantime, the person dealing with the broken tractor won’t have the needed information to figure out exactly what is going on. Ideally, many of them would like to be able to troubleshoot the problem themselves, without having to use the company’s proprietary software.
“They’re still not giving us access to that next level that we have to have for some of the most difficult problems that we encounter,” Wilson says.
Willie Cade, a board member of the advocacy group Repair.org and frequent critic of John Deere, takes that a step further.
“They’re just monopolists that want to make money and as much as they possibly can,” Cade says. “Their real customer is not the farmer. Their real customer is Wall Street.”
At the demo, I ask about the repair advocates and what they get wrong about John Deere. Hindman says he doesn’t mind the pressure.
“We have the best intentions of making sure that we have the ability to give customers the tools that they need to keep their equipment up and running,” Hindman says. “We share that goal in common. Are there things that we need to continue to work on? I’m sure that there are. But let’s not forget that we are a long way towards moving the needle to a much better state.”
The repair advocates are still pushing on John Deere. Agricultural equipment like tractors are some of the most durable goods, built to last for years and even decades of hard manual labor. If society isn’t able to establish a precedent to let people fix these machines, advocates argue, it becomes harder to pass legislation or judicial rulings that would solidify people’s rights to fix their own personal devices.
“This is an issue that’s concerning agricultural equipment,” Wilson says. “But it’s really the vanguard of a much bigger and persistent problem that affects every aspect of our society.”

President Donald Trump on Sunday said he would remove tariffs on Irish whiskey after golfer Shane Lowry and the Irish prime minister did the unthinkable: They asked him.
"Everybody's been bugging me," the president said during remarks at the Irish Open. "They're saying, can you do me a favor? It's so unfair what's going on."
The crowd cheered wildly after the president said he would lift the tariff, which sits at 10%.
Ireland's national public broadcaster said last year that about 45% to 50% of Irish whiskey is exported to the United States, making the US its biggest export market.
In May, the Irish whiskey association said the tariffs on whiskey should be removed.
"Reducing the tariff for Irish drinks would benefit the many US companies who have Irish premium products in their portfolio," the association said in a press release. "It would avoid uncertainty for the US consumer and strengthen the cask trade in Kentucky, Tennessee and other US states."
Trump placed the 10% tariff in February as part of his temporary global tariff on most imports. Popular Irish whiskey brands include Jameson, Bushmills, Tullamore D.E.W., and Redbreast.
Trump's tariff policies in his second term have upended markets, thrown business for a loop, and strained relations with long-standing allies, most recently Canada. They've also landed his administration in legal trouble.
Trump has said the tariffs are meant to rebalance what he calls unfair trade relations, jump-start American industry, and give the US leverage in international negotiations, like border security and drug trafficking.

The national song Vande Mataram, written by Bankim Chandra Chattopadhyay, was played ahead of the national anthem Jana Gana Mana at an international sporting event for the first time, before India’s opening T20 International against Afghanistan in New Delhi on Sunday. The move followed a directive from the Union Home Ministry, under which all six stanzas of Vande Mataram were played at the Arun Jaitley Stadium. The national song lasted 3 minutes and 10 seconds, while the national anthem took 52 seconds, bringing the combined duration to 4 minutes and 2 seconds. News agency PTI citing BCCI sources said Vande Mataram will now be played before the opening match of every home series. Quick answers to key questions Vande Mataram was played ahead of the national anthem at India's T20I against Afghanistan following a directive from the Union Home Ministry, marking its first rendition at an international sporting event. The BCCI announced that Vande Mataram will be played at the start of every home series, specifically before the first match of each series. The Ministry of Home Affairs issued guidelines stating that the official version of Vande Mataram should last 3 minutes and 10 seconds, with attendees required to stand at attention during its performance. Vande Mataram was adopted as the national song by the Indian National Congress in 1937 and received official recognition as the 'National Song' by the Constituent Assembly in 1950. It remains uncertain whether both Vande Mataram and the national anthem will be featured at upcoming ICC events, as this was the first instance of the song being played at a sporting event. "Vande Mataram will now be played at the start of every home series, before the start of first game," PTI quoted a BCCI source as saying. The Ministry of Home Affairs issued guidelines on February 6 outlining the protocol for singing or playing Vande Mataram as part of events marking 150 years of the national song. Under the guidelines, the official version of the song has been set at 3 minutes and 10 seconds. All those present are required to stand at attention during its rendition. The complete six-stanza version has also been approved for select occasions, including formal government events attended by the President or Governors, broadcasts of presidential addresses on radio and television, ceremonies involving the National Flag being brought on parade, and other similar functions. The first two stanzas of Vande Mataram were adopted as the national song by the Indian National Congress (INC) in 1937. Car manufacturers are ditching CarPlay in 2026: Here's why
Drivers and auto makers alike have enjoyed CarPlay since its inception, but many manufacturers are turning their backs now.
Apple CarPlay has given drivers a great alternative to clunky car infotainment systems for over a decade. It has a simple premise: connect your iPhone and use the apps you already know. Like Android Auto, CarPlay is a service that vehicle manufacturers have adopted in great numbers and with relative enthusiasm — at least, until lately.
Some of those same manufacturers are starting to backtrack. General Motors, for instance, has been removing CarPlay from its EVs and plans to phase it out completely. Tesla and Rivian have never offered support for it, although Tesla has reportedly tested out CarPlay.
Removing CarPlay erases a layer of convenience for you as the driver. But for the manufacturer, it gives greater control over data and the services you use. Automakers might argue that removing it provides better integration with the car, but with CarPlay Ultra looking to close the gap, this disagreement is likely going to get bigger.
Apple CarPlay became the best way around bad car software
Apple CarPlay's biggest strength is consistency. You can step into any compatible car and, no matter the type of display or its size, you'll see the same interface. The apps you use on your phone, along with your contacts, are all accessible. You don't need to port anything or create new accounts to get going.
Drivers don't need to worry about whether built-in infotainment systems are any good, since you can ignore them with CarPlay. Before the the CarPlay and Android Auto era, drivers were stuck with whatever infotainment system the manufacturer had built. This wasn't consistent, nor were many long-lasting: MyFord Touch on Ford and Lincoln cars lasted just five years. BMW, meanwhile, tried to charge $80 a year for access to CarPlay. Navigation was a common problem with older systems. Maps would quickly become out-of-date and sometimes required a costly fee to update.
It made sense for manufacturers to add CarPlay (and Android Auto) support to their vehicles: they could hand over the bulk of functionality to Apple's (or Google's) system while focusing on other areas. Apple CarPlay now supports over 800 different models, so the arrangement has certainly taken hold.
For manufacturers, though, handing over the dashboard to Apple has become a bit of a problem. Electric cars in particular require much more integration between the dashboard software and the vehicle itself. A whole host of features on EVs aren't an ideal fit for Apple CarPlay, including battery preconditioning and manufacturer-specific charging controls. Standard CarPlay sits on top of the car's own software to effectively act as a mirroring app for your phone, and you may need to leave it if you need a feature Apple's solution doesn't support.
CarPlay support matters to drivers. Apple claimed at WWDC 2022 that 79 percent of car buyers wouldn't choose a model without CarPlay support, while a more recent survey suggested losing CarPlay was a "deal breaker" for 55 percent of its users. The consistency makes CarPlay familiar and easy to use. For those making the cars, though, Apple controlling the parts of the on-screen experience we see and use the most means manufacturers have less control and power. Some companies are deciding that this compromise no longer works for them.
GM wants complete control over the in-car experience
General Motors is the one making the biggest pivot with CarPlay so far. It's already begun the process by removing CarPlay and rival Android Auto support from its newest electric models, including the Chevrolet Blazer EV. It's also expected to begin removing support from gas-powered cars once its own centralized computing platform is released around 2028. You won't see support suddenly dropped from existing cars, but newer models will only be left with GM's alternative.
Ironically, that alternative is being built around Android Automotive (not Android Auto), Google's standalone car operating system. Rather than simply mirroring your phone apps, Android Automotive runs apps directly on the car itself. You won't need to connect a smartphone at all.
General Motors argues this gives its software a much deeper understanding of the vehicle underneath. Navigation is an obvious example. While running GM's new Android Automotive-based system, Google Maps can factor in an EV's remaining charge and estimated range into its route planning, giving you suitable charging stops along the way.
The thinking is that you won't need your phone to act as a middleman, a fact GM executive Mike Hichme mentioned in a 2023 interview. He suggested that he didn't want GM's infotainment system to be "dependent on a person having a cellphone" like it is now.
Of course, keeping it all native means GM has more control over the data when you use those services. It can learn more about how drivers use the car, particularly when they plan routes or charge their EVs. If the built-in apps rely on the car's own data connection (instead of your phone's mobile plan, adding yet another expense), some could require a subscription once any free period expires. It also has more opportunities to sell connected services later.
Better integration is GM's public argument, but keeping the dashboard to itself could pay off, too. That control comes with a trust problem, though. In January, the FTC banned General Motors from selling driver data for five years after it allegedly collected and sold behavior data without informed consent.
CarPlay Ultra could make the disagreement even bigger
GM might suggest that standard CarPlay is too limiting, but Apple does have an answer to that criticism. CarPlay Ultra goes far beyond mirroring iPhone apps on your car's display. It's a solution for the entire car, including the instrument cluster, where it can show your car's speed and tire pressure alongside Apple Maps directions.
CarPlay Ultra is Apple's biggest attempt to close this gap. It manages the systems a driver interacts with, including radio and climate controls, so you won't need to jump between interfaces. Manufacturers will be able to create their own themes to fit with the car's aesthetics.
The downside is that you'll still need your iPhone. GM's complaint about the iPhone dependency issue isn't solved by CarPlay Ultra, as it still relies (for now) on the processing power in your phone to work. It also doesn't solve the Apple problem itself; manufacturers will have to share vehicle data and work closely with Apple to integrate the system. For companies like GM who want to own the entire software experience, CarPlay Ultra would arguably be a step in the wrong direction.
That might be why CarPlay Ultra adoption has been slow, at least for now. Aston Martin is the only manufacturer currently offering it, although brands like Hyundai and Kia have suggested they will at a later (unconfirmed) date. Thankfully, CarPlay remains available across hundreds of car models, allowing you to carry on with the iPhone experience as you drive for years to come.

At Apple’s recent hardware event, the software powering its foldable iPhone Duo stood out, with translucent Liquid Glass effects and vertically stacked icons. But you don’t need to snatch a folding smartphone to reap the benefits of Apple’s iOS 27 updates.
When iOS 27 leaves beta on Monday, Siri AI’s standalone app and smartphone search integration will likely be the most immediately obvious change for many iPhone users. But it’s worth digging even deeper to uncover helpful additions to key apps, like Apple’s Safari browser, as well as revamps to underutilized apps, like Shortcuts.
The version of Safari available in iOS 27 looks fairly similar to the last iteration, with a few key updates tucked away in the settings. These Safari features are powered by Apple Intelligence, which requires an iPhone 15 Pro or newer (they're also available on iPadOS 27 and macOS 27).
Notify Me
If you’re shopping online and want a quick price-drop notification, you can use the “Notify Me” feature to scan a webpage on a certain cadence and look for changes. First, head to the page you want to track and tap the three-lined hamburger menu icon in the top right corner of Safari. About halfway down, you’ll see this option listed.
“Safari can let you know when a website updates the content you’re interested in,” reads the feature’s description. Here you’ll find an open text box where you can describe what change in content you want Safari to scan for, as well as how often you want it to check.
For example, my couch is broken, so I’ve been eyeing a few different replacement options. I have two final contenders from CB2, but both are out of my price range. So, I set up a “Notify Me” for Safari to scan the pages each day for a significant discount. Whichever one goes on sale first will likely be what I decide to get, and now I don’t have to refresh the pages manually every day.
While many other browsers have similar shopping features, like the price-tracking bell in Google Chrome, I appreciate how this feature stretches beyond just buying stuff. You can also use Safari to scan for ticket drops, privacy policy changes, and other content updates.
Describe an Extension
If you’ve experimented already with the “Describe a Shortcut” feature for iPhone automation, then “Describe an Extension” for Safari will seem familiar. It's located under the same settings menu as the “Notify Me” tool, just a little further down.
The feature asks you to type what you want the extension to do, then generates a custom option. Some of the suggested prompts in Safari revolve around boosting productivity, like “display a reading time estimate as a badge on the extension,” maintaining better focus, like “make the web page grayscale,” and more random ideas, like “show a colorful and explosive firework every time I tap.”
It took only a few seconds for each of those three examples to generate. Safari also suggests pre-made extensions during the process that could fit what you’re looking to do. As I scrolled through the internet with all three of the new extensions activated, everything worked as expected. While I’ll likely only keep the grayscale one to help me focus while reading online articles, the fireworks felt whimsical in small doses.
Organize Tabs
I am a glutton for mobile tabs, especially on Safari. I’m rarely ever exiting out of anything and always just pop open something new, which leaves me with hundreds upon hundreds of loosely connected, completely unorganized tabs—until now.
This feature is in the wider browser tab view accessible by tapping the two overlapping squares at the bottom-right corner of your screen. Swipe to a tab group brimming with websites and look for the three-lined button in the top-left. Here’s where you can choose to allow Safari to “automatically create topics” based on those tabs.
It takes a few seconds to organize everything after you activate this feature, but it did a great job of finding helpful trends in those 500+ tabs. For example, it grouped all the WIRED articles I had open and created a tab topic for upcoming San Francisco event pages and comedy clubs I was considering checking out.

'People are still afraid of those three letters': Fighting the stigma of HIV
RIO DE JANEIRO -- "People are still afraid of those three letters," says Gareth Thomas, a former Welsh rugby star.
He's talking about HIV. Thomas became a global champion for people living with HIV when he announced that he was HIV positive in 2019.
Since then, he has been a strong advocate for sharing knowledge about the virus –- and what it's like to live with it.
This summer, he came to Rio de Janeiro to participate in the International AIDS Conference and to spread his message as part of the Tackle HIV campaign.
"I thought I was gonna die"
That message resonates with another advocate: Welton Gabriel, a 36-year-old event organizer from Sao Paolo.
Sitting in a bar overlooking the world-famous Ipanema beach, Welton Gabriel recalled the night 12 years earlier when he learned he had tested positive for HIV.
"I thought I was gonna die," he remembers.
For a while, his life did hang in the balance. Gabriel had contracted a treatment-resistant strain of HIV — he believes that the sexual partner who infected him had been taking medication but decided to stop, allowing the virus to mutate. It took seven months before doctors were able to get the infection under control.
"The amount of virus in my body was really high," he says. "I was initially started on a medicine that gave me a lot of problems with my liver, and my eyes became yellow. But then I was changed to the treatment that I am still on, which is working."
Despite the trauma he'd endured, and the fact that his condition was under control, when Gabriel chose to tell close friends that he was HIV positive, many cut contact. "They did not want to talk with me," recalls Gabriel, who lives in São Paulo.
Such discrimination remains one of the biggest hurdles to ending AIDS as a public-health threat in Brazil, a country of about 214 million which has the greatest number of people living with HIV in Latin America — nearly 1.1 million.
While Brazil's public healthcare system provides free access to medications that can suppress HIV and prevent transmission, allowing people to live normally, many still face a lifetime of stigma. Research from UNAIDS Brazil, a nonprofit that works closely with government agencies in the country, suggests that more than half of all HIV positive individuals in the country have experienced some form of discrimination. Gabriel lost friends, and others have been excluded by their own family or denied opportunities at work after disclosing their HIV status.
Today, Gabriel works as an activist with Barong, an organization that supports vulnerable communities across Brazil by offering mobile testing, education and information about HIV protection. He has come to realize that much of the discrimination stems from a place of fear.
Despite advances in HIV science — highlighted at this summer's AIDS 2026 conference in Rio, where researchers discussed developments from a monthly pill that can block HIV transmission to new strategies aimed at long-term remission — Gabriel says perceptions of HIV in Brazil have changed little since 1990, when the iconic Brazilian singer Cazuza died of AIDS at age 32.
Charismatic and talented, Cazuza went from school dropout to wealthy superstar during the 1980s and captivated the Brazilian public. His struggle with the debilitating effects of AIDS turned HIV into a household discussion topic within the country. However, Gabriel says that many people are unaware of the extent to which medical science has changed the prognosis of HIV over the past three and a half decades. As a result, he says that HIV is still commonly viewed as a death sentence.
"For a lot of Brazilians of that generation, that's still the symbol of HIV," says Gabriel. "When I learned I was HIV positive, I looked on Google, and the first thing I saw was the story of Cazuza."
'You can live a normal, happy, healthy life"
Gabriel had come to Ipanema Beach to speak with teenagers from disadvantaged communities as part of a Tackle HIV event organized in partnership with Thomas, Viiv Healthcare and AIDS-related charities. The effort aims to shift public attitudes by bringing accurate information to young people who are often left out of mainstream health outreach.
Speaking at the event, Thomas suggested that people still ostracize those living with HIV because of a lack of knowledge about the virus. He says it's common for people to be unaware of the modern medications that can prevent and control HIV.
""Many people don't know that you can live a normal, happy, healthy life if you start medication straight away, and so people avoid getting tested, avoid the result or avoid the medicine taking," says Thomas.
The consequence is preventable deaths. In Brazil, national health data shows that 27% of HIV positive people are only diagnosed and treated once their condition has progressed to a late stage, known as advanced AIDS. By that point, their immune system is severely weakened, leaving them highly vulnerable to life-threatening infections. In 2024, the most recent year for which data is available, more than 9,000 people in Brazil died from AIDS.
"We're losing ground every year"
Beatriz Grinsztejn, a Brazilian infectious-diseases specialist and former president of the International AIDS Society, describes this as tragic, given the availability of free tests and treatments. "People don't access what is available, and this is really painful," she says.
Even when timely diagnoses are made, convincing people to keep taking their medication is another challenge, even if that treatment is keeping them alive. Government figures show that 82% of HIV-positive individuals in Brazil are taking HIV-suppressing antiretroviral drugs — a seemingly impressive number yet well short of the U.N.'s target of 95%.
Gustavo Passos, equality and rights officer at UNAIDS Brazil, says this gap undermines the country's push to eliminate AIDS as a public-health threat. "On the treatment part, we're losing ground each year," he says. "The data we have implies that it's related to how people connect with health services."
Passos says that many people living with HIV feel stigmatized even by healthcare professionals, fearing that their status will be illegally disclosed without their consent, which causes them to lose trust in the system meant to support them.
Gabriel sees this dynamic play out in daily life. "It's about being judged if you're seen taking your treatment each day, and the pressure that puts on people," he says. "If someone feels judged, a lot of times they will stop the treatment."
"A lot of homophobia and transphobia"
While Brazil is commonly depicted to outsiders as a place of uninhibited sexuality — on social media, it's popularly described as one of the most promiscuous countries in the world — the reality is quite different.
Since 2014, lawmakers at federal, state and municipal levels in Brazil have proposed more than 200 pieces of legislation to ban all discussions of sex and gender education in schools. The legislative trend has continued to surface elsewhere: Two years ago, protests broke out in major cities over a proposal to equate abortion with homicide.
As Grinsztejn points out, Brazil has very high rates of violence against sexual minorities, citing Rio as a notable example. "The best gay destination in the country has a lot of homophobia and transphobia," she says. "The number of murders of trans people is one of the worst on the planet." Most victims are young: While general life expectancy in Brazil is 76, the transgender population's life expectancy is 30-35, which Grinsztejn says has been attributed to high rates of violence.
She says that this feeds into wider perceptions of HIV as a disease of immorality and deviance, driving discrimination.
Her fiancé never spoke to her again
Fabiana de Oliveira, a 57-year-old activist with the National Network of Women Living with HIV, an organization formed by women living with HIV and AIDS, says HIV discrimination in Brazil is also heavily gender-skewed.
She recalled her own experience of being diagnosed with HIV at 26. Her fiancé and partner of eight years, whom she suspected of giving her the virus, never spoke to her again. "I never saw him after that day," she says. "His family came to the hospital to check if I had HIV, and told me that I was no longer welcome in their house."
Living in Catanduva, a municipality in the state of Sao Paulo with just 100,000 people, she grew accustomed to feeling the judgment of others and even herself. "Women in Brazil are never the ones who are being cared for," says de Oliveira. "We are expected to take care of everything, the husband, the children, so it's hard to equate HIV as being part of your identity. You end up asking yourself, 'Was this my responsibility?' and it places a lot of burden on your mental and emotional health. Many women living with HIV in Brazil end up isolating themselves."
When it comes to the persistently damaging effects of stigma, the irony is that Brazil has also played a major role in innovations which have the potential to ultimately end the HIV epidemic. Lenacapavir, a twice-yearly injectable drug which can block HIV with virtually 100% effectiveness, was recently approved by regulators after reviewing global clinical trial data, including research carried out in Brazil. The country is now leading a large real-world study of lenacapavir across multiple cities to understand how the drug can be effectively implemented in public-health settings.
But de Oliveira is skeptical about whether such innovations can have the necessary impact without wider education campaigns and more openness in discussing HIV.
"People are more afraid of how society is going to perceive them than they are of the virus," she says.
Yet Gabriel has also seen firsthand how mindsets can change when people learn more about HIV. In the months and years after he disclosed his status, he was able to explain to his family and friends that he wasn't going to die, and correct misconceptions about how the virus could be transmitted.
"When I was able to explain more, some of my friends did eventually come back," he says. "Even if I originally felt discriminated against, it later allowed everyone to be more present and more aware."

Erling Haaland’s Man City goal decision vs Man Utd an ‘error of judgement', says Pro Ref
Sunday 13 September 2026 21:36, UK
Refereeing body Pro Ref has admitted an error in awarding Manchester City's winner at Manchester United in their 1-0 victory at Old Trafford.
Erling Haaland's goal was initially disallowed for offside on the pitch before VAR overturned the decision.
The VAR officials deemed that Haaland was played onside by Man Utd defender Patrick Dorgu. However, Man City's Enzo Fernandez was in an offside position as he attempted to play the ball before it reached Haaland.
Despite not touching the ball, Fernandez's movement appeared to impact the defending of Man Utd's Lisandro Martinez before Haaland's back-post finish, which by the laws of the game should have led to the goal remaining disallowed.
