Since 2022, Sweden has been governed by a three-party minority government led by the Moderates party (often referred to simply as M) leader Ulf Kristersson, with Ebba Busch’s Christian Democrats (KD) and Simona Mohamsson’s the Liberals (L).
They are currently supported by – but not formally joined in the government – by the far-right populist and anti-immigration Sweden Democrats (SD) party, led by Jimmie Åkesson. They are one of, if not the, key talking points of the night.
A win for the centre-right bloc of parties would most likely see them formally join the government, breaking another taboo in Swedish politics.
The opposition is led by former prime minister Magdalena Andersson’s Social Democrats (S – not SD), which is the largest party in the parliament. Other parties of the opposition bloc are: the Centre party (C) of Elisabeth Thand Ringqvist, the Left party (V) of Nooshi Dadgostar, and the Green Party (MP) of Daniel Helldén and Amanda Lind.
The left-wing bloc has been leading in the polls for the majority of the current parliamentary term, with Andersson’s party alone polling at times in mid 30s, leaving many experts thinking that a change of government was all but certain.
But in recent months the polls have substantially narrowed, giving the combined opposition only a very slim lead going into the election day. They are the favourites to win, but it’s still all to play for.
“The opposition parties have had a lead in the polls, often a very comfortable lead … so if there were to be any other outcome than an opposition victory, it would be sort of sensational because the lead has been so consistent and so long established – but it’s not impossible,” Aylott tells me.
“The big challenge the Social Democrats would face in the quite likely event that they will be forming a government is that their constellation of allied parties, which would comprise the majority, is very diverse,” he adds.
“One of the aspects of this diversity is that some of them take a much more permissive view on things like law and order and migration, so keeping this diverse constellation of currently opposition parties could be difficult.”
Arriving at her election night, Social Democrat leader Magdalena Andersson says it has been an “intense” campaign, and adds “there are still a few minutes left to choose a new direction.”
Arriving at his Moderate party’s election night, prime minister Ulf Kristersson said it has been “a fantastically enjoyable campaign” of “hard work … and great enthusiasm.”
He would say that, right?
But he also says he is “confident” as the party has had “the wind in our sails for several weeks now.”
“Now it’s up to the Swedish people to decide,” he says.
How the far-right changed Sweden's conversation on migration
Ashifa Kassam
European community affairs correspondent
The Swedish polls have narrowed in recent weeks making many nervous, particularly as the right-leaning ruling coalition has for the first time said it would offer ministerial posts to the far right if it wins.
Those who have borne the brunt of the far right’s time propping up the government worry that Sweden, long held up as a leading light when it comes to equality and freedom, may have been irrevocably changed, regardless of what happens on Sunday.
“It’s a kind of Pandora’s box that has been opened,” said Munir Niazi.
During the government of the centre-right prime minister Ulf Kristersson, the far-right Sweden Democrats have used their leverage to steer policies on migration and crime, seizing on the spotlight to spread rhetoric linking the two and scapegoating migrants, Muslims and other minorities for all that ails the country.
The result had shifted Sweden’s national conversation to the right, said Niazi.
“In the past four years, the biggest opposition party, the Social Democrats, have slowly adopted and even voted with the right wing on migration, on crime. In the near future, at least, we don’t see the country going back to the policies of the 80s and 90s.”
The changes to immigration policy, including recently introduced rules barring most asylum seekers from accessing permanent residency, were an example of how the political conversation in Sweden had been transformed by the far right’s time as power-brokers, said journalist Bilan Osman.
Among those caught up in the crackdown on asylum seekers was an undocumented 14-year-old who, despite being born in Sweden, was facing deportation to Armenia, along with his single-parent mother and his younger brother. “It’s like hell. I’ve been here my whole life,” he told the Guardian. “I feel Swedish.”
Sweden needs 'new direction,' opposition leader Andersson says
Opposition leader Magdalena Andersson, voted on Sunday morning in the Stockholm suburb of Nacka, and said the campaign had been “a tale of two sides”.
“There have been a lot of lies and bickering, but at the same time there are so many sensible people out there across the country,” she told SVT. “The focus is on winning and setting a new direction for Sweden.”
“We’ve become a harder society, a quieter society, but also a poorer society as we’ve had growth far below our potential and where households see their paychecks buy less and less,” she told Reuters.
Separately, Abba’s Benny Andersson showed his support for the Social Democrats’ leader by performing a reworked version of Mamma Mia to supporters at the party’s headquarters, replacing the words “Mamma Mia” with “Magdalena”.
Prime minister Ulf Kristersson cast his ballot today, rocking up to vote with his family members and welsh springer, Winston.
He told journalists he expected “a very, very exciting” evening, and insisted “the momentum” was on his side – even as his party appeared to be losing support in recent polls.
But Kristersson’s focus appeared to be on winning as a bloc to continue the work of his government. “We are team leaders, that is our role in Swedish politics,” he said.
“The precondition for getting things done is actually the ability to compromise, to have a clear vision but be pragmatic,” he said. “If we get people’s votes we will continue to do that for the coming four years.”
Opposition bloc leads in polls by somewhere between 5 and 0.3%
As mentioned earlier, polls have long pointed to an opposition victory tonight – but the gap has narrowed significantly in recent weeks and leaving the question of the result tonight quite open.
Over the last few weeks, Andersson’s Social Democrats fell below 30%, from near 35% at the beginning of the year, and were expected to secure around 28% of the vote.
The far-right Sweden Democrats are expected to come second at 19%, narrowly ahead of Kristersson’s Moderates at 17%.
The remaining parties are all around 7-8%, with the Liberals noting a surprising surge in recent weeks amid concerns if they would make it above the 4% threshold. After polling at just 2% in August, they were at 6-7% in the latest round of polls.
The latest round of polls showed the opposition bloc lead by between 5.6% and 0.3%, giving it a slight edge in today’s race.
While the two main contenders were busy debating on TV, deputy prime minister and Christian Democrat leader Ebba Busch and Liberal leader Simona Mohamsson went behind the bar in central Stockholm to serve some drinks and so mark the end of the campaign.
There are some great pictures from their big pre-election night out in the Swedish press.
“On a Saturday night you want to be where Sweden is, and many people are at the bar,” Busch told reporters.
Other ministers also joined the party leaders, including Sweden’s top diplomat Maria Malmer Stenergard.
But as the polls narrowed in recent days, the unusually polarised and tense campaign took a further nasty turn this week as a canvasser for the Social Demorats was physically assaulted on Thursday evening when knocking on doors in Bromölla.
An 18-year old man was later arrested in connection with the incident.
And during last night’s TV debate Andersson also disclosed that Social Democratic Gothenburg mayor Jonas Attenius was aggressively confronted when out campaigning on Saturday afternoon.
Opening last night’s TV debate, she insisted that “words matter” as she urged politicians to be more considerate of the language they use when describing their rivals in an apparent swipe at the far-right Sweden Democrats party.
PM Kristersson said he had no knowledge of the incident, and condemned it as “appalling.”
A Sweden Democrats spokesperson rejected any implied link with their party, while also saying “no one should ever be threatened.”
Two frontrunners clash over visions of Sweden in key televised debate
The two leading candidates for the post of Sweden’s next prime minister – the incumbent Ulf Kristersson and the challenger Magdalena Anderssen – faced each other on live TV last night in the last debate of the campaign.
During the 90 minute duel, they set out their competing visions for the economy, crime, education, and other long-term challenges. A separate bloc of questions also looked ahead to Sweden in 2040, tackling an ageing population, low birth rates, climate ambitions, and energy policy.
Ultimately, though, this was the final chance for both Andersson and Kristersson to pitch their vision of government directly to voters.
Andersson repeatedly called for a different style of politics – one that would never be “governed by extreme forces” in the far-right Sweden Democrats.
Yet she repeatedly evaded questions on the exact composition of a future administration. While criticising the growing polarisation in Swedish politics, she maintained she would be open to cooperating with every party except the SD.
Her diplomatically vague stance reflects the complex internal dynamics of the centre-left bloc, where policy disputes and party rivalries make the shape of a potential coalition hard to pin down.
In sharp contrast, Kristersson presented his bloc – the three coalition parties plus the Sweden Democrats – as ready to step straight back into office.
He argued they “have proven that we are up to the task,” and insisted they would be prepared to start coalition talks the day after the vote.
Pressed by Andersson, he refused to speculate on which ministries the SD might get in the next government, but claimed he offered a “stable, safe alternative” to Andersson’s “left-wing experiment.”
Despite record-high number of people casting their votes early, long queues were reported in parts of Sweden on Sunday, with voters waiting up to three hours to vote.
Swedish public broadcaster SVT spoke to voters in Umeå, who complained about the queues and waiting times at the polling station, while Expressen reached out to two elderly voters who go home because the queueing was too exhausting (but were planning to come back later).
Lots of people also take to social media to express their frustration with the wait.
The Swedish Election Authority said it was “unusual” for voters to have to wait for so long, and – perhaps not surprisingly (18:03) – suggested simplifying the voting system a bit.
Over 3.5m voters cast their ballots early, including far-right leader Åkesson
Over 3.5 million voters are believed to have cast their votes early to avoid the election day rush.
It’s a somewhat unusual system, with voters given an extended window - which started on 26 August – to take part in the election.
Among them, the Sweden Democrats leader Jimmie Åkesson who chose to cast his ballot in Rinkeby, a heavily immigrant-populated area of Stockholm, which critics said was another polarising PR stunt before the polling day.
Using it to hammer home his central anti-immigration message of the campaign, he said the area “did not look like Sweden” and “Sweden should not look like this,” in what Swedish media said was a reference to Muslim head coverings worn by some women in the area.
The Sweden Democrats have pledged to ban both the niqab and the burqa if they get into government.
Voters uneasy about difficult campaign as they cast ballots in Stockholm
Jakub Krupa
in Stockholm
Outside a polling station at Adolf Fredriks Musikklasser in central Stockholm, as many as three competing groups of pupils and students set up stalls offering coffee and pastries, hoping to raise funds on the back of election day.
A mid-morning rush saw some voters pause for a kanelbulle and a chat, while others hurried straight inside to cast their ballots.
Mikael, 51, felt voters in the middle were particularly squeezed by a polarised campaign.
“I’m slightly nervous as someone who is in the middle. We are either going to have a centre-right government, dependent or with a far-right party in the government, or a centre-left government, dependent on a leftist party that I see as problematic. There is no perfect ending for me,” he said.
“I would like the parties to focus on policy more – on your own policy, and not on what is bad with the others’ [proposals],” he said.
A man in his thirties agreed it had been “a very intense” election campaign as he declared his support for the right-wing governing coalition.
“I feel that in the past four years they have been [growing] the Swedish economy, and making Sweden a better place again, much safer than it used to be,” he said.
Rebecca, 46, said she was holding “mixed feelings” about the vote and admitted she could not decide who to support until the very last minute.
“I am hoping for the red side to win,” she eventually declared. “I think it’s important for everyone to be valued equally. I do not think we are going in the right direction now. Sweden was a lot better and more open minded before,” she said.
Voting about to close in Sweden with far right eyeing first role in government
Miranda Bryant
Nordic correspondent
Voting is under way in Sweden in a high-stakes election that could lead to the far-right Sweden Democrats (SD) entering government for the first time.
It comes after an unusually heated and polarised campaign punctuated by personal attacks between leaders, accusations of misinformation and Maga-inspired ads.
The right-leaning bloc, made up of what are known as the Tidö parties, has been in power for four years. It is formed of the Moderates, the Christian Democrats and the Liberals with a supporting role for SD, Sweden’s second biggest party.
The opposition left-leaning bloc is formed of Sweden’s biggest party, the Social Democrats, the Centre party, the Green party and the Left party.
The rightwing coalition broke a longstanding taboo in 2022 by going into partnership with SD, which has neo-Nazi roots.
SD has attempted to make itself more palatable to the mainstream by toning down its overtly racist rhetoric, while arguing that immigration is responsible for Sweden’s crime problems.
After four years in a supporting role for the Moderates-run coalition government, however, during which it has shifted much of the Swedish establishment to the right, SD’s approach to the election has been more brazen. If the right-leaning coalition wins, the party has been promised a prominent role in the government, including key ministerial positions.
The prime minister and leader of the Moderates, Ulf Kristersson, has put considerable focus in the final days of campaigning on the penalty discount applied to criminals convicted of various offences. He accused opposition leader Magdalena Andersson of not standing up for female rape victims. In response, she accused him of weaponising men’s violence against women.
Voters say the most important election issues are healthcare, law and order, immigration and the economy. But much of the election debate has been focused on personal finance, said Radio Sweden’s senior political correspondent, Fredrik Furtenbach.
“The parties have tried to outdo each other with promises of more money. It has been a sort of auction.”

Between surviving an illness and returning to regular life, lies a journey of a thousand small victories. Physiotherapy helps people take those victories, one step at a time.
There is a moment after a heart attack or stroke that very few people talk about. It is not the moment the ambulance arrives. It is not the moment the doctors say the patient is out of danger. It is the moment when the hospital doors close behind you, you return home, and everyone expects life to slowly return to normal.
But what does ‘normal’ mean?
For someone who has had a stroke, it may mean learning to walk again, using an arm that suddenly feels unfamiliar, finding their balance, or simply getting out of bed without someone holding their hand. For someone who has survived a heart attack, it may mean taking that first walk outside without constantly wondering whether their heart can handle it.
And sometimes, the hardest part is not the physical limitation. It is the fear. “What if it happens again?” That question can stay with a person long after they have left the hospital. This is where physiotherapy becomes much more than a set of exercises.
What rehabilitation entails
We often imagine rehabilitation as someone working hard in a gym, lifting weights or walking on a treadmill. The reality can be much quieter.
For a stroke survivor, the first goal may simply be to sit upright without support. Then to stand. Then to take a few steps. For the family watching, it may seem like very little. For the person doing it, it may feel like climbing a mountain.
A physiotherapist is there for these moments. Not just to count repetitions or measure strength, but to help someone understand that progress does not always have to be dramatic. Sometimes, progress is one extra step. Sometimes, it is standing for ten seconds longer. Sometimes, it is being able to walk to the bathroom without asking for help. And sometimes, it is simply finding the confidence to try.
What patients go through
Imagine being someone who used to walk to work, play with their children, exercise regularly or climb four flights of stairs without giving it a second thought. Then you have a heart attack. Suddenly, your heartbeat becomes something you constantly notice. You begin questioning every sensation. Is this normal? Am I too tired? Is my heart rate too high? Should I stop?
That fear can lead people to become overly cautious and inactive. Cardiac rehabilitation can help break that cycle. With appropriate medical assessment and supervision, patients can gradually return to physical activity, improve their exercise capacity and learn how to manage their cardiovascular health with greater confidence. The physiotherapist’s role is not simply to say, “Push harder.” It is to say: “Let us understand what your body can safely do today—and build from there.”
Not only for the elderly
A stroke or heart attack is often imagined as something that happens late in life, after the age of 60 or so. But when it happens to a younger person, the shock can be enormous. Someone in their 30s or 40s may suddenly find themselves worrying about things they never expected to question. Will I be able to go back to work? Can I take care of my children? Can I travel? Can I exercise again? Can I return to the sport I love?
They may look perfectly healthy from the outside. But inside, they may be dealing with fatigue, weakness, uncertainty and fear about what comes next. That is why rehabilitation cannot simply be based on a person’s age or diagnosis. A younger patient may need to return to a physically demanding job. A sportsperson may want to return to competition. A parent may simply want enough energy to play with their children. Rehabilitation has to fit the life that person wants to return to.
The patient is not a diagnosis. This may be one of the most important things a physiotherapist learns. A medical report might say stroke. It might say heart attack. It might list numbers, test results and medications. But none of those words explain who the patient is. They do not tell you that the patient loves taking their morning walk. They do not tell you that someone has a child waiting at home. They do not tell you that being able to climb the stairs independently means more to that person than almost anything else. Good rehabilitation starts with a simple question: “What do you want to get back to?” The answer may be different for every person. And that answer becomes an important part of the treatment.
Preventive goals
Physiotherapy is also about preventing the next story. Rehabilitation should not only begin after a crisis. Physiotherapists also have an important role in helping people become more physically active, develop healthier movement habits and reduce preventable health risks. Physical activity is an important part of cardiovascular health, but exercise is not a prescription that can simply be copied from one person to another.
The right type, intensity and amount of activity depend on the individual. For someone recovering from a cardiac event, exercise may require appropriate medical guidance and monitoring of symptoms, heart rate, blood pressure and exercise tolerance. For someone recovering from a stroke, rehabilitation may involve improving balance, strength, coordination, walking and everyday functional activities.
The goal is not to push everyone to do more. The goal is to help each person do what is right for them—safely and consistently. The greatest thing a physiotherapist restores is not movement. It is the part of someone’s life they thought was gone forever.
We often say that physiotherapists help people move. But perhaps that does not quite capture the whole story. Physiotherapists help people return to the things that make life feel like life.
(Shanthi Dass is a sports physiotherapist and managing director of Synergy The Clinic, Chennai. synergytheclinic@gmail.com)

The precise composition of ancient Egyptian paints, binders, adhesives, and similar materials used to make artifacts is largely unknown, in part because a full analysis would require taking samples that would damage those valuable artifacts. The development of cutting-edge, non-destructive techniques has been helping to unlock those secrets, aiding conservation efforts.
Most recently, researchers have used mass spectrometry-based proteomics to analyze the glues and adhesives in a broad set of Egyptian artifacts, according to a new paper published in the journal Science Advances. They found plenty of expected sources, such as animal collagens and egg proteins, but also plant proteins, specifically from sesame and drumstick tree (moringa) cereals.
As previously reported, the ancient Egyptians had a highly formalized (and easily recognizable) painting style, and there has been considerable interest in gaining insights into the specific pigments and painting techniques employed. Common pigments included hematite and realgar for red; goethite and orpiment for yellow; Egyptian blue; Egyptian green; carbon-based black; and calcite, gypsum, anhydrite, and huntite for white. (Just last year, Washington State University researchers were able to re-create Egyptian blue by mixing together silicon dioxide, copper, calcium, and sodium carbonate in varying proportions and heating them at very high temperatures akin to those of ancient kilns.)
Many pigments available to ancient Egyptian artists have elemental markers detectable by X-ray fluorescence imaging. Macro-XRF imaging in particular has previously been used (in combination with hyperspectral imaging) to study a Greco-Roman painted funerary portrait from the second century CE, as well as to determine the remnants of color on marble at Delphi in Greece. In 2023, scientists used a portable MA-XRF imaging device to study ancient Egyptian paintings, part of a broader project investigating tomb chapels in the Theban Necropolis.

Platinum-based chemotherapy — in particular cisplatin and carboplatin — are a lifeline for children with certain cancers. These treatments, for instance, transformed the prognosis of hepatoblastoma, a rare cancer of the liver that is the most commonly diagnosed in childhood, from a five-year survival rate of 20% to more than 80% for localized tumors.
However, these medications work by damaging the DNA of cancer cells, and they are also known to cause mutations in the DNA of healthy cells, potentially raising the risk of new cancers later in life. The mutations have been documented in adults, but the picture is less clear when it comes to children. A new study published Thursday in Science sought a clearer understanding of the long-term impact of platinum agents in children treated for hepatoblastoma.
The study looked at children who had received platinum therapy followed by surgery to remove the tumor. The researchers sampled tissues from the liver — both healthy and cancerous — and the patient’s blood, analyzing them through a sophisticated DNA sequencing technique called NanoSeq.
They then compared the sequencing results to those from children who had been treated with different drugs, or had not been treated prior to surgery, as well as to fetal liver tissue. They found that being exposed to platinum agents led to hundreds of mutations in genes (on average 2,200 per liver sample), a burden of mutation usually found in adult livers. In other words, platinum aged the liver cells of treated children, making them look more like adult liver cells.
Mutation load also increased proportionally to platinum exposure: children who received only cisplatin had a smaller number of mutations than those who received both cisplatin and carboplatin. These mutations could increase the likelihood of liver pathologies, or the emergence of secondary tumors, the authors said.
“We found lots of cancer genes but also genes associated with long-term changes in liver metabolism,” said Foad Rouhani, one of the authors of the paper and a professor at King’s College in London. However, he stressed that “by no means does that mean that these cells will definitely become cancerous in time. All we talk about is there was evidence for potential for these cells to eventually cause problems further down the line.”
Liver cells showed many more mutations than blood cells, even though chemotherapy is a systemic treatment. “The platinum is doing something differently to liver cells than other cells. Either it’s been metabolized differently or the liver cells are repairing differently, we don’t really know yet,” said Rouhani. This could mean that the liver was more susceptible to the effects of platinum, or it could be the other way around: The extent of the mutations may explain why that liver got sick in the first place.
In a perspective article, Sanjeev Vasudevan and Donald Williams Parsons, both professors at Baylor College of Medicine in Houston, wrote that the findings “provide strong evidence for conducting survivorship studies of children that have undergone treatment for liver cancer beyond their third decade of life.”
For the study authors, its primary contribution lies in establishing that the damage occurs, so clinicians can monitor these patients more closely during their lifetimes, said Rouhani, and identify issues at an earlier stage.
But there could be a prospective impact on treatment. “If we understand the mechanism, can we then eventually be able to design next-generation chemotherapies which are highly effective at treating the cancer but actually leave the background tissue largely untouched?” said Rouhani.

Mumbai Police on Sunday (September 13, 2026) denied Maratha reservation activist Manoj Jarange-Patil permission to hold an indefinite hunger strike at Azad Maidan from September 19, even as he alleged that there was a conspiracy to have him shot during his planned march to the capital city.
“There is a conspiracy to shoot me during the Mumbai march. They do not want to kill Marathas, but want to target me,” Mr. Jarange alleged while speaking at Antarwali Sarati in Jalna district as his hunger strike entered the 16th day.
“I will accept death, but I will not surrender,” he said. There is so far no independently verified evidence to substantiate the alleged assassination plot.
Mr. Jarange-Patil plans to continue the protest at Antarwali Sarati until September 15, when he and his supporters are scheduled to begin their march towards Mumbai. The mobilisation is intended to culminate in an indefinite hunger strike at Azad Maidan from September 19 as part of his renewed agitation for Maratha quota in jobs and education.
Why Mumbai Police has refused permission
However, Azad Maidan Police on Sunday (September 13, 2026) refused permission for the proposed indefinite protest.
Police cited restrictions governing demonstrations at Azad Maidan, including rules prohibiting indefinite hunger strikes, limits on the duration and size of gatherings and the possibility of traffic and public-order disruptions.
They also referred to problems during previous demonstrations, when movement around south Mumbai, including the CSMT area, was affected, and said the Ganeshotsav period would already place substantial demands on the city’s police force.
Reacting to the decision, Mr. Jarange-Patil questioned how the authorities could presume that protesters would violate conditions before the agitation had even begun. “Why do they think we are going to violate the rules even before the agitation begins? Under what law are you running the state?” he said.
He also questioned whether Ganeshotsav processions would be stopped on similar grounds and maintained that the agitation in Mumbai would proceed through peaceful and democratic means.
He also escalated his ongoing hunger strike on Sunday (September 13, 2026), announcing that he would stop taking water, saline and medical treatment. “From today, saline, water and treatment — everything is stopped,” Mr. Jarange-Patil said, as he hardened his position following the police refusal.
The police decision comes two days after the Bombay High Court declined to issue pre-emptive directions stopping Mr. Jarange-Patil’s proposed march to Mumbai.
A division bench of Chief Justice Mahesh Chandra Tripathi and Justice Advait M Sethna on Friday (September 11, 2026) refused to restrain the march merely on the basis of apprehensions that it could lead to law-and-order problems.
“Merely on the basis of an apprehension in a petition, we are not going to take such a call. State machinery is capable to handle all these situations,” the bench observed. The court also noted that the right to protest is protected in a democracy and expressed confidence that Mr. Jarange would act as a law-abiding citizen.
Referring to the court’s observations while reacting to the police decision, Mr. Jarange-Patil questioned why his movement was being stopped when the High Court itself had declined to prohibit the march.
Allegations of attempting to weaken agitation
Mr. Jarange-Patil also accused the State government of attempting to weaken the agitation and alleged that efforts were being made to create trouble during the Mumbai mobilisation. He claimed that people associated with ruling parties could be sent into the march to provoke violence and create a law-and-order situation. The allegations have not been independently established.
Despite those allegations, the activist has repeatedly instructed his supporters to keep the mobilisation peaceful and avoid stone-pelting, arson or other violence. He has said that if police barricades prevent protesters from advancing, supporters should sit peacefully at the spot rather than attempt to force their way through.
The renewed agitation centres on Mr. Jarange’s demand that eligible members of the Maratha community be issued Kunbi caste certificates based on historical and gazette records, allowing them to access reservation benefits available to Kunbis under the Other Backward Classes category.

Neena Gupta has spoken openly about raising her daughter Masaba Gupta as a single mother and the choices that shaped their lives. In a recent conversation with Zoom, Neena reflected on Masaba’s childhood and her experience of growing up without her father, former West Indies cricketer Vivian Richards, being present in her everyday life.
Neena Gupta says she apologised to Masaba Gupta for growing up without her father: “It is my fault”
Neena revealed that she has apologised to Masaba over the years for the circumstances of her upbringing. She acknowledged that some decisions made when she was younger had consequences that became clearer with time.
“I am so honest with her that many times I have said sorry to her that you didn't have a father with you when you were young. It is my fault, but she understands. We all make mistakes. When we are young, our parents tell us certain things and we don't listen. That wisdom comes later,” she said.
Neena also explained that she made a conscious effort to ensure Masaba learned about her father and their relationship directly from her. Rather than allowing her daughter to hear about the circumstances from others, she chose to have honest conversations with her as she grew older.
“I made her like her father. I told her why and what had happened as she grew up. So, there was no malice or anger towards me because I told her the truth. It is very important because, rather than her hearing something from outside, I thought it was better that I told her myself. I think that was a very sensible thing that I di,” she added.
Neena and Vivian Richards welcomed Masaba in 1989. In her autobiography Sach Kahun Toh, the actor had previously spoken about their relationship and the circumstances surrounding her pregnancy. "Vivian and I had an affair and I got pregnant. He had already returned home when I found out," she recalled.
She also remembered telling Richards about her pregnancy and asking whether he would object to her having his child. “I'm pregnant,” she told him. “Would you have a problem if I were to have your baby?" According to Neena, Richards told her to go ahead with the pregnancy.
The two continued their relationship for a few years despite often living apart. Neena later married chartered accountant Vivek Mehra in 2008. Masaba went on to establish herself in fashion before also entering acting. She married Satyadeep Misra in 2023, with both her parents present at the wedding.
On the work front, Neena was most recently seen in Netflix’s Chumbak, alongside Deven Bhojani, Arjun Bijlani, Sumeet Raghavan and others. The sitcom revolves around five multigenerational families living in row houses in the fictional Chumbak Colony. The series was created by Aatish Kapadia and Jamnadas “JD” Majethia.

MP woman kills husband with axe

Iran is set to unveil temporary Hormuz agreement to Gulf nations on Monday
Iran has indicated any deal will not amount to a full reopening of the waterway and it will still decide on which ships can cross the strait
Iran plans to formally unveil an agreement on a temporary shipping lane through the Strait of Hormuz on Monday, after a flurry of diplomatic activity including a rare meeting between senior officials from Tehran and Abu Dhabi.
The Islamic Republic is set to reveal to Gulf nations its agreement with Oman on a temporary new shipping lane, according to a person familiar with the matter.
Negotiations on details such as the fees ships may be charged will continue between the two countries later, they said, asking not to be identified when discussing private deliberations.
Talks between Tehran and Muscat over the waterway, a global chokepoint for energy exports, have progressed in recent weeks and the latter had been aiming to bring together foreign ministers from the Gulf Cooperation Council on Monday in Salalah, a southern Omani city.
Tehran has indicated any deal will not amount to a full reopening and it will still decide on which ships can cross the strait. Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi described the proposed meeting as an “important event” and a step towards building trust, in an interview with Al Araby Al Jadid newspaper.

International Oscar Submissions: Nepal, Singapore, Israel, Romania, South Korea, Chile and More Join the List
The campaigns for the Oscar for international feature film are gaining momentum, with final submissions due by Oct. 1. The Oscars shortlists will be revealed on Dec. 15, with 15 international films selected to be voted on by Academy members in all branches who commit to watch all 15 films. Oscar nominations will be revealed on Jan. 21.
This year’s entries include titles like Romania’s “Fjord,” which won the Palme d’Or at Cannes; Chile’s “The Meltdown,” which screened in Un Certain Regard; and Germany’s “Everytime,” which won Cannes’ Un Certain Regard prize.
France has not yet submitted a film, but faces several disparate choices.
Meanwhile, a new Academy rule allows any film that wins the top prize at one of the six biggest festivals — Cannes, Berlin, Venice, Sundance, Busan and Toronto — to be entered in the international feature race even without a national committee’s backing.

Beijing bans drone possession in the city after earlier moves to tighten rules
Beijing is tightening its drone ban to include possession within city limits
BEIJING -- Beijing is banning the possession of drones within city limits in new rules announced Sunday that further tighten its regulations on drones, which already include a May ban on sales of the devices. The ban on possession will come into effect in mid-November.
Beijing has barred unauthorized drone flights, citing security reasons, and has designated the city’s administrative area as restricted airspace.
The latest revised rules come after a fatal accident in late June when a small aircraft crashed into a Beijing skyscraper, killing the pilot and injuring 13 others.
Under regulations approved in March and which came into effect May 1, existing drone owners in Beijing had to register their devices with their real names and identities, but owners have been allowed to keep their registered drones under strict requirements.
However, according to the revised regulations approved this month, which will be effective from Nov. 15, the possession or storage of drones or key components within Beijing's city limits will also be banned. The revised rules were released Sunday by authorities.
Authorities can confiscate the drones of those who do not comply and can impose fines on individuals and companies.
Beijing authorities will be offering subsidies for existing drone owners to sell their devices at designated buyback locations, according to the state-owned newspaper Beijing Daily. Drone owners can also consider scrapping and recycling their drones with a small subsidy provided, or shipping them outside of Beijing before the new rules come into effect.
Drone users can still fly drones outdoors in other parts of the country, but real name registrations are required. Beijing, the Chinese capital, often has more stringent security rules than other parts of China.
Bringing drones into Beijing from outside the city, including by tourists, is already prohibited.

China’s intelligence chief warns of risks from AI as ‘new arena for strategic rivalry’
State data, business secrets and personal privacy are at stake, State Security Minister Chen Yixin warns as he calls for stronger safeguards
Chen underscored Beijing’s view of the technology as a key geopolitical battleground. AI has become “a new arena for strategic rivalry among major powers”, he wrote for China Cyberspace, a journal run by internet watchdog body the Cyberspace Administration of China.
The article was published on the journal’s social media account on Sunday.
Chen called for maintaining security boundaries while seizing new opportunities as he highlighted the risks of AI development.
AI could have a systemic impact on ideological security, he warned, including being “leveraged by hostile forces” to generate rumours and mass-produce harmful information.
The technology also posed serious risks to critical information infrastructure, Chen warned, arguing that advances marked by next-generation US-led models such as Anthropic’s Claude Mythos and OpenAI’s GPT-5.5-Cyber could significantly lower the technical threshold and costs of executing cyberattacks.

EXCLUSIVE: The Walsh Sisters are coming back. Irish pubcaster RTÉ has greenlit a Season 2, which the BBC will once again show in the UK. The new series, based on Marian Keyes’ novels, will stream on Stan in Australia.

Watch on Deadline

KSEB seeks nod to buy additional power at higher price amid Keralam power crisis
Kozhikode , The KSEB has decided to approach the state government seeking permission to procure additional power at higher prices to meet the rising demand amid a power shortage in the state, Electricity Minister Sunny Joseph said on Sunday.
Keralam has been experiencing power outages, particularly at night, amid a sharp rise in consumption and difficulties for the Kerala State Electricity Board in procuring additional electricity from other states.
"We are currently exploring all options to procure as much power as possible from central government institutions and other states. Even if it means buying at a higher price, permission should be granted by the state," Joseph told reporters here.
He said he would write to the chief minister seeking permission to purchase additional electricity at higher prices and a similar request would be made to the Kerala State Electricity Regulatory Commission.
KSEB board members will also visit other states and hold discussions with electricity department officials there to explore the possibility of arranging additional power supply to Keralam, he said.
"The CM has granted permission for it. I have spoken with the KSEB Chairman regarding this, and the board members are also ready," Joseph said, adding that he would not elaborate on the proposed visits at this stage.
Asked whether solar power could be an option, he said it was worth considering.
"We have solar production, but the mechanism to store and process it for nighttime use-like Battery Energy Storage Systems-has not become effective yet. We will think about ways to encourage and bring everyone into it. They need to be given incentives," he said.
He also said the state is prepared to purchase electricity generated by consumers for nighttime supply at a higher price.
"This period has brought difficulties that compel everyone to think. A new policy is needed-a policy aimed at increasing production," he said.
The minister also appealed to the public to avoid unnecessary electricity consumption and said the current situation required responsible use of available power.
He said former minister V M Sudheeran had drawn his attention to street lights remaining switched on during the day.
Joseph said street lighting was mostly managed by local self-government bodies and not directly by the KSEB.
He also urged people to reduce unnecessary decorative lighting at night.
"When a resource is scarce, if we understand our limits and use it carefully, there will be some change," he said.
The minister said the KSEB and state government should not be blamed for the present power shortage.
He also said the current crisis could have been avoided if the long-term power purchase agreement signed during the Oommen Chandy government had continued.
According to Joseph, the Electricity Regulatory Commission had decided to scrap the agreement, while the previous LDF government decided to challenge the decision only after six months, by which time the supplier had withdrawn from the agreement.

I cannot overstate the importance of having an air purifier that not only has enough power to actually purify a room's air but also caters to your home's particular needs. Pollutants like wildfire smoke, pollen, unventilated gas stoves, pet allergens, and even litter box odors can be potentially harmful additions to the air you breathe in your home.
Air purifiers from Coway have been a consistent top pick in our guide to the Best Air Purifiers for years, including the Coway Airmega Mighty2, which was released in March this year. Its predecessor, the Coway Airmega Mighty, had been our reigning “Best Affordable Air Purifier” for many years as well. I was excited to test the newest mid-size option built for medium to large rooms in Coway's Airmega line, where it sits between the compact Airmega 50 or 100 and the higher-capacity 350 or 450 models.
Released at the end of August, Coway’s Airmega Halo is an affordable, lightweight air purifier that aims to deliver whole-room air purification at an accessible price point. Plus, its focus is on promoting a healthier night's sleep with smart sleep features and quiet noise levels when in sleep mode.
Overall, it delivers on most of its promises, but I ran into some problems during field-testing that made me question its sensor, and I wish it had more transparency with pollutant levels.
Simple Design That’s Maybe Too Simple
The Halo is only 9.7 pounds, making it lightweight and portable as far as air purifiers go, but it doesn't have accessibility features like a top handle or wheels for easier moving. It has a small cutout in the back to grip, but because I have an upper-limb disability, moving it was awkward—I essentially had to hug the purifier to maneuver it, since I don't have large hands that can easily grip the inlet.
The purifier's cylindrical design with a 360-degree air-intake structure draws in polluted air from all sides, making for fewer spatial constraints and more options for placement around the home. The inside of the machine uses Coway's HyperVortex filtration system, which is an aerodynamic fan and duct design that Coway states is “inspired by eagle wings and golf ball dimples.” It uses wing blades to stabilize airflow, along with aerodynamic blades for powerful airflow for the generator fan and dimples to reduce air resistance for smoother air intake.
Setup was extremely easy—I just needed to unscrew the bottom, remove the filter from the plastic protective covering, screw the bottom back on, and plug it in. There's no need for a Wi-Fi connection, no app, and no remote. I started testing air purifiers earlier this year, and I've found I actually like having a connected remote, or better yet, an app that allows me to monitor air quality and adjust settings from afar. This model had neither. I also appreciate getting transparent numbers of pollutant levels directly from the machine rather than relying on colored lights, but this machine had the latter.

Pennsylvania says an unvaccinated woman has died from measles-related complications
An official in Pennsylvania has confirmed the measles-related death of a 40-year-old woman. Jefferson County Coroner Greg Furlong told NPR that the woman, who died on Saturday, was unvaccinated.
"This is a heartbreaking loss for the family and an unfortunate reminder that measles can be a serious and potentially life-threatening disease," a statement from the coroner's office said.
Officials have not released the woman's identity, but said she was a resident of Jefferson County. This is the third death that Pennsylvania state officials have linked to measles this year. No other states have announced measles deaths in 2026.
On Friday, the Pennsylvania Department of Health reported 676 measles cases so far this year. It also reported 52 new positive cases from Wednesday to Friday.
Pennsylvania officials and the federal government have clashed over the number of measles-associated deaths in the state in recent weeks, as the U.S. faces a nationwide resurgence of the illness. The Centers for Disease Control and Prevention declared that the highly contagious virus had been eradicated from the U.S. in 2000.
Last week, the CDC reported more than 3,200 confirmed measles cases in the country.
The agency said it was reviewing whether to count two measles-related deaths involving infants in Lancaster County, Pennsylvania. After Gov. Josh Shapiro announced the state's first two deaths, U.S. Department of Health and Human Services Secretary Robert F. Kennedy, Jr. said on X the announcement appeared to have been "premature" and "may even have been altogether fabricated by one of the Governor's hopeful staffers."
This clash is notable, as NPR's Rob Stein has reported. "The CDC usually defers to the state's determination" of cause of death in this kind of outbreak, "so the agency can alert the public, doctors and health officials around the country."
The CDC lists the number of measles cases reported in each state for 2026, as well as the number of hospitalizations. The agency has not listed the number of deaths for this year. Instead of giving a figure, there is an asterisk that explains: "The National Center for Health Statistics (NCHS) does not currently have any death records from 2026 that indicate measles is the underlying cause."
Kennedy has said on X that NCHS "will update as it receives and reviews submitted records."
The Jefferson County Coroner's Office also emphasized measles can lead to severe complications at any age.
"While cases of severe illness remain uncommon, this tragedy highlights that measles should not be taken lightly," said Chief Deputy Coroner and Public Relations Officer Jason Stiver in a statement. "Public health measures, early recognition of symptoms, and consultation with healthcare providers are important tools in protecting our community."
The county coroner's office is working with the Pennsylvania Department of Health on the case. Pennsylvania and South Carolina have the highest numbers of confirmed measles cases in the U.S., according to federal data.

Everything Trump Wants to Do Causes Inflation
Does he not understand, or does he just not care?
This is an edition of The Atlantic Daily, a newsletter that guides you through the biggest stories of the day, helps you discover new ideas, and recommends the best in culture. Sign up for it here.
Just call it the Five-Grand Old Party. This week, at the Republican Party’s midterm faux-convention, President Trump announced something called (inevitably) the “Trump Dividend.” The premise is simple. “If the Republicans win the House of Representatives and the United States Senate, both of them,” Trump said, “I will issue a dividend to every adult citizen in the United States of America for $5,000.”
Problems abound. First, this is wildly inappropriate, for obvious reasons: It’s an attempt at using taxpayer money to bribe voters into supporting the president’s party. Because Trump is not premising the supposed payout on individuals’ votes, it might be legal, though the White House would presumably require congressional approval for the estimated $1.3 trillion cost. A Republican Congress might sign off; a Democratic one might be more inclined to start impeachment proceedings.
Second, the payments almost certainly won’t happen. (If you disagree, I’d be happy to sell you a nice bridge in Brooklyn if you sign your Trump Dividend over to me.) Trump has promised to cut checks to Americans before and not followed through, and this proposal appeared to catch many of Trump’s advisers, as well as Republican lawmakers, by surprise. Florida Governor Ron DeSantis, Trump’s rival for the 2024 GOP nomination, quickly criticized the pledge.
Third, injecting more than $1 trillion into the economy wouldn’t just blow up the deficit and national debt—it would also drive up prices. Giving every American $5,000 to spend would create demand that couldn’t immediately be met, encouraging sellers to raise prices. I could quote lots of economists from left, right, and center who have already said that the payouts would be inflationary, but you could also just take it from Trump himself, who has repeatedly blamed inflation on high spending during the Biden administration—including in the same speech where he floated the dividend.
A paradox of this moment is that inflation is a big reason for Trump’s cratering approval and his party’s sinking odds in the midterm elections, but nearly every one of his signature policy ideas is inflationary. The basic challenge is not novel to this president—voters hate inflation, yet most anti-inflation measures the government can take will hurt the economy, which voters also hate. But Trump’s strategy seems to be to commit to new proposals that would drive up costs.
In some cases, inflation is incidental to the president’s goal. When Trump launched the war in Iran, he apparently believed that it would end quickly—and might even result in the United States gaining control over Iran’s huge oil reserves. Instead, the war is dragging on into its seventh month, with no end in sight. The de facto closure of the Strait of Hormuz, as well as attacks in the Bab el-Mandeb Strait, have strangled shipping of oil as well as other goods, driving prices higher. The average price of a gallon of diesel fuel in the U.S. topped $6 today for the first time, and because so many goods move via diesel trucks, the rise drives further inflation.
Trump’s efforts to crack down on immigration also have the collateral effect of pushing prices up. The administration has not only tried to secure borders and deport unauthorized immigrants; it has also revoked legal status from more than 1 million people who were permitted to live and work in the United States under Temporary Protected Status. Many of these people were employed in industries such as construction and health care that are difficult and low-paid; for example, more than 20,000 Haitians with TPS worked in caregiving last year. Housing shortages plague many parts of the country, and more building could alleviate them. Perhaps Americans will be willing to take these difficult jobs, but with unemployment rates already low, that will likely require higher salaries—which will mean higher costs, and therefore higher prices.
Other Trump policy ideas are directly and explicitly inflationary. For decades, Trump has espoused protectionism, saying that the United States should impose tariffs in order to close trade deficits with some partners. Regardless of the other merits of this plan (and they are dubious at best), tariffs are by definition inflationary. The goal is to raise prices on certain products. A tariff is a tax on goods, and someone has to pay it.
Faced with economic headwinds and voter dissatisfaction, Trump has at many times dismissed voter concerns, but he has also pressured the Federal Reserve to lower interest rates. Trump attempted to oust former Fed Chair Jerome Powell and the board member Lisa Cook, and made clear that he expects his newly appointed chair, Kevin Warsh, to lower rates. By law, the Fed is required to promote maximum employment and stable prices. (It aims for 2 percent inflation.) Trump wants lower interest rates because they encourage economic growth, but they drive inflation for the same reasons: Lower rates encourage borrowing, which produces spending, which has a similar effect on prices as sending every American adult a $5,000 check.
Writing off Trump’s pursuit of inflationary ideas as cynical is tempting, if only because so much of what he does is cynical, but years of evidence suggest that Trump actually has little idea how economics works, as the journalist Steve Benen recently noted. The president’s obsession with trade deficits is nonsensical; Senator Rand Paul memorably quipped that because he gives money to his grocer and gets food in return, he’s running a trade deficit with the supermarket. Last week, Trump perplexingly suggested that the United States could simply cut off commerce entirely: “We could do tremendous good for ourselves by just not trading with countries.”
Perhaps Trump doesn’t understand that his ideas will drive up prices. Perhaps he does, but concludes that dangling free money in front of voters is worth the hit. Either way, new numbers released today show that inflation rose 3.4 percent from one year ago. Trump’s policies are working.

Defense agencies of Mexico and the US have announced they are implementing a new collaborative strategy to combat drones used by criminal organizations. The operation, dubbed High Eagle, or Águila Alta, builds on recent tests of anti-drone technologies carried out along the border between the two countries.
The first phase of the strategy took place between August 31 and September 2 along the border between San Diego and Tijuana, Mexico. Initially, both military forces—simultaneously on the ground from their respective territories—tracked commercial drones used by criminal entities. In the second phase, the agencies neutralized the unmanned aerial vehicles, with support from fixed and mobile anti-drone systems. These activities began on September 7 and will continue through September 21.
The information released by Mexico’s Secretariat of National Defense, known as SEDENA, does not specify the kind of technology involved in the mission. However, US Northern Command has suggested that the operation might employ high-energy lasers. These extremely concentrated beams of light can—in various phases—detect, track, illuminate, damage, or destroy drones from a distance.
The US Army has invested in a particular laser system known as the Locust platform, which is designed for mounting on military vehicles. Authorities have had this technology at their disposal since September of last year, when the company that produces the system, AeroVironment, delivered the first two functional prototypes to the Armed Forces.
So far, it has not been confirmed that these systems are being used in Operation High Eagle, though the Mexican authorities have increased access to these state-of-the-art weapons. Last month, SEDENA and the US Department of Defense signed an agreement allowing the Mexican military to access the US Army’s digital marketplace for acquiring anti-drone systems at competitive prices.
Representatives from both countries have stated that the aim of this new operation and recent agreements is to strengthen efforts against organized crime, especially human and drug trafficking. Earlier this month, the US Northern Command announced it had disabled or destroyed approximately 300 drones linked to criminal activity this year, a third of which were taken down in August. Within recent weeks, 11 of the targets were involved with cartels.
The operation stems from the US-Mexico Bilateral Implementation Group. According to SEDENA, it aims to ensure security on both sides of the border, while respecting the national sovereignty of both nations and “prioritizing the interests of the Mexican State at all times.”
The US ambassador to Mexico, Ronald Johnson, stated that the agreement would strengthen both countries’ ability to combat cartels and address bilateral security challenges.

The Eiffel Tower has reopened after a one-day strike was called in response to the landmark’s management ordering female staff to keep out of sight at the request of a visiting religious group.
City Hall, which operates the Paris landmark, has apologised for breaching France’s republican principle of equality and ordered a full inquiry.
Workers at the tower walked out on Monday, closing the landmark to visitors, after female colleagues were sidelined and replaced during a visit organised by a Hindu religious group at the weekend.
In a statement, staff said they objected to “professional instructions that led to female employees being sidelined, replaced and made invisible because of their sex” during the visit.
“Some were asked to leave their posts and wait in separate rooms. In some posts, women were replaced by men. All female employees were instructed not to pass through or enter certain areas while the [Hindu] delegation was present,” they said in a statement.
Employees said they were shocked to find themselves in a situation that was “deeply contrary to the values of equality and nondiscrimination”.
“The Eiffel Tower is the symbol of France. We believe it must also be exemplary in the values it promotes and the way it treats staff,” the statement said.
The Bochasanwasi Akshar Purushottam Swaminarayan Sanstha (BAPS) spiritual movement, whose members made the request in advance of a visit on Saturday, apologised.
“To our knowledge, nobody was refused access to the Eiffel Tower at any moment. Nevertheless, We offer our sincere apologies to anyone who may have been hurt or offended by this situation,” it wrote in a statement.
BAPS is close to India’s ruling Hindu nationalist party, Bharatiya Janata, and was in France to consecrate its first major temple in the country on Sunday.
The public-owned Eiffel Tower operating company (SETE) acknowledged that BAPS had requested that “interactions with women” be limited, and said it should not have accepted these conditions. “They are not in keeping with SETE’s values or the principles of equality between women and men and the neutrality that must guide the organisation of visits to the monument,” it said.
Emmanuel Grégoire, the mayor of Paris, has promised an investigation to “get to the bottom of this as soon as possible”.
He said moving female staff out of sight was unacceptable.
“These are not my values nor those the Eiffel Tower must represent,” he wrote on X.
Ariel Weil, mayor of the Paris Centre district and president of SETE, said he was unaware of the “shocking and unacceptable” conditions afforded the visiting group.
“I confirm again the Eiffel Tower’s commitment to republican values and gender equality,” he said.

Eye donation is said to be one of the most meaningful forms of donation, as a single donor can potentially restore sight to two individuals through corneal transplantation. India has made considerable progress in eye banking; the country currently has 396 functional eye banks, and corneal collections increased from 62,370 in 2022–23 to 69,848 in 2024–25. However, the need for donor tissue substantially exceeds its availability. There are approximately 2 million corneally blind people in our country, but only 40,000 corneal transplants performed per year.
Role of stakeholders
The government has a crucial role in strengthening the eye donation ecosystem through the National Programme for Control of Blindness and Visual Impairment (NPCBVI). Government support includes funding for eye bank infrastructure and equipment, training of ophthalmologists and eye bank technicians, promotion of eye donation, and provision of corneal storage media. Government hospitals can further improve donation rates by establishing Hospital Cornea Retrieval Programmes (HCRP) and integrating eye donation into routine end-of-life counselling.
Non-governmental organisations and service organisations have an equally important role in creating awareness, dispelling myths, encouraging pledges and, most importantly, counselling families at the time of death. Organisations such as eye bank networks, Lions Clubs and other community-based groups can take the message of eye donation to schools, colleges, workplaces and rural communities.
Private eye hospitals and institutions can complement these efforts by establishing or strengthening eye banks, developing efficient corneal retrieval networks, maintaining high standards of tissue evaluation and preservation, and providing advanced corneal transplantation. Recent initiatives such as the expansion of the National Eye Bank at AIIMS, Delhi through partnerships with additional hospitals demonstrate the value of collaborative retrieval networks.
Building strong PPPs
Ultimately, the future of eye donation in India lies in a strong public–private–NGO partnership. Awareness must translate into timely family consent, consent into retrieval, and retrieved tissue into high-quality transplantation. Strengthening this entire chain will be essential to bring down the burden of corneal blindness and make the gift of sight a reality for many more Indians.
The goal is clear: to transform the gift of eye donation into the gift of sight. Every donated cornea carries a legacy of compassion—allowing one person’s life to bring light into another’s.
(Dr. Mohan Rajan is chairman and medical director and Dr. Sujatha Mohan is executive medical director, of Rajan Eye Care Hospital. drmohanrajan@gmail.com)

Editor’s note: After more than a decade, this is the last WIRED Security News This Week. “The roundup,” as we call it internally, started as a way to ensure that our readers knew about the latest key cybersecurity and privacy news even if we didn’t write about it ourselves. It was a simple way to highlight our own work and the wealth of other great journalism and research published in this realm every week.
Over the years, the roundup has developed a devoted following, and some editions have even become viral hits—which is honestly weird, but the cybersecurity community is great and weird, so it feels right. Rest assured that something new and exciting is coming in the roundup’s place, so stay tuned for that! For now, as always, stay safe out there.
Meta failed to catch roughly 350 AI child abuse ads, according to new research this week, including some that included images of real kids. In one case, a child depicted in an ad was a member of a European royal family. Lawmakers have said they intend to investigate, and the San Francisco City Attorney’s Office ordered the company this week to stop “allowing” AI child abuse ads.
In other Meta news, the company announced a new personal AI agent this week that can book your plane tickets or sell your car, but it emphasized heavy investment in security and privacy features, seemingly anticipating mistrust from consumers. In this vein, the company was hit with a proposed class action lawsuit this week over alleged illegal harvesting of Facebook and Instagram photos for training AI and face-recognition systems.
Clearview AI is testing a previously unreported prototype AI tool known as InquiryIQ that would help law enforcement find a target’s associates, social media accounts, and other personal information. And Apple announced a set of new “audio intelligence” features for its Apple Watch Series 12 and Ultra 4 devices this week that involve processing audio in a user’s environment. The company extensively emphasized the security and privacy protections built into the features, perhaps anticipating that they could come across as, well, creepy.
The US and Mexico have a new joint operation to detect, track, and take down drones at the border using laser tech. And there’s a new GTA V mod that lets you make (in-game) money destroying (in-game) Flock license plate recognition cameras.
But wait, there’s more! Here’s the security and privacy news we didn’t cover in depth ourselves this week. Click the headlines to read the full stories.
From State-Sponsored Hacking to Bioweapons, Claude Abuse Is Simply Everywhere
Anthropic has been perhaps more vocal than any other AI company about the ways in which its tools are prone to misuse. It published some of the first reports of its AI service Claude being used in cybercriminal hacking operations and the discovery that its AI agents had, like those of its competitor OpenAI, escaped their sandbox and autonomously breached the networks of several organizations as part of their attempts to fulfill their users’ commands.
This week, the company released a new overarching report on how Claude has been abused over the last eight months, and the results are staggering in their breadth—if, perhaps, inevitable in a world where AI is simply used as a productivity shortcut for just about everything. In case study after case study, the company documents how Claude was exploited for state-sponsored and cybercriminal hacking, disinformation campaigns and influence operations, and even attempted development of bioweapons. In all of these cases, Anthropic says that it disrupted the activity in progress.
In one case, a group of Russian state-sponsored hackers identified by Microsoft as Midnight Blizzard used Claude for reconnaissance, breaching targets that included Ukrainian and other European government networks, and stole data and maintained access. Cybercriminal group ShinyHunters used Claude in practically every stage of its hacking and extortion campaigns. Disinformation campaigns focusing on politics everywhere from Kenya to Bangladesh used the tool. And perhaps most disturbingly, in a handful of cases, Anthropic discovered what appeared to be users of its tools attempting to develop potential bioweapons like disease pathogens and toxins.
While Anthropic touts its success in the report in heading off these threats—while implicitly humblebragging at the power of its tools—the effect of the case studies is more unnerving than reassuring. After all, there’s no guarantee Anthropic has spotted every malevolent use of its AI. Factor in its competitors and less safeguarded open-source AI tools, and the report reads like less of a victory lap for AI’s guardrails than a preview of AI-enabled chaos to come.
US Feds Disrupt Xinbi Guarantee, the Internet’s Biggest Black Market
Xinbi Guarantee, over its four-year lifespan, grew into the biggest illicit marketplace on the internet. It carried out an estimated $30 billion–plus in sales, most of which took the form of money laundering for “pig butchering” crypto scam operations—largely based in Southeast Asia—but which also included sex trafficking and harassment for hire. All of it thrived on the Telegram messaging service, which shut down Xinbi a year ago only for it to rebuild and eventually grow larger than ever. This week, finally, the US government stepped in to do what Telegram did not, seizing the Xinbi’s channels on Telegram’s platform and sanctioning the market. The Justice Department simultaneously announced raids on 13 scam compounds in Madagascar—a sign that Western law enforcement is beginning to take seriously the epidemic of forced labor crypto scamming, but also evidence of how widely the operations have spread.
Conti Ransomware Gang Member Sentenced to 4 Years in Prison
The ransomware gang Conti was, until it officially disbanded in 2022, one of the most dangerous hacker crews in the world. According to US law enforcement, it hit more than a thousand victims, extorting millions and at one point disrupting government systems in Costa Rica so completely that it triggered a state of emergency. Now one member of that group is facing justice: 44-year-old Ukrainian Oleksii Oleksiyovych Lytvynenko was sentenced to four years in prison this week, in a rare example of a ransomware actor who will see the inside of a US prison.
Meta Left AI-Generated Child Abuse Videos Online After Reporters Flagged Them
Facebook is hosting a large network of accounts uploading AI-generated videos that depict violence against children, according to Futurism, which spent days cataloging the material and kept finding more than it could count. The clips show young children being beaten, burned, confined, and starved. Many attract thousands of reactions from users who appear to think the footage is real. Futurism said it found most of the accounts by opening one and then following Facebook’s recommendation feed, which supplied a continuous stream of similar videos—a sign Meta’s own systems can already identify the category of content the company says it bans.
Futurism reported eight of the accounts through the standard user channel. Meta removed two, one of them after first rejecting the report. Several decisions took more than a week. The company deleted most of the videos sent to its press office, but initially left others up, including one showing a child locked in a freezer.
In addition to blanket bans on child sexual abuse material, Meta’s written policy bars depictions of nonsexual child abuse whether real or synthetic, with exceptions for art, cartoons, movies, and games. It does not say whether AI-generated video falls under those exceptions. In a statement, Meta told the reporters that some flagged links did not break its rules and asked them not to write otherwise.

Hindi's progress meaningful only with respect for all Indian languages: Amit Shah
On Hindi Diwas, Home Minister Amit Shah said Hindi should advance while protecting all Indian languages. He said linguistic diversity strengthens India's unity and cultural memory.
Home Minister Amit Shah on Monday said the progress of Hindi is meaningful only when it moves forward while ensuring the dignity, promotion and protection of other Indian languages. Greeting people on Hindi Diwas, he said India’s linguistic diversity is one of its biggest strengths and not a weakness.
Shah said every Indian language carries its own history, folk traditions and way of looking at life, and helps shape the values of the younger generation. He also said Hindi has played an important role in connecting different sections and communities across the country as a language of dialogue, bond and coordination.
In his message, Shah said, "Everyone says that our languages are diverse. That is our weakness. But I believe that our greatest strength is that we have so many languages." He said every language contributes to the country’s cultural richness.
He added, "Our linguistic diversity strengthens the sense of unity in diversity in India."
Shah also said a language is not merely a medium of communication but the "memory" and "self-awareness" of a society.
He said Hindi should not be seen as representing any one language, but as an important link among India’s languages and national unity. "The progress of Hindi is only purposeful when it moves forward while ensuring the dignity, promotion and protection of other Indian languages," Shah said.
He added that while his own mother tongue is Gujarati, Hindi allows him to connect directly with people in different parts of the country.
Hindi Diwas is observed every year on September 14 to mark the adoption of Hindi as an official language by the Constituent Assembly on September 14, 1949.
Shah also urged the youth to learn as much as possible from the world without giving up their language, and appealed to parents to speak to their children in their mother tongue.
"Language is what connects us to our mother, our soil, our history and our culture," he said, underlining his message that the growth of Hindi must go hand in hand with respect for all Indian languages.

Vladimir Putin has arrived in India’s capital of Delhi ahead of an 11-member Brics summit set to be dominated by wars in the Middle East and Ukraine, as well as economic challenges.
The Russian president and his Iranian counterpart, Masoud Pezeshkian, were due to hold talks with India’s prime minister, Narendra Modi, while Chinese leader Xi Jinping was also expected to attend the two-day meeting.
Putin arrived at Palam air force Station in Delhi, where he was greeted by India’s minister of state for external affairs, Kirti Vardhan Singh, according to footage broadcast by Russia’s Ria Novosti news agency.
The summit will mark Xi’s first visit to India since 2019 and is seen as the biggest step yet in a cautious thaw between the rival neighbours, six years after a deadly military clash along their disputed Himalayan border.
Ties between the nuclear-armed Asian giants have been warming again recently, with flights, visas and high-level contacts gradually being restored.
However, deep mistrust remains, with their contested frontier, a widening trade deficit and strategic rivalry still complicating ties.
On Friday posters of a beaming Modi lined streets in Delhi, along with heavy deployments of security forces across the capital and widespread traffic restrictions in central districts. Delhi police have urged people to be patient and cooperative.
Brics was created in 2009 as a forum for major emerging economies seeking greater influence in institutions dominated by western powers.
It has since expanded and now includes Iran, Saudi Arabia and the United Arab Emirates, three countries with sharply differing positions on the war launched by the US and Israel in February.
“The Gulf conflict is going to be the central fault line this time during the Brics summit,” said Harsh V Pant of India’s Observer Research Foundation. “What was seen until last year as an achievement – the expansion of Brics – today looks like a big constraint on Brics”.
It will be Pezeshkian’s first visit to India as Iranian president, and will put the Middle East conflict firmly on the agenda.
“The war in Iran will provide a stern test of the [expanded] group’s cohesion,” said Shilan Shah of Capital Economics, noting the failure of the Brics foreign ministers to agree on a joint statement when they met in Delhi in May.
India maintains cordial relations with Iran and Israel, but is also careful to strike a delicate balance in its ties with Washington.
India has navigated the energy crisis caused by the Iran war in part by turning to Russia, one of its most important strategic partners and its most controversial fuel supplier in recent years as the war against Ukraine drags on.
Putin last visited India in December 2025 but he also met Modi in Bishkek, the capital of Kyrgyzstan, this month.
India’s foreign minister, Subrahmanyam Jaishankar, visited Kyiv this month, when the Ukrainian president, Volodymyr Zelenskyy, said he was “grateful to India for its commitment to ending this unjust war”.

Don't file petition in air: HC raps lawyer over claim people trapped in PG debris
The Delhi High Court declined to urgently hear a plea against demolition besides the collapsed five-storey Satya Niketan hostel, which killed seven people.
The Delhi High Court on Monday refused to urgently list a plea over the Municipal Corporation of Delhi's decision to demolish the building next to the five-storey Satya Niketan PG that collapsed last week. A lawyer told the court that the demolition was being carried out without clearing debris from the hostel's basement and that some people might still be trapped.
A bench of Chief Justice DK Upadhyaya and Justice Tejas Karia questioned the basis of the claim and said the authorities would have carried out an assessment before ordering the demolition. The court said the plea would be listed in due course and declined to take it up urgently.
When the matter was mentioned for an urgent hearing, the lawyer said the authorities had gone ahead with the demolition without removing debris from the basement of the collapsed hostel. The lawyer told the court that some people could still be trapped there.
The bench, however, asked what material was available to support that submission.
“What's the source of information that there are persons below the debris? How do you know? They must have conducted some type of technical audit before deciding to demolish the adjoining building. It's all your guesswork that there might be some people. You should have some basis for making such submissions,” the court told the lawyer.
The bench added that the plea would come up on its normal course. “What's so urgent? You should not file the petition just in air. What is the technical information available to you?” it said.
The Satya Niketan building, which housed a boys' paying-guest accommodation near Delhi University's South Campus, collapsed on September 6 while repair work was underway. On September 7, the High Court ordered a high-level MCD inquiry into the collapse, which left seven people dead, and said the government could not evade responsibility.
The court had said the incident was not only unfortunate but also raised deep concern over inadequate housing facilities, including hostels run by Delhi University or the government, the safety and security of students, and the inadequate measures used by the MCD and other authorities to regulate such paying-guest facilities.
On September 8, the civic body began a controlled demolition of the adjoining building after declaring it dangerous. The building housed a girls' paying-guest accommodation and had been evacuated after the collapse of the neighbouring five-storey structure.
