Critics celebrate Céline Dion's 'high-stakes' comeback show in Paris
- Published
Iconic Canadian pop singer Céline Dion has kicked off her long-awaited comeback show in Paris on Saturday, after a six-year hiatus due to health issues.
The 58-year-old superstar was diagnosed with a rare neurological disorder called stiff person syndrome in 2022, which forced her to pull back from touring.
Dion, one of the best-selling musical artists of all time, has not performed a full show since a 2020 concert in New Jersey - the last before the Covid pandemic cut her tour short. In 2024, she performed just one song at the Paris Olympics closing ceremony.
Saturday marked the first of Dion's 26-show residency at the Paris La Défense Arena, Europe's largest covered concert arena.
"I made a promise," she told the Paris audience of about 30,000 people in her emotional return.
"I made a promise to come back, to be back on stage. And here I am. Singing for you, and singing for me," she said.
"I am everything I am because you loved me," she told the crowd.
She also broke down in tears after finishing a song, telling the audience: "I had promised myself not to cry."
"But I'm so happy to see you all. I missed you."
They weren't the only tears of the night, as the star appeared to be overcome with emotion several times.
Dion will be performing in Paris throughout September and October and into the New Year.
The Mirror's Lucy Needham, external noted that the singer was 50 minutes late to start, and may have needed extra time to "compose herself" for the "emotionally charged return".
"Eyes-brimming, the veteran singer gave herself little nods of approval after every line, before finally breaking down at the end of the track, seemingly overwhelmed at having made it through."
After beginning her set in a black gown, she later changed into a trouser suit "to show off some of those signature kooky dance moves," says Needham, adding that she appeared "to be having the time of her life, gyrating and slapping her thighs with glee".
The night was a "a tense, tearful, joyous affair probably even more so for the singer than for her loyal audience," writes The Telegraph's Neil McCormick, external.
She started out slow, he says. "Her voice sounded fragile and exposed, but at least it was her distinctive voice, not some autotuned approximation."
"At first, she was clearly struggling to hold herself together," he continues. "Her vocals wobbled dangerously, as if about to crack or collapse. But she was gaining confidence with every moment back on stage."
She broke down in tears as the audience roared in approval after the first song, and addressed the crowd in both French and English during the set.
"This was a high-stakes, high-wire return, perhaps the riskiest comeback in the history of showbusiness," McCormick continues, referring to her health condition.
But he concludes: "I honestly think I prefer this less superhuman Céline. Her voice is still great, but a bit more raw and real, with a rougher tone, less smoothness in the runs and more edge to her whoops and shrieks."
Sarah Leavitt, reporting from Paris for the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation (CBC), external, said the crowd "was left without words" by the stunning performance.
She noted that she didn't want to cry, but "of course she cried right away."
Dion also "endeared herself" to the crowd by saying during one song that she wanted to stop and start over.
Will Hodgkinson at the Times of London, external writes in his review, "miraculously, her art will go on," that the performance was "overwhelming".
She "looked suitably humbled and tearful" as she emerged, he said, going on to praise the stage direction.
"Truly, she was throwing the love at the crowd, who threw it right back at her. There was no holding back. It was quite overwhelming, actually," he writes.
The performance was "complete with both costume, key change and air of tragic, important romance".
"Céline Dion's strength lies in being a diva with the common touch while being as French as they get, even if she is Canadian. She fulfilled that role with all the verve you could hope for," writes Hodgkinson.
"The concert had a spiritual feel, with visual interludes steeped in biblical imagery alluding to a pilgrimage," Elsa Keslassy writes for Variety., external
In video clips, Dion is seen wandering in a desert. "The set design was highly cinematic, with a monumental staircase sweeping up one side and a moon dominating the stage, while the backdrop appeared to have a stark, almost brutalist gray texture."
The star, known for power ballads like My Heart Will Go On and Because You Loved Me, has said she will not let her diagnosis control her life.
"The way I see it, I have two choices. Either I train like an athlete and work super hard, or I switch off and it's over," she told French Vogue magazine, external in 2024.
"I've chosen to work with all my body and soul, from head to toe, with a medical team."
When Dion announced the first leg of her Paris residency back in March, nine million fans signed up for early access tickets to the concerts, French outlet FRI reported.
The shows sold out so fast that her management company soon announced an additional 10 shows scheduled for May 2027, which have also since sold out.
Fans who were unable to snag tickets to one of the highly anticipated shows have not been left out entirely - events honouring Dion's comeback have dominated Paris in recent weeks.
Céline Dion tribute boat cruises on Seine - complete with costume contests, sing-alongs, DJ sets, are happening throughout September.
Ahead of Saturday's show, fans gathered outside Dion's Paris hotel, LeRoyal Monceau, as early as 06:00 local time to catch a glimpse of the star.
Paris City Hall organised a massive karaoke event on Friday night, attended by thousands, to celebrate Dion's return to the stage.
"I couldn't get tickets to the concert. I'm still keeping my fingers crossed and hoping, but I thought to myself: at least I can share a moment here with all the fans," Rania, a participant at the event, told Reuters.
Earlier this week, thousands of fans also gathered at a historic theatre in central Paris for two nights of karaoke and activities inspired by Dion's music.
And Paris venues and night clubs are hosting Dion-themed events around the city on Saturday night for fans who couldn't get tickets to the actual show.

It wasn’t that long ago that ClickFix attacks were exotic. Now the technique has become mainstream as attackers reap its simplicity and effectiveness in infecting users of PCs and Macs alike. All that’s required is a compromised website—a painless enough task—a fake CAPTCHA overlay, and the inclusion of a single terminal command. So many visitors get suckered into pasting and running the command that just about every malware pusher has adopted the technique. Even Kremlin-backed hacking groups are joining in.
“Reddit is becoming post after post after post of people getting their computer infected via ClickFix,” independent researcher Kevin Beaumont observed Thursday. “Legit websites everywhere [are] getting hacked to serve the fake captcha prompts.”
How many of us make things worse
More seasoned Internet users—a fair number who read this site—are quick to dismiss the attack. They typically blame the people who fall for the scams and marvel at their gullibility and lack of attention. The reality is that for more casual users, using computers and the Internet has become so difficult—think impossible-to-close interstitials, CAPTCHAs with an endless series of pictures to analyze, and constantly changing interfaces that bury the features they’re looking for—that they have grown desensitized to instructions that seem ridiculous and burdensome.
ClickFix attackers are capitalizing on this fatigue. Typically, attacks begin with a simple CAPTCHA image, often masquerading as one from Cloudflare. After engaging with the box, the user sees a line of text, often obscured in a way to mask any malicious commands. Then the user is instructed to copy the text and paste it into the Windows Run, PowerShell, or macOS terminal and click Enter.
The instructions come from websites people have used for years. The directions seem no more suspicious than things they’ve been required to do for a decade. Why would someone without a firm grasp of computer security have any reason to hesitate?

Giotto's famed fresco cycle depicting St. Francis of Assisi restored in Florence
A cycle of frescoes by Italian 14th-century master Giotto, depicting key moments in the life of St. Francis of Assisi, has been unveiled after a four-year restoration
FLORENCE, Italy -- A cycle of frescoes by Italian 14th-century master Giotto, depicting key moments in the life of St. Francis of Assisi, has been unveiled after a four-year restoration.
The newly vibrant “Stories of St. Francis” were shown to the public last week in the Basilica of Santa Croce, just in time for the 800th anniversary of the saint’s death on Oct. 4.
Giotto, who died in Florence in 1337, is considered by many to be the greatest Italian painter of his time and is considered the father of European painting. His artistic innovations informed the Renaissance style that developed after he died.
Painted between 1317-1325 and adorning a side chapel in the basilica, the St. Francis frescos have regained their richness following the restoration and offer new insights into Giotto’s revolutionary techniques and style, restorers said.
Emanuela Daffra, superintendent of the Opificio delle Pietre Dure, said the restoration removed layers of film and subsequent additions to the frescoes that had obscured Giotto’s original vision and now show his “profound capacity for expression.”
“Today, we can clearly interpret the gazes,” of the various figures in the scenes, she said. “He knew how to orchestrate them within spaces that emphasized the meaning of the scenes,” with a high degree of detail.
The frescoes had been covered by several layers of lime whitewash that had been applied in the 18th century, a common fate for frescoes considered outdated at the time. In 1851, while preparations were underway for a new decoration of the chapel, some of the whitewash was removed, but the process also damaged the works. The frescoes underwent further interventions in the 1950s, before the latest restoration began in 2022.
The restoration project consolidated the most fragile parts of the cycle, reduced signs of deterioration, removed deposits and altered materials, and replaced much of the old synthetic grouting from previous restorations with mixtures more compatible with the original plasterwork, restorers said.
During the project, restorers used an innovative no-touch device for ground-penetrating radar analysis of the works, thermal imaging cameras and a laser scanner, used to create a 3D model of the chapel.
The Basilica of Santa Croce is one of the largest Franciscan churches in the world and houses the tombs of Michelangelo, Galileo and Machiavelli.
The frescoes cover some 180 square meters (nearly 2,000 square feet) within the Bardi Chapel, to the right of the central altar, and recount seven key episodes in the life of Francis.
Among them are scenes depicting Francis’ renunciation of worldly goods, the approval of the Franciscan Rule, and the trial by fire, in which Francis offers to walk through fire to convert the Sultan of Egypt.
The Bardi family – among the wealthiest and most powerful bankers in Europe – acquired the patronage of the chapel and commissioned Giotto to paint its frescoes.
Today, that tradition of patronage has evolved into a collective effort to fund the restoration. Some 250 private donors contributed 700,000 euros toward the total restoration cost of 1.3 million euros, according to the Opera di Santa Croce, the organization that cares for and manages the basilica.

NASA has released a document that provides some initial details about the proposed United States Space Academy, and it’s clear that the space agency wants to move quickly in establishing the institution.
According to the document’s timeline, NASA seeks a groundbreaking for a permanent campus no later than next year, the first class to be enrolled and begin studies in temporary facilities in 2028, and a transition to a permanent campus in 2031.
What will that campus look like?
NASA is seeking a permanent site with at least 300 acres for the Space Academy, which aims to “prepare a new generation of leaders to explore, build, operate, secure, and defend the space domain.” Proximity to NASA facilities or university campuses could be a plus. The campus will initially support 1,200 undergraduates, with the potential to expand to up to 4,000 students.
Let the bidding begin
The document is called a “Request for Information,” and it essentially kicks off the bidding process among US states to house the Space Academy. This is expected to be a hot competition, with states such as Texas, Florida, and Alabama expected to put forth attractive bids to the federal government.
All 50 states are invited to submit a single response, specifying their contributions such as land, infrastructure, funding, and more. Respondents are also asked to provide a “rough-order-of-magnitude” estimate of the cost to establish and operate the Space Academy at their proposed locations. Submissions are due back to NASA by October 26.
The 14-page document sets up a competition that may look something like a major corporate relocation, with states pitching packages of free land, university partnerships, state funding, and more to lure the federal government to choose their state.

An enemy that swarmed the battlefield in large groups while under fire, seemingly oblivious to the dangers of drones and fire from automatic weapons. An elite corps of ghost soldiers who chose suicide over surrender. They fought and died in their thousands, then apparently vanished from the battlefield.
North Korea's soldiers were sent to fight by Pyongyang alongside Russian forces as they sought to repel a Ukrainian offensive on Moscow's territory at the end of 2024. They paid a heavy price, as many as 3,000 killed in action from the 13,000 deployed.
Ultimately, they would adapt their tactics, and with Russia would drive Ukrainian forces from its Kursk region. In combat terms, little has been heard of them since, but according to Ukraine's president, Volodymyr Zelensky, North Korean forces, and their weaponry, are soon to make a dramatic return to Russia's war in Ukraine.
Last month, Zelensky warned that up to 50,000 North Koreans will be deployed in Russia, revising an earlier estimate of 30,000 troops. He called on South Korea to provide support for his country's air defence.
But why, after such heavy losses, would North Korea send more men to fight for Russia, and what happened to its soldiers sent in the first place?
"They're still there", said Dr Yang Uk, research fellow at the Asan Institute for Policy Studies, Center for Foreign Policy and National Security in Seoul. "They are defending Russian territory for another counterattack from Ukraine. And we believe that some of the engineer corps or workers might be in [the Russian-occupied] Donbas area but that's not the combat troops."
The Main Intelligence Directorate of Ukraine's Ministry of Defense, HUR, estimates that 8,500 North Korean servicemen are still on Russian territory. They are organised into four brigades, which operate as part of the "North" Group of Forces and are assigned to protecting the state border of the Russian Federation in the Kursk Region from Ukrainian incursions.
"They do not participate in active combat operations. Units of the Korean People's Army have not been observed in the temporarily occupied territories of Ukraine," HUR said in a statement to the BBC.
A first for North Korea
For North Korea's leader, Kim Jong Un, the Kursk deployment was a gamble, its largest combat force ever sent overseas. (In 1973, North Korea sent 1,500 military personnel and instructors to Egypt during the Yom Kippur war with Israel, and in the late 1960s, an estimated 87 North Korean pilots fought for the North Vietnamese against US forces).
And despite the bloodshed, it was a gamble that paid off, reaping countless benefits for the isolated and impoverished country, transforming both its economic and military fortunes. And one that could serve as a blueprint for even deeper military cooperation.
North Koreans, "now know what modern combat is about", said Yang.
The soldiers sent to fight in Russia were from Storm Corps, the elite of the North Korean armed forces. Extremely isolated, totalitarian North Korea is a militarised and heavily indoctrinated state.
At first, neither Russia, nor North Korea, even acknowledged their presence. Ukrainian forces first clashed with them in November 2024, and the first live North Korean prisoners of war wouldn't be captured until January of the following year.
It wasn't until April 2025 that Russia first acknowledged their role, when Valery Gerasimov, chief of the General Staff of the Russian Armed Forces, described their "heroism" on the battlefield.
Yang continued, "North Korean soldiers are very brave I mean, especially those of Storm Corps. They are willing to die for their country. But the problem is that passion doesn't mean efficient combat skills... [They suffered] a lot of bloodshed in the early stage of the Kursk campaign, but they learned the lessons of modern drone warfare."
"Cannon fodder", is how "Sultan", a soldier with Ukraine's 95th Air Assault Brigade described North Korean troops. He faced them in the battle for Kursk at the end of 2024.
"They would begin with one large assault group, then another 15–20 men would be sent into the same position, and then more after that. The North Koreans operated differently. They kept moving all the time. That gave them a certain advantage, but not a decisive one," he recalled recently in Kyiv.
Communication between them and their Russian allies appeared poor, he said, and their soldiers were inadequately equipped.
After combat, Sultan and his men would search enemy corpses for documents and intelligence information. On the Russian dead they would find personal belongings, identification and equipment. "But when we searched the North Koreans specifically, the only thing we found on them was simply ammo. We checked absolutely all the small pockets - there were no documents, nothing at all," he explained.
Other Ukrainian soldiers reported the North Koreans lacked body armour, winter clothing and helmets.
In one chilling video from a Ukrainian assault, a wounded North Korean soldier lies prone on the snow-covered ground in a wooded area. As the Ukrainians approach, he detonates a grenade under his chin, after calling out, with his last words, the name of his leader, Kim Jong Un.
In April 2025, at a memorial service in Pyongyang at the newly created Museum of Foreign Military Operations, Kim praised heroes who choose suicide over capture.
In a speech to relatives, with Russia's Defence Minister Andrey Belousov in attendance, he said they were "heroes who unhesitatingly opted for self-blasting, suicide attack, in order to defend the great honour".
While North Korea has never officially acknowledged the death toll from the Kursk operation, a BBC Korea analysis of the memorial site estimated that 2,300 soldiers were killed fighting for Russia.
Ukraine's intelligence arm, HUR, puts the figure at 3,000 killed and 1,500 injured.
But aside from the combat experience, why did North Korea sacrifice so many of its best troops in a foreign war?
An economic windfall
The deployment has been a much-needed economic windfall for the country and a geopolitical win, according to Lim Soo-ho, a senior research fellow at the Institute for National Security Strategy, in Seoul.
He estimates that arms sales to Russia and the troop deployment have netted the impoverished country close to $10bn.
"North Korea's annual GDP is estimated at around $30bn (£22bn)," he told me. "That means they earned a third of a year's GDP over two and a half years through weapons exports and troop deployment, which, for an economy as small as North Korea's, is a very significant effect."
In exchange for its manpower, North Korea gets food, oil and hard currency. While China says it complies with sanctions against Pyongyang, Russia does not.
But equally important, the cooperation with Russia has shifted North Korea's long-term dependency on China.
So in Beijing in September last year, Kim Jong Un was able to stand shoulder to shoulder with China's leader Xi Jinping and Russian President Vladimir Putin, in the first public meeting of all three. Not quite as an equal, but no longer reliant on China alone.
This is significant, said Lim, "It's a major geopolitical shift".
"Whenever things got difficult under isolation, North Korea would reach out first toward South Korea, Japan, or especially the US to try to normalise relations, that was the pattern of Korean Peninsula diplomacy. But now that ties with Russia have tightened, Kim Jong Un argues that the world is in a new Cold War, a multipolar system."
The arrangement with Russia, which began as economic and military expediency appears to be developing into something deeper and longer-term. At this year's 9th Party Congress of the Korean Workers' Party, Kim Jong Un was emboldened and spoke of accomplishments that his grandfather Kim Il Sung and father Kim Jong Il never achieved.
But dangers lie ahead. To date, no North Koreans have fought on Ukrainian or Russian-occupied Ukrainian land. If they did so, there would be diplomatic consequences, not least in South Korea, an ally of Ukraine, albeit one which so far has only provided "non-lethal" aid.
This is something that President Zelensky has emphasised as he presses for Seoul to provide advanced military hardware, including air defence systems. He said that since June, preparations have been underway in Russia's Voronezh region to receive fresh North Korean forces and claimed that Pyongyang was preparing to transfer additional ballistic weapons to Russia.
"Russia is helping North Korea learn modern warfare, improve its weapons, and gain real combat experience. This poses a threat to every country in Asia that lies within range of North Korean missiles," he said in a presidential address in July.
Only two North Korean soldiers were captured alive in battles with Ukrainian forces. That's a staggeringly low number, given that between 11,000 and 14,000 fought in the Kursk campaign. (Another was captured alive but died from combat-related injuries, according to the South Korean National Intelligence Service).
Like their comrades who choose suicide over capture, neither man intended to be taken alive.
"For Joseon (North Korean) soldiers, becoming a prisoner of war itself is a crime. That just isn't an option. We can't become POWs," one of the captured men told a South Korean MBC documentary crew who interviewed him in prison in Ukraine.
Baek Pyeong-gang, not his real name, lay wounded from a drone strike for four days before being captured. He was tricked into surrendering when he mistook Ukrainian soldiers for his Russian allies.
The second prisoner, Lee Kang-eun, also a pseudonym, told the journalist Kim Young-mi that he felt guilty he was still alive. Barely conscious, he was found by Ukrainian soldiers on the battlefield with extensive injuries to the arm and jaw.
"I had no grenade or knives on me to self-blast (end my life)," he explained.
He described scores of his colleagues killed by drones, early in the war. The battlefield "reeked of the smell of blood", he said.
Neither man wants to return to North Korea, Lee said he believed that his family members would be "wiped out" as punishment for his capture. Both have said they want to be sent to South Korea, and Seoul is willing to take them.
Only Russia, not Pyongyang, has asked for their return.
But Ukraine, still intent on pressuring Seoul for military aid, has not committed to handing them over to South Korean authorities. Kyiv has said it will honour international human rights obligations which prevent the forced repatriation of prisoners of war.
Their fate remains undecided, but what appears certain is that more North Koreans will join Russia's war. Their service has enormous economic and political value to Pyongyang; but Russia desperately needs them too.
Four and a half years into Moscow's full-scale invasion of Ukraine, it is facing a desperate manpower shortage. Western and Ukrainian intelligence agencies estimate that it is losing some 6,000 more troops a month than it can recruit. So, Moscow has been forced to turn to foreign fighters, from Colombia, Kenya, Cameroon and North Korea, to sustain its ranks.
For Russia and North Korea, it is a mutually beneficial relationship, a coalition at a price. Ultimately, North Korea will continue to send its soldiers to fight in Russia's war, but only for as long as it is profitable to do so.

Turkish police detain dozens in raids on gay bars and homes of LGBTQ+ activists
- Published
Police in Turkey have detained 47 people in a series of raids on gay bars and the homes of LGBTQ+ activists, officials say.
Raids took place in 12 provinces over the weekend as part of a campaign dubbed "My Family is Safe" that the Turkish government says has been designed to protect family values.
One of the targets of the operation was LGBTQ+ association Kaos GL.
Same-sex marriage is not recognised in Turkey, with growing pressure on gay couples. Human rights groups in Turkey have accused the government of using the campaign to target the LGBTQ+ community.
Officers detained 26 people and seized drugs, digital equipment, smuggled alcohol and a firearm during the raids, according to the Istanbul chief prosecutor's office.
In a separate statement, the Ankara chief prosecutor's office said another 21 people had been detained as part of an investigation into Kaos GL.
The organisation said 50 activists had been detained, more than 10 taken after police raids on their homes.
It said that authorities had blocked several websites and social media accounts linked to LGBTQ+ organisations.
According to the group, authorities have accused Kaos GL of making "obscenity" in online posts that are available to children and had demanded the shutting down of the Kaos GL X account, as well as those of around 15 other LGBTQ+ organisations.
Same-sex relations are not an offence in Turkey but homophobia is common, with President Recep Tayyip Erdogan describing LGBTQ people as "perverts" responsible for the falling birth rate.
As part of "My Family is Safe", Turkish Justice Minister Akin Gurlek says legal proceedings have been started against more than 160 people and a number of organisations and companies across the country.
Gurlek did not say how many people had been taken into custody, but said the raids came in the context of the "Decade of the Family" campaign.
However, the Turkish Human Rights Association says the Turkish government has been using the campaign to target the LGBTQ+ community in recent years.
"The real name of this operation is not 'My Family is Safe'; it is state-led discrimination, politics of fear and the dismantling of civil society," the organisation said on X.

Solheim Cup 2026: Europe captain Anna Nordqvist dismisses USA captain Angela Stanford's 'dig' at course set-up
Team Europe captain Anna Nordqvist defended the Solheim Cup course set-up after suggestions from Team USA that the greens had been deliberately slowed down; the home side regained the trophy with a 15-13 win after prevailing in Sunday's singles at Bernardus Golf
Sunday 13 September 2026 19:54, UK
Team Europe captain Anna Nordqvist was quick to shut down suggestions the Bernardus Golf course set-up had been tailored to suit the home team at the Solheim Cup.
Nordqvist's side completed a 15-13 victory over Team USA after prevailing in Sunday's singles in the Netherlands.
The scores were tied at 8-8 following the opening two days, but USA captain Angela Stanford felt her side had been at a disadvantage throughout the tournament due to the slowness of the greens.

Stanford said at her post-tournament press conference: "Europe played well. I don't think we played bad. I think we just didn't make enough putts.
"And if you listen to everything I've ever said, Europeans always putt better. I don't know why. I still don't know why. I mean, I have a good idea, but I'm not going to say it right now.
"Apparently I didn't get to know the superintendent [grounds manager] as well as I should have."
When pressed further about whether she was referring to the green speeds being different to what she had been expecting, Stanford added: "Even when we showed up in July here, they were faster.
"And I don't think it had anything to do with the rain either. Now, saying that, it's my responsibility to get the team ready.
"This is the one thing I am kicking myself is that I just didn't keep pushing, you know, we got to figure out how to hit our putts a little bit harder, which is really difficult, to change the way you putt.
"So I'm a little frustrated with myself that I didn't drive that point home."
'We're in Europe in September'
Nordqvist was a little surprised by the apparent dig at the greens when it was put to her at her own press conference.
"We're in Europe and in September. We know how the weather can be," she said.
"I'm not sure I believe a lot in setting up a way to fit Europe because these girls play the same golf courses week-in and week-out competing.
"We came here in July, it was a very hot and dry summer, so the course played a little bit different then.
"So if anything it was just really trying to manage firmness. But then it's obviously been raining a lot in the past couple weeks and then this week we saw a lot of rain.
"So if anything they were probably just playing a little bit softer than we all thought coming here. But that's obviously the weather, we can't control that."
Stanford: You don't want to take away those moments
The Americans were pictured celebrating on Saturday evening after Jennifer Kupcho had sunk two brilliant putts to snatch a late victory for the visitors and level the match at 8-8 rather than going into the final day trailing 9-7.
But Stanford dismissed suggestions they had reached an emotional high too early.
"That's kind of tricky because you don't ever want to take away from that moment," she said.
"The worst thing I could have done is go in there and be like, 'okay, y'all. Come off this high'. So you don't want to take away from those moments.
"We're never going to see anything like that again. I think they handled it very well.
"But I talked to Kupcho and everybody and they're like, 'yeah, we got good rest but, yeah, it did take a minute to come off because it was a pretty high high'."
What's next?
The Ladies European Tour heads to Spain next for La Sella Open, beginning Thursday and held at La Sella Golf Resort, while the LPGA Tour takes a week off before the Walmart N Arkansas Championship from September 25-27.

For 26 days, India watched as Sonam Wangchuk wasted away. His hunger strike, held in solidarity with India’s “Cockroach” youth protest movement, would prove to be one of the most politically consequential fasts held in the country’s modern history.
Many in the country view the gruelling fast, which began on 28 June, as the crucial spark that helped propel the Cockroach movement into one of the most formidable challenges to the government of prime minister, Narendra Modi, in more than a decade.
Abhijit Dipke, the founder of the Cockroach movement, said Wangchuk had “awakened the conscience of an entire nation” through his sacrifice.
The Cockroach movement was launched in May, following the cancellation of a key nationwide exam to enter medical college after a paper was leaked. The cancellation was devastating for the 2 million students who had already sat the exam, a dozen of whom reportedly took their lives.
The movement took its name from comments made by India’s chief justice, Surya Kant, who had compared some unemployed young people to cockroaches and parasites in a court hearing.
Dipke’s demand for education minister, Dharmendra Pradhan, to show accountability for the leak by resigning struck a nerve, and anger that had been seething below the surface surged out on to the streets.
The protest ballooned into a nationwide movement. For weeks, deadlock prevailed between the government and Dipke, backed by thousands who flocked to his sit-in protest in Delhi. Eventually, after an unprecedented police crackdown which further influenced public opinion in its favour, the protesters triumphed and Pradhan resigned on 25 July.
The victory was not a foregone conclusion and Dipke has acknowledged the importance of Wangchuck’s fast in determining the outcome. Unlike the students, Wangchuck was a well known and respected figure, recognised for his decades-long efforts to secure educational reforms and environmental protection. Last year, he was arrested in Ladakh on charges of inciting anti-government protests.
The timing was also key: crowds at the Delhi protest site had been thinning before he started his fast on a stage there on 28 June, injecting new energy and momentum into the movement.
Wangchuk had declared he would not end his strike until the government had listened to the demands of India’s protesting youth. He lay outdoors at the Cockroach protest site in the heart of Delhi, day and night, enduring rain, torturous heat and mosquitoes. Already a lean and slight figure, he lost 11kg over the 26 days.
“I felt confined, trapped … like a prison,” he told the Guardian. “The heat and humidity were awful.”
In the aftermath, Wangchuk, a softly-spoken engineer, environmentalist and educationist, remains humble about his role. “I was a known entity and that helped,” he said. His reverence is reserved for the hundreds of thousands of young people in the Cockroach movement, which he says has changed Indian politics for good.
Wangchuk is adamant that the Cockroach movement’s success is far bigger than a single resignation. In an era where dissent is routinely criminalised, young people, he said, had seized back the power of political protest.
“They have stripped away the curtain of fear that existed,” he said. “They are now engaged. They have tasted success in getting results and I expect them to continue.”
The 60-year-old admits the hunger strike took a gruelling toll. By the time he broke his fast on 24 July, he had pushed his body to the limit and was perilously close to organ failure. But as thousands of young people and politicians flocked to his side, his spirit remained unbroken throughout.
The greatest test, he says, came when he was forcibly removed by police from the protest site and taken to hospital against his will. Videos of his frail body being dragged away by burly police went viral and Wangchuk was hailed by young people online as a national hero. When mass protests erupted the following day, Wangchuk’s name was chanted and held aloft on placards.
Wangchuk was not always an obvious figure of anti-government resistance. Born in Ladakh, he rose to international prominence as an engineer and environmentalist, best known for inventing the ice stupor, a unique technique for water storage in human-made glaciers. He became a prominent champion of the rights of Ladakhis and set up his own school and cultural and environmental institution.
He had been a vocal supporter of several prominent policies of Modi’s Bharatiya Janata party (BJP) but it soon turned to resistance as he accused the BJP of failing the people of Ladakh. Last year, as protests in Ladakh escalated, he was imprisoned by the government for almost six months under draconian anti-terrorist laws.
While his focus has been on rebuilding his body in recent weeks, regaining about 60% of his previous weight, Wangchuk has also continued his call for political reform, albeit without any overt criticism of the Modi government.
In a video message posted before India’s independence day in August, Wangchuk called for a “second independence movement” and urged Indians to choose men and women of “character and substance” to lead the country.
He has urged people to share the names of individuals of integrity who can be trusted and once he has a list, he plans to meet them in Mumbai and Delhi to discuss how elections can be cleansed of those with a criminal background.
“Indians have to trust those at the top,” he said. “At the moment, there is no trust in anything, not in elections, not in exams, not in civil servants. Clean and honest leaders are the first step to a better future.”
He expressed his support for the decision by the Cockroach movement to resist calls to become a political party and instead focus on being a pressure group, championing issues of education. “When we used to talk during the long days of the fast, I used to advise them that being a pressure group is the best way to keep clean and neutral,” he said.
For now, he is back living quietly in Ladakh, finally able to enjoy the one food that lingered on his mind during his hunger strike. “I did dream of apricots,” he said, “but that was just because I was wondering if mine back home had ripened.”

In Summary
- New Apple CEO, John Ternus, announced a range of products at the Surprise and Shine event.
- While most of the focus was on the iPhone Duo, Apple’s first foldable phone, there was much more to the event than just devices and a CEO debut.
- We bring you eight takeaways that were buried in the buzz around the new devices, which might have escaped your attention.
It might not have surprised too many people – the leaks messed that up – but Apple did a fair bit of shining at its recent Surprise and Shine event. The event, which also marked John Ternus’ debut as Apple CEO at a launch, went on expected lines, with Apple revealing new AirPods, Apple Watches, new iPhone Pros and, of course, the iPhone Duo, which has grabbed the most attention. There was, however, much more to the event than just the launches. Here are our eight biggest takeaways from the day on which the world saw Apple’s new foldable and the CEO on stage:
Table of Contents
New Era? Presentation-wise, Apple is still Cook-ing (Pun intended)
Yes, it was John Ternus who held the reins at Surprise and Shine. But in terms of presentation style, the template that was followed was still from the menu of the preceding chef, Tim Cook. We had multiple speakers, elaborate backdrops, and a similar race through a number of products, leaving the most time for the star of the show (it was the Air last time around, the Duo this time). Yes, in terms of presentation style, Apple remains well ahead of the competition, although we miss the wit and humor of the past; this launch was more from the Cook manual than the Ternus one.
No surprises (Sigh)…
It’s been a while since Apple surprised the Dickens out of us at a launch, but in recent years, the brand’s product announcements have often been leaked out well in advance. And that was pretty much true this time around. From the iPhone Duo to the shades of Burgundy to the fact that there would be no suffix-less iPhone at the event, the leak community got a lot of things right, which, as we have said in the past, takes some of the mystique and surprise out of the event. Mind you, Apple did pull one rabbit out of its hat.
…except for the AirPods 5
There were no suffix-less iPhones at Surprise and Shine, but there sure were suffix-less AirPods. And while most of the noise was about Apple’s first foldable, the AirPods 5 might have emerged as the silent, value-for-money heroes of the show. While most people had been expecting new AirPods Pro with perhaps a camera built into them, Apple brought in a new version of the classic AirPods, complete with better ANC and battery life, even while retaining the “open” fit and, surprise, surprise, the same price tag as its predecessors. Not too many noticed…until the price of the Duo was announced, and suddenly a device with no price increase became the belle of the tech ball.
Hooray, we will now have TWO iPhone launches every year
Surprise and Shine marked the beginning of a new iPhone era, in which Apple will release its iPhones in two tranches over a twelve-month period. While Apple has released iPhones at two different times of the year in the past, the second launch has generally been a relatively low-profile and soft one (of the SE and ‘e’ mainly). That is set to change now. Even if Apple does a soft launch for the iPhone 18, the iPhone Air 2 and the iPhone 18e, rather than a full-fledged event, the fact is that close to half of the iPhone portfolio will be launched in the second half of the year, and the remainder in the first half of the next year. The iPhone schedules just got tweaked.
Apple is getting REALLY serious about AI (no, really, this time)
Two years ago, Apple launched the iPhone 16 series, saying it had been designed from the ground up for Apple’s avatar of AI, Apple Intelligence. However, AI is one area where the Cupertino brand has been found trailing the competition. So it was not surprising that the brand was clearly out to write a new chapter at Surprise and Shine. Every device it announced – iPhones, Apple Watches, AirPods – had a strong element of AI, which different presenters stressed would work wonderfully well, even while preserving the users’ security. Well, we have heard that a few times in the past, but never in such a comprehensive manner. Is Apple finally going to crack the AI puzzle? Based on what we saw, it would be no Surprise if it went on to Shine in that department in the coming months.
Whoop, Whoop, the Apple Watch is now a full-fledged fitness and health device, and is targeting Whoop
It started out trying to be a computer on your wrist, complete with apps, notifications and alerts, but the Apple Watch has of late graduated (or been demoted, depending on your perspective) to being mainly a health and fitness tracking device. And Surprise and Shine saw this trend continuing, with most of the talk about the Apple Watch 4 Ultra and Apple Watch Series 12 revolving around better sensors and measurement. The highlighting of features like Readiness Scores and Health Age seems to indicate that the Cupertino brand now has the screenless Whoop, which popularised these features, in its sights.
The narrative is unmatched, but is now very hardware-driven!
Processors, camera apertures, health sensors, ANC, battery life…these formed the major part of the narrative around Surprise and Shine, showing how Apple’s has shifted from storytelling to specs at its launches in recent times. This might be fine for some, but we do miss the time when an announcer would walk us through nuances of design and amazing (or they called amazing, and often, unbelievable) features on devices.
Yes, Apple remains the lord, master, and commander of product launches, but we prefer tales to tech, and a live presenter on stage to edited videos, no matter how sleekly edited. The fact that the Duo section stood out from the others because of its stress on design and UI only reinforces our belief that Apple might perhaps reconsider going back to its storytelling roots, and leave the specs on the spec sheet, rather than on the speech notes. Everyone else talks specs anyway.
Cosmic orange is out of the Apple cosmos… and Black is back!
This was so typically Apple. After making orange the color of the last twelve months, courtesy of the Cosmic Orange variant of the iPhone 17 Pro series, and making a number of brands come out with orange phones and other devices (JBL even had a pair of headphones in orange), the Cupertino giant pushed the shade out of its color palette. It also brought back the one color that everyone had missed in the Pro series – Black. Henry “Any Color As Long As It Is Black” Ford and AC/DC would approve of the return of the color, and so do we. We are not shedding any tears for orange, although we suspect those orange Pros are going to have great antique value some day.
And one more thing…
Craig Federighi’s hair looks as awesome as ever!

India’s senior living market is expected to become a $ 10.1 billion opportunity by 2030, requiring $ 7.7 billion capital investment to meet new supply under a policy-driven scenario, according to a ASLI-JLL report “India’s Silver Economy: From Niche to Necessity”.
“With over 166 million Indians aged above 60 and the number projected to double by 2050, there is a need to build an ecosystem of senior citizens. The organised senior living facility penetration is just 1.5%. The opportunity is about building a strong, accessible, and trusted senior care ecosystem,” G. Rajagopal, chairman of the Association of Senior Living India (ASLI), said in a press release.
The addressable market of urban, financially independent senior households in India is expected to grow from 1.7 million in 2026 to 2.1 million by 2030. The opportunity is not just in senior living friendly properties and communities but includes assisted care, healthcare, specialised care, rehabilitation, and other supporting services, says the report.
The organised senior living sector reached 25,050 dwelling units as of June 2026 (at 1.5 %) compared with 6-7 % in the U.S. and 14-15% in New Zealand. The sector registered 14.2 % CAGR between 2024 and first half of 2026.
“We are looking at a market that could scale from 25,050 units to 74,000 units by 2030, unlocking $ 7.7 billion in capital deployment. But the real story is not just independent living, it is the assisted living crisis. We have barely 2,100 assisted living beds today against a projected need of 11,000 by 2030, while the population of 75 plus years is growing at 7.8% annually,” said Karan Singh Sodi, Senior Managing Director, JLL.
However, despite 80 % – 85% occupancy at well-managed facilities, skilled caregiver shortages and high real estate costs remain key constraints. Affordability is a critical barrier, according to the report.
Rental and service-led models are likely to gain significant traction in the coming years, with rental models expected to overtake outright sales. Financial innovations such as repositioned Reverse Mortgage Loans and insurance-linked products could help convert existing assets into viable funding mechanisms for senior care.
The Maharashtra Housing Policy 2025 has formally recognised senior housing through dedicated planning standards and healthcare linkages, while Haryana’s policy combines licensing clarity with Floor Area Ratio incentives to improve project feasibility. Such policy measures can take the market penetration to nearly 2.4 % within four years.
Operators are also investing in digital health infrastructure, including electronic health records, monitoring wearables and telemedicine, alongside quality and accreditation frameworks, the report said.

India condemns attack on ship off Oman as seafarer remains missing; 13 Indian crew members rescued
Thirteen other Indian seafarers who were part of the crew of MT El Gaia were rescued following the attack off the coast of Oman
India on Sunday condemned an attack on a Panama-flagged oil tanker that resulted in one Indian seafarer being reported missing, and said the targeting of merchant shipping and civilian infrastructure is unacceptable.
Thirteen other Indian seafarers who were part of the crew of MT El Gaia were rescued following the attack off the coast of Oman, the external affairs ministry said.
Also Read | A distress network for seafarers at sea: What Modi proposed at BRICS, and why India needs it
The attack came a day after Prime Minister Narendra Modi proposed creating a “Seafarers' Emergency Support Network” at the Brics Summit to safeguard mariners facing heightened risks due to regional conflicts. Ten Indian seafarers are among 16 Indians killed so far in the West Asia conflict, while another five Indian seafarers have died in strikes on merchant vessels in the Black Sea.
“We condemn the attack on the commercial vessel MT El Gaia off the coast of Oman earlier today. Of the 14 Indian crew onboard, 13 Indians have been rescued so far,” the external affairs ministry said in a statement.
“Search and rescue operations for the missing Indian national are continuing. Our embassy in Oman is closely monitoring the situation and proactively coordinating with the Omani authorities in the ongoing search and rescue operation,” it said.
The Indian side thanked Omani authorities for their support in rescuing the Indian seafarers.
Also Read | From Hormuz to Black Sea, PM Modi pitches BRICS distress network to rescue seafarers
“We reiterate our call for immediate de-escalation of tensions and pursuance of dialogue and diplomacy to bring peace to the region,” the statement said. “The targeting of commercial shipping, seafarers, civilians, and civilian infrastructure in the region is unacceptable.”
The Indian side also called for the restoration of free and safe navigation and flow of commerce through international waterways in the region at the earliest.
Indian seafarers make up more than 12% of the global merchant shipping workforce, second only to Philippine nationals. India contributes almost 312,000 of the global total of 2.57 million seafarers.

Tucker Carlson backs Democrat Abdul El-Sayed in Michigan Senate race
Mike Rogers is ‘unfit to serve’, right-wing commentator writes, after wave of Islamophobic abuse against El-Sayed and Zohran Mamdani over 9/11
A wave of Republican attacks against two Muslim Democrats has ended with one of the most prominent right-wing commentators in the country endorsing Abdul El-Sayed for Senate.
Tucker Carlson wrote in his newsletter on Friday that El-Sayed’s opponent, Mike Rogers, was unfit for office and defended him over his past criticism of the war on terror.
The Michigan Democrat emerged from this past week after a wave of attacks were hurled at him and Zohran Mamdani, the first elected Muslim mayor of New York, around the anniversary of the 9/11 terrorist attacks. Both men were the subject of intense focus from media organizations on the right and even some mainstream outlets as the two faced differing but related accusations of anti-American sentiment impossible to separate from their Muslim faith.
For El-Sayed, it included accusations that he didn’t sufficiently care about American victims of the attacks given that he’d made statements criticizing the War on Terror launched in their wake, including one where he mentioned that he would spend September 11th mourning the attacks’ victims, and the next day mourning victims of the wars.
Carlson, who is now the most vocal critic of Donald Trump’s war with Iran on the right, leapt to El-Sayed’s defense on Friday, the anniversary of the attacks, after Mike Rogers’ campaign said El-Sayed’s attitude was “disgusting”.
“Hold on a second. Disgusting? Understanding that the Bush administration was wrong to kill hundreds of thousands of people and waste trillions of dollars in Iraq, even though, again, Iraq did not do 9/11, is disgusting?” asked Carlson.
“El-Sayed did not celebrate airplane hijackings or cheerlead Al-Qaeda; he simply said that the U.S. conducting terrorism of its own in response to 9/11 was not exactly an appropriate reaction. He is obviously right,” wrote Carlson.
Carlson is passionately opposed to the war in Iran and called the strikes launched by the U.S. and Israel to begin the war in February “disgusting” and “evil”. In June, he warned that the war would be the end of both the Trump presidency and the Maga movement, predicting that it would consume both, leaving the president’s legacy in tatters.
“What’s the Bush presidency about? It’s about the Iraq war and the financial collapse of 2008. Those are its defining facts. And that will be you,” Carlson said he told Trump during a Sky News interview. “It doesn’t matter what else ... you’re the Iran war guy if you do this. He knew that. Boy, did he know that. But he did it anyways.”
The latest remark from Carlson is bad news for Rogers, as it signals that the efforts of his campaign to paint his opponent as a radical extremist aren’t paying off.
Polling has trended in El-Sayed’s favor since the primary and support for Trump’s war in Iran continues to drop as well. The president’s own approval ratings hover in the 30s, dragged down by economic woes brought on by the war.
In Michigan, Democrats are hoping to hold on to a Senate seat held by retiring Sen. Gary Peters as they pursue a majority in the upper chamber in the upcoming midterms. The party needs to hold Michigan and net four other seats to take back control of the chamber.
But El-Sayed’s win of the primary in Michigan followed a bitterly divisive campaign against him by AIPAC and supporters of the Democratic Party’s relationship with Israel, which has frayed severely since the Israeli siege of Gaza began in 2023. The primary fight mirrored the New York mayoral race won by Mamdani, who faced a similar wave of anti-Muslim attacks labeling him a “jihadist” and supporter of radical Islamist terror groups, cheered on by a right-wing media sphere and even some conservative Democrats.
El-Sayed has sought to embrace Mamdani’s playbook and has been relentless in trying to refocus the conversation around his campaign whenever media outlets attempt to draw him into disputes about his Muslim faith, his past comments about 9/11 or other issues or the support his campaign has received from Hasan Piker, an avowed anti-Zionist Twitch streamer who also faced blowback over comments about 9/11 and criticism of the war on terror.

Following a restructuring of the Bharatiya Janata Party’s (BJP) digital wing, the party has intensified its social media campaigning, increasingly employing violent memes and videos.
On August 27, the Karnataka unit of the BJP shared a meme featuring a clip from the film ‘KGF: Chapter 2’, in which the protagonist unleashes a barrage of gunfire on his opponents. In the meme, the shooters were depicted as the BJP’s state units, while the opponents were labeled ‘Dimagi Naxals’ — a term used by Prime Minister Narendra Modi during his Independence Day speech to describe individuals with a “Naxalite mindset”.
The accompanying caption stated, “We will not stop, we are confronting ‘Urban Naxals’ with full force.” The BJP Karnataka unit posted this video on Instagram as a collaborative post with the BJP units of Delhi, Goa, and Jammu & Kashmir.

The Punjab BJP posted an AI-generated video showing an angry parent slapping Punjab Chief Minister Bhagwant Mann inside a government school. In the video, a teacher is seen writing an incorrect spelling on the blackboard while Punjab Chief Minister Bhagwant Mann and Aam Aadmi Party convener Arvind Kejriwal watch. Suddenly, the parent spots errors in their child’s notebook and, in a fit of rage, slaps the Chief Minister.
Unlike posts featuring memes from the film KGF or the web series Mirzapur, the Punjab BJP’s post did not use fictional characters to make a point. Instead, it used AI to create a scene depicting a physical attack on a state’s elected Chief Minister, creating a fabricated image of violence directed at a real, identifiable individual. Following widespread criticism, the Punjab BJP deleted the post.
The Origins Of ‘Dimagi Naxal’
The term ‘Dimagi Naxal’ recently entered India’s political vocabulary and is now becoming a weapon wielded by BJP and its affliates to attack dissenters and opposition on social media.
The term originated during Modi’s Independence Day speech at Red Fort, wherein he declared that while the country had eliminated the armed Naxals hiding in the forests, ‘Dimagi Naxals’ remained active within society. He claimed that individuals with a Maoist mindset had entrenched themselves in the corridors of power and influenced policies while serving as advisors on government committees, he emphasised the need to identify and isolate them.
The Prime Minister did not directly mention any specific individual or organisation. However, critics believe that, much like terms such as ‘Urban Naxal,’ ‘Tukde-Tukde Gang,’ and ‘Andolanjeevi’, the term ‘Dimagi Naxal’ is another such label to attack dissenters.
Union Minister Kiren Rijiju tweeted: ‘Dimagi Naxals’ are those who support Maoists and do not accept the Indian Constitution, who stand with separatists and support Article 370, and who want to sever the ‘Chicken’s Neck’ to separate the North-East from India.
In a follow up tweet, Rijiju posted a video of political prisoner Sharjeel Imam, while writing: “…Kapil Sibal and Company who are trying to save this person and his Tukde-Tukde Gang members, P. Chidambaram should clarify if he too supports this statement. Dimagi Naxal can be proven by a person’s actions and expressions. #DimagiNaxal”
Besides Kapil Sibal and Company who are trying to save this person and his Tukde-Tukde Gang members, P. Chidambaram should clarify if he too supports this statement. Dimagi Naxal can be proven by a person’s actions and expressions. #DimagiNaxal pic.twitter.com/jq98cU3Q4s
— Kiren Rijiju (@KirenRijiju) August 17, 2026
The most alarming aspect of the campaign waged against this fabricated concept of ‘Dimagi Naxalism’ is not any single video, but the dangerous pattern underlying it. ‘Dimagi Naxal’ has become a label coined not for actual terrorist groups, but merely for those holding dissenting views, people whom memes have depicted as being brutally beaten or riddled with bullets.

A New York high school senior was suspended on her first day of classes after bringing a cup of coffee to school and refusing to throw it away. This dispute has now prompted the district to the revisit how a new rule should be introduced. Julie Kaputa, a senior and honours student at Beaver River Central School in Castorland, New York, received an in-school suspension on September 3 after arriving with the drink. The incident centred on a new addition to the school's code conduct prohibiting students from bringing outside food and drinks onto school premises. According to Kaputa, she walked into her first-period classroom with the coffee when her teacher gave her three options: discard it, consume it immediately or report to the office. “I walked in, I had my coffee with me,” Kaputa told local broadcaster WWNY. She said the teacher told her she would need to “dump that out or consume it on the spot, or go down to the office”. It's clear Kaputa chose which option. What followed was not simply a disagreement over a drink. The student said she was concerned about how the new policy had been adopted and whether the required process had been followed before it came into effect. The outside food and drink restriction was a new provision in Beaver River Central School's code of conduct for the current academic year. Kaputa and her mother, MaryAnne, argued that the district had not properly notified the public about a hearing where the policy could be discussed. Julie said transparency in government was important to her and that the absence of what she understood to be a properly announced public hearing was what prompted her to challenge the rule. Her mother similarly questioned when the required hearing had taken place, saying the family searched for an announcement but could not find one. MaryAnne later said her daughter was aware of the new rule but deliberately refused the instruction as a form of protest. She described Julie's decision as an act of civil disobedience and said the teenager, who serves as student body president, believed she had support from other students over the issue. The dispute has since moved beyond Julie's suspension. Beaver River Central School superintendent Todd Green said an August monthly board meeting had been intended to serve as the public hearing required as part of the district's annual review process. However, he acknowledged that the meeting's advance notice did not explicitly identify it as a “Public Hearing”, meaning members of the public may not have understood that they had an opportunity to speak about the code of conduct. “Because we hold ourselves to the highest standard of compliance, we are correcting this administrative detail,” Green said in a statement issued on September 10. Green also praised the student for challenging the process. “It’s good to see students standing up for what they believe in,” he told WWNY, adding that the district was trying to follow open-meeting laws and would make changes when problems were identified. A new public hearing is scheduled for 14 September, giving students, parents and other members of the community an opportunity to address the controversial policy. The incident has also drawn attention because the punishment was tied to a relatively ordinary item: a cup of coffee brought from outside the school. Kaputa has said the suspension will not appear on her permanent record. She also told WWNY that she was not angry with the district and that her main concern was seeing the system operate as it was intended to. The school eventually allowed her to return to class with her coffee, according to her mother. The previous year's policy reportedly restricted food deliveries unless they had been approved or ordered by staff, but did not prohibit students from bringing their own food and drinks. The new provision therefore represented a significant change for students arriving at school with beverages or food from outside. The controversy has led to petitions circulating locally, with some students, staff and parents reportedly questioning whether the new rule is unnecessarily restrictive and how practical it will be to enforce. Book Box | Inside Hammock: Literary magazine in an AI age
Founding editor Abhay Puri, a South Asia Speaks Fellow, counts Granta and The Stinging Fly as his literary magazine favorites.
A literary magazine is like a lucky dip — you never know what will come your way.
This is what draws me to these publications. I subscribe to the New Yorker, the Mekong Review and now Hyphen and open up every issue with excitement - Will I find something dark and strange? A story that leaves me wondering why I have never read this writer before? Or a laugh out loud treat?
Almost certainly, literary magazines are where offbeat work turns up long before it reaches the regular bookshelves.
So it is with the first print edition of Hammock magazine, an olive-green paperback titled The City and priced at Rs. 899 (Kindle e-book: Rs.449). The anthology includes a horror story set in Chennai, a picaresque tale of a city bus in Bengaluru, slices of life from Mumbai, and a newly translated story by the well-known Bhisham Sahni
Founding editor Abhay Puri, a South Asia Speaks Fellow, counts Granta and The Stinging Fly as his literary magazine favorites. We talk about what it means to publish a print literary magazine in the age of AI, when the economics of print publishing have become difficult. Here are edited excerpts from our conversation:
What was the inspiration for Hammock?
I think every writer dreams of starting a magazine, and I was silly enough to actually go ahead with it. I felt that the literary ecosystem in India needed more avenues for new writers to publish work, have a community, or simply read things that were not news or ‘lifestyle’ centric.
When the first print anthology came out earlier this year, it felt like we’d actually launched, even after publishing digitally for more than three years.
You have a Master’s in Creative Writing from Birkbeck College, University of London. Has this degree helped your writing career?
For a long time, I was skeptical about whether creative writing could really be taught. Many writers I admire worked in post offices or dead-end jobs, or were housewives.
There is an ‘MFA voice’ that the publishing industry seems to aspire to. There are certain styles and dogmas. For instance: avoid the passive voice. ‘Show, don’t tell.’ Erase dialect or stories that make a reader work harder. All of these things are true in some contexts. But they are also rooted in what works for the Western market and can leave many books feeling flat and detached.
I do think, though, that my editorial work and everything I’ve done with Hammock benefited a great deal from studying creative writing. My course also gave me time to write and an amazing community of writer friends whose feedback helps me develop my work.
What has it been like publishing in the age of AI? Are there ways AI can be helpful to writers, and are there things writers should guard against?
There’s already a noticeable increase in the number of submissions that feel like they are AI-generated, but for now it’s quite easy to identify them.
I’ve never used AI, and I don’t plan to. I think the societal, environmental and cognitive costs are not worth the trade-off.
I really resent how technology companies are essentially forcing AI on people without their consent. I am sure it has its benefits in terms of handling huge amounts of data or medical applications or solving climate problems, so people should use it for that and keep it as far away from the arts as possible.
What’s been the hardest part?
As a small, independent magazine with limited budgets, you need to figure out all the administrative tasks yourself. The biggest problem is that we live in a time where there is so much being produced, published and posted every single day that capturing attention is very difficult.
Can you talk about the economics of publishing a literary magazine?
I’ve done a combination of self-funding and raising some money, but I am still working on other avenues to generate funds, like grants and fellowships. I definitely think there needs to be more of an arts ecosystem in India which allows small ventures to create freely — I think these kinds of projects can have value beyond just the balance sheet and take time to mature.
Many countries in the West have robust government funding for small publishers and artist-led initiatives, and it’s also a way to build soft power and cultural relevance.
For instance, one of the big reasons that Korean film, music and literature has blown up so much in recent years is because their government decided to hugely expand arts funding a couple of decades ago, and now you can see the impact that’s having globally. Hopefully India can go in that direction too, though obviously there are many other problems to address first.
Tell us about your own reading life.
I was lucky enough to grow up before the internet era, in a home where both parents are big readers. I remember my mother often reading to my sister and to me at night — anything from picture books to Enid Blyton to Harry Potter. Our family would visit bookshops like Strand in Mumbai or the Kemps Corner Crossword, where we were always allowed to get whatever we wanted. In school in Singapore in the 11th grade, we were assigned Dostoevsky and The Great Gatsby for English. That was one of the first times I realized all that a novel or story can be.
You’ve lived in both Mumbai and London. What are your favourite city books?
Mumbai: Rohinton Mistry’s novels, Jayant Kaikini’s short stories, Jeet Thayil’s Narcopolis, Jerry Pinto’s Em and the Big Hoom, Katherine Boo’s Behind the Beautiful Forevers
London: Ben Judah’s This Is London, Zadie Smith’s White Teeth, Rachel Cusk, Ian McEwan, Virginia Woolf
And back to your City anthology, if you had to pick a story that stayed with you the most, which one would it be?
There were aspects of each that I really loved: the honest, unique voice that Shruti Sonal and Prithviraj Solanki bring to their pieces, the propulsiveness and surreal nature of Dinesh Shrinet and Namita Krishnamurthy’s stories, the unique topics like single screen cinema halls or ice factories or rampant tourism that are the focus of the pieces by Sagar Kumar, Rama Raghavan and Rishu Nigam.
Finally, what next?
We’re going to expand our print publishing in the next year, and have more anthologies released. Our next anthology is themed around immigration and the diaspora, and that should be out in two months.

Top-level online schooling offers route to leading universities
As an elite international school with an online delivery model for seven- to 18-year-olds, Crimson Global Academy prepares students for places at the world’s best universities.
[The content of this article has been produced by our advertising partner.]
For families who are regularly on the move or simply looking for a high-quality alternative to traditional modes of teaching, an easy-to-access option is now available offering flexibility, rigour and a proven track record.
Operating since 2019, the Crimson Global Academy (CGA) conducts small live group classes alongside one-to-one classes where a more personalised pace is helpful. Everything follows a well-structured weekly timetable, with a choice of curricula that lead to globally recognised qualifications including the IGCSE, international A-Levels, AP (advanced placement) programmes, and the US high school diploma.
The aim at all times is to provide an education which is effective, challenging and transformative. This is done by giving students access to cutting-edge technologies, a global learning environment, and even an AI chatbot on hand to offer extra support when needed.
Results show it is an approach which can accelerate academic performance and broaden perspectives, while also allowing sufficient flexibility to adjust personal timetables and pathways or opt for one-to-one classes in certain subjects if preferred.   
“We have rolling admissions, but students will join one of three virtual campuses – centred in Hong Kong, London and the United States – where live classes, with an average of 8-10 students – are taught remotely in the morning or early afternoon in each time zone,” says Liya Sun, CGA’s admissions officer for Asia.
“Each campus follows its own academic year, but we make it easy to switch between them if families or students move, and there are the usual term breaks, internal exams, reports, parent-teacher exchanges and check-ins with group tutors.” 
Already, children from more than 70 Hong Kong families are studying with CGA, usually choosing to do so for one of three reasons. 
“There is an onboarding process where we set up student accounts and links to portals for classes, schedules and other activities,” says Sun, noting that CGA’s reach now extends to more than 75 countries, with over 400 subject specialists teaching 3,000-plus pupils. “Each class lasts an hour, the discussions are very interactive, cameras must be on, all students are called on to present and contribute, and we send parents email reminders if there is any issue.”
Every student must also take a weekly “learning for life” course which covers topics such as time management, classroom ethics and essential life skills.
“To bring people together, we host regular in-person events each quarter where students, siblings and parents in the same city can meet up,” says Ella Liu, CGA’s senior marketing associate for the Asia region.
There are also numerous extracurricular activities, including a popular cooking club where students prepare and share recipes from the own culture , and general PE sessions to keep pupils fit and active.
While there can be challenges in switching to online learning, most young people only need to refamiliarise themselves with the type of processes and protocols they had to follow during the pandemic.
“New joiners have to get used to the platforms and chatbots, but students of this generation adapt really quickly,” Sun says. “Usually, it is the parents who take longer to understand the portals and what to do.”
“We are accredited by four leading bodies: WASC (the Western Association of Schools and Colleges), Cambridge Assessment International Education, Pearson Edexcel, and the College Board (AP), and are registered in the US and New Zealand, so colleges recognise us as a private school,” Liu says. “We have had 160-plus admission offers from Oxbridge, Ivy League and other universities among the world’s top 50, and we are working towards steady expansion, maintaining the current momentum for our next intakes and well beyond.”

When Seher Hashmi speaks about mental health, her words do not stem from textbook theories or clinical observations. They carry the raw truth of a survivor. Having battled severe clinical depression and Borderline Personality Disorder (BPD), and having survived multiple suicide attempts and self-harm, Seher knows the darkest corners of anguish. Today, she is converting her trauma into a movement, traversing thousands of kilometres across India on her Royal Enfield motorcycle to shatter the silence surrounding mental illness.
Her ongoing nationwide campaign, titled ‘Beyond the Horizon – A Ride for Resilience,’ has reached Keralam after completing its north Indian leg. Together with a group of fellow riders, Seher is engaging with youth to transform societal attitudes towards mental health.
Seher’s life began under difficult circumstances. Abandoned by her biological parents at just nine months simply for being their third girl child, she was adopted by renowned social activist Shabnam Hashmi and scientist-writer Gauhar Raza. She is the niece of Safdar Hashmi, the iconic street-theatre activist who was murdered in 1989. Growing up alongside deeply committed parents whose demanding public lives sometimes left little room to process her childhood anxieties, Seher’s struggles gradually worsened into severe mental health challenges.
Path to recovery
Her path to recovery was forged through personal determination, medical intervention, and the empathy of her loved ones. Emerging from that dark space, Seher rebuilt her life as a motivational speaker, fashion stylist, and mental health advocate.
For Seher, every kilometre ridden is a step towards dismantling social stigma. By sharing her own story of survival, she offers young people across the country something far more powerful than advice—proof that resilience is possible, and that no struggle has to be faced alone.
Second journey
This motorcycle odyssey marks her second major awareness journey. Her first expedition took place in 2025, covering over 3,000 kilometres from Delhi to Kashmir and back, reaching thousands of students across 20 cities. Her current campaign—the south Indian leg—was flagged off on August 20, 2026, at the Constitution Club of India in New Delhi by veteran actor Sharmila Tagore. Spanning 55 days, 11 States, and over 7,000 km, the initiative aims at covering 100 venues across schools, colleges, and rural community spaces.
Entering Keralam on September 9, 2026 through Kasaragod, the team will cover nine districts—Kasaragod, Kannur, Kozhikode, Malappuram, Thrissur, Ernakulam, Alappuzha, Kollam, and Thiruvananthapuram—before heading to Kanyakumari on September 18. In Keralam, the campaign is supported by the Yuva Samithi of the Kerala Sastra Sahitya Parishad (KSSP). Parishad volunteers are accompanying the team on motorbikes throughout the State, organising mental health awareness sessions and interactive discussions in educational institutions.
