Anthropic said Thursday it has blocked efforts by bad actors to use its artificial intelligence models for malicious activity such as cyberattacks, surveillance, and research that could have led to biological weapons.
As AI models grow more powerful, elaborate cyberattacks no longer require sophisticated skills and even lone individuals can create threats that would not have been possible even a year ago, Anthropic said. The company said it has added stronger safeguards in its latest models to restrict biological research that could also be used to make weapons.
“The cases we share here aren’t typical misuse, but rather examples of the most notable and novel threat activity we’ve identified to date,” Anthropic said in its third report since March 2025 describing AI misuse. The report includes snippets of the malicious code and AI prompts Anthropic said it found, and urges governments and AI competitors to identify and prevent similar abuse.
“We’re publishing this work because we believe we have a responsibility to disclose malicious misuse of our services. As models become increasingly capable, their risks will increase, unless AI developers and society’s defenders act to make them safer,” the company said.
The lengthy report by the AI startup, which is planning an initial public offering this fall, was published two days after one of its researchers announced he's resigning over concerns that Anthropic and its competitors are not acting responsibly in AI development. He echoed concerns raised inside and outside of the industry about the technology’s potential to elude human control.
Between December 2025 and August 2026, researchers at Anthropic found misuse by actors ranging from spyware vendors and “politically motivated individuals” to state-sponsored groups spreading propaganda.
Among the findings in the company's report are unnamed actors attempting to use its models for research that could have led to biological weapons. In one instance, Anthropic said its systems blocked a request for Claude’s assistance in authoring a grant application for scientific funding.
“The work discussed in the application involved gain-of-function research (that is, research that genetically alters an organism to create a new or enhanced biological property) on the chikungunya virus. This gain of function research was aimed at the virus’ transmissibility and immune evasion properties,” the report said.
Chikungunya is a mosquito-borne virus that causes debilitating symptoms such as severe pain and fever. The request involved a grant proposal for research seeking to enhance mutations to make the virus progressively more harmful. While such research could “certainly” be used to develop better vaccines and treatments, Anthropic said, “it could also be used to make the pathogen more dangerous.”
None of the cases Anthropic included in its report were found to be using its newer, more powerful Claude Fable or Mythos-class models, with the exception of one illicit distillation case that Anthropic described as “an industrial-scale, covert campaign to extract a model’s capabilities and replicate them in another model without authorization.”
Anthropic said its older models, such as Claude Opus 4 and Claude Sonnet 4.5, from 2025, “were well below the threshold where they could meaningfully assist a sophisticated user in carrying out dangerous biological research.”
“As a result, safeguards on these models were less stringent, directed mostly at preventing access to content that might uplift novices in recreating known bioweapons,” the report said. “But for today’s models — which are capable of assisting in a range of complex scientific research tasks — the evidence is no longer certain, and we cannot make that same assurance.”
Because of this, Anthropic has applied “stronger safeguards that restrict access to a wide range of dual-use biological research queries” in its more recent models, such as Claude Fable 5, the report said.
As companies introduce increasingly powerful AI models, experts have called on governments to regulate the technology, rather than relying on the industry to police itself.
John Thickstun, an assistant professor of computer science at Cornell University, said it is an uncomfortable position for companies like Anthropic and OpenAI to be in when they are expected to determine what is safe vs. unsafe behaviour and make "value judgments at societal scale without any kind of democratic or deliberative oversight.”
Anthropic also found groups that created hundreds of social media accounts that look like they belong to ordinary people and then posted material amplifying the same political view over the course of a week. The company outlined nine such cases it found, originating in Russia, Iran, Turkey and across the Persian Gulf, South Asia, Africa and Europe.
While social media companies can detect influence operations on their platforms once posts are circulating, “we may see it on Claude while the operation is still being built.”
Anthropic released this report after one of its researchers, Jacob Coxon, announced he's resigning amid fears the company and its chief rival OpenAI “are racing straight to self-improving superintelligence and gambling with our lives.” Coxon's post warned that some of his colleagues now believe AI could threaten human life by the end of the decade.
But Anthropic said it has blocked each of the malicious activities it identified, used the experience to strengthen safeguards and shared information with government authorities and industry partners.
“We hope that the findings in this report will help other developers recognize similar patterns on their own platforms, give governments and civil society a clearer view of how emerging threats take shape, and strengthen collective defenses,” Anthropic said.

If you want to bring your music everywhere, the humble Bluetooth speaker is your best bet. You’ll lose some audio quality compared to bookshelf speakers, but these days, Bluetooth speakers sound pretty great, and let you blast the tunes wherever you go—the backyard, the beach, and beyond.
Since they first appeared on the audio scene back in 2010, the team at WIRED has reviewed hundreds of Bluetooth speakers at every price range. My top pick for most use cases remains the portable, durable, and affordable JBL Flip 7 ($150), but I’ve got specialized recommendations for nearly every use case and budget. From outdoor parties, beach days and poolside fun, to at-home listening in every room, these are the best speakers for everything you do.
Don’t forget to check out WIRED’s other audio guides, including the Best Soundbars, Best Wireless Earbuds, and Best Computer Speakers.
Updated September 2026: I’ve added the LG xboom Stage 501 and JBL Go 5 to my recommendations, refreshed the Honorable Mentions list, and updated pricing and copy with the most up to date information.
How I Test Bluetooth Speakers
WIRED’s audio experts have spent countless hours listening to, carrying, charging, dropping, and dunking Bluetooth speakers. I’ve been testing audio equipment for more than 20 years and remember the excitement surrounding the launch of the industry-changing Jawbone Jambox way back in 2010. It helped take wireless speakers mainstream and kick-started an entire industry. Since then, I’ve lost count of the number of Bluetooth speakers I’ve tested, but looking around my office today, I count at least 20 cluttering up the place.
Every speaker gets extensive listening with a wide mix of music, podcasts, and recordings of varying quality, including basic Spotify streams and high-resolution lossless audio from Qobuz and Tidal. This guide focuses on portable, battery-powered speakers, so there are inevitable compromises in sound compared to hi-fi speakers, but the difference between the best and worst is still remarkable.
Where possible, I compare similarly priced and sized speakers directly. A $50 speaker does not need to compete with a $500 one, but it does need to outperform the alternatives you might realistically buy instead.
I also test portability, controls, apps, Bluetooth reliability, useful extras, and battery life against manufacturers’ claims. The latter takes increasingly ridiculous amounts of time these days, especially with many speakers breaching the 50 hour mark.
And if a brand says its speaker is built for the beach, backyard, or pool, I test that too. Admittedly, WIRED doesn’t get as many pool days as it would like, but there’s always the bath.
What Should I Look for in a Bluetooth Speaker?
That entirely depends on what you plan to use it for. The best advice we have is to start with how and where you’d like to listen to music and work backwards to a specific model from there. Speakers include tiny keychains, larger boomboxes, and everything in between. We select speakers based largely on how they perform in their specialty, whether that’s audio quality, durability, or some other particular niche.
As far as durability, we look for speakers with solid IP ratings for dust and water resistance and tend to prefer long battery life; batteries with larger capacities tend to still work well even after a few years of degradation.

Small enough to go almost anywhere but big enough to let you properly enjoy your music, the JBL Flip 7 hits a sweet spot that makes it an easy recommendation. It sounds remarkably good for something this compact (and affordable), with plenty of bass and punch, clear vocals, and refined detail. Build quality is excellent too, with IP68 water and dust protection and some drop-proofing (within reason)..
JBL keeps improving the Flip with every iteration. It now has 14 hours of battery life (or 16 with the bass-reducing Playtime Boost mode), and Auracast lets you link newer compatible JBL speakers together for a surround sound experience. The app also has a useful seven-band EQ if you like to tinker with your tones.
As a nice bonus for those who care about bit rates, the Flip 7 can play 24-bit/96kHz lossless audio if you plug it into a source via the USB-C, which is a surprising extra feature at this price point. JBL continues to be the brand to beat in the land of Bluetooth speakers.

If your house is already full of Sonos speakers, the Sonos Play is an easy addition to justify, with ample smarts and connectivity built-in. It sounds significantly better than the smaller Sonos Roam 2, with an audio performance closer to the brand’s excellent Sonos Era 100, despite being battery powered.
Wi-Fi connectivity means access to the full Sonos ecosystem and app, including more than 100 streaming services, voice control, automatic Trueplay tuning, and multiroom playback. Leave it on the supplied charging base and it’s a great Sonos speaker. Pick it up and switch to Bluetooth, and you have a portable speaker with a huge 24 hours of battery life and IP67 protection.
At 2.9 pounds, it’s just about portable enough for travel, although I was very aware I was carrying it in my backpack. You can also charge your phone from it or add an analog source using Sonos’ optional line-in adapter. If you’re already invested in Sonos’ ecosystem, and don’t mind a regularly-changing Sonos app, it’s hard to think of a more smart speaker.

Great looks, cute size, and instantly stolen by my tweenage daughter, the Go 5 is my ideal tiny speaker. It weighs next to nothing and fits in the palm of my hand, but the 4.8 watt output sounds considerably less weedy than it has any right to.
The already excellent JBL Go 4 is a little cheaper, but the Go 5 brings fuller, deeper bass, clear mids, and enough punch to make music sound good. Its tough little enclosure is drop-proof and IP68 dust and waterproof. Connectivity is also impressive with Bluetooth 6.0, Auracast, 7-band app EQ, and clever pairing (where you bump two Go 5s together to create a stereo pair).
It’s speakers like this that remind me just how we’ve come since the days of sticking my phone in a mug to amplify the tiny built-in speaker. If only I knew where my daughter had put it.

I’m happy to admit when I’m wrong, and for a few years, I dismissed Marshall’s mini guitar amp aesthetic as a good looking gimmick. But having spent time with the Kilburn III, I hold my hands up. It’s not "serious" hi-fi, but the design and attention to detail—the tactile, spring-loaded, knurled metal power lever, and illuminated control knobs are a joy—stand apart. It just looks fantastic, and with 50 watts of power and 50 hours of playtime, it plays loud and long. I love being able to charge devices from the speaker’s USB-C port too.
Marshall does not include the charger needed for the fastest recharge, which is a bit annoying, although most laptop users will have one already. There’s no stereo pairing option either, but I find it hard to imagine needing two of these in the size of room it’s designed for.
In his Marshall Kilburn III review, reviewer Simon Cohen was ebullient about the speaker’s performance, and I agree. It’s loud enough for small- to medium-sized rooms, and cut through when used outdoors, with weighty bass, decent balance, and no obvious distortion when pushed. The 360-degree presentation spreads music evenly too, so it feels less directional than many rivals.

Paying $250 for a portable Bluetooth speaker is hard to justify if all you need is something loud enough for a picnic blanket, but the Kef Muo feels more like a compact hi-fi component. The seamless aluminum body is beautifully tactile and flawless, although it looks almost identical to the model they first launched in 2015. Maybe I’m just feeling old because I remember that launch like it was yesterday.
While the Muo is getting on a bit aesthetically, its connectivity is bang up to date. The drivers have been rebuilt around a new racetrack-shaped 2.5 x 5-inch mid/bass driver, paired with a 0.74-inch (19mm) tweeter and 40W of Class D amplification. A neat pleated edge to the drivers does brilliant things to the bass too, which is beyond impressive given the size.
Audio quality is seriously impressive here and you may be surprised by how often you reach for it. I heartily recommend plugging in a hi-res streaming (24-bit/48 kHz) source via USB-C and enjoying all the speaker has to offer.
The app is a basic affair, and some might lament the speaker’s lack of Wi-Fi, but with IP67 protection and 24-hour battery life it’s a great buy when fidelity matters.
Best Party Bluetooth Speaker
Specs
| Battery Life | Up to 25 hours | 
| Dust/Water Resistance | IPX4 | 
| Connectivity | Bluetooth 6.1, USB-C audio, USB-A, 3.5-mm aux input, two 6.3-mm mic inputs | 
| Special Features | AI Karaoke, AI Lighting, app EQ and DJ effects, Auracast, multipoint, replaceable battery | 
| Dimensions | 11.73 x 23.38 x 11.56 inches | 
| Weight | 25.79 pounds | 
Part of LG’s xboom collaboration with producer, Black Eyed Peas star, and tech obsessive will.i.am, the Stage 501 is a mighty 25.8-pound party starter. Its 2.2-channel setup combines twin 5.25-inch woofers with two 2.5-inch full-range drivers. Together they’re capable of 160 watts on battery or 220 watts plugged in. In simpler terms: It easily filled a huge workshop space with rave-ready bass, and enough volume for a proper party.
What surprised me more than the party capabilities was that it also sounds acceptable at low volume in my office. I was expecting a pint-sized PA system, but dialled back to casual listening volume and it remained composed. Often, speakers designed for loud really struggle with quiet, and just sound muddy, but that wasn’t the case here. Yes, it prefers it when people are dancing, but it manages well when you’re chilling out too.
The xboom app is excellent, with EQ, AI Karaoke, synchronized lighting, and some cheesy but irresistible DJ punch buttons. LG has also included two very sensible smartphone/tablet stands that position your device at the perfect angle for karaoke nights. It comes with two mic inputs, but you will need to buy microphones separately.
Battery life is “up to” 25 hours, and the battery itself is replaceable. It’s big, and not as grown-up sounding as the Soundbox Mix, but it is cheaper and has a surprisingly good LED light show feature that I expected to hate, but didn’t. Party on dudes.
Honorable Mentions
Bang & Olufsen Beosound A1 (Gen 3) for $399: Gorgeously designed, flawlessly finished, and one of the most covetable Bluetooth speakers around. The brushed aluminum puck has barely changed since 2016, which says plenty about the strength of Cecilie Manz’s original design. The latest version adds a richer, more powerful 360-degree sound from its 3.25-inch woofer, 0.6-inch tweeter, and 60 watts of amplification. It is IP67 rated, lasts up to 24 hours, and is appreciably more repairable and upgradable. I love it, but it’s just a little too expensive when the KEF Muo exists and sounds as good as it does.
Soundboks Mix for $799: The 21.4-pound Soundboks Mix is tremendously loud, with a 10-inch woofer, 1.2-inch tweeter, and 40-hour replaceable battery. WIRED writer Parker Hall measured 111 decibels from a meter away, and was surprised at how musical it remained rather than just battering you with volume. IP65 protection, sturdy handles, and rubberized tennis-ball style corners make it particularly well suited to outdoor parties. It’s expensive and heavy compared to the new breed of party speakers from brands like LG and Sony, but it is superb at what it does.
JBL Charge 6 for $150: It’s just too big to be our absolute favorite Bluetooth speaker, but it was a close run thing between two superb JBL options. The great sound and portability of the Flip 7 won out, but the 40 watts from the Charge 6 deliver more bass and scale, while maintaining detail. Battery life stretches to 24 hours, and you also get IP68 protection, Auracast, app EQ, USB-C lossless playback, and reverse charging. Currently on sale too, making it a real bargain at $150.
Bose SoundLink Plus for $269: Sitting neatly between Bose’s little Flex and chunky Max, the Bose SoundLink Plus weighs 3.37 pounds but produces surprisingly substantial sound, with excellent detail, robust bass, and plenty of power without any rawness at volume. IP67 protection is solid, the 20-hour battery is replaceable, and it can also charge your phone over USB-C. There’s multipoint Bluetooth, app EQ, stereo pairing, and aptX Adaptive for Android too. It takes an irritating five hours to recharge, however. Bose could do with a refresh soon, as the competition has caught up with them.
Sonos Roam 2 for $179: The Sonos Roam 2 is a superb little speaker and if the hugely versatile Sonos Play didn’t exist, it would be one of my top picks. It lacks a bit of punch and scale compared to the larger option, but can still be connected over Wi-Fi or Bluetooth, so it remains ideal at home, in the garden, or out and about. IP67 protection means beach sand and bathroom splashes aren’t a concern. Battery life is a meager 10 hours, though, and it costs considerably more than similarly sized Bluetooth-only rivals, but if you’re a Sonos fan, you won’t be disappointed.
Ultimate Ears Megaboom 4 for $200: If you don’t mind something a bit large, the 9-inch tall Megaboom 4 is one of the best outdoor speakers you can get, according to former WIRED writer Ryan Waniata. It blasts sound in 360-degrees, with enough bass in every direction to please most listeners. It’s also IP67 dust and waterproof, and it floats, making it especially suited to pool and beach days. Like other Ultimate Ears speakers, you can pair multiple Megaboom 4s together through the app and adjust settings like EQ.
Beats Pill for $150: Remember the Beats Pill? WIRED loved the revived 2024 model when it launched, and it remains an excellent choice if you’re wedded to Apple’s ecosystem. You get one-touch pairing, Find My support, and a friction-free setup Apple does so well. Android gets similarly easy pairing and Find My Device support too. Sound is unmistakably Beats, with crisp treble, impressive clarity, and a whole pile of bass, although there’s still no EQ adjustability (you need to use your streaming service’s settings) to tame some occasional brightness. The 24-hour battery, IP67 protection, reverse USB-C charging, lossless playback over USB-C, and stereo pairing keep it competitive, especially since it’s often on sale.

Washington Spirit sign Luvanga - but is it a record deal?
- Published
Tanzanian striker Clara Luvanga has joined the Washington Spirit from Saudi Arabian club Al-Nassr in a deal believed to be one of the most costly in the history of women's football.
The fee paid by the National Women's Soccer League side has not been officially disclosed.
Some are reporting it to be $2.3m, external (about £1.7m), which would make Luvanga the most expensive female footballer in history.
BBC Sport has not been able to verify this figure, although a well-placed source said they believed it ranked in the top five most expensive signings in the women's game.
The Spirit declined to comment on the fee involved when contacted by BBC Sport.
Luvanga, 21, has signed a contract running to the end of the 2029 NWSL season.
If the reported record figure is correct, it would mean the fee passes the £1.4m that London City Lionesses are said to have paid to Paris St-Germain for Grace Geyoro last year.
However, the Geyoro fee has been disputed, further illustrating how transfer figures in the women's game are often kept private.
With her move, Luvanga becomes the first Tanzanian player in NWSL history.
Luvanga won the Saudi Women's Premier League in all three of her seasons with Al-Nassr, as well as the Saudi Women's Cup, Saudi Women's Super Cup and West Asian Football Federation (WAFF) Women's Clubs Championship.
She also claimed the league's golden boot last season after scoring 24 goals in 14 appearances.
The Washington Spirit are owned by Michele Kang, who also owns London City Lionesses.
London City made a series of high-profile signings during the summer transfer window, including two-time Ballon d'Or winner Alexia Putellas who arrived from Barcelona on a three-year deal.
Luvanga made her senior international debut for Tanzania in 2024. Before joining Al-Nassr in 2023, she played for DUX Logrono in Spain, having developed through the youth system at Tanzanian club Yanga Princess.
When discussing her new club, Luvanga said: "I am very excited to join the Washington Spirit and to take on this new challenge in the NWSL.
"I know I am arriving with the season already under way, but I'm really excited to play in a new league and a new country."
Spirit sporting director James Hocken said: "Clara adds an exciting new dimension to our attack as we head toward the play-offs.
"Despite her young age, she has demonstrated the ability to score goals in different ways and has the profile to be very successful in this league."
Inspired by Ronaldo, dancing her way to the top - analysis
Luvanga's rise from Tanzania to one of the world's most competitive women's football leagues has been remarkably rapid.
She began her career with Yanga Princess in her native country before her big international breakthrough came in August 2023, when she joined Spanish side DUX Logrono. But Spain was only a brief stop on her career journey.
By October of that year, Luvanga headed for Saudi Arabia to join Al-Nassr, a move that would prove transformative for her career.
Over three seasons in the Middle East, she helped Al-Nassr win the Saudi Women's Premier League title each time, establishing herself as one of the division's most prolific forwards.
Her time at Al-Nassr also provided an opportunity to meet one of football's biggest stars, Cristiano Ronaldo, who plays for Al-Nassr's men's team. Luvanga has spoken about modelling aspects of her own career on the Portuguese forward.
"The focus and determination that he has, when you look at his life, I wish to live like that," she told BBC Sport Africa in 2025.
There is another side to the Tanzanian forward that goes beyond the goals.
Her former team-mate at Al-Nassr, goalkeeper Sara Khalid Al-Dossary, described Luvanga to BBC Sport Africa as a great player and colleague but also revealed another of her talents: she is a great dancer.
Now Luvanga is taking both her football and her personality to the United States.
Her move to the Washington Spirit makes her the first Tanzanian woman to play in the NWSL, another significant milestone in the internationalisation of Tanzanian women's football.
She will also enter a dressing room containing a sizeable African contingent, with the Washington Spirit's roster now featuring seven African internationals.
For all her success at club level, Luvanga has not enjoyed the same impact in Tanzania colours at senior international level. Her 12 goals for Tanzania have come at youth level — 10 for the U-17 side and two for the U-20 team, while fitness problems have limited her involvement around the past two Women's Africa Cup of Nations campaigns.

Assam man, 23, held for rape, murder of woman over alleged affair: Police
The officer said that victim’s body was sent to Assam Medical College and Hospital (AMCH), Dibrugarh for postmortem
A 23-year-old tea garden worker from Assam’s Dibrugarh district was arrested for allegedly raping and strangling a 22-year-old woman over an alleged illicit affair, police said on Sunday.
The woman, who went missing on Friday morning, was recovered from an abandoned pit in Chabua area on Saturday afternoon, and police detained the accused later.
“As per the initial investigation, the woman was sexually assaulted and strangled to death before her body was thrown into an abandoned pit,” officers said, adding that the accused was known to her and they were allegedly having an affair.
The woman, a mother of a two-year-old boy, separated from her husband nearly a year ago and was staying separately in the Chabua area of Dibrugarh.
Police said she had been missing since Friday morning and her family members reported it at the Chabua police station the same day. “A search operation was launched based on the complaint and her body was found on Saturday,” officers said.
Victim’s family members later lodged a first information report (FIR) against Sumit Kalandi (23), who according to them was in contact with her for several months.
“He was forcing her to stay with him but she was not ready because she had just separated and was raising a little kid. They used to fight and when she went missing, we informed the police about it,” family members said on Saturday.
Police said they detained Kalandi after recovering the body, and he later confessed to the crime. “He said they were having a relationship but she was also keeping contact with others, which is why he killed her,” a senior police officer said.
He said that Kalandi has been arrested for rape, murder, kidnap and other charges and the matter is under investigation.
The officer said that victim’s body was sent to Assam Medical College and Hospital (AMCH), Dibrugarh for postmortem on Saturday and they are waiting for the report.

Games may be life with all the hard bits removed, but they provide a way to study why people make the choices they make. Traditional games are usually played against a static background: the rewards per outcome are constant. That limits their relevance to behavior because, in real life, the rewards and consequences of strategic choices are ever changing. Now, researchers have used a mathematical model to study a series of games that include evolving strategies and randomly varying returns.
A bit of history
Perhaps the most famous game-theory contest is the prisoner’s dilemma. In the prisoner’s dilemma, a pair of thieves have been captured and are being separately interrogated by the police. If both clam up, they will be punished for a lesser crime. If one prisoner makes a deal (defects) then that prisoner gets to go free and the other gets a heavier sentence. If both make a deal, they both get an in-between punishment.
The person running the game can start it with different rewards for cooperating and defecting to explore how the optimum strategy varies with reward and risk, which the players can figure out by varying the strategies across multiple rounds. Depending on the balance between the reward for staying silent (cooperating) and betrayal, the game stabilizes with everyone betraying everyone. In this simple situation, everyone loses.
Similar dynamics can be found in games of chicken, rock-paper-scissors, and more. The evolution of strategies can lead to stable populations, bistable populations (where the population flips between two stable strategies), or limit cycles, where the population shifts continuously among multiple strategies.
There is also a rich history of changing a game as it is played. Usually, these are within-game variations. For instance, you can set a limit on the amount of reward available, so strategies evolve to take into account increasingly limited resources as the number of rounds goes up. In other words, most of this older work studied situations where the player’s behavior in the current round changed the resources or rewards available for the next round.

The Chinese president, Xi Jinping, has received a red-carpet welcome in India for a summit of Brics developing nations, as regional rivals Beijing and Delhi make a public display of thawing relations while quietly competing to lead at a time of shaky US global dominance.
As Xi stepped off the plane, he was walked past an honour guard of Indian soldiers and traditional dancers in colourful dresses.
The Russian president, Vladimir Putin, and Iranian president, Masoud Pezeshkian, had already been welcomed by the Indian prime minister, Narendra Modi, who is hosting one of the group’s most closely watched gatherings since its inception.
The summit marks Xi’s first visit to India in seven years and is seen as the biggest step towards reconciliation after a deadly 2020 military clash along the disputed Himalayan border, in which 20 Indian and four Chinese soldiers were killed.
Ties between the nuclear-armed Asian giants have been warming recently, with flights and high-level contacts gradually being restored. China was “willing” to work with India to properly manage differences and be “good neighbours and friends”, China’s foreign ministry said on Friday.
Leaders and diplomats have been convening in India for the annual gathering of the Brics grouping, named after five of its earliest members – Brazil, Russia, India, China and South Africa – that was conceived as a counterweight to western dominance.
This summit comes as wars in Ukraine and the Middle East, along with rising US-China tensions, test the bloc’s ability to find common ground.
Since its inception in 2009, Brics has expanded as a forum for major emerging economies to include Egypt, Ethiopia, Indonesia, Iran, Saudi Arabia and the United Arab Emirates (UAE). The group now rivals the US-dominated G7 forum of advanced economies, accounting for half of the global population.
But its growth has also created new fractures and disunity – Iran was bombing Saudi Arabia and the UAE earlier this year, and Brics foreign ministers failed to agree on a joint statement when they met in Delhi in May.
Reuters reported on Saturday that India’s summit would result in a generic joint declaration that would show unity by condemning unilateral war, but was unlikely to name any single country.
Jiang Shixue, vice-president of the expert committee of the China thinktank Council for BRICs cooperation (China), said the 11 members “cannot speak with one voice on many issues”.
“The only solution is to continuously strengthen political consensus,” he told the South China Morning Post.
Beijing and Delhi have differing views on the role of the group.
China has sought to expand Brics power as a counterweight to the US under Donald Trump’s leadership, which has launched global tariff and trade wars and retreated from multilateral institutions such as the UN, which afforded it international credibility.
India has taken a more cautious approach, seeing Brics as a bridge between the west and the developing world.
Chietigj Bajpaee, a senior research fellow for South Asia in the Asia-Pacific programme at Chatham House, said this week that Delhi had found it hard to maintain its policy of “strategic hedging” during such a disruptive US presidency.
“India’s position can appear out of sync in a forum whose membership includes countries with more overtly anti-western agendas, including China, Russia and Iran. And two other Brics countries, South Africa and Brazil, have suffered high-profile diplomatic disputes with the US,” he wrote.
“The challenge for Delhi is that it wishes to promote this worldview in a way that is non-western but not explicitly anti-western.”
Agence France-Presse contributed to this report

Malaysian boy acquitted for murder of schoolgirl on grounds of insanity
- Published
A Malaysian teenage boy charged with the high-profile murder of a female schoolmate has been acquitted, with the judge finding the boy was mentally unsound during the incident.
He had fatally stabbed Yap Shing Xuen in a toilet at their secondary school on the outskirts of the capital Kuala Lumpur.
The killing of the 16-year-old girl had shocked Malaysia and sparked debate about the effects of social media on children.
Police previously had said they suspected social media could have influenced the boy, who was 14 at the time. The case was seen to have spurred authorities to limit children's access to social media, which began earlier this year.
The boy - who cannot be named under Malaysian law as he is still a minor - had pleaded not guilty to the murder charge.
During the trial defence lawyers did not deny that the boy killed the girl, but argued that he had suffered from poor mental health for years and asked for his acquittal on the grounds of insanity.
An expert witness, a psychiatrist, testified that the boy had schizophrenia, and had suffered from mental illness and experienced delusions since he was nine years old.
The boy's condition was said to have worsened during the pandemic and when he eventually returned to school. Lawyers had said that the boy would need medication for the rest of his life to manage symptoms.
On Monday the judge ruled that the boy would be acquitted, but also ordered for him to be detained and to receive treatment at a psychiatric hospital.
He will stay at the hospital until he is deemed fit to be released back to society, and would likely be subject to yearly assessments.
A defence lawyer told reporters on Monday that upon hearing the verdict, the boy appeared "neutral in emotion, but he understands what is going on, [that] it's a very serious matter".
The trial and verdict hearings were held in a closed court, which meant that the public and media could not attend.
- Malaysian boy on trial for allegedly murdering girl in school 
  - Published3 August
The case has profoundly shocked Malaysia and sparked a nationwide conversation about the negative effects of social media on children.
Much of this conversation was triggered by the contents of a note that police had found on the boy at the time of his arrest, which was leaked online and widely circulated.
Some people had compared the case to the Netflix series Adolescence, which featured a storyline about a young boy killing a female schoolmate and explored the theme of online radicalisation.
Last year, the country's Prime Minister Anwar Ibrahim was asked about the case as well as other recent cases of violence in schools.
He was quoted by local media as saying that "almost all of these issues stem from the use of mobile phones and social media", and vowed to look into stricter measures.
Authorities have since put in place new rules which they say will protect children and reduce their exposure to harmful online content.
Since June, Malaysia has banned all children under the age of 16 from having accounts on major social media platforms.
Additional reporting by Diyana Nawwar

On April 12, 1955, America threw a vaccine party.
That morning, Thomas Francis Jr. — who had overseen trials of polio vaccines developed by Jonas Salk — held a press conference to announce the results.
Only it wasn’t a press conference. It was an event.
Reporters packed the room. Tens of thousands of physicians gathered in movie theaters to hear the broadcast. Millions of Americans huddled around their radios.
The verdict: The vaccine worked. A disease that had devastated families for decades had finally met its match.
A documentary describes the reaction: “Factory whistles blew, school children cheered, parents wept.” Newspapers ran headlines like “POLIO IS CONQUERED” across their front pages. Store owners wrote “Thank you, Dr. Salk” messages on their windows. Salk took the stage at the press conference to a prolonged standing ovation, on his way to becoming a living legend.
Fast forward 71 years, to 2026.
On Sept. 2, major medical societies released an independent research evaluation covering flu, Covid-19, and RSV shots. There was another press conference, and more good news: These vaccines are still safe and continue to provide strong protection against death and severe illness.
But this was no event.
Experts talked about “informed decisions” and “shared commitment” and “restoring trust.” The American Medical Association launched a new website with JAMA articles and PDF charts, but no real people or stories. The tone was somber, the mood dour.
So much for a party.
As a communications consultant, I have spent years supporting vaccine advocates. Every conversation right now feels bleak. Measles has come roaring back. Vaccination rates keep dropping. The Centers for Disease Control and Prevention is a wreck. Robert F. Kennedy Jr., the ringleader of the country’s vaccine critics, is somehow still in charge of the Department of Health and Human Services.
For the pro-vaccine side, this is all excruciating. We spend our days debunking and fact-checking. We debate repeatedly whether to confront wellness influencers or engage them. We search endlessly for just the right analogy or metaphor to reach the hesitant parent.
We take vaccines really, really seriously. As we should. It’s a matter of life and death.
Somewhere along the way, though, we forgot how to celebrate. We are sorely lacking in optimism and excitement. There’s no sense of togetherness or belonging. We’ve gotten wound up so tightly that there’s no joy in what we’re doing.
We need to remember how to have fun again.
Consider how Children’s Health Defense, the organization Kennedy previously led, rallies people to its cause. This group is deceitful and dangerous. But it knows how to build a movement.
They fight for “health freedom.” Their volunteers are “defenders” who join an “army of truth.” They hold banners and make street signs. They host book clubs and movie screenings. They sell merch. They encourage people to “grab a couple friends” on the first Saturday of every month and go around debating opponents.
Right now, no pro-vaccine equivalent comes close to matching that energy. Which is a crying shame, because that’s exactly what’s worked for us in the past.
Francis’ press conference in 1955 was the culmination of a movement that had been building for years. More than 1.8 million children participated in Salk’s vaccine trials. They were known as “polio pioneers.” Each received a keepsake card, which many kept for decades. Moms and dads across the country rallied Americans to contribute research donations. Millions did so.
The campaign paid off. Less than a decade after that national vaccine party, cases of polio in the U.S. dropped by 97%.
We experienced a similar surge in vaccine enthusiasm during the pandemic. I received my first Covid vaccine in the parking lot of a Six Flags amusement park; everyone honked their horns after getting a shot. On social media, people posted vaccine selfies and wore “I got vaccinated” stickers. States got creative with all sorts of financial incentives, from million-dollar prizes to college scholarships. Major League Baseball offered free tickets to games.
Once again, the campaign paid off. Covid vaccines saved millions of lives.
Of course, this time, the enthusiasm didn’t last. The ensuing backlash to Covid vaccines seems to have convinced the pro-vaccine side to become more cautious, more restrained, and more clinical in our approach.
Problem is, we’ve learned the wrong lesson.
To increase vaccination rates, we need to match our seriousness of purpose with a renewed spirit of possibility. We need to give people who support vaccination — and those who aren’t sure — something to get excited about and a team they feel good about joining.
That should start with how we talk about vaccines. One thing I never see in any vaccination messaging guide is an exclamation point. Vaccines are incredible! They do amazing things! Let’s try getting people fired up for a change!
It should also include incentive programs for vaccinations. Evidence from the pandemic was mixed, but these programs showed more than enough potential to warrant additional exploration.
But the biggest opportunity lies in building our team. Think of everything we could do with just one vaccination clinic. Much as election officials recruit volunteer poll workers, health departments could recruit volunteers to staff information tables. Cities could match volunteers with older residents who need rides. Civic groups could “adopt” a clinic and bring food and swag. Schools could provide service learning hours to students who lend a hand.
Our side will always stand up for science, data, and facts. But some of the best vaccine pushes in history were marked by factory whistles blaring, car horns honking, and people cheering for a cause bigger than themselves.
It’s gotten far too quiet on the pro-vaccine side. Let’s start making some noise again.
Adam Zimmerman is a public health communications consultant.

CBS News is getting employees hyped about the first full season of "60 Minutes" under top editor Bari Weiss, months after a string of high-profile exits.
"We don't often send notes to the whole newsroom. But today calls for it. It's a big moment for 60 Minutes and CBS," newsroom leaders, including Weiss, wrote about the new "60 Minutes" season in a memo sent to staffers on Sunday.
The memo teases an interview — that "everyone has been chasing" — with a US Air Force officer who was rescued from Iran in April.
The 59th season of "60 Minutes" will have 10 regular contributors, including five correspondents: Lesley Stahl, Bill Whitaker, Jon Wertheim, Norah O'Donnell, and Ross Douthat, who joined CBS from The New York Times in July.
"60 Minutes" is kicking off its highly anticipated season following a turbulent early-summer stretch for the storied news program.
Lead producer Nick Bilton, who was handpicked by Weiss in May, started his tenure by firing longtime correspondent Scott Pelley after a noisy confrontation in front of "60 Minutes" staffers.
Pelley had publicly questioned Bilton's qualifications, pressed his new boss on why fellow correspondents Cecilia Vega and Sharyn Alfonsi were let go, and accused Weiss of "murdering" the iconic Sunday night telecast while trying to "kill" CBS News.
Weiss later addressed the firing, telling staffers she's "only interested in working in a newsroom that is built on trust and mutual respect." Bilton told "60 Minutes" employees that his first week had been "a trying and difficult few days."
Veteran correspondents Whitaker, Wertheim, and Stahl — who's been with "60" since 1991 — decided to return to the program, saying that they "don't want to see 60 Minutes die." They said they're "working to build trust" with Bilton and "heard all the right things" in his memo.
"If we can continue doing the work that made this show what it is — committing acts of independent, fearless journalism and storytelling — we're here for it. If not, we leave," Stahl, Whitaker, and Wertheim wrote in their memo.
Read the full memo sent to CBS News staffers here:
All -- 
We don't often send notes to the whole newsroom. But today calls for it. It's a big moment for 60 Minutes and CBS.
Ahead of our premiere, we wanted to congratulate the team on the launch of what will be an exciting season—and to thank everyone across the CBS newsroom.
Tonight's episode is a powerful start with three original, revelatory stories that showcase 60 at its best. We begin with the interview everyone has been chasing. Then, a hidden camera investigation and a profile of a NFL superteam's wunderkind coach. We also have a cameo from one of our new correspondents on the story of our time: AI.
We are deeply thankful to everyone across CBS News for the support over this summer. That especially goes for social, digital, graphics, marketing, and, above all, the investigative unit.
Last but not least: You've probably seen the great "It's Time" campaign everywhere. That push continues through tonight's game. We'd be grateful if you can spread the word to your friends and followers by sharing these promos today.
This is just the start and there's so much more to come. See you tonight at 7:30pm!
Nick, Bari, and Tom

Rules Designed to Create Chaos
The Trump administration is hoping to put so many restrictions on mail-in balloting that people simply won’t be able to vote that way at all.
Donald Trump hates mail-in voting. He has described it as “dangerous,” “corrupt,” “horrible,” and “a fraud.” Last year, in a Truth Social post festooned with capital letters and exclamation points, he announced that he would be signing an executive order to do away with mail-in ballots entirely. That order never materialized, possibly because the president has absolutely no legal authority to carry out such a ban. The federal government plays only a small role in administering elections, and the Constitution locates those authorities with Congress, not the president.
But now, with some ballots already heading to voters as the midterms draw near, the Trump administration is waging another fight against voting by mail, this time through its control over the U.S. Postal Service. Trump’s plan wouldn’t outright prohibit mail-in voting but would throw so many wrenches into the machinery that it could grind to a halt. Federal courts at both the district and appellate levels have blocked the rule, and now the Supreme Court is in the process of weighing whether to allow this effort to move forward before the midterms; it could make a decision as soon as later today. If the justices let USPS take these steps in the coming weeks, the risk, the election-law expert Rick Hasen told me, is “mass disenfranchisement.”
Historically, the Postal Service has simply mailed every ballot provided by state and local election officials. But in a March executive order, Trump directed USPS to develop a new plan that would erect a series of hoops for election workers to jump through before a ballot can be sent to an expectant voter. If the rule goes into effect, USPS will require state and local jurisdictions to obtain federal sign-off on the design of the envelope and then mark each ballot envelope with barcodes. States must also upload a full list of every voter receiving a mail ballot to a so-called federal ballot mail portal. Only then, once USPS cross-checks the barcodes with the voter list in the portal, will the ballot be delivered.
In the abstract, this might sound inoffensive. But the process is so hopelessly tangled that it seems almost designed to fail. Take the portal, which is still not online. On September 3—a week ago—the Postal Service stated in a court filing that the website would be ready “by sometime next week.” Even if the portal were functional, it might not operate fairly. A whistleblower recently filed a disclosure warning that the Postal Service is planning to use the system with a “zero percent failure rate.” USPS will scan ballots in large batches, the whistleblower says, and if a single ballot fails to match the uploaded list of voters, none of the ballots in the batch will be mailed.
Election rules take a long time to change, and states begin preparing the polls long before Election Day. When Trump announced the order, in March, experts did not immediately think that the midterms would be affected. “I had assumed that this was going to be put on hold” until after November, Hasen said. But USPS quickly began putting together the detailed plans requested by the White House, even though the order itself faced multiple legal challenges and was racking up court judgments against it. (Another section of the executive order directed the Department of Homeland Security to produce a mechanism by which states can review “citizenship lists” of potential voters. DHS has yet to provide these lists, and the nonprofit Electronic Privacy Information Center recently sued to block the agency from compiling and distributing them.)
The Supreme Court ruled on August 24 that the executive order’s challengers had gone to court too soon, before USPS’s plans were far enough along. Now the Postal Service claims that its work is ready—mostly—to be rolled out, if the justices will let it.
The court dockets are crammed with statements by election experts and state and local officials explaining all of the different problems created by the rule. In their breadth and variety, these declarations are a reminder of just how big the United States is, and how many people must work together across multiple states and levels of government to pull off a successful election season. Hawaii has spent more than $79,000 printing ballot envelopes, the state’s chief election officer wrote in one filing; he worried that if officials need to order new envelopes, they may not arrive from the continental U.S. in time for the election. Rhode Island’s deputy secretary of state explained that the state’s laws regulating ballot-envelope design effectively prohibit officials from affixing the two barcodes required by USPS. In Wisconsin, some rural jurisdictions may not have the ability to print the required barcodes, the chair of the Wisconsin Elections Commission said. The elections director in Oregon, which conducts all of the state’s elections completely by mail, worried that the state’s “aging” computer systems are not equipped to efficiently upload 3 million voters’ personal information into the USPS portal. “If the system fails,” she wrote, “Oregon may be unable to mail ballots to voters at all.”
Election officials who have long relied on the Postal Service are now thinking through alternatives. Cisco Aguilar, Nevada’s secretary of state, told me that he has reached out to private mail carriers about delivering ballots in a pinch. “We got a quote from UPS of about eight bucks per ballot, which is about three dollars more than we pay the Postal Service,” he said. “With 2.1 million ballots in Nevada, that’s a pretty significant expense.” Nevada sends mail-in ballots to voters by default, and mail-in voting is popular: 60 percent of Nevadans voted by mail in the state’s primary elections, Aguilar said. Now his office is figuring out how to communicate clearly with voters who may be alarmed or confused if USPS refuses to mail Nevada’s ballots. “Do we just start to message, Hey, just skip the mail ballot altogether and show up in person?”
Experts are hoping that the Supreme Court takes these concerns seriously. Because of the emergency status of the litigation, the justices can consider not just the legality of the federal government’s actions but also the “equities”—that is, the potential harms suffered by each side depending on how the Court rules. There are strong legal arguments that the administration has no authority to put such a program in place. (Perhaps tellingly, the federal government has been reduced to arguing that the Post Office can impose requirements for mailing ballots in the same way that it can put safeguards in place for mailing cremated human remains.) On the equities, though, the matter seems particularly stark. If the Supreme Court allows the policy to go into effect, the outcome could be catastrophic. But if the policy remains blocked, what is the harm to the federal government? The administration’s briefs make little attempt to answer this question other than vague insinuations about voter fraud.
Then again, a victory at the Court wouldn’t appear to gain much for the administration, either. If the goal is partisan sabotage, there is little reason to think that the USPS plan would help Republicans. “If this actually happens, the burden is going to fall hardest on the most vulnerable of our voters—the elderly, the disabled, rural voters, voters on reservations, voters in the military,” Hasen said. Older voters and rural Americans have tended to be reliable GOP constituencies, and in a season when the Republican Party is struggling to build up voter enthusiasm, there is a real risk that inconvenienced voters who never receive a ballot will simply stay home. Democrats furious with Trump, meanwhile, may be more motivated to find a way to the polls.
Still, the widespread confusion that the USPS rule would inevitably create may have its own appeal to the White House. A group of election officials, including several Republican secretaries of state, warned in an amicus brief before the Supreme Court that “a chaotic election erodes confidence in the result.” For a president long obsessed with undermining Americans’ trust in elections, perhaps that’s victory enough.

The Best Mushroom Coffee
Featured in this article
The world has been addicted to caffeine for centuries, and in the year 2026, the scientific argument over whether coffee is good or bad for you remains unsettled. One might believe the lack of consensus is a Mainstream Media™ psyop to keep people scrambling for marketable solutions to a problem that’s completely made up, but the cottage industry of coffee alternatives that’s proliferated during this endless tug of war is an interesting outcome regardless of which side you’re on. This is where mushroom coffee makes its inevitable entrance.
Some quick googling revealed the known players in the game, all of which offer their own riff on a common base formula of dried mushrooms–usually a combo of lion’s mane, chaga, and cordyceps—boosted with buzzy add-ons like probiotics and nootropics. I spent a week with each, including our top pick, Atlas Coffee Club’s Latte Superblend ($26), swapping out my morning coffee for each brand's recommended dose of powder and hot water. After day five I allowed myself to experiment with sweeteners and milks, which you’ll need with almost all of these to get through the entire cup without gagging.
Some hit like a mild cup of coffee, some were actual coffee, and others were uncanny concoctions no normal person would ever crave unless they were fully indoctrinated in the heady lifestyle this unique alt-beverage industry revolves around. I laughed, I cried, I got the runs, and I crashed on my couch in the early afternoon more times than I could count, all for science, and all so you don’t have to try this on your own.
Be sure to check out our other coffee and caffeinated coverage, including the Best Coffee Subscriptions, Best Coffee Makers, Best Energy Drinks, and Best Electric Kettles.
Updated September 2026: We've added new mushroom coffees from Wunderground, Bullet Proof, and Vahdam; moved some previous picks to honorable mentions; and ensured up-to-date links and prices.
Love WIRED? Add us as a preferred source on Google to see more of us.
Others Tested
Lifeboost Mindflow for $45: The flavor of this instant powder is snappy and astringent at first, then it mellows into a warm middle ground after a few sips and a short cooling period. By the middle of the cup I forgot I was drinking something other than coffee, and the mild acidity on the finish–likely a product of the CognatiQ Coffee Fruit Extract that’s lauded on the back of Mindflow’s mylar pouch–tastes similar to a nice cup of Ethiopian or Rwandan coffee if you close your eyes and pretend for just a moment. Regarding its potency, if mushroom supplements were attendees at a state college keg party, Lifeboost would be the unremarkable guy pacing himself in the back while everyone else is getting blitzed like the world is ending. It’s unassuming yet self-assured, patiently waiting for all other entrants to crap out so it can make its move. I copped a mild buzz just a few sips in, and I felt alert and wide-eyed for a good two hours after the silty final sips of the cup were consumed. Electrolytes are uncommon in this space, which means this is a rare entry in the mushroom supplement world that purports to be a good pick if hydration is a trivial concern.
Four Sigmatic Organic Coffee for $20: Four Sigmatic’s Focus blend is labeled as a dark roast, but it’s missing the cigarette-butts-and-bowling-alley aftertaste that looms on the finish of similar blends. Despite my preference for lighter beans, this hit like a hug from an old friend after weeks of sipping murky silt. The caffeine buzz normalized after two days of using Think in lieu of more standard shroom-based coffee replacements, so I added a three-quarter-teaspoon hit of the powdered Focus blend to my daily cup to see what would happen. Within 10 minutes I felt an overwhelming urge to sort my finances spreadsheet in preparation for tax season, then I set up a new template in Loopy Pro to accommodate a friend who planned to join my basement jam session that evening. He bailed, but I was jacked on Genius Adaptogens so I played all the instruments myself into the wee hours of the night.
Terrasoul Superfoods Sun Alchemy Cognitive Coffee for $15: Sun Alchemy plays directly to the interests of busy professionals who only recently stopped using the #riseandgrind tag on their LinkedIn posts, with a greatest hits collection of buzzy adjuncts punctuating the top of its ingredient list. Fans of the bulletproof coffee craze will love the addition of MCT oil and organic coconut milk powder, while mushroomheads of all stripes will find the blend of mushrooms in the sachet to be standard and proper. The package recommends a frothing wand for stirring, but I tried whipping this up in a Wawa with hot water and a stir stick to see if it might be a good fit for a haggard road warrior like me. A fair amount of sediment remained in the bottom of the cup in both scenarios, rendering the last sip or two basically undrinkable. Until that point, this is a totally fine drink, with prominent notes of medium-roast pre-ground grocery store coffee, a light tickle of coconut on the finish, and a sharp, mildly bitter nose a newbie might dislike but a lifelong coffee addict will find endearing.
Everyday Dose Premium Adaptogenic Mushroom Coffee for $40: One month of this fantastical dust promises better sleep and boosted mood. Two months promises a healthy gut, and three months promises glowing skin and boosted immunity. It’s easy to acquire three months of Everyday Dose because its subscription-only model is damn near impossible to cancel. It’s difficult to drink this daily for even a week, though, but best of luck if a guy with an alpha jawline and yacht full o’ thots in Croatia told you otherwise! Unlike MUD/WTR (below), which seems to be the closest analog as far as aesthetics and cheekiness go, Everyday Dose boasts a wee bit of caffeine, which is appealing for coffee addicts like yours truly. I first mixed 1 tablespoon of the powder with 8 ounces of hot water and drank it straight up, which yielded an unappetizing liquid that tasted like a mix of Chex Mix and bong water. Some frothed oat milk and a squirt of simple syrup turned out to be the most drinkable form, but I’d be lying if I said I enjoyed any of it.
Om Master Blend Organic Mushroom Powder for $20: The bulk of Om’s catalog is billed as “dietary supplements,” so its Master Blend is not exactly the kind of thing you’ll want to drink on its own. I tried this for science, of course, and it wasn’t terrible! There’s a vegetal flavor on the sip that tastes like potato water, and the finish has an astringent tingle that’s akin to the tiniest dose of Sichuan peppercorns steeped in hot water. Om really shines when it’s added to a cup of coffee brewed with beans from the Global South. One teaspoon of this sand-colored dust added a savory pop that smoothed out the brightness of my favorite Colombian Supremo beans from Costco, and the requisite jitters that usually kicked in after three cups of the brew felt mellower than usual with Om mixed in. The silty residue at the bottom of the cup is best avoided, but it won’t harsh your vibe too much on the whole.
North Spore Functional-5 Mushroom Coffee for $18: Most mushroom-infused ground coffee blends are filed under the “Medium Roast” category, which is typically a safe catch-all that grocery store brands and discount purveyors describe their preground product as to avoid pissing off discerning light-roast aficionados such as yours truly. Nine times out of 10 they hit like a dark roast, with an ashy taste and a healthy dose of the oil that seeps out of the beans during the elongated roasting process, shimmering and swirling around the top of your cup like a puddle in a parking lot. This coffee from North Spore, which makes our favorite mushroom-growing monotub and spray-and-grow mushroom kit, lacks all of those off notes while still retaining a sturdy, earthy flavor that’s far enough removed from the citric and buttery notes I love most about classic high-end light roasts to stand up as its own unique thing. There’s a hint of mushroom flavor on the swallow if you really look for it, but you could easily swap this in for someone's morning cup of Folgers or Illy medium roast and they’d be none the wiser.
Ryze Superfoods Mushroom Coffee for $75: One could consider two different approaches to how purveyors of mushroom coffee dial in the flavor profile of their product: They can go all in with a bombastic brew filled with spices and overtones, or they can play it safe and concoct the base of a beverage that tastes more like memories of other drinks than a beverage with an identity of its own. The underwhelming flavor of Ryze falls in the latter camp. In fairness, there are plenty of folks who have no interest in savoring their morning beverage and instead need to put the liquid inside them as fast as possible so they can “adult” that day. Twenty-one-year-old Pete thought people who claimed to enjoy espresso were insane, yet here I am, two decades later wishing I could sip bitter bean water instead of this sour cup of forgettable swill that curdled the whole milk I tried to cut it with. A week with Ryze did little to boost my mood, focus, or energy. It mostly made me cranky and sad.
Cuppa Medium Roast Mushroom Coffee for $30: Like the friendly foreigner who calls his daily cup of tea or coffee his “cuppa,” this newcomer is polite, congenial, and inoffensive. The first sip brought to mind a really good cup of coffee at a nameless diner, with a light body and very mellow acidic notes on the swallow. The small dose of ruddy powder pulled from the bag with the included plastic scoop dissolved thoroughly with a few stirs, and the pristine lack of sediment in the cup was exactly as advertised. The boost of energy is also unassuming and easy to relegate to the background, which could be a welcome respite from the blast of caffeine many coffee addicts think they need right when they wake up every morning. After a week with Cuppa I started to enjoy easing into my daily brain vibrations rather than white-knuckling it off the rip at 7 am on the dot every morning.
Not Recommended
MUD/WTR Original Blend for $60: The packaging of MUD/WTR isn’t quite as unhinged as a bottle of Dr. Bronner's, but it’s definitely in the same realm. The spicy dust inside the can is a maximalist circus of weirdness as well, with herbaceous stalwarts like turmeric and masala chai holding it down alongside the usual shroom suspects. It took me a few days to realize that properly emulsifying this ruddy power per the suggested instructions—1 tablespoon with ¾ cup of water, battered thoroughly with the included handheld immersion blender—is an impossible task, so I started experimenting with supplemental ingredients in hopes that some blend of milk, fat, and sugar would minimize the gritty aftertaste that overwhelms the palate. I landed on 1 tablespoon of simple syrup and 4 ounces of whole milk frothed in my trusty Subminimal NanoFoamer Pro. The final result hits somewhere between a chai latte and the kind of hot cocoa you’d order at a coffee shop with boring ’90s music, mean baristas, and a dirty bin full of stale vegan + gluten-free snacks next to the register. I didn’t hate it, but the bottom quarter of the cup is an undrinkable gunky mess. And don’t get me started on the chunky brown lacing that clings to the edge of the cup. The physical and mental effects of MUD/WTR felt more like a facsimile of a boost than a visceral kick in the pants, but a placebo high is better than nothing, right? Combine that with the amount of adjunct ingredients required to make this drinkable and I ended up with a beverage I would only drink every now and then as a treat on a chilly day rather than a daily sipper I can rely on for increased focus, energy, virility, and the million other things this product promises within the wall of text that adorns its packaging.

BCCI secretary Devajit Saikia heaped praise on the Indian women’s cricket team, which won its eighth Women’s Asia Cup title by beating Sri Lanka in the summit clash in Dubai on Sunday.
“Everything went very well. We won, and everyone is extremely happy. Everyone is proud of their performance, and the biggest thing is that our country’s name is shining bright. There could be no greater cause for happiness than this. Everyone put in complete hard work; the entire team performed exceptionally, and our support staff worked tirelessly, which resulted in us winning this tournament so easily,” he told IANS hours after the game.
The dominant performance of the Indian side has been overshadowed yet again by its decision not to collect the winner’s trophy and cheque from Mohsin Naqvi, the president of the Asian Cricket Council. This mirrored the decision of the India men’s team which did the same after winning the men’s Asia Cup beating Pakistan in 2025.

“Our men’s team won the Asia Cup a year and a half ago. And our whole situation, since the April 2025 Pahalgam incident, changed after that. So, after that, there was pressure on us from our citizens that we shouldn’t keep any relations with our neighboring country and not play cricket with them. But our government has a policy that we must play against every country in multinational tournaments...
“But that doesn’t mean we will follow every condition laid out for us. Our military conflict is still ongoing. One of the main leaders who is working against the interests of our country; we can’t receive the trophy from him. The Women’s team has expressed solidarity with the decision taken by the men’s team last year. It doesn’t diminish the performances of our team. We have won all our matches in a one-sided manner. Women’s cricket has been growing so well in India and there’s no bigger evidence of that than this. Our whole planning is geared towards the 2026 ICC T20 World Cup. The happiest part of this tournament is how India has left everyone else behind and surged so far ahead.”
Saikia was also asked about visuals of himself and BCCI vice president Rajiv Shukla speaking cordially with Naqvi in the Royal Box that went viral.
“It’s not as if we wouldn’t meet anyone. I was sitting outside in the Royal Box seats right from the toss until the end of the game. Having sat there, I remained in that same place throughout the match. Everyone who came met me during the match; someone sat next to me, then Shukla came and sat with me. The person you mentioned also came and sat alongside Deputy Chairman Khalid (Khalid Al Zarooni) sahib. That’s just a normal tradition—whenever anyone comes, we meet and talk with everyone. We tried to solve today's situation, but our efforts were not successful. We don’t have any regrets. Our ultimate priority and ambition was not to focus on who would give the trophy. We wanted the Indian team to win and we’ve achieved that.”

The Sapiens Health Foundation has welcomed the Tamil Nadu Government’s announcement of a salt reduction campaign in the Assembly on Tuesday.
Reducing salt intake could help lower the burden of hypertension, stroke, heart attacks and kidney disease. In a press release, the foundation cited the UK’s salt-reduction campaign, initiated in 2005 by Graham MacGregor of the World Action on Salt, Sugar and Health (WASSH), which resulted in a reported 30% reduction in salt in bread.
The Foundation’s salt-reduction campaign began in 2010 with a walkathon at Marina Beach, followed by similar events in Tiruchi and Puducherry and awareness programmes in colleges. In 2014, its founder-chairman Rajan Ravichandran received the Notable Achievement Award from the World Hypertension League for the campaign.
The Foundation has written to more than 300 food manufacturers seeking reductions in salt content and cited reductions in salt in noodles by Nestlé and Hindustan Lever as examples of industry response. It also organised international conferences on salt and health with IIT-Madras and IIT-Bombay in 2017.
The Foundation has conducted salt and health workshops for more than 500 physicians in Chennai, Mumbai, Delhi and Vijayawada. It also welcomed the growing focus on front-of-pack food labelling and said the State’s decision to take forward the campaign will be an important step towards improving population health.

25 years after 9/11, the GOP has never been more anti-Muslim
The GOP wants America to fear Muslims.
Hi readers — today marks 25 years since 9/11. In New York City, Washington, and Pennsylvania, survivors, families, and politicians are gathering to grieve and commemorate the attacks.
Today, we wanted to focus on one small part of the story in New York City, where former Mayor Rudy Giuliani singled out Mayor Zohran Mamdani, who is Muslim, with an Islamophobic screed about Mamdani’s participation in memorial ceremonies.
Giuliani’s rant, to be clear, is not really news in its own right; 25 years on, he’s less “America’s mayor” than he is the twice-disbarred, disgraced former lawyer of President Donald Trump. (And Mamdani did attend the event, even shaking hands with Giuliani.)
But Giuliani’s remarks are, unfortunately, emblematic of a disturbing trend in Republican politics, where open, aggressive Islamophobia is on the rise — 25 years after a particularly ugly brand of it emerged in response to 9/11. One major difference between then and now? In 2001, many politicians tried to tamp it down rather than inflame it.
As Nathan Lean, an assistant teaching professor at North Carolina State University and author of the book The Islamophobia Industry, explained to my colleague Christian Paz last month: “Islamophobia has passed the dinner table test. You can say things about Muslims with basic impunity today. And it’s institutionalized in the way that prejudice that targets other marginalized communities is not.”
The GOP is running on Islamophobia in 2026
The 2026 midterm elections have provided a particularly clear showcase for the right’s Islamophobic turn.
On Thursday, at the second and final night of the GOP’s unusual midterm convention in Dallas, Texas, Sen. Ted Cruz (R-TX) told attendees that “communism” and “Islamism” were allying against Republicans. “They share the same enemies,” he said. “They hate Christians. They hate Jews. They hate capitalism. They hate the Constitution, and they hate America.”
At another point in Cruz’s speech, attendees screamed “he should be shot” as Cruz name-checked Mamdani, Michigan Democratic Senate candidate Abdul El-Sayed (who is Muslim, and who Cruz said “says he has an obligation to Sharia Law”), and Texas Democratic Senate candidate James Talarico.
As Christian reports, Michigan and especially Texas have both been on the front lines of rising Islamophobia.
Michigan has a large Muslim population in cities like Dearborn and Hamtramck, and El-Sayed has drawn particular vitriol; Rep. Nancy Mace (R-SC) wrote last month that “Every single Muslim holding public office in America is a Trojan horse, and a threat to both national security and our republic.”
And in Texas, as the New York Times reported at length last month, Islamophobia has become a matter of policy as well as rhetoric from Republican Gov. Greg Abbott and other politicians in the state.
El-Sayed, in Michigan, has described the attacks as an attempt to distract voters from other issues. “They’re going to point at me, they’re going to point at my name, like, ‘Wow, he’s different,’” he said last month. “My name is not raising your gas prices. My name is not taking us to war. My name is not the reason you can’t afford your groceries.”
Without much else to run on, though, Republicans seem to have decided they’re all-in on Islamophobia.

Carney says Canada planning to discuss 'unique alliance' with EU, but not membership
Comments follow media report Canada is seeking to be 'associate member'
Prime Minister Mark Carney says Canada plans to begin discussions for a "unique alliance" with the European Union — but not membership — as he gears up to address the European Parliament this week.
"We're not looking to become a member of the European Union," Carney said Sunday evening on the red carpet of the Toronto International Film Festival. He attended the festival shortly after giving a speech to kick off the two-day Canada Investment Summit, which begins Monday.
"What we are looking — and will begin discussions for — [is] a unique alliance with the European Union. We share the same values, we have the same priorities and we have very complementary strengths."
Carney's comments come after the Wall Street Journal reported on Saturday that Carney has been pushing to bolster Canada's relationship with Europe's 27-nation bloc, and tasked his team to identify the most ambitious possibilities short of full membership.
The Journal further reported that Carney suggested Canada take on a new title of "associate member."
The report sparked a fierce pushback from Conservative Leader Pierre Poilievre, who said on social media Sunday evening that Carney "could not be more out of touch."
"We will NEVER be the 51st U.S. state," Poilievre wrote. "And we will NEVER be the 28th EU state."
A senior Canadian official, who offered information to CBC on a not-for-attribution basis, said there have been ongoing conversations about how Canada can deepen its relationship with Europe.
The official said Canada is not trying to give up its independence for access, and the federal government is less concerned about the "associate member" label and more about what deepened ties can achieve for the country.
The official added that the "associate member" label is one of a few being considered and that Canada did not propose it.
Canada, the EU and the U.S.
In recent days, cabinet members have spoken up about Canada bringing itself closer to Europe as one way to ease the country's economic dependence on the United States.
"I think Canadians should be reassured by the fact that we are looking at partnership in a market which is basically bigger than the U.S. consumer market," Finance Minister François-Philippe Champagne told CBC's The House on Friday.
Canada and the U.S. remain locked in a bitter trade war, with the Canadians launching their $27.6 billion counter-tariffs earlier this week. The United States responded by announcing it would ban the import of Canadian alcohol, motorcycles and other products beginning Sept. 29.
In an interview with Power & Politics earlier this week, the EU Ambassador to Canada Geneviève Tuts said the two sides already work well together, but both sides seek to "go further than that."
"Not just a new partnership, but something very new, and in a way something unique," Tuts said. "We want to reimagine the relationship between the EU and Canada."
Carney will travel to Strasbourg, France, on Tuesday and will address the European Parliament on Thursday, at the invitation of President Roberta Metsola.
Canada will also host a summit with the EU at the end of October.
